en: The ritual injunction is that the two shoulders and the chest are auspicious, while the webbed fingers are inauspicious; likewise, upon birth and death, shaving should be performed on the tenth day. Shaving must be carried out by kinsmen and relatives on the day of the funeral rite.
They likewise know that the birth-impurity (sūtaka) must be observed on the tenth day.
Even for one who is pregnant, [the shaving] must be performed only upon the death of the parents;
otherwise, if he were to perform the shaving, it would be equal to the murder of a Brahmin.
Upon the death of senior sapindas, as well as of the mother-in-law and father-in-law,
and of an elder sister or her husband, there shall be the shaving of the head.

Even for those who have died at night, having performed the water-libation rites (*udakakriyā*), shaving (*vapana*) is not permitted at night; rather, the act of shaving shall take place on the following day. He who goes [to the cremation ground] for the sake of the deceased, and likewise he who consumes [the funeral food], [is subject to the following].
One should avoid those [acts] for a day and night, such as recitation (*japa*), fire-oblation (*homa*), and so forth.
In the absence of fire or the absence of clarified butter, there is consecration by means of the *gāyatrī*.
Having drunk ten mouthfuls, one becomes pure again through bathing.
Upon the death of [his] paternal uncles, elder brothers, maternal uncles,
teachers, their wives, his father’s sisters,
his mother’s [sisters], and even a pregnant sister, he should have [the hair] shaved.
Except on the day of the commencement of the initiation (*dīkṣā*), the shaving of the disciples should take place prior [to that day]; however,
on that very day, during the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsa*), the shaving of the Guru occurs.
One should cause [the rite] to be performed there during the consecration festival together with the Mūrtipas.
Thus ends the procedure for shaving (*kṣauravidhi*) composed by the illustrious Ghorāśivācārya. (p8a. blank), (p8b, l1.)
Regarding the formal procedure for brothers who have arrived from another country to see one another, Atri states:
"There should be either an announcement by hearing or by sight, depending on whether the difference between them is perceived through hearing or sight."
The newspaper may serve as the primary witness; there is no fault here in this remaining [point].
If [the death] should occur after twelve days, what is the rule for the witness in this case?
Or how might there be a witness among brothers born of the same womb?
Thus says the Guru; herein Marīci states:
[This is] for those born of the same womb, for kinsmen, and especially for brothers, who desire the full increase of their lifespan together with their sons, wives, and others.
Or how could there be a meeting with those who have arrived from other lands?
[One should perform it] before Śaṅkha, Likhita, and Dakṣa; before one's father, mother, and teacher;
or before one's parents and teacher; or in the assemblies of great Brāhmaṇas.
In the temple, in the presence of the deity, one should perform the mutual gazing (*anyonyadarśana*),
having lit a lamp and placed a vessel containing water before it.
Having drawn a curtain across the middle, one should offer clarified butter (*ājya*) preceded by the waving of the staff (*daṇḍapūrvaka*).
"One should ensure mutual sight," so said the Blessed Manu.
"One should perform the feeding of Brahmins for the sake of the disease and for the granting of its fruit;
he who does this with discernment shall attain long life. Thus from the Smṛti of Bodhāyana.
In the southwest corner there are six [triangles], in the west five corners, and in the northwest there would be sixteen;

in the north there is a triangle, and in the northeast a two-cornered [triangle]. These, combined with their respective powders, should be placed in order starting from the east. One should worship Lakṣmī in the station of Brahmā... according to the rule as it should be known by the most excellent [practitioner].

O best of the twice-born, the five Brahmās are indeed established in the [inner] arrangement; the eight Lords of Knowledge (Vidyeśvaras) are considered to be established in the outer [arrangement], as are the eight Lords of Form (Mūrtīśvaras). Within [the inner circle] are Vāmadeva and the others, numbering twenty-five; likewise, there are eight Lords of the Gaṇas (Gaṇeśvaras) in the outer [circle], headed by Aṅguṣṭha. Then, there are the eight Krodhas, and the Śatarudras, numbering one hundred, in the cardinal directions.

And: "By this [method], fifty deities are considered for the ablution (*snapana*). Here, by means of the unsurpassed [mantra] alone, it is considered equal to fifty. In the middle, the Lords of Knowledge (*vidyeśvaras*) are declared;

the hundred Rudras are likewise intended. Thus they say it is threefold: one hundred and eight, one hundred and eight, and one hundred and eight. The deities in the middle are the Lords of Knowledge, but elsewhere, indeed, there is only Śiva."
May he, who is especially praised as "Sahasranāman" (*sahanāt mā sahasraiḥ*),

whose heart is given to hearing the *ḍaṅkāra* sound of swarms of bees hovering about his pair of ears that are gently swaying like palm leaves, the delighter of Śrīśailajā; and who, by means of his service, destroys the darkness of obstacles and radiates light— [may he protect you].

I bow to Sāgara, the abode of the husband of the ocean-born goddess and the Lord of Vighnas (Gaṇeśa), the venerable Vaidyeśa-liṅga, served by hosts of supreme sages; [I bow] to the one whose eastern and other [directional] forms are joined with the ages and the Manus, in the form of liṅgas. Having prostrated before Śambhu named Ananta, whose mind is fixed upon the ocean of the compassion of his excellent Guru, [he who is] most proficient in the *Śrīmat-siddhāntasārāvali*...

For the sake of accomplishing the hidden meaning, when knowledge had been set forth, thirty-two [verses] were composed; of those, eighty-eight were offered as oblations by calculation in the *Karmaṇyatārā* chapter. The Sage [is] Yoga-rāja.

The *Siddhāntasārāvali* is composed by one who has mastered the calculation of the number of pairs of arms [of the gods], and who is ever engaged in the reckoning of the sixty-four systems established by the lords of sages.

Therein, first of all, Trilocana Śivācārya— who dwelt at Āmardaka-maṭha and had reached the further shore of all the Āgamas— having examined the various divisions of the Siddhāntas such as the *Kāmika* and others arising from the well-established lineage of the Āgamas, as well as the *Mṛgendra* and other scriptures, [proceeds] therein with respect to both word and meaning...

Desiring to compose the treatise titled *Siddhāntasārāvalī*— which establishes its meaning through numerous verses that attain the status of authoritative means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) by implication, which consists of three topics, and which comprises four quarters— he [first] [commences] for the sake of the unimpeded completion of the work he intends to compose...

For the sake of the extensive completion [of this work], he pays homage to Śiva with the first verse by means of the specific utterance of the partless root-mantra (*niṣkalamūlamantra*), which reveals the nature of the state beyond the fourth (*turyātītāvasthā*): "By whom this entire world of moving and non-moving beings is woven as the warp and all is ever interwoven as the woof; and by whose grace even bound souls (*paśu*) shine forth from the mass of fetters—[to Him I bow]. (*Note: The asterisks indicate the end of the verse portion.*) (l2. By whose grace even bound souls shine forth from the mass of fetters—[to Him I bow].

With my intellect, I take refuge in that radiant light called Śiva—the subtle, pervasive, and supreme light—which is contained within the resonance of the utterance "Om" and so forth, and which illuminates all luminous things.

Just as the warp [of a cloth] serves as the instrumental cause for the production of a garment, even so, by means of Paramaśiva, who possesses a pervasive nature and acts as the instrumental cause, this [universe is produced]. (Verse 3)

(14) That which is perceived in the form of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) is the "moving and non-moving" (*carācara*), namely, that which moves and that which does not move. Here, by the word "moving" (*cara*), that which is mobile in nature is meant; for example, the nature of speech and so forth belonging to animals and the like. (15)

By the word *acara* (immobile), that which consists of the stationary, such as mountains and so forth, is indicated; by the term "mobile nature" (*carasvarūpatva*), the subtle bodies common to all souls (*ātman*) are meant. By the phrase "that which consists of the stationary," the worlds (*bhuvana*) are denoted. Furthermore, that which consists of both the mobile and the immobile is of two kinds.

According to the distinction between pure and impure natures, there are fifteen worlds within the *kalā* of the sphere beyond peace (*śāntyātīta*). There are eighteen worlds within the *kalā* of peace (*śānti*). These thirty-three worlds are indeed pure in nature, belonging to those souls who reside in the pure worlds.
(…) the twenty-seven worlds in the *vidyā* and *kalā* [tattvas] are indeed pure. In the *nivṛtti-kalā*, there are fifty-six worlds;

in the *nivṛtti-kalā*, there are one hundred and eight worlds. Those (l2) (…) one hundred and eight worlds are impure. The bodies of the selves residing in the impure worlds are indeed impure. All this, being thus constituted, is entirely...

In this context, by the word "all," the world well-known [to common experience]— beginning with the Great Principle (*mahat*) and ending with the specific elements (*viśeṣa*)— is what is called "the world. According to the Vedāntic and other systems, however, the term "world" refers to the entire cosmic order starting from the principle of primordial nature (*prakṛti*) down to the element of earth.

In the Śaiva system, the principle of Śiva (*śivatattva*) is designated by the word "Great" (*mahat*); the earthly principle, characterized by the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*), is designated by the word "Specific" (*viśeṣa*); and that which is not that [earthly principle], namely the world, is indicated by the word "All" (*sarva*). By the word "Śiva," the principle of Power (*śaktitattva*) is signified. The world-sphere of the Point-principle (*bindutattva-bhuvana*), situated within the [power] residing in the [heart-]lotus, is to be known. Thus, this world, beginning with the pure worlds, is at all times—perpetually—woven warp and woof, created in the form of an upward and downward extension.

The upper world is the Śāntyatītā [kalā]; the world situated within the Vidyā [kalā] is the lower world, which is contained within the Pratiṣṭhā and Nivṛtti kalās. And it has been said: "Nivṛtti and Pratiṣṭhā operate in the lower portion; likewise, Vidyā and Śānti [operate] in the upper."

"But Śāntyatītā is presided over. Just as threads are the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) with respect to a cloth, in the same way, the pure realm is woven and interwoven by Bindu—which serves as the inherent cause in relation to the pure worlds—and by Paramaśiva, who serves as the instrumental cause (*nimittakāraṇa*); it is made [manifest] and pervaded by his own nature. The word "and" (*ca*) indicates pervasion.

Through the destruction of the impure world—which is the destruction of Māyā, who serves as its inherent cause (samavāyikāraṇa)—and through the gateway of Ananta and others, who serve as its efficient causes (nimittakāraṇa), the impure world is created and pervaded.
Thus it has been said: "The Lord is the efficient cause."

Their substrate is Sabindurāṭ. Śiva is declared to be the agent in the pure sound (*dhvani*), while Ananta is the Lord in the white [sound]. Above *māyā* is *mahāmāyā*; by *mahāmāyā*, the meaning is *bindu*. Thus, by Paraśiva, for the sake of the enjoyment of bound souls (*paśu*), worlds, and bodies born of the worlds, as well as for the ripening of the accumulation of karma, both creation and withdrawal are performed at all times.

This is the meaning. He asks: when does the occasion for the sprinkling (*prokṣa*) of the selves (*ātman*) residing in the worlds arise? He says: "The bound souls" (*paśavaḥ*). There are three kinds of bound souls: the *vijñānakala*, the *pralayākala*, and the *sakala* through their differentiation. The *vijñānakala* is endowed with *mala* alone; the *pralayākala* is endowed with *mala* and *karman*. (Fragmentary text follows).

*Kala* (limited time), conjoined with *mala*, *māyā*, and *karman*, is the *sakala* (the bound soul). By the force of the word "also" (*api*), eight others—Ananta and the rest—are mentioned; these eight, such as Ananta and so forth, are said to be those whose impurities (*mala*) have reached a state of maturity through a gradation relative to [the lower levels]. From the mass of fetters (*pāśanikara*)—that is, from the collection of the five fetters consisting of *mala*, *māyā*, *karman*, *bindu*, and *rodhaśakti*—of him [who is liberated from this].

The meaning is that [beings] are led to enjoyment (*bhoga*) and liberation (*mokṣa*) in succession through the five acts at the conclusion of the grace (*prasāda*) of Paramaśiva. The essential point is that liberation does not occur through mere self-knowledge (*ātmajñāna*) without the grace of Śiva; and likewise... (l. 8).

"...by the Lord. Even though they are liberated souls (*muktātman*), they are called 'auspicious ones' (*śiva*); yet, by the grace [of the Lord], they are said to be 'liberated'—this is the meaning. Through the differentiation of the recitation of the root mantra (*mūlamantra*), from the locations such as the heart (*hṛdaya*) and so forth, [the soul] attains the state of being a cause (*kāraṇatva*) such as Brahmā and the others. Just as [beings] are bound by ropes, so too, by the fetters (*pāśa*) of impurity (*mala*) and the rest, one is awakened [to bondage] and thus becomes known as a *paśu* (bound soul). And it has been said: 'The *paśu* is the state of being a *paśu*... (l. 2)"

"Not one" (*aneka*) means he is not singular; "of manifold kinds" (*anekaprakāra*). "With a Lord" (*seśaḥ*) means impelled by the Lord (*īśvara*) toward experience and so forth. And it has been said: "This creature is ignorant and lacks mastery... (l3) ...therefore it goes toward what is auspicious or indeed inauspicious. The word "and" (*ca*) is used to indicate that [the Lord] is the indirect impeller. Among the *vijñāna-kalas*, the Lord is directly [the impeller]... (l4) ...the "all-pervading" (*vibhuḥ*) means omnipresent. "Of little knowledge" (*alpavit*): one who knows (*veti*) or perceives (*jānāti*) only a little, something small, is "of little knowledge. Within himself, existing...

Because of [the possession of] knowledge such as omniscience... (l5) ...due to being bound by [impurity], I have declared that the atom (*aṇu*) is "one who knows only a little" (*kiñcijjña*). Because it is free from beginningless impurity, this one is "all-knowing" (*sarvajña*); therefore, he is Śiva. This is according to his own composition... (l6) ...the agent of action (*karmakartṛ*)—the letter *ca* is used for the purpose of indicating dependence (*pāratantrya*). Being an agent of action through dependence, he is the enjoyer of the fruits of action... (l7)

The sense is that [the bound soul] depends upon a unifier because of its state of being half-insentient (*ardhakajaḍabhāva*). Likewise, in the *Parākhya*: "For one whose power of consciousness is obstructed by the state of being a bound soul (*paśutva*), [it requires] a unifier; that unifier is the Great Lord (*maheśāna*), for he is powerful by his own will.
(l. 8) [... it depends upon that unifier. That unifier is the Great Lord, because he is powerful by his own will.
Likewise, in the Mahābhārata, [it is said] regarding Vāsudeva:
"Having understood the Dharma... and there is no turning back for me; whatever I am enjoined to do by whichever deity resides in my heart, that I shall perform. (Folio 12a, line 1, broken).

(... they say that is incorrect; the status of being an enjoyer (*bhoktṛtva*) is not possible for the sense organs (*buddhīndriya*) because of the absence of connection with another birth. [The Self is] eternal, devoid of destruction, and imperishable... (l2) ...because it has been stated that there is conjunction even with Maheśvara, who is all-pervading (*vibhu*). Having thus stated the characteristics of the selves (*ātman*), [the text proceeds] with "the *prabodhākala*" etc., [describing] the threefold [classification] of the selves...

[he] does not perceive [the world], yet he is bound; this is the time of awakening. The meaning of "Vijñānakala" is that he is endowed with only the impurity (*mala*); "vijñāna" refers to knowledge...
The state of *vijñānakevalya* is the manifestation of Śiva who has been concealed by the power of innate impurity (*sahajamala*).
Likewise, in the *Mṛgendra*: "Those who have transcended *māyā*...

[Śiva] is beyond the paths (*adhvātīta*) and stainless (*nirañjana*)," which refers to the *prabodhākala*. The singular number is used for the class because there are many such individuals. For the self... [end of fragment].

(... ) there are many living beings; thus it has been said: "There are many selves (*ātman*), consisting of consciousness, yet defiled by impurity, [and obscured] by the impurity of *māyā* and *karman*. (l. 7) (... ) in *māyā* there is the *pralayākala*; above *māyā*, below *śuddhavidyā*, and veiled solely by impurity, there exists the other, the *vijñānākala*. (l. 8) (... ) it should be understood that both the *sakala* and the *niṣkala* are innumerable. Since that which is made is rendered impure, it is called *kṛti*; and *kṛti* consists of *karman* and *mala*. He who possesses these is... (l. 9) ...he is the *sakala*. Thus, the *sakala* is the one who possesses the three impurities (*trimala*). The *niṣkala* is the one who is free from the three impurities. The *pralayākala* is the one who possesses two impurities. The *vijñānākala* is the one who possesses only one impurity. The *māyākala* is the one who possesses *māyā* alone. The *māyāvinirmukta* is the one who is liberated from *māyā*. The *māyāsambaddha* is the one who is bound by *māyā*. The *māyābaddha* is the one who is fettered by *māyā*. The *māyāmukta* is the one who is released from *māyā*. The *māyāyukta* is the one who is joined with *māyā*. The *māyārahita* is the one who is devoid of *māyā*. The *māyāśūnya* is the one who is empty of *māyā*. The *māyāvarjita* is the one who is abandoned by *māyā*. The *māyāpetaka* is the one who is bereft of *māyā*. The *māyāhīna* is the one who is destitute of *māyā*. The *māyātyakta* is the one who has cast off *māyā*. The *māyāvimukta* is the one who is disengaged from *māyā*. The *māyāviyukta* is the one who is separated from *māyā*. The *māyāvigata* is the one who has departed from *māyā*. The *māyāvirahita* is the one who is separated from *māyā*. The *māyāvipramukta* is the one who is completely freed from *māyā*. The *māyāviprayukta* is the one who is dissociated from *māyā*. The *māyāviśliṣṭa* is the one who is detached from *māyā*. The *māyāvicchinna* is the one who is cut off from *māyā*. The *māyāviyuta* is the one who is parted from *māyā*. The *māyāviyogin* is the one who possesses the separation from *māyā*. The *māyāviyogavān* is the one who possesses the state of separation from *māyā*. The *māyāviyogabhāj* is the one who partakes in the separation from *māyā*. The *māyāviyogayukta* is the one who is endowed with the separation from *māyā*. The *māyāviyogasaṃyukta* is the one who is joined with the separation from *māyā*. The *māyāviyogasaṃpanna* is the one who is perfected in the separation from *māyā*. The *māyāviyogasampanna* is the one who has attained the perfection of separation from *māyā*. The *māyāviyogaprāpta* is the one who has reached the separation from *māyā*. The *māyāviyogalabdha* is the one who has obtained the separation from *māyā*. The *māyāviyogādhigata* is the one who has realized the separation from *māyā*. The *māyāviyogānubhūta* is the one who has experienced the separation from *māyā*. The *māyāviyogānubhavita* is the one who has caused the experience of separation from *māyā*. The *māyāviyogānubhāvita* is the one who has brought about the experience of separation from *māyā*. The *māyāviyogānubhāvitavat* is the one who has become like one who has caused the experience of separation from *māyā*. The *māyāviyogānubhāvitavatī* is the one who has become like one who has caused the experience of separation from *māyā*. The *māyāviyogānubhāvitavatvant* is the one who has become like one who has caused the experience of separation from *māyā*. The *māyāviyogānubhāvitavantī* is the one who has become like one who has caused the experience of separation from *māyā*. The *māyāviyogānubhāvitavantvat* is the one who has become like one who has caused the experience of separation from *māyā*. The *māyāviyogānubhāvitavantvatī* is the one who has become like one who has caused the experience of separation from *māyā*. The *māyāviyogānubhāvitavantvattva* is the state of having become like one who has caused the experience of separation from *māyā*. The *māyāviyogānubhāvitavantvattvavat* is the one who possesses the state of having become like one who has caused the experience of separation from *māyā*. The *māyāviyogānubhāvitavantvattvavatī* is the one who possesses the state of having become like one who has caused the experience of separation from *māyā*. Thus,

[the term] *pralayākala* refers to one who, even during the dissolution (*pralaya*)— when the principles (*tattva*) such as Time (*kāla*) and the rest have been withdrawn— remains conscious of and perceives the principle of *māyā*.
[The remainder of the sentence concerns] the subtle...

"...because he possesses that, this refers to the subtle [state] whose object is the *pralayākala*. However, for the *sakalas*, there is the supreme Śiva, who is beyond *unmanī* and consists of both the subtle and the gross. 'I remember him through a consciousness whose essence is the state of "I am He" (*so'ham*),' he says; [this refers to] the mantra beginning with *oṃ*, which resides in the elevated sound.
That which has *oṃ* as its beginning is "beginning with *oṃ*" (*omityādi*); and that is also the mantra..."*demaha*...* (l2) [fragmentary].**

*Dimanu* is the *prāsāda-mantra*, which denotes Paramaśiva. By means of that, *uccāra* refers to the sound (*dhvani*)—namely *nāda* and *nādānta*—which has arisen during the act of utterance. From that sound, it is "internal" (*antargata*), meaning it has gone far (*dūra-gata*), existing at a distance;
this is the sense. Alternatively, it may be explained as being internal within that sound through an extremely subtle utterance. It is the light situated in the midst of the sound.
Based on the statement, "Śiva is situated in the midst of light," there is the recitation of the *prāsāda* mantra.

This [recitation] is of various kinds, distinguished by short (*hrasva*), long (*dīrgha*), protracted (*pluta*), subtle (*sūkṣma*), and other such subtle divisions. Short recitation ends with the *bindu*; long recitation ends with the half-moon (*ardhendu*); protracted recitation ends with the *nirodhinī*;
and subtle recitation is...
That which does not end with *nāda* is the extremely subtle utterance ending in *vyāpinī*. By the short utterance of the *prāsāda* mantra, there is the abandonment of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra;

therein, the letter *a*, which denotes Rudra, is abandoned by Rudra, who is its denoted object, in the middle of the palate. By the long and protracted utterances of the *prāsāda* mantra, there is the abandonment of Īśvara; [the point] of the *bindu*, which denotes Īśvara, is abandoned by Īśvara, who is its denoted object.
(7) Abandonment at the center of the eyebrows (*bhrūmadhya*).

Within that very place is the inclusion of the Half-moon (*ardhacandra*) and the Obstructress (*nirodhinī*). Through the subtle and ultra-subtle utterances (*uccāra*) of the Prāsāda mantra, there is the abandonment of Sadāśiva.
This refers to the Nāda—which denotes Sadāśiva—along with the End of Sound (*nādānta*), by means of that which is its denoted object (*vācya*). (8)

Indeed, by Sadāśiva, there is a renunciation at the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmabila*); right there, extending up to the Pervasive Power (*vyāpinī*), is the pervasion of Sadāśiva. Through the sequence of renouncing the five causal lords beginning with Brahmā—up to the utterance of the mantra *Oṃ* and so forth—the powers of Sūcī and Vyāpinī are included within the pervasion of Sadāśiva. Above the aperture of Brahmā, at a measurement of three finger-breadths, is the station of Śakti; above that, at a measurement of three finger-breadths, is the station of Vyāpinī.

It becomes the All-Pervading Space (*vyomavyāpin*). Above the All-Pervading, at a distance of four finger-breadths, the location of Samanā is said to be situated. Because it pervades that, it is called the All-Pervading Space;
it is Anāhata Śiva. Beyond that All-Pervading Space...

By that which exists above, the abandonment of the Unstruck Śiva (*anāhata-śiva*) is indicated; at its end, Paramaśiva is to be perceived as the Mind (*manaska*), through the abandonment of the recitation of the Prāsāda mantra, by means of the Prāsāda in the form of *unmanī*. Likewise, it is stated in the Śruti:

"Those who have well-ascertained the meaning through the knowledge of Vedānta, who are self-controlled through the yoga of renunciation, and whose essence is purified—they, at the time of the final end, are liberated from the supreme death in the world of Brahman."
"All" refers to this: here, by the word *veda*, the *praṇava* [is meant];

by the word *anta*, the *nāda*; those for whom the meaning consisting of the fragrance of the knowledge of that [nāda] is well-ascertained are "those whose purpose is well-ascertained through the knowledge of Vedānta. They are ascetics who have conquered their senses, whose being is pure, and whose selves are purified by initiation; they [reside] in the world of Brahman.

In the *brahmabila* [the aperture of Brahmā], which is the world of Sadāśiva—the word "tu" (*but*) serving to emphasize—there are the bodies of Brahmā and Sadāśiva because of their nature as Brahmā. Abiding in that world at the time of the end of the supreme, that is, at the time of the dissolution of the supreme *unmanā*, there occurs through the yoga of renunciation (*sannyāsa-yoga*) the complete casting away (*samyak prakṣepaḥ*) of the presiding deities of the letters beginning with 'A' into their respective causes; this is renunciation. By means of that yoga...

Having united their own self with Śiva through the supreme nectar of the knowledge of Paramaśiva, they are completely liberated; that is to say, they are released from saṃsāra and attain the state of Śiva. Having withdrawn the forms of the effects, beginning with Brahmā, each into its own cause...
"Having thus disciplined the mind, one should unite the self with the supreme Śiva in Śiva," so said Yājñavalkya. Alternatively, renunciation may be performed in another manner:

by the renunciation of the Lord (*Īśvara*), who is the sovereign of the *bindu*, the half-moon (*ardhacandra*), and the *nirodhinī*, there is the renunciation of the two breaths (*prāṇa* and *apāna*). By the renunciation of Sadāśiva, who presides over *nāda* and the end of *nāda* (*nādānta*), there is the renunciation of both. Anāhata-Śiva is the sovereign of Śakti, Vyāpinī, and Samanā.
By the abandonment of that [state], there is the abandonment of the triad beginning with *rakta*.

(l2) In this context, by the word "space" (*vyoma*), the locus of the triad beginning with *śakti* is expressed. Through the subtle utterance (*sūkṣmoccāra*) of the temple-mantra (*prāsādamantra*), there is the abandonment of Sadāśiva;
through the ultra-subtle utterance (*atisūkṣmoccāra*), there is the abandonment of Anāhataśiva. Thus it was said by the Blessed One: (l3) [jña...]

(…) Śivācārya states in his *Pūjāstotra*: "By means of the crest of the resonance (*nāda*) arising from the venerable Root Mantra, one abandons the stages beginning with Brahmā up to Sadāśiva; this sequence of movement culminates in the pure void (*vyoman*) situated at the zenith.
Likewise, (l4)

In the *Svacchanda*, the letter A, the letter U, the letter Ma, the Bindu, the Half-moon, the Nirodhī, the Nāda, the end of the Nāda (*nādānta*), the Śakti, and the Vyāpinī—these are remembered as the eleven [levels], ending with the Samanā. That which transcends these is called the "Beyond" (*tatītata*); that which is beyond that is the "Untainted" (*nirāmaya*). Those who possess light are called "possessors of light" (*jyotiṣmantas*); they are so called because they have lights within them.

The meaning is that [the aforementioned] Hataśiva, Sadāśiva, Īśvara, [and so forth], as well as Viṣṇu, Acyuta, Brahmā, and the others, possess lights (*jyotīṃṣi*) only by means of the light of Paramaśiva, which shines everywhere and illuminates them. Thus says the Āgama:
"Of all luminous bodies... (l7).

"...and the Lord Śiva is the treasure; because he illuminates everything, he is remembered as *tejas* (splendor) and *jyotis* (light). Likewise, the Śruti also says: "May that one light, which travels far by means of light, my mind, be intent upon Śiva. That light named Śiva, whose name is Śiva, is said to shine everywhere in its fullness. And it has been stated: "That splendor which arises from the contact of fuel and fire, and that which is produced from the moon, the sun, and the gem—" from that [comes all light].

I take refuge in that which is perfectly full, luminous, and the supreme light, with the thought "This is it. The meaning is: by means of an intellect whose nature consists of the contemplation of "I am He," I contemplate my own self as dissolved in the Supreme Śiva. Now, one might object:
the intellect is indeed one among the internal organs (antaḥkaraṇa), characterized by such categories as individuality, genus, and so forth.

Knowledge accompanied by conceptual construction (*savikalpaka-jñāna*) is achievable through the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*); however, the apprehension of the mere nature of reality in non-conceptual knowledge of Śiva (*nirvikalpaka-śiva-jñāna*) is not achievable through the internal organ, because the internal organ is itself a bond (*pāśa*). And it has been said:

"That which is called consciousness (*bodha*), being a modification of the internal organ, is not capable of manifesting the Great Lord, because it is a bond like shackles and the like. How, then, can one attain Him through the intellect (*dhī*)?
In response to the doubt as to whether this has already been stated, the refutation is as follows:

the initiated, stainless, and excellent practitioners, through the sequence beginning with the arousal of the root-mantra as previously described, perceive the partless Śiva by means of an intellect that illuminates their own consciousness; thus [the Prāsāda-mantras... (l5).

By the power of its [own] abiding state, it is said that through the vision of consciousness empowered by the rays of Śiva’s solar energy, one perceives Śiva together with Śakti and the other [principles], and thus there is no longer any obscuration of the Self. Who is this peaceful one who performs all things? He who is the possessor of all... (l6) ...consciousness, self-luminous, and manifesting others; he who is beyond Brahmā, beginningless, incomparable, subtle, great, a mass of consciousness, pervasive, and a friend to the liberated.

Śakti is stainless and diligent; she is called Brahmāṇī, the sovereign of the Sakala [state], and resides in the white resonance (dhvani). Ananta and Rudra reside in the white [resonance]. Now, for the purpose of explaining the cause of creation and so forth, [there is] Sadāśiva and the others, who are conjoined with the Supreme Śakti and are beyond the Supreme Śakti, conjoined with the Supreme Śakti.

He states that there is another designation: "the Peaceful" (*śānta*). He is peaceful because he is free from passion, hatred, and so forth, due to the impossibility of the impurities (*mala*) and other causes thereof.

"The All-doer" (*sarvakṛt*): he is the all-doer because he performs everything; by virtue of his sovereignty, he is the one who desires all things. (p14b, l1) "The Imperishable" (*avyaya*): decay (*vyatha*) means destruction. During the great dissolutions (*mahāpralaya*), manifested things abide in the form of their powers (*śakti*); because of his perfection, he is [free] from that... (l2)

The term *tvādavyayaḥ* means the imperishable one. *Sakalavit* means he who knows everything; that is, he knows the entire whole (*sakalam samastam*) through the power of his knowledge, and thus the meaning is "all-knowing" (*sarvajña*).

*Svānyaḥ* means he for whom his own self (*sva*) is itself other (*anya*); the meaning is that he is one alone. *Prakāśaḥ sarvatra* means shining everywhere. Alternatively, *svānya* refers to both the self (*sva*) and the other (*anya*); *svānyaprakāśaḥ* means the manifestation of those two, or alternatively, he who manifests both the self and the other.

Self-luminous (*svaprakāśa*) means that which illuminates itself and others. That is to say, it is illumination. Just as the sun, having dispelled the mass of darkness for the world, becomes the illuminator of itself and, by generating light in others such as sun-crystals (*sūryakānta*), [acts as their illuminator].

The meaning is as follows: just as [the sun] becomes the illuminator of others, so too, having removed the impurity that serves as an obscuration for the selves residing on the path of the Siddhas, and having presided over them by means of its own rays of power, it becomes self-illuminating; furthermore, by generating the splendor of Śiva even for those such as Ananta who are fashioned by its own capacity, it becomes the illuminator of others. It is "immovable" (*acala*), meaning devoid of movement.

In performing an action, [he is] like a potter and so forth... (l7) ...due to the absence of movement in his own body and so forth, he is devoid of motion because all effects are accomplished by mere volition; this is the meaning. "Immeasurable" (*ameya*) means devoid of objects of measurement (*meyarahita*), not to be delimited by knowledge derived from means of valid cognition such as direct perception (*pratyakṣa-pramāṇa*); [this refers to] speech... (l8)

The meaning is that he has transcended the path of both [the manifest and the unmanifest]. He is "supreme" (*para*) with respect to Brahman—that is, superior to the Brahman propounded in the Vedānta scriptures and other texts; the sense is that this is known from the Vedic revelation: "The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme" (*brahmavid āpnoti param*).

(p15a, l1) ... [He is] established by his own nature, incomparable (*atula*), devoid of similarity, subtle (*sūkṣma*) in form, great (*mahān*) in essential nature, [greater] than the minute and greater than the great.
The meaning is "most great. *Cidghana* means that whose bodily form is a mass (*ghana*) of consciousness (*cit*), by which term [is meant] the powers of knowledge and action;

thus, *cidghana* means devoid of a material body, such as the body consisting of the *bindu*. It is all-pervasive (*vyāpī*) because the *bindu* and so forth are not all-pervasive, and because it is itself devoid of any other pervader. It is pervasive (*vyāpaka*).

It has been stated [in the Śi... that he is pervasive within the Three Jewels (*ratnatraya*), pervading the names of the worlds and so forth, together with the *bindu*. This *bindu* is not pervaded by anything other than Śakti and Śiva; thus it is "Śiva.

He is the "friend of the liberated" (*muktasakha*)—meaning he is the friend of liberated souls (*ātman*) and the one who effects liberation. He is joined with the Supreme Śakti, and is stainless (*amala*), being devoid of primordial impurity (*anādimala*).

By means of the word "api" (also/even), having raised the objection that it is improper for the Stainless One to perform creation and so forth, the word "api" is employed to indicate that it is indeed appropriate for Him to perform creation and so forth for the sake of those selves who have accumulated karma prior to the great cycle of existence (*mahā-saṃsāra*) in order to experience the results of that karma. Thus it is understood.

One should proceed with diligence; "brahmagaḥ" refers to one who moves toward the *brahmans*—that is, the *mūrti-brahman*, the *tattva-brahman*, and the *bhūta-piṇḍa-sakala-brahman*. Thus, "brahmagaḥ" means one who goes to the nature of the *brahmans* consisting of the forms (*mūrti*) and so forth.

Likewise, in that which is called "pure," there is first the *mūrti-brahman*; the *tattva-brahman* would be the second; the *bhūta-brahman* would be the third; the *piṇḍa-brahman* would be the fourth; and the fifth is—
The *kalā-brahman* is that which is impelled by the five *brahmans*. Thus, [there are] the five beginning with Sākalya;

the *praṇava* is the *mūrti-brahman*. On the surface of the *śaddha*, there are the five *prāsādas* named after the pure root-principles (*mūlatattva*) and so forth. The *tattva-brahman* consists of the syllables *la*, *va*, *ra*, *ya*, and *ha*.
The *bhūta-brahman* consists of the lords of the five *piṇḍa-brahmans*, such as Sadyojāta and the others, which are born from the seed-syllables of Śiva.

The *kalā-brahman* begins with "of all sciences" (*sarvavidyānām*) and so forth. The *pada-brahman*, recited in the midst of the *vyomavyāpin* formula beginning with "to the head of Īśāna" (*īśānamūrdhne*), consists of various types of *pada-brahman* according to the divisions of the *vyomavyāpin*. Because it is Brahman and because it pervades everywhere due to its vastness, it is the body of Sadāśiva, the *Brahman*. As it has been said: "Because of its greatness (*bṛhattvāt*) and because of its being Brahman (*brahmaṇatvāt*), Brahman is the body of Sadāśiva"; thus it is called *sādākhya*.

The one named Sadāśiva is the lord of all (sakalādhipa) on the white path, the pure path; he is the lord of Ananta and the others. The ellipsis implies that by virtue of his sovereignty, he is the agent. Ananta, Ananteśvara, and Rudra—namely Śrīkaṇṭha-Rudra—are both lords on the black path, the impure path. Regarding the domain of the pure and impure, Ananta [is the lord] on the impure [path].

The meaning is that Śrīkaṇṭha is the subject regarding the phoneme *dh*. One should understand the lineage as follows: from Paraśiva comes Sadāśiva; from Sadāśiva, Ananteśa; and from Ananta, Śrīkaṇṭha.

Thus it has been stated by the venerable Jñānaśiva: "Indeed, the Lord was grasped as Paraśiva; therefore, that region is Śiva, consisting of Sound (*nādātmā*), [and comprising] the Sakala and Akala [levels]. From that Lord comes the venerable Ananteśa-bhaṭṭāraka."
Therefore, at that time, the eminent sage named Durvāsas—the teacher who was the incarnation of the Tantras—was the Śrīkaṇṭha Rudra who [incarnated] as Aṇḍaja, Viṣṇu, Vāsava, and Vidhi. ||2||

Those who know the Veda say that his form is independent and designated as Śiva, while it is also dependent upon another and called Śakti; he whose nature is non-different from these is Dharmīśa, and he is also the nature of Dharma. He states that the nature of existence has arisen through the union of the natures of Dharma and Dharmī in Paraśiva and Sadāśiva.

"Independent of another" (*parānapekṣam*) means that from Paraśiva comes Anāhataśiva, and from Anāhataśiva comes Sadāśiva; therefore, it is said to be dependent on Anāhataśiva alone and not on Paraśiva, because there is an intervention in between—this is the intended meaning. Furthermore, the term "dependent on another" (*parāpekṣam*)—meaning that which depends on another (*param apekṣate*)—is used here with the sense of conjunction (*api*), implying that both Paraśiva and Anāhataśiva possess the quality of pervading space (*vyomavyāpikatvena*).

Because it is partless, there is indeed unity and no duality; thus it is said to be independent of anything else. Those who know the Vedas, those who know the Āgamas, and the teachers together declare that such is the nature of Sadāśiva, produced from the supreme Śakti and the secondary Śakti called Parā. They have stated this regarding the supreme Śakti and Paraśiva.

The meaning is that the teachers, considering there to be no difference due to their being of the same essence (*samavedatā*), have established [the reality] as being called "Power" (*śakti*). It is of a non-different form from that;

that is, it is of a form non-different from that Supreme Śiva, a form of unity; this is to be explained as "for that reason," O Lord. Sadāśiva is "possessing the same attributes" (*sadharma*); he whose attribute (*dharma*) is the same is *sadharma*, like the form of lightning in the sky.

That which is luminous in every way, devoid of arising and destruction, endowed with the qualities of consciousness (*caitanya*) and so forth, and whose nature is light—that is *dharma*, and that is Paramaśiva. He is "of the nature of *dharma*" (*dharmarūpa*); that is, he whose form is the possessor of *dharma* (*dharmī*), for he possesses *dharma*.
This is the *dharma* of Sadāśiva and Paraśiva.

By virtue of its nature as *dharma*, Sadāśiva exists in the form of the embodiment (*mūrti*) of Paraśiva; however, Paraśiva exists within Sadāśiva as his inner essence. The form that arises from the union of these two is called *sādākhya* because it consists of both states. For the purpose of meditation and worship for all, it may be either partless (*niṣkala*) or with parts (*sakala*). ||3||
The power (*śakti*) is the body of consciousness (*cittanu*) of the Lord; it is the instrument for [perceiving] objects of knowledge and for effects.

Through its various manifestations, that [power], being endowed with Him, undergoes differentiation according to its qualities (*guṇa*), whether as action or cognition. That [power] is eternally present in all other agents; its function is directed toward the pure and white [state] that is not the path of worldly benefit.

That very same [Śakti], following her Lord, performs the ten [functions]... Thus, having demonstrated through the union of Paramaśiva and Sadāśiva— the two whose nature is that of the substratum— that they are the source of all states which serve as the means for ritual practice, [the text describes] the activity of the world for Sadāśiva who has attained the state of authority...

He states that there exists an instrument (*karaṇa*) consisting of his own power (*svaśakti*). He says "power" (*śakti*) because, since Sadāśiva is partless (*niṣkala*) and thus devoid of body, senses, and so forth, his status as the creator of the universe would not be possible; therefore, it is indicated that he acts by means of his own capacity.

Furthermore, in order to make known that even this power does not possess the nature of a transformation characterized by insentient qualities—unlike *māyā* and the *bindu*—it is called "the mind-body" (*cittanu*).

Because *māyā* and the *bindu* are the material causes (*upādānakāraṇa*), and because the world cannot arise without an inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*). And it has been said by Bhojadeva: "There is no effect without an agent, nor likewise without the two material causes."

Consciousness (*caitanya*), whose essential nature consists of the acts of knowing and acting, is grasped as *cittanu*: that power (*śakti*) whose body (*tanu*)—that is, its form—is consciousness itself. This is the Supreme Power (*parāśakti*) of the Lord Sadāśiva.

She is the instrument (*karaṇa*), considered the means of accomplishment (*sādhaka*) and the supreme benefactor, with respect to objects worthy of being known among those things to be known, and with respect to things worthy of being done among those things to be performed; she is to be known through the power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*).

The meaning is that [Śiva] performs the action of producing an object through the power of the cognition of objects (*viṣayajñāna*). Cognition is twofold: conceptual (*savikalpaka*) and non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*). Among these, the conceptual pertains to Śiva’s domain of enjoyment (*bhoga*), while the non-conceptual pertains to his domain of dissolution (*laya*). The conceptual...
Non-conceptual [cognition] consists in the association with name, genus, and so forth; it is free from conceptual construction and apprehends the mere thing-in-itself.

Thus it is stated in the Pauṣkara: "And that is held to be of two kinds, by virtue of the presence or absence of association with conceptual construction. The apprehension of the mere essential nature of the object is non-conceptual. In that very state, the powers of the object of dissolution—since their activities such as exertion have ceased—abide in Śiva alone.

And that very [reality] is indeed partless (*niṣkala*), with its nature as the effect withdrawn. At that time, when it is not established in a state of differentiation, that reality is called *laya*; for that alone is the *śivatattva*. In that very state, there is conceptual cognition (*savikalpaka*) accompanied by the connection of names, genera, and so forth;
this conceptual cognition is dependent upon the sense faculties.

"Likewise, it is independent; and it is considered to be the natural yoga of the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*) with all objects, being entirely free from bondage and independent of the organs of action. Action is also twofold: consisting of volition (*saṅkalpa*) and consisting of the performance of acts (*ākaraṇa*). Of these, the former belongs to Paraśiva and liberated souls (*muktātman*), while the latter belongs to those bound by bondage (*bandhātman*).
Thus it is said in the Pauṣkara: "Indeed, pots are not made by potters through mere intention alone;

rather, by the mere intention of Śiva, [the power] always effects the agitation of the *bindu*. Since she is intent upon action (*kriyā*) regarding her office and is authorized in all tasks—both that which is to be done and that which is to be performed—[she consists of] the recollection of the intentions of the *guṇas*..."

The term *pāra* is said to denote the Lord’s act of making that [object] his own object; therefore, it is established that His agency and subjectivity consist of the nature of knowledge. Thus, the activity of Śiva regarding the universe is fivefold, consisting precisely of the recollection of qualities (*guṇa-smaraṇa*) and volition (*saṅkalpa*).

By that [activity], His power (*śakti*), when conjoined with and attained through various modes—the distinctions of those objects of knowledge, effects, and so forth—is subordinate (*apradhāna*) by virtue of its qualities.
Action [arises] from knowledge; action... (p17b, l1).

Here, in the phrase "from knowledge and so forth" (*jñānādita*), the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) should be understood as elided. By the word "and so forth," the powers of will (*icchā-śakti*), activity (*vāmā-śakti*), and the others are included. It goes to—that is, it attains—diversity, which is of various kinds. (l2)... the power of fire... (l2).

Just as fire receives the designations "liquefier," "burner," "shatterer," and "cooker" according to the distinctions of its limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) such as iron, wood, salt, or rice, so too does Śiva-Śakti, though one, assume various forms. As stated in the *Mṛgendra*: "The instrument is not other than Śakti; Śakti is not insentient, for she is consciousness (*cit*). Due to the restriction of objects, she is one in both cognition and action; and that [instrument] is likewise. The meaning of this is as follows: [text continues]

The production of another instrument by means of power is not [possible] for that [instrument]. Śiva’s most effective means (*sādhakatama*) is not something distinct; rather, the intended meaning is that it is simply his inherent power (*samaveta-śakti*). The power of consciousness (*citaḥ śaktiḥ*) is not insentient, nor is it of the nature of sentience;
this is because there is no restriction regarding objects, and because of the manifoldness of effects, just as... (l5)

In awakening (*bodha*), knowledge (*jñāna*), and likewise in action (*kṛtya*) and the performance of that action (*kārya*), there is only one instrument (*tatkaraṇam*); for that reason, it means from the nature of the instrument of power (*śakti*).

[She] consists of the powers such as *vāta* and so forth—that is, she is the nature of the nine powers beginning with *Vāmā*; by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), *Jyeṣṭhā* and the others are included. She alone is the one who follows the Lord (*pati*), being inherent (*samavetā*) in Paramaśiva, the Lord who is followed [by her].
The Supreme Power (*parāśakti*),

on the pure path (*vartman*) or way (*adhvan*), constantly— that is, at all times— performs the fivefold activity (*pañcakṛtya*). For the purpose of making it known that the Supreme Power proceeds as a wife among the deities beginning with Sadāśiva in the form of Manonmanī and others, she is equal to the Lord (*pati*).
Thus it was said: "Vata.

Likewise, in the *Kāmika*: "Wherever the form of Sadāśiva is conceived, there [the power] is conceived; then, O Brahmin, she receives the name Manonmanī, for she is the source of both the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and the action of Kuṇḍalinī. The particle *eva* [indicates] that these are synonymous names.

When it is considered that "having performed the action" refers to the power *kuṇḍalinī* alone and nothing else, one must understand that [this statement] was made by certain teachers for the purpose of excluding [any other agent]. Thus it has been said by the teachers: "Some declare that the *bindu* is inherent (*samaveta*) in Śiva; therefore, this *kuṇḍalinī*, like the power of vision (*dṛkśakti*), is the power of action (*kriyāśakti*). These two powers are both inherent in Śiva."

These two consist of knowledge (*jñāna*) and action (*kriyā*). Among them, the first is called *sañciti*; it is the supreme *kuṇḍalinī*. Through the power of knowledge she discerns, and through action she creates the world. For action alone bestows fruit upon men; knowledge by itself does not grant fruit. There is no separation from these two for him [the soul], nor do they exist without Śiva, just as curd exists in the form of milk within *kuṇḍinī*.

Considering that [the power] is identical with Śiva by virtue of being His transformation (*pariṇāma*), the teachers—thinking that it cannot be a synonym for the *kriyāśakti* known as Kuṇḍinī—have established that the origin of mantras occurs through the *kriyātmikā* (action-natured) power residing within the embrace of Śiva, and not through the power of Kuṇḍalinī.
This has been stated: ... [l5] ... the origin of mantras is the action-natured [power] existing in the embrace of Śiva; it is not the power of Kuṇḍalinī. Thus it was said.

Mahāmāyā, the source of mantra, who abides as the encompassing [power]... (l6) ...by means of this tradition of the three nights, all individuals [attain liberation]. Thus, this power of the Lord, whose nature is action, is eternally manifest. This elaboration was stated by the teacher Trilocanaśiva.
That which, within itself, produces the multitude of various worlds along with diverse bodies, enjoyments, sense organs, and so forth, is called *bindu*.
By logic, it is a transformative entity (*pariṇāmin*), like *pradhāna*, and is subject to transformation.

(Verse 8) It must necessarily be insentient (*jaḍa*) by nature, just as milk is. If it is insentient, how can there be an inherence (*samavāya*) of this [insentience] in Śiva? [One might argue: "Because of the relationship of identity (*sahitādātmya-sambandha*), it brings about insentience through its union with the insentient."

However, due to delusion, the dull-witted person conceives of Śiva—who is in truth the singular essence of incomparable, partless, and dense consciousness—as an insentient Lord. For him, there is neither logic nor scripture, nor even a name, and no deity exists for him. He is to be avoided by the wise, as he is excluded from all who profess the existence of God. Therefore, this power of action belonging to me, which resides on the pure path (*śuddhādhvan*), was performed by me for the sake of the mantra... (l2)

For those who are pure consciousness alone (*vijñānakevala*), this [impurity] exists as the reality of experience (*bhoga*) in the form of *mala*, *māyā*, and *karman*. How does it exist among the bound souls (*paśu*)? Established as the state of being a bound soul characterized by the impurity that binds one to office (*adhikāra-nibandhana-mala*), it exists within the bound souls. It impels the bound souls toward various kinds of worlds of experience (*bhoga-bhuvana*). Therefore, it is this very [impurity] that performs the function of *karman*, which is the basis for the diversity and gradation of experiences for those dwelling on the Pure Path (*śuddhādhvan*).

The maturation of impurities (*malaparipāka*)—[as intended by] karma—is what is meant here, and not dharma or adharma in their own nature; for since [dharma and adharma] are causes of pleasure accompanied by suffering, they cannot exist in this context.
Therefore, one must accept that karma is something entirely different, distinct from dharma and adharma which are the sole causes of pleasure.

And that [cause] ought to be stated as being precisely what is called the "maturation of impurity" (*malaparipāka*), on account of the parsimony of conceptualization (*kalpanālāghava*). It is established that in the pure path (*śuddhādhvan*), the *bindu*—which is the pure material cause (*śuddhopādāna*) of the pure body, senses, and so forth that are heard of there—is indeed that very *bindu*. The Supreme Lord directly agitates this *bindu* by means of His own inherent power of consciousness (*cicchakti*), and although that power of consciousness is one, it is...

It is said that [Śiva] is the cause of dissolution (*laya*), enjoyment (*bhoga*), and authority (*adhikāra*) due to the distinction of the three kinds of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*). By means of that [power], which possesses distinctions based on limiting adjuncts, Śiva is designated as possessing dissolution, enjoyment, and authority; and he comes to have the names, in their respective order, of Śiva, Sadāśiva, and Īśvara.

Thus, the activity of Śiva is indeed threefold: *adhikāra* (empowerment), *bhoga* (enjoyment), and *laya* (dissolution). Among these, *adhikāra* is the activity consisting of creation and maintenance, by which [beings] are empowered by Śiva; *bhoga* is that which is enjoyed or protected—meaning the activity consisting of the protection of the material causes (*upādāna*) of the world following dissolution, or the granting of experiences according to the fitness of individual souls.

The meaning is "disappearance" (*tirobhāva*). As for "dissolution" (*laya*), it is the process of merging; it is an activity characterized by withdrawal (*upasaṃhāra*), and that [activity] is of two kinds: consisting of re-emergence and not consisting of re-emergence. Among these, that which consists of re-emergence is the residual potentiality (*śaktiśeṣa*) of the effect within its material cause (*upādānakāraṇa*).

Furthermore, for those whose nature of production has been destroyed by the descent of power (*śaktipāta*) and who are bound by the fetters of cause and effect and so forth, liberation—characterized as dissolution—is the withdrawal of that power;

this is what is meant by "grace in the form of reabsorption" (*saṃhārasvarūpānugraha*). Alternatively, when the *bindu* has reached a state of readiness for agitation, the Lord’s enjoyment consists in his merely being intent upon agitating it. When [this occurs]...
When the *bindu*, having transcended the state of exertion (*udyoga*),

transforms into the nature of the effect, then it is the domain of the Lord (*deva*), because he is the cause of that effect. When the *bindu*, having shaken off the state of the domain of experience (*bhogādhikāra*) and having internalized the entire web of its own effects...

Then, because it is caused by that [state], there is the dissolution (*laya*) of Śiva. Alternatively, Śiva himself—whose *bindu* has transcended and who is of the nature of pure consciousness (*kevalacidrūpa*)—receives the designation "dissolution.

This is precisely the intended meaning when it is said: "The function of those entitled to dissolution and enjoyment (*layabhoga*) arises from within the *bindu*. Therefore, by metaphorical attribution (*upacāra*), the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*), or even Śiva himself, is the one entitled to dissolution and enjoyment along with that *bindu*.

In that same way, because of the rule that Śiva does not act without Śakti, through the relationship characterized as that of agent and instrument, Śiva also is designated as possessing the authority for dissolution (*laya*) and enjoyment (*bhoga*). Just as [the fire] in the act of burning... (p19b, l1)

Just as fire is the burner when blazing, and its user, Devadatta, is also called the burner, so too Śiva receives the designation of "absorption" (*laya*). This is exactly what was stated by Trilocana-Śiva: "In that state, he becomes agitated; enjoyment (*bhoga*) occurs within the *bindu* which consists of bliss. When [the *bindu*] is agitated, there is the Lord's authority (*adhikāra*); absorption (*laya*) is that which has transcended the *bindu*. That alone is the power of consciousness (*cit-śakti*) of Śiva. (L2)

In the substrate (*samavāyin*), through the differentiation of the three limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) of consciousness, there arises that which possesses the authority over dissolution (*laya*), enjoyment (*bhoga*), and sovereignty (*adhikāra*).

In this very manner, because it is thus connected, the one God becomes threefold: Śiva, Sadāśiva, and Īśvara, who possess the authority over dissolution, enjoyment, and sovereignty respectively. She herself consists of the powers (*śakti*) such as Vāmā and the others.

It has been stated that the Supreme Power (*parāśakti*) performs the fivefold cosmic action (*kṛtya*). By this, it is illuminated that the powers beginning with Vāmā perform the effects of earth and the other elements within the domain of the Pure Path (*śuddhādhvan*), assuming the forms of the eight manifestations (*aṣṭamūrti*) starting with earth.

For example: Vāmā is the form of earth; Jyeṣṭhā is the form of water; Raudrī has the appearance of fire; Kālī has the appearance of wind; Kalavikaraṇī is the form of space; and Balavikaraṇī is the form of the moon.
Balavikaraṇī has the form of the sun;

Balapramathanī has the form of the self; Sarvabhūtadamanī and Manonmanī are of the nature of the supreme power (*parā-śakti*). The meaning is that she performs the effects of earth and the other elements through these powers. And so it has been said: "The forms beginning with earth... (l. 7).

The powers beginning with Vāmā are extended from You; by the word *vāma*, beauty (*saundarya*) is expressed as being endowed with five qualities. Because water and the other elements possess four, three, two, and one quality respectively compared to the state of possessing all qualities in their entirety, [Vāmā] is described as such. Having the form of Vāmā, she is the *pṛthivī-tattva* (the earth principle); she whose nature is Vāmā is the cause of emanation (*sṛṣṭi*). She is Vāmā, and Śarva is the Lord whose form is the earth (*kṣiti-mūrti-pa*); he is indeed that very one.

Vāmadeva is his power, and she is celebrated as Vāmā. Jyeṣṭhā consists of water; therein, "Sv" is the form of the material cause (*upādāna*). His lord is Aghora, and from Jyeṣṭhā comes Jyeṣṭhā. Because Agni has the nature of Rudra, Raudrī is the fiery energy, and her lord is Īśvara; he is indeed Paśupati, who is Rudra, and Raudrī is recognized as his power. As for... [the remaining portion of the verse].

Because she is the form of time (*kāla*), Kālī is the power (*śakti*); Īśāna, whose form is Vāyu, is renowned as Time (*kāla*). Kālī is his power, consisting of space (*ākāśa*), and is Kalavikaraṇī because she causes the transformation (*vikaraṇī*) of the *kalās*. Since *kalās* are parts and those [parts] are void (*śūnya*), she is their transformer because space is devoid of parts; thus she is its transformer. Because of that, there is the absence of *kalās*, which is the casting away (*vigatakṣepaṇa*); therefore, he is Bhīma, whose form is the sky (*gagana*).

Kalavīkaraṇa is proclaimed; its power is Kalavikaraṇī and Cāndrī. Balapūrvikā is Vikaraṇī, and Bala is indeed the specific cause of Śakti. Because he is the Lord of the Moon (Sudhāṃśu), Mahādeva is its Īśvara; he is indeed Balavikaraṇa, and his mistress is Balapūrvikā-Vikaraṇyākāmayī.

Because she crushes the power of Śakti, and because Rudra is indeed the lord of the form of the Sun due to the sun’s fierce rays, he is Balapramathana; the Lord is the one who releases from bonds, and his [consort] is Balapramathanī, who likewise subdues all beings. Because one experiences one's own merit and demerit through that [bond], the Self is indeed all beings, and it is remembered as the sacrificer; thus, she is the Śakti who subdues all beings.

The Śaiva power Manonmanī has been proclaimed [as such], because she leads the bound soul (*paśu*)—along with all his sins—to the state beyond, to Śiva-hood, by means of the supreme instrument of dissolution. She is called Manonmanī; the Supreme Śiva resides within her.
Those who abide on this pure path are directly under the control of the Supreme Lord.

The *yogya* [souls], who are exclusively pure consciousness (*vijñānakevala*), are of two kinds according to the distinction between those whose impurities are matured and those whose impurities are immature. Among them, the eight beginning with Ananta have matured impurities; however, the seven crores of great mantras known as *vidyās* have immature impurities.

With regard to these, the Supreme Lord—desiring to emit [the universe] through connection with the pure path, the pure principles (*tattvas*), instruments (*karaṇas*), worlds (*bhuvanas*), and so forth, by bestowing pure enjoyment, by establishing [them], and by dissolving that [impurity]—[acts].

The meaning is that, being endowed with the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*)—which serves as the instrument for both the withdrawal of all things and the favoring [of souls] by rooting them out—he becomes the performer of the fivefold act (*pañcakṛtyakara*). Having thus shown the act whose object is the pure path (*śuddhādhvan*), [the author now asks:
"In what manner does he exercise his authority over the impure path (*aśuddhādhvan*)? [This is the beginning of the following section.]

It moves by means of the sixteen digits (*kalā*), beginning with *karman* (action). Homogeneity consists of all actions, the threefold intellect (*buddhi*), mind (*manas*), ego (*ahaṅkāra*), ignorance (*vidyā*), speech, and the powers of action (*kṛti-śakti*). These are the sixteen digits. Action is twofold, distinguished as merit and demerit; the intellect is threefold, distinguished as passionate (*rājasa*), dull (*tāmasa*), and pure (*sāttvika*); likewise, the mind and ego are [divided] according to the distinction between knowledge and action, and the sense organs are twofold.

Together with *vidyā*, *vāk*, and *śakti* (l5), the number of *kalās* is sixteen. And it has been said by one who abides in the instrument (*karaṇastha*), through the distinction of his own consciousness (*svaciti*) and also [other distinctions]: "The two divisions of *vāk* and *śakti*, along with the *puṃs-kalās*, are traditionally taught as sixteen. Alternatively, [there are] the *karma*, *buddhi*, and *manas*... (l6)

The meaning is that it performs its functions by means of the feet. That which is called the "eightfold city" (*puryaṣṭaka*) exists, according to the fixed allotment for each individual, from the time of creation until the great dissolution or until liberation. Starting from the earth element up to the *sakala* [state], this subtle body consists of thirty principles (*tattva*s) and has a common form. Thus it is stated in the *Tattvasaṅgraha*: "This group of principles, beginning with the earth and ending with the *sakala*, is fixed for each person. Among the sixteen digits (*kalā*s)...

By the word "mind" (*manas*) being established [in its function], the six principles (*ṣaṭ-tattva*)— namely, the internal organs (*antaḥkaraṇa*), the limited powers (*kalā*), time (*kāla*), necessity (*niyati*), attachment (*rāga*), and the constituent qualities (*prakṛti-guṇa*)— are said to be the instruments in the person’s activity of enjoyment. By the words "intellect" (*buddhi*) and "action" (*karman*), the five gross elements (*pañca-bhūta*), beginning with space (*ākāśa*), which are the objects of perception through their determination by those [internal organs], are indicated.

The causes of those [gross elements] are called the five *tanmātras*, such as sound and the rest. Thus it was stated by Bhojadeva regarding the *pralayākalas*: "Those whose impurities (*mala*) and karma have ripened go, joined with the body of the *puryaṣṭaka*, into all wombs (*yoni*) by the power of karma. Here, by the word *yoni*, the worlds (*bhuvana*) are meant, and not the *mātrā-yoni*.

When she is established—meaning situated—in those who are the "other agents," namely Ananta, Īśvara, Śrīkaṇṭha, Viṣṇu, Brahmā, and so forth, who are themselves devoid of other agents; and when she resides within the impure self, which is the domain of the impure path (aśuddhādhvan), she performs the fivefold activity (*pañcakṛtya*). On the domain of the pure path (*śuddhādhvan*), she is inherent in the Lord (*pati*); on the domain of the impure path, she is the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*) itself, abiding through the medium of Ananta and the others, performing the fivefold activity.

The meaning is "he acts. ||4|| (l5. The embodied one is distinct [from the Self], the impure bound soul (*paśu*); the innate-consciousness [bound soul] is not one; the awakened-incomplete (*prabodhākala*) and the incomplete-with-a-lord (*seśa-pralayākala*); the complete-incomplete (*sakala*) is possessed of *mala*, *karman*, and *māyā*, all-pervasive, possessing subtle limbs, limited in power, enjoying its own creations, and an agent; and the Lord is eternal. (l6.)

Indeed, one who has performed the ritual of consumption (bhuktakṛti) shall, in due course after a long time, be liberated by Śarva. Having thus explained the distinctions among the categories of the Lord (pati), he now begins to explain the distinctions among the categories of the bound soul (paśu). "Distinct from the body" (dehānya) means other than the body and so forth; that is, distinct from the body, senses, and the like, having the nature of innate, inherent consciousness (caitanya), where consciousness consists of the forms of vision (dṛk) and action (kriyā).

Thus, although it has been stated that this [state] exists in the self at all times, nevertheless, that impurity is bound by beginningless impurity; the meaning is that its nature as consciousness is obstructed by the power of impurity. And so it has been said: "The state of Śiva, which is the purity of the self, though clearly present, does not attain its full manifestation for men due to impurity, because that [purity] is obstructed."

(... immediately thereafter, he becomes the bestower of liberation even through the conjunction of *kalā*, because it has been stated that "we are not subject to the *kalās* like the multitude of bound souls (*paśu*)". Other than these [is he];

therefore, the Supreme Lord is the bestower of liberation for those who dwell upon the path where the impurities of karma have ripened and are mixed. As for the *sakalas*, they are those who dwell within the worlds situated inside the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*), wherein karma, impurity, and *māyā* have fully ripened. For these, the ripened...

However, due to the equilibrium of karma and according to the descent of power (*śaktipāta*), those in whom aversion toward *saṃsāra*, faith in liberation, devotion to Śiva, service to the Guru, and so forth arise, are indeed those who are ripened;
whereas for those who are unripened, there is simply an absence of such reflection. For the ripened ones... [text fragment].

The Supreme Lord, assuming the form of the Guru, bestows the state of Mantreśvara and other ranks according to the degree of ripening of one's impurities and so forth, and thus becomes the giver of liberation. ||5||
Like mist, like the [sound] of a river, like the dust of youth...

(l5) It is like the dark glow of copper at twilight; it is that which destroys its own office, which is perceived by each individual person, and which possesses manifold powers. It is to be bound, to be purified, and to be awakened, since from it arises the state of being an enjoyer, characterized by dependence on activity and karma. (l6)

O Consort of Śaśakti, this has been composed by Deryoga. Now, he explains the classification of the categories of bondage (*pāśa*), beginning with impurity (*mala*): "Nīhāra" means impurity (*mala*), because it is stated among the synonymous names for *mala*.

Thus it is said in the *Mṛgendra*: "By means of the impurities of animality (*paśutva*), the obscuration of the bound soul (*paśunīhāra*), death, and fainting; by means of ignorance (*avidyā*), disease, exhaustion, the root of sin, destruction, and so forth.

The meaning is that because there is no other cause, its beginninglessness is established as being innate (*anādi-svābhāvika*); it is not adventitious (*āgantuka*), like the bonds of karma and *māyā*. Therefore, it is one, even though it exists in a state of insentience (*jaḍa-bhāva*).

Because it would otherwise be multiple due to its permanence, it would be impermanent like a jar; thus, "co-arising with humans" (l9) means co-arising with the selves of humans, having arisen together. Here, by the term "co-arising," one should not suspect that when the self is born, then the defilement is born, because the self has no birth from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*). By the term "co-arising" here (p22a, l1)...

Therefore, by means of that beginningless self which is established [as real], the impurity (mala), being internal, is described as a real entity (*vastu*). It is indeed a real entity, like a cataract in the eye; for if impurity were not a real entity, it would follow that it is non-existent, like a hare's horn. Furthermore, there would follow the absurdity that all means—such as initiation (*dīkṣā*) and knowledge (*jñāna*), which serve as the causes for the cessation of the root [impurity]—would be useless. He strengthens the [impurity’s] beginninglessness and other qualities with an illustration: "or like the blackness of copper" (*tāmra-kālikā*); that is, in the case of copper.

The existence of *kālimā* (blackness/darkness) as a single, beginningless, and innate property is established; likewise, the beginninglessness of impurity (*mala*) is established. This is because, in the case of the blackness of copper and so forth, since there is no other cause [for its arising], its status as a beginningless entity is proven.
Thus it is stated in the *Kiraṇa*: "Due to the connection with beginningless impurity, blackness resides in the gem; due to being freed from beginningless impurity..."

Purity resides in Śiva. Such is the nature established by those two as pure and impure according to their true state. Just as a pure crystal, or as copper with its dross, so too is the relationship between the individual soul (*ātman*) and Śiva.

By the example of copper and its dross: just as the dross that covers copper is removed when it is pierced by the power of the elixir (*rasa-śakti*), so too is the impurity (*mala*) that veils the Self.

The meaning is that one becomes liberated by means of Śiva’s power. Just as husks are the cause for the growth of sprouts from rice grains, so too is impurity (*mala*) the cause for the production of the body and other attributes of the self (*ātman*). The self is all-pervasive; because it is that which covers [the self], impurity is also entirely pervasive. For this very reason, it is eternal.

Since there exists a relationship characterized by beginningless mutual concealment between the *bhūtamala* and the self (*ātman*), their separation can never occur; thus, [if one were to argue] that liberation would be impossible due to this inherent nature, [the author] says: "The power of concealment is manifold, directed toward each individual soul (*pratipuruṣa*) until the destruction of its own office. Here, "its own office" (*svādhikāraḥ*) refers to the office of impurity (*malādhikāra*).

This is the meaning: because it possesses the authority (*adhikāra*) to veil the consciousness of the Self, at its end—that is, at its conclusion—since impurity (*mala*) is a substance (*dravya*), a "cooking" (*pāka*) is possible, just as a film on the eye is removed; this refers to the state of complete maturation (*paripākāvasthā*).
At that point of destruction, those which are all [the powers] ending with their own respective authorities...

Since *mala* is of a single nature, one might raise the objection that because the state of maturation belongs to a single self among all selves, when the *mala* consisting of *nivṛtti* is removed from that one self by the power of Śiva, the consequence would follow that liberation occurs for that one self and, by extension, for all selves. Anticipating this, he says: "The power that obstructs vision is manifold for each individual person. This means that for each person—that is, for each individual self—the power that obstructs vision is distinct.
He is thus described as one who possesses manifold powers (*aneka-śakti*) and abundant capacities.

For the eternal and unimpelling *mala*, there exist multiple, non-eternal powers residing in each individual soul (*pratipuruṣastha*) that obscure knowledge; these manifold powers are to be sought here [in this context]. Otherwise, if [the obscuration] were a single entity, then when the *mala* was removed from even one self—

There would be liberation for all at the same time; since simultaneity in liberation is not possible, one must therefore accept that the pervasive impurity (*mala*) possesses an abundance of power (*śakti*), because its eternity is admitted. Just as the burning power of fire is quickly suppressed by a mantra such as *stambhana*, so too [is it suppressed] by the power that constitutes the grace of the Lord (*īśvara*).
The meaning is that, because the power of impurity (*mala-śakti*) is obstructed, it is figuratively said that the impurity is "separated from the person" (*puruṣa*).

Thus it is stated in the *Kiraṇatantra*: "The destruction of this pervasive impurity is effected through its power; by means of the [spiritual] method, the obstruction of the power within the impurity is somehow brought about."
Just as the burning power of fire is quickly suppressed by a mantra, so too, because that power is suppressed, he is called "distinguished" (*viśiṣṭa*). Thus, even by the power of Śiva,
it occurs only at the stage when one's innate impurity (*mala*) has reached maturation.

The meaning is that the power of impurity (*mala-śakti*) is brought to cessation just as the husk and such, which cover the grain, are brought to cessation only at the stage of ripening and not otherwise; for example, just as the ripening stage of the grain results in the destruction of the grain itself through striking with a pestle and so forth, so too, if [the impurity] were brought to cessation while it is still in the state of ripening, there would follow the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the Self undergoing modification (*vikāritva*).
There is no destruction of the subtlest [element].

Thus it is said in the *Kiraṇa*: "The *saujā* is *kālikā* in copper; there is no destruction of that because of its destruction. Just as there is destruction in copper, so too is there the destruction of the impurity of the person (*puruṣa*)."

It should be understood that in the case of copper ore (*tāmrakālikā*), the state of ripening arises at the very moment of contact with the liquid (*rasa*). For this very reason, the destruction of the power of impurity (*malaśakti*) is made manifest during the state of ripening.
Thus it is said in the *Mṛgendra*: "That one [power], which is beginningless, dense, and great, residing within each individual self until the end of its own time for all beings..."

"Like a multitude of nooses and powers"—thus, he explains the distinction between the states of being bound and so forth due to the existence of impurity (*mala*) in the self. Because of the presence of impurity, that self is a "bound soul" (*paśu*); it is "bound" (*pāśya*) because it has not escaped the noose, meaning it is impelled by impurity and the like. For this very reason, it is "to be purified" (*śodhya*), meaning it is fit to be purified by initiation (*dīkṣā*), which consists of the nature of the *viḍadhva* (the path of excrement) as the means of purification; [this applies] to the self within the mind and so forth.
The meaning is that, although devoid of instruments, it is to be purified because it is veiled by impurities.

(l5) Immediately after being purified, it is to be awakened; it is fit to be awakened by means of the instrument consisting of the scripture—that is, by the knowledge of Śiva endowed with omniscience and other qualities—even when all innate defects have been destroyed, [it remains] by virtue of the mere existence of the Self. (l6)

The meaning is that because [the Self] exists and because there is no destruction of qualities such as omniscience, it is to be realized (*bodhya*). The word "becomes" (*bhavati*) is to be connected with every instance. Since, due to impurity (*mala*), he becomes a bound soul (*paśu*), one who is subject to bonds (*pāśya*), and one who is to be purified (*śodhya*), it is established that upon the cessation of impurity, there follows the cessation of the functions of being bound and so forth, in due order.

And so it is said in the *Kiraṇa*: "By its very nature, the bound soul (*paśu*) is here considered to be one who is to be bound, purified, and awakened. The functions such as being bound, in which its various states are established, come into being only when impurity (*mala*) exists; and not only [the state of] being an enjoyer (*bhoktṛtva*), but also dependence (*pāratantrya*) arises for the self through its connection with karma and so forth, precisely because of the existence of impurity. (l8–l9)

[Objection regarding] Connection: "But surely the self possesses the status of an enjoyer through its very actions; even in the case of enjoyment, since passion (*rāga*) and so forth are the causes, how can there be a connection with impurity (*mala*)? To this, the following is the rebuttal: Just as in the world, when a person is seen to be engaged in theft, he is bound by means of shackles and the like, so too the self, being joined with impurity, is bound by passion and so forth. Otherwise, how [could this be]?"
