Being bound by passion (*rāga*) and the other [afflictions], it is for this very reason that the direct cause of impurity (*mala*) is said to be the state of being an enjoyer (*bhoktṛtā*). The bond of *māyā* is the indirect cause, while the bond of karma (*karmabandha*) is the cause for the arising of the body and the cause for experience (*bhoga*) consisting of pleasure and pain.
Thus it is stated in the *Kiraṇa*: (....)

For, just as one observes the seed [to understand] the binding of shackles, so too, observing the state of being a bound soul (*paśutva*), the principle of passion (*rāgatattva*) functions. Indeed, through this state of being a bound soul, there is the status of being an enjoyer; the bond of *māyā* resides in the two bodies, and experience (*bhoga*), consisting of pleasure and pain, is established for the bound soul (*paśu*) by means of karma. It is declared that there is no other way for this bondage of being an enjoyer of experience than from the very self that has cast off impurity (*malatyakta*).

Since dependence on [external] factors such as karma is established regarding the consumption of food, one might ask: "Do the powers of impurity (mala-śaktayaḥ) bind or release the self by its own autonomy? To show that this is not the case, he says: "In this regard, [one should] contemplate the effect (kṛti) of this impurity—that is, its causal activity consisting of bondage and liberation. (L5–L6)

The sense is that those [powers], being imitative, are themselves the binder and the remover; [the phrase] "the binder" refers to the power of concealment (*tirodhāna*). The remainder [of the thought] is that there exists the power of the Lord (*īśa-śakti*), which is the power of Śiva (*śiva-śakti*). Here too, the power of Śiva does not act by itself, because agency belongs to Śiva alone; for this very reason it is called the "power of the Lord. Power is the instrument (*karaṇa*), while Śiva is the agent (*kartṛ*).

It is well known that when this very Śiva-śakti is gracious, she is called "the bestower of grace" (anugrāhikā). Thus it is said in the Mṛgendra-tantra: "Among those [powers], the power of Maheśvara is the auspicious one who bestows grace upon all; it is only because she follows [the individual's] dharma that she is metaphorically designated as 'bond' (pāśa)."

The word "tāsām" (of those) refers to the impure powers (*mala-śakti*); the phrase "from among them" (*madhyataḥ*) is to be supplied as an ellipsis because this was stated in the section on impurity (*mala-prakaraṇa*). He transforms them, and they bring about the manifestation of hardness, cruelty, and so forth, up to the point of obstruction; at that time, they are called "gracious" (*anugrāhikā*). Thus [it is said].

As for the question "What is the power of impurity (malaśakti)?", it is that very Lord who is the Sun; His desire to conceal [the soul] by means of the light of knowledge which has taken refuge [in Him] is what is metaphorically called the power of obscuration (tirodhānaśakti), meaning it is the very nature of the fetter (pāśa). ||6||

Karma— characterized by the causes for union with the body and so forth, producing various and manifold diverse experiences, subject to destruction and origination, determined by beginningless impressions, perceived through its subtle state, accomplished through the body and objects, and possessing the capacity to generate results— is [the cause], as are the restraints (yamas) and other [observances].

That which is fit for sleep, having reached its maturation through *māyā*, and being conjoined with the principle of persistence (*sthiti*), shall grant enjoyment until the end of *kalā*. Thus, having explained the fetter called "obstruction by impurity" (*malarodha*) which pertains to the self and the *vijñānakalā*, he now describes the fetter characterized as *karman* (action), which pertains to the self and the objects of the *pralayākala* and *sakala* states. By the words "by the body and so forth," the word "and so forth" includes the senses and their objects; by this, the following meaning is established.

The cause of yoga is the connection—by means of the body, that is, the gross and subtle physical forms; by the senses, that is, the cognitive and active faculties such as the mind; and by objects, that is, the sense-objects such as sound and so forth—with the conscious self (cidātman). [This refers to] the yoga of the conscious selves with respect to the body and senses...

The connection of the conscious selves with the body and so forth—which is the cause, the instrumental factor for the connection with objects—is perceived through direct observation. Therefore, having established whether this connection with the body arises from [past] action (*karman*), it is inferred that action alone is the cause of the connection with the body and so forth; the meaning is that otherwise, such a connection with the body and so forth would not occur. Having thus stated the general cause, [the author now discusses] its specific nature.

To demonstrate this, he says "variously" and so forth. "Variously" means that among the various types of connections involving the self through bodily actions, the diverse bodies, sense faculties, and abodes of living beings are observed. Among these, the bodies first consist of the dwellings of gods, *kinnaras*, *gandharvas*, humans, *piśācas*, animals, and so forth; and among humans, [the distinctions of] Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, and so on.

First, regarding the sense faculties (*indriya*): elephants possess the quality of turning back [to look behind]; snakes possess the quality of hearing with their eyes; owls possess the quality of being blind by day; cats possess the quality of extreme luminosity at night; and humans possess the quality of slight luminosity at night.
Thus it is stated in the *Kāmika*: "Just as the eye of a cat is distinct... [and so forth].

Regarding the phrase "yoḥ" [meaning "those who see"]: elsewhere too, there are living beings blind by day, while others are bound [blind] at night; likewise, some living beings have equal vision by day and by night. Thus, the objects of experience are as follows: for *cātaka* birds, it is subsisting on drops of water falling from masses of clouds; for swans and bees, it is tasting the nectar of lotus filaments; and for cattle and other animals, it is feeding on grass and the like.

The meaning is that the gods have nectar as their food (*amṛtānnatā*), while humans have rice and other grains as their food (*vrīhyādyannatā*); furthermore, the word "of" (*naḥ*) is used in the singular genitive case denoting a genus (*jāti*), and by the word "human" (*nṛ*), the selves (*ātman*) are intended; for them, there is the production of manifold enjoyments (*citrabhogaprasūtiḥ*), consisting of various kinds of enjoyment (*nānāvidhabhoga*).

It is the locus of origination, just as the heavenly realm and other such places are the causes for various kinds of enjoyments for the gods, and the earthly realm and other such places are for humans; even there, some possess sovereignty, some possess wealth, and some possess poverty— this is the remainder [of the meaning]— accompanied by destruction and production, that is, accompanied by the aforementioned destruction and production of the body, sense organs, and so forth.

By the word "also" (*api*), it is indicated that variegated enjoyments and so forth possess the quality of arising and perishing at some time or other. For this very reason, [the result] is determined for each individual (*pratiniyatanarāṇām*); that is, it is determined for each person (*prati-puruṣāṇām*) as birth, lifespan, enjoyment, and so forth, in accordance with their karma.

The meaning is that [the Lord], being endowed with *niyama*, is capable of bestowing, according to the respective gradations of the various worlds, the diverse types of perishable bodies, senses, and objects—which are determined for each individual and destined to arise in future births—upon the inhabitants of those respective worlds. [Objection: Is it not the case that karma, like the fetters of beginningless impurity (*anādimala-pāśa*), is inherent as the cause for the instruments of experience? [Response: True, but "experience" (*bhoga*) consists of the forms of pleasure, pain, and so forth.
Action is the cause of that; for only when there is the arising of a body from that [cause] does the acquisition of action occur immediately thereafter.

For this very reason, at the time of the first creation, the connection with a body and so forth is accepted as being due to some other cause. It is not accepted that the connection with a body and so forth is caused by action.
Therefore, it is from that very cause that [the connection arises], not from action.

The argument that the consequence of beginninglessness is not tenable is addressed here by this rebuttal: even at the time of the first creation, the selves possess connections with various kinds of bodies; otherwise, from where would these various bodily connections have arisen?

Thus it is said in the *Kiraṇa*: "O Lord of Gods, this action which is declared to be the cause of experience—since the acquisition of action occurs only when a body exists, from where does the body come at the time of creation? Just as his impurity is beginningless, so too is his action beginningless. If [action] were not established as beginningless, by what cause would there be such diversity? This is stated by the venerable Rāmakaṇṭha in his commentary on the *Kiraṇa*.

For, in every respect, because the diversity of bodies and enjoyments among persons would otherwise be inexplicable, [the existence of] karma is established; for even at the time of the initial creation, there is the perception of a diversity consisting of beasts, birds, wild animals, reptiles, immovable things, humans, and so forth, and this remains true even during the great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*).

It has been explained that through *siddhi* (accomplishment), the bondage of the body for the performance of activities such as the emission (*pravāha*) and so forth is accomplished. For this very reason, by virtue of the logic of the seed and the sprout, the beginninglessness of karma is indeed established.

It is called "karma" because it is performed in its subtle state; it is said to be "seen" because it exists in the self in a subtle form consisting of withdrawal (*saṃhāra*), due to its capacity to generate activity.

And it is said in the *Mṛgendra*: "Because it is produced by the operation of karma, the visible is called the subtle state. Just as in the world, a man may attain a certain conclusion merely by [seeing] the ground, yet suffer the loss of his life by falling from a branch above merely by approaching the foot of a tree—these two results, arising in the form of merit and demerit, are called his "visible" [consequences]. Therefore...

Thus, its true nature is unperceived, yet it is to be accomplished through speech, mind, and action—where "speech" (*vāk*), "mind" (*dhī*), and "action" (*kārya*) are the means by which it is to be achieved. By the word *dhī*, both the internal organ (*manas*) and the intellect (*buddhi*) are understood.

By the word *artha*, wealth, grain, and so forth are meant; or alternatively, the recitation of hymns concerning Śiva is of the nature of speech, meditation on Śiva is of the nature of mind, and the worship of Śiva and other such acts are of the nature of action.

The construction of the abode of Śiva and so forth is the "form of the object" (*artharūpa*) because it is being performed with wealth; the meaning is that it is to be accomplished by these means. It possesses the production of fruit, it is the producer of fruit, and it is the sustainer and the object of enjoyment for the selves, solely for the sake of experiencing the fruits of their karma.

And it has been stated in the *Gṛhendrarāja* that [the Lord] is the progenitor of the body, the senses, the worlds, and so forth, by means of a fixed time alone, and He is also the object of experience (*bhogya*) through the bestowal of fruits that sustain them: "He is the progenitor, the sustainer, and the object of experience; the means for the internal [self] and so forth is dharma and the rest. By the word "and the rest" (*ādi*), the status of being a cooperative cause (*sahakāritva*) is understood as the essential nature of dharma.
The meaning is that the insentient [matter] depends upon Īśvara and others.

Likewise, in the *Mṛgendra*: "Because it depends upon Īśvara, Vidyā, and so forth, it is called a 'cooperative cause' (*sahakārin*). Thus, the bond (*pāśa*)—which bears the names of both karma and non-karma—has its maturation reached through Māyā at the time of universal dissolution during deep sleep; that is, it has attained a transformation through Māyā.

The meaning is that, accompanied by *sthitimati*—that is, joined with the cognition of persistence—it exists within *māyā* in the form of a latent impression (*saṃskāra*). Precisely because it exists within *māyā* in the form of a latent impression, it is destroyed immediately after its fruition; thus [it is said in] the Mantra... (p26a, l1). Likewise, it is stated in the *Mṛgendra*: "It abides in *māyā* until the end, and when unattached, it goes to destruction. Furthermore, elsewhere it is said: "Action once performed must necessarily be experienced."

Neither auspicious nor inauspicious, karma is not exhausted even in hundreds of millions of kalpas; rather, it is at the time of the equalization of karma that the manifestation of Śiva-nature occurs. Thus it is stated in the *Kiraṇa*: "When karma has become equalized, then, by virtue of the lapse of time, one is initiated by a Guru through the descent of the intense power (*tīvra-śakti*). At that moment, the transmigrating soul becomes fully manifest as the nature of Śiva, and remains so eternally until the end of the *kalās*."

It is the bestower of experience (*bhoga*); from the *pṛthvī-tattva* up to the *kalā-tattva*, it provides the experience of pleasure, pain, and so forth for the selves residing therein. That which is called *māyā* is fully pervaded by manifold powers; it is the seed of the single path of suffering, eternal, situated within karma, and the dwelling place of the intellect produced by its own actions. Due to the manifestation of the diversity of effects, it renders one insentient and inauspicious, and is delusive during the state of sleep.
Or rather, that very [Self] is the universal soul; furthermore, that white cause is the awakener.
Now, he describes the nature of the noose of Māyā, which has become the object of the entire soul—namely, that which is called "Māyā," the one whose name is Māyā, possessing manifold diverse powers.

By implication, it is that which is excluded from [other causes], inherent, partless, subtle in form, and the sole seed of the path of suffering (*kaṣṭavatman*). It is the primary material cause—the single seed—of the entire universe, which consists of both the world of the impure path (*aśuddhādhvan*) comprising the worlds situated within the principles (*tatva*) beginning with *kalā*, as well as the bodies born of those worlds; for there can be no arising of the universe without a material cause. This is expressed by the word "sole" (*eka*).

It has been established that what is called "māyā" is indeed one alone. In the world, things such as jars and cloths are seen to be multiple, insentient (*acetana*), produced from causes, and possessed of origination. This [māyā], however, although insentient, exists without being produced from causes or possessing origination;
therefore, it is one, whereas the sentient is manifold.

The point is that impermanence is established by consensus, and thus it is one and the same. Now, one might object: "Let the multiplicity of that which is called *māyā* be admitted; what is the purpose of postulating a single essence?

Just as in the world we see the production of a single cloth from many constituent materials, so too let the creation of the entire universe be performed from multiple causes. To this, the following is the rebuttal: in that regard...

Just as the material cause (*upādānakāraṇa*) of a cloth is one and of the same nature as that [cloth], because it is produced from a single substance called cotton, so too is the production of the world from the single entity called *māyā* established; and because it possesses manifold powers (*citraśaktimat*), the creation of diverse manifestations and so forth is established.

Thus it is said in the *Mṛgendra*: "A cloth is produced from a collection of threads and so forth; everything [arises] from multiplicity. Even that [multiplicity] is born from a seed which is likewise multiple. Thus, even during the great dissolution (*mahāsaṃhāra*), because Māyā persists like Śiva and like the Self, as he will state:

(…) [the categories] ending with the *paśu*, the *suśakti*, the stainless *śambhu*, and the two-fold *māyā*. If *māyā* were impermanent, then the production of the world would not occur; if *māyā* were destroyed during the great dissolution (*mahāsaṃhāra*), then at the time of the commencement of creation again, from what material cause (*upādāna*) would the world arise? Therefore, *māyā* must be eternal; for if it were not, there would be an absence of the world due to the absence of a material cause. Thus, *māyā* is eternal.
It must not be accepted that the Lord is the creator of the world.

[The claim] that at the beginning of creation He creates the material cause by His own power alone is not tenable; for even regarding a material cause, there can be no production without another material cause, and thus another material cause would have to be postulated, which would itself be subject to impermanence.

Therefore, Māyā must indeed be eternal, because she exists in the form of power (*śakti*) at the time of dissolution. (p. 27a, l. 1) [The term] *karmāntara* means that which obstructs the end of one action and the beginning of another—that is, it binds the end of actions. The "authority" (*adhikāra*) of an action is simply its capacity to yield a fruit; just as the taking up of a tool like a hammer requires auxiliary factors such as a wheel, so too does Māyā. (l. 2)
It is established that [the cause] depends upon karma as a cooperative factor (*sahakārin*) by virtue of being its material cause (*upādāna*).

Likewise, in the *Mṛgendra*: "That single, non-auspicious seed of the world, which possesses variegated powers, is eternal, pervasive, and obstructive until the end of the period of its own activity; it resides in its own creation, within its own effect. (III.1.3)

The phrase "dwelling in its own creation" (*svakṛtinivāsana*) refers to the effect of Māyā, which is twofold: external and internal. Among these, the external exists at the time of emanation (*sṛṣṭi*) in the form of the manifestation of worlds and other principles situated within the categories (*tattva*) such as Time (*kāla*), while the internal exists in a subtle form within the womb of Māyā at the time of reabsorption (*saṃhāra*). The meaning is that [Māyā] persists through these two types of effects.

And it is said in the *Mṛgendra*: "Then, in the course of transmigratory existence (*saṃsṛti*), those things which are of the nature of power (*śakti*) function as effects in their unmanifest state; in the state of transformation (*vikṛti*), they function as effects in their manifest state for the accomplishment of purposes. Therefore, [the Lord] is the pervader of His own effect; and in the absence of a pervader, there would be no manifold effects situated everywhere in the form of the entire universe and so forth.

Since there could otherwise be no origination, the pervasiveness of *māyā* must necessarily be admitted. To refute the position that [the world] is non-existent because it manifests from the conscious Self (*caitanya-ātman*) alone—thereby being merely a state of being—he states that *māyā* is indeed the absence of consciousness: "From the manifestation of the consciousness of the effect," meaning within the effects such as *kalā* and the rest.

Because it manifests as non-consciousness in the form of the body, the organs, the worlds, and so forth—that is, because it manifests as insentience—it is "non-conscious" (*acit*). Non-consciousness itself is Māyā. Just as in the world, an effect such as an insentient jar is seen to have insentient material causes such as clay, so too, by observing that the effects of Māyā—namely the elements, the worlds, and so forth—are non-conscious, one perceives the non-consciousness of Māyā, which serves as the material cause of the worlds and other such things.
This is indeed established.

And it has been stated in the *Mṛgendra*, in the chapter on the characteristics of Māyā: "That [Māyā] must be insentient, because its effects are seen to be insentient. Now, one might object: since sentience is absent, how can insentience be known? What is the rule in that regard?

Because that which has a different nature arises from that which has a different nature, and because that which has a certain nature arises from that which has that very nature, everything would arise from everything due to the absence of any restrictive cause. Consequently, why is it that water is not inferred from the cognition of smoke—which is a mark indicating fire? For this very reason, the cognition of one thing could never arise from a mark other than its own.

It is not possible [that the insentient arises from the sentient], for the production of insentience from sentience is not established. And it has been said: "For those who claim that even the insentient is produced from a cause whose nature is consciousness, why is water not inferred by means of the mark of smoke? That which produces what is inauspicious is, precisely because it is distinct from the knowledge of Śiva, a producer of ignorance; for this very reason, it is also delusive. Now, as for Māyā itself...

Because there is an absence of bondage. It has been stated that knowledge and action, by means of the *kalās* and so forth, are both binders and illuminators; this is true. However, how [can they bind] one who has arisen from *māyā*, since [such a person] knows something merely through knowledge and so forth regarding the non-self (*anātman*) and the like?

The meaning is that it is called "delusion" (*moha*) because it generates the conceptualization of a self and so forth. Just as a lamp in great darkness, even while shining, is said to be "delusive" because its light causes a contrary cognition—such as perceiving a blue lotus as a red one—it is established that knowledge produced by *māyā* is indeed delusive. Thus, at the time of sleep and at the time of cosmic dissolution, the Abode is the Self of all, [pervading] all selves.

Having described the characteristics of the commencement, maintenance, and means of subsistence for the *sakala*, *pralayākala*, and *vijñānākala* [states], he states the characteristic of the Great Māyā known as the Bindu with the words beginning "In this way" (*evam*).
Thus, it is of the nature of the aforementioned mode, and is also called the Supreme Bindu (*paramabindu*).

It is indicated that there exists a specific characteristic (*viśeṣalakṣaṇa*) for that which is explained as the *bindu*, characterized by [the aforementioned general] characteristics. He states that specific characteristic: "White" means having the nature of the Pure Path (*śuddhādhvan*); it is the "cause" (*kāraṇa*), meaning the material cause (*upādānakāraṇa*) of the Pure Path; it is "illuminating" (*bodhaka*) because it is the illuminator of all objects, such as the means of knowledge (*jñāpaka*); its essential nature is that of an illuminator by means of the material cause of sound (*śabda*) through the vision of pure entities beginning with Śiva; and it is "not deluding" (*amohaka*), unlike *māyā*. Thus [it is described].

The meaning is that this is well-known in all the scriptures (*āgama*) in this manner. This [reality] called *bindu*, which possesses the characteristic of *māyā* and is endowed with manifold powers (*citra-śakti*), is partless (*akala*) and eternal;
yet it is joined with two types of effects—internal and external—within the sphere of the authority of impurity (*malādhikāra*). However, in this case...

The external effect consists of the worlds and other entities situated within the principle of Śuddhavidyā, such as Śakti; the internal effect, however, is its abiding in a subtle form within the Śiva-principle in the form of the *bindu* during the process of withdrawal (*saṃhāra*).

It pervades the entire universe, which is the pure path (*śuddhādhvan*), by means of the five *kalās*—Śāntyatītā and the rest—which are its own transformations. Due to the manifestation of the consciousness of the effect, it is of the nature of insentience (*acit*).
At the time of their dissolution, the abode of the mantras and the lords of mantras, such as Ananta and the others, is [the heart]; thus everything should be gathered together. ||8||

From *udyoga* (exertion), the principle of power (*śakti-tattva*) emanates from the Lord; and from that [power], the principle called *adhiṣṭhāna* (presiding), which is similar to vision and action, arises prior to the *bindu*. In the state of sovereignty, the principle of the Lord (*īśa-tattva*), accompanied by the Lord of Mantras (*manupati*), arises through the union with the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*); and through the union with the power called knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*)... (Note: The provided text contains several lacunae indicated by ellipses and scribal marks such as "ḍyu" and "ḍhyul". The translation reflects the legible portions of the Sanskrit.)

[He describes] the principle (*tattva*) called Pure Knowledge (*śuddhavidyā*) through [the faces of] Manu and so forth. Thus, he states that for the sake of the enjoyment (*bhoga*) and liberation (*mokṣa*) of the selves (*ātman*), the mantras, the lords of mantras (*mantreśvara*), and the thirty-six principles beginning with Śiva—which were created by Paraśiva—there exists [this reality], starting from the stainless [principles]. Regarding the phrase "from exertion" (*udyogāt*): when the Bindu, during the state of its authority over enjoyment, having shaken off the entire web of its own effects and remaining while internalizing them within itself...

Then, having transcended the *bindu*, Śiva, who is pure consciousness (*cidrūpa*) alone, attains the designation of the *śivatattva*, which is the nature of dissolution (*layasvarūpa*). At that time, the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*), though inherent (*samaveta*), also becomes indifferent (*udāsīna*) by nature, because Śiva lacks attachment to activity and because the *bindu* itself is insentient (*acetana*). What [connection] could there be with those things that serve as its substrata? What connection with Śiva’s inherence (*śivasamavāya*) [could there be]? *(Note: The text fragment provided ends abruptly at "kaiva śivasamavā", suggesting the sentence remains incomplete. The translation reflects this truncation.)*

The power (*śakti*) receives the designation "dissolution" (*laya*); by being completely merged with that [power], the one God becomes designated as "dissolution. When the God is appointed to a task, then the power is appointed to that task. When there arises the desire to perform acts such as creation, then the very power of Śiva, acting as the agent of creation and so forth, becomes the substrate for the causal point (*bindu*), and thus performs its own work.
"It acts" refers to the Lord who desires to emit;

thus it has been stated in the *Tattvaprakāśa*: "All powers, beginning with Will (*icchā*), having merged into this [Lord], perform their respective functions; therefore, they call this [Lord] the one who bestows grace upon all. Thus, for the Lord who desires to emit—that is, who wishes to create—the Supreme...
"From the exertion and activity of the Lord, from the *bindu* which constitutes the first material cause known as Śiva-nature.

Thus it is stated in the Pauṣkara: "When the *bindu*, having withdrawn its effects, remains established, then that very state is called the principle of dissolution (*layatattva*) or the principle of Śiva (*śivatattva*). Previously, at the very beginning, it was described as being enriched by *kalā*—meaning pervaded by the *kalā* of peace (*śāntikalā*)—and abounding with worlds (*bhuvana*)."
And [it is said]: "The collection of worlds resides within the *tatva* of *kalā*.

This well-known *śakti-tattva*, known by the name *prasara* or *jāyate*, arises from the transformation of the *bindu* which serves as its primary material cause; this is the meaning of "the *śakti-tattva* is born. By the word "and" (*ca*), it is indicated that the *śiva-tattva* resides at the summit of the *śānti-kalā*.

The world beyond tranquility (*śāntyatīta*) is said to be *saṃjñā*. And it has been stated that the principles beginning with *prakṛti* are agitated by the *bindu*; however, that which is not agitated therein is its *bhoga*, and that is the *kalā* beyond tranquility (*śāntyatīta*). That transformation whose nature consists of the worlds beginning with *śāntyatīta* is the *bindu* itself; that is what is called the *śivatattva*. Thus, by means of the intervention of the *śaktitattva*, he speaks of the principles beginning with *sadāśiva* through the passage beginning with "by [the powers of] will and action" (*drakriyābhyām*).

Similarity (*sāmyam*) means likeness through the two powers of knowledge and action (*jñānakriyābhyām*). From the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*), who has attained his office (*adhikāram*) as the creator (*sraṣṭṛtvena*) over that which is under discussion; that which is the material cause (*upādānam*) of the aforementioned *bindu*—that second state of being transformed (*pariṇāmitvam*), whose nature is the equilibrium of knowledge and action—is the principle (*tatvam*) called *sadeśa*.

The meaning is that "the collection of principles" (*tatvajāta*) refers to that which bears the name Sadāśiva. Here, the principle of Sadāśiva and so forth is of two kinds: the form of the creator (*sraṣṭṛ-rūpa*) and the form of the created (*sṛjya-rūpa*).

First, when [Sadāśiva] himself experiences the designation of the principles beginning with Sadāśiva while remaining in the state of persistence (*sthiti*), then Śakti and Śiva alone are called the "form of the creator. The "form of the created," however, consists of the thirty-sixth principle together with its actual nature (*tāttvika-rūpa*) as endowed with the worlds (*bhuvana*) and other elements that have been established therein.

For in that [text], the nature of emanation (*sṛṣṭi*) consists of the principles (*tattva*) beginning with Sadāśiva, which are differentiated by the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) of the various functions regarding the objects to be emanated; these principles, such as Sadāśiva and the rest, consist of Śiva’s own nature and take the form of the authority for experience (*bhoga-adhikāra*).
Likewise, in the *Mataṅga*, it is stated that there are three principles known as dissolution (*laya*), experience (*bhoga*), and authority (*adhikāra*).

"By way of illustration, this first category of entities is proclaimed to be named 'Lord' (pati). Thus, even for this [category] which has the form of the Creator—namely the reality (tattva) beginning with Sadāśiva—there is no dependence upon a material cause (*upādāna*). This is because, while distinctions are conceptually constructed through the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) of the various operations of power (*śakti*), there is in ultimate reality (*paramārthatas*) no actual division; as it is said in the *Tattvaprakāśa*: "In reality, the single principle known as Śiva is inlaid with hundreds of diverse powers; yet, due to the distinction in the activity of those powers..."

These [categories] are imagined as its distinctions; thus, within the principles (*tattva*) beginning with Sadāśiva, which consist of the forms to be emitted, there exists for those individual souls (*aṇu*) karma that has attained the status of a field of experience and serves as the counter-correlative to the Creator. In that regard, there is a requirement for material causes (*upādāna*); therein, Śiva—distinguished by the three states beginning with Sadāśiva which are conditioned by limiting adjuncts (*aupādhika*)—is the agent, and His power alone is the instrument.

Therefore, the divided *bindu-śakti* itself is the material cause (*upādāna*). This is the intended meaning: for the Blessed One, who is distinguished by the desire to emit the objects consisting of the principles (*tattva*) beginning with Sadāśiva, there occurs an activity for the purpose of their manifestation;

and this activity takes the form of an equal division between the powers of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*) and action (*kriyā-śakti*). Due to the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) of those various activities, that Supreme Lord [is designated as] the principle of enjoyment (*bhoga-tattva*) and the principle of Sadāśiva (*sadāśiva-tattva*).

It is designated as such. And it has been said: "The wise declare that state which is the expansion [of consciousness] due to the absence of any decrease or increase in the two powers known as knowledge and action—that is the reality called Sadāśiva. That [reality], when differentiated by the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) of the various distinctions in its activity, is termed *bhoga* (experience).

The Supreme Lord (Parameśvara), through the power of the Point (Bindu) and Energy (Śakti), brings about the reality of Sadāśiva-tattva; and that act of creation occurs solely through the operation characterized by the unfolding of knowledge and action, owing to the connection with the power of action (kriyāśakti). From the Supreme Lord, distinguished by his connection with the power of action, there arises predominantly the principle known as Īśvara-tattva, which is accompanied by Manupati and endowed with Ananteśvara and the others, and constitutes the principle of Tadīśa.
[This state] is born from the expansion below the [level of] Sādākhya through the excellence of the power of action (*kriyāśakti*).

Here too, when [Śiva] becomes preeminent in the activity of creation and so forth, then Śiva himself, as qualified by the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of that activity, is designated as the *adhikāra-tattva* and the *īśvara-tattva*.

And it is said elsewhere: "That wherein action attains its elevated state known as the knowledge of power (*śakti-jñāna*) is here called the *Īśvara-tattva*, which is always the agent of all things. Furthermore, the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*), characterized by the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of that activity, brings about the essential aspects of the *Īśvara-tattva* through the *bindu* and *śakti*. And that instrument (*karaṇa*) arises precisely from the operation characterized by the unfolding (*unmeṣa*) of the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*). Of this [world] that has been created...

He states that [the Lord] effects protection through the activity of maintenance and so forth, both for the reality of Sadāśiva and the other principles, and for the collection of individual souls (*aṇu*) residing therein. And that protection arises from the connection with the power called knowledge (*jñāna*), which is characterized by an abundance of knowledge;
it is from the Supreme Lord, distinguished by His relation to the power of knowledge, that [protection proceeds], just as [it was granted] to Manu.

Accompanied by the seven crores of great mantras headed by the [mantra] Ha-mukha, there is the collection of principles known as Śuddhavidyā. For here too, the excellence of knowledge belongs to one whose task is accomplished, consisting in the protection of that [knowledge] and so forth; its activity is conditioned by [its own] adjuncts, and Śiva is designated as the principle of Vidyā, which is termed the "gross office" (sthūlādhikāra). And it is said elsewhere: [The text continues: ...it becomes [so].

Wherein the reality known as *vidyā* attains an intensification called the power of the agent and knowledge, Śiva— characterized by the adjunct of the activity of that intensified knowledge and designated as the "gross office"— effects the true [entities] of the *vidyā-tattva* through the power of the *bindu*. Thus, [this pertains to] the adjunctual [state] of the one whose form is the Creator.

Because the Śiva-state, which consists of the categories beginning with Sadāśiva, lacks any substratum such as the worlds (*bhuvana*), for this very reason, [the following applies] to the *vijñānakevalas*— namely, the *vidyās*, *vidyeśvaras*, and so forth— who abide within those ultimate principles (*tattva*) designated as Sadāśiva and the rest, which are being emitted as planes of experience (*bhogabhūmi*).

Even beautiful women, who are lovely by nature with their various worlds and so forth—[the Supreme Lord], the Parameśvara, creates those withered enjoyments and the limbs of the instruments through the powers of knowledge and action inherent within himself; as it is said in the Śivāgama:
"Among those principles, for those who are *vijñānakevalas*... (l2).

Śiva, whose essence is action (*kriyātman*), brings about the diverse worlds, beloved ones charming by their very nature, enjoyments, and even the organs whose limbs are slightly withered; this occurs through the power of his non-differentiated Śakti. From the conjunction [of these], the principles of *kalā*, time (*kāla*), and necessity (*niyati*) emerge; from time arise knowledge (*vidyā*) and attachment (*rāga*); and from this, which is the friend of primordial nature (*prakṛti*), emerges that which is associated with Rudra as a secondary attribute (*gauṇa*).
And from that [intellect], I am the threefold [ego-sense] endowed with qualities...

by means of the senses, the mental [faculty], the objects of past karma, the measures, the distinctions of the multitude of its own qualities, and the five elements from those [measures]. Having thus described the five pure principles, [he describes] the pure Māyā.

He speaks of the principles (*tattvas*) beginning with *kalā*: "From *māyā*. From *māyā*—which is the material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*) of the impure principles—from the principle of *māyā*, due to its connection with Ananteśvara, who is established as the agent of the impure principles through his union with Ananta; and having understood that the karmas of these souls have ripened during the dissolution (*pralaya*), [Ananta] [acts] upon *māyā* by means of the infinite powers presided over by his own power.

And having caused agitation, he makes [Māyā] oriented toward the production of *kalā*; thus it is said: "The Lord of the Sovereign Kings of Vidyās, the King of Mantras, impelled by the procedure of Śiva’s will and joined with the powers beginning with Vāmā, having agitated Māyā, brought forth *kalā*. (l. 8)

Thus, having agitated *māyā*, by means of that very empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*), [the Lord] emits the diverse subtle and gross bodies and the worlds belonging to the *pralayākala*s and the *sakala*s; and *kalā*—the principle of *kalā*, the principle of *kāla*, along with the principles called *niyati* and *aniyati*—is born from *māyā*. This triad of principles arises from *māyā*.

The meaning is that it has arisen. Likewise, in the *Mṛgendra*: "Hara creates for those [souls] that which favors them—the principle called *kalā*, which is luminous (*taijasa*)—for that is indeed the supreme limb for their engagement with *māyā*."

Thus, in the *Tattvaprakāśa*: "She who consists of manifold powers is victorious; first is the principle of Time (*kālatattva*) itself, then follows Necessity (*niyati*) in the form of restriction, and after that arises Māyā. From Kalā [comes] the principle of Kalā, then Knowledge (*vidyā*), Attachment (*rāga*), and the principle of Knowledge. The principle of Sovereignty (*rājatatva*) is born from the principle of Sovereignty as Ananteśvara. And having made Kalā inclined toward the agitation and production by his own power..."
The principle of *vidyā* gave birth to the principle of *rāga*, as it has been stated:

"For that purpose, the Lord, having caused agitation, was born as *kalā*, the radiance; he created the principle of *vidyā*, the companion [of *rāga*], which is the instrument of the Supreme Self. Furthermore, elsewhere it is said:
"From the principle of *kalā*, two principles, *rāga* and *vidyā*, came into being, O Guru. Thus.

He states that after the five principles produced from *māyā* have arisen, the principle of *prakṛti*, which serves as the material cause (*upādānakāraṇa*) for the secondary principles (*gauṇa-tattva*) and so forth, is born from the principle of *kalā*.
Thus he says: "The *prakṛti*"; from this principle of *kalā*, the principle of *prakṛti* is born.
Likewise, in the *Mṛgendra*: "Then the principle of Pradhāna was produced from the principle of Kalā; that which is the cause of the secondary [evolutes] is the cause of the seven knots.

Regarding the phrase "of the seven knots," it has been stated by the venerable Nārāyaṇakaṇṭha: "Pradhāna is the cause of the Great Principle (mahat), the I-principle (ahaṅkāra), and the five subtle elements (tanmātra)—thus, of the seven knots."

Having explained [the category] as "the source of effects," he states that there exists a principle called Puruṣa, which arises from Māyā, completes the principles beginning with Prakṛti, and has its locus in the Bhuvana-path of Rudra: "the companion of Prakṛti," meaning it serves as an assistant to the principle of Prakṛti.

Since the principle of *prakṛti* is accepted as being accompanied by the effect along with the principle called *puruṣa*, it is well known as "prakṛti and puruṣa. For this very reason, it is stated that [the *puruṣa*] is the friend of *prakṛti*. As Rudra has said: "The *puruṣa*-principle, produced from *māyā*, arises from that very [source]; it is the basis for the cognition of 'person' (*puṃ-pratyaya*), the fulfiller of *pradhāna* and the rest, and it rests upon Rudra within the world of beings (*bhauvana*). Thus, in this way...

The meaning is "from the principle of *māyā*. Now, one might object: since the *puruṣa* is conscious by its very nature, it is impossible for it to be counted as an *adhvan* among the principles (*tattva*) which are insentient like Śiva; therefore, its inclusion as an *adhvan* within the midst of the *tattvas* is not logical. How then can it be said that "the pair of Rudras is associated with *prakṛti*"? True, [but this is said] in relation to the five principles beginning with *kalā*.

In ultimate reality, the *puruṣa*-principle, whose nature is bondage, is designated as the "experiencer" (*bhoktṛ*). For it, there exists neither the state of being a temporal path (*adhvatva*) nor the state of being the support of the worlds (*bhuvanādhāratva*). Therefore, it is stated in the Āgamas that those worlds abide within the *rāga*-principle. Thus it is said: "Then Vāmadeva, Bhīma, Ugra, he known as Bhava, Sarva, Īśāna, Ekavīra, Pracaṇḍa, Īśvara, Pumān, and Umā."

His lord is Ananta, and Śiva alone is also [the lord] thereafter. For these Rudras, fierce with intense power, abide in the principle of Rāga. In that very place, the Puruṣa is to be known as the protector of the grasp of Pradhāna;
thus, for this very reason, [it pertains to] the principle of Puruṣa.

In the initiation for Nirvāṇa, after the purification of the *prakṛti-tattva*, there is no fault whatsoever in reciting [the subsequent categories] above *prakṛti* and below the *rāga-tattva* for the sake of purifying the impurity of the individual soul (*puṃstva-mala*).
From this *prakṛti-tattva*, the secondary qualities of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*— namely, the *rūpa-guṇa-tattva*— are known.

Thus, in the *Tattvaprakāśa*: "From the Unmanifest arises the principle of the Guṇas, which consists of manifestation (*prakhyā*), activity (*vyāpāra*), and restriction (*niyama*); here, Sattva, Rajas, and Tamas are also [known as] pleasure, pain, and delusion.

Therefore, from the principle of the Guṇas, which possesses this threefold form, the principle of the Intellect (*buddhitattva*)—consisting of Sattva, Rajas, and Tamas—is produced. And it is said: "From the three Guṇas..."
Intellect (*dhī*), which consists of the determination of objects and so forth, is also threefold according to its qualities (*guṇa*) in accordance with past karma.

Therefore, from the principle of intellect (*buddhitattva*), [the ego-principle] arises, endowed with the three qualities—joined with the qualities consisting of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*—and further joined with the names of the qualities beginning with *sattva*: namely, *taijasa*, *vaikārika*, and *bhūtādi*. This is the ego-principle (*ahaṃkṛt*).

The principle of *ahaṅkāra* has arisen and been described; it is born again as threefold through the divisions of *sāttvika*, *rājasa*, and *tāmasa*. It breathes forth under the names *taijasa*, *vaikārika*, and *bhūtādi*. Here, the word "first" (*prāk*) at the outset indicates the *taijasa* and the others. Therefore, the principle of *manas*, whose nature is the *taijasa-ahaṅkāra*, is born together with the organs of action and the organs of perception from the *rājasa-ahaṅkāra*.

The organs of action (karmākṣāṇi), which are the organs of action (karmendriyāṇi), are born from the ego (ahaṅkāra) characterized by the element of activity (bhūtādi). Likewise, the subtle elements (tanmātrāḥ) are born [from the same]. Similarly, in the *Mṛgendra*, it is said: "The ear, skin, eye, tongue, and nose, together with the mind, are composed of light (taijasa) due to their connection with illumination; they are sattvic, and so is speech. (l6)

The hands, the organ of generation, the anus, and the feet—these are the "arising from passion" (*rajobhava*) *mātrās*. By the word *mātrā*, the objects such as sound and so forth are understood, distinguished according to their own qualities.
As for the qualities of their respective [elements] such as sound and so forth:

in the case of earth, there is sound in the form of [the noise of] jars, cloths, and the like; touch in the form of cold and heat; color in eighteen varieties, such as white, red, black, and so on; and taste in the form of sweet, bitter, and the like.

Taste is also of six kinds; smell is of two kinds, being both fragrant and non-fragrant. These elements, such as earth and the rest, having attained their own qualities (*svaguṇagatāḥ*), "divide" them—that is, they exist in a state of differentiation from them—and thus they are called *svaguṇagatābhidāḥ*. Some maintain that the feminine suffix *ṭāp* is applied after a word ending in *hal*, so it ends in long *ā*.

The meaning is that the subtle forms (*tanmātra*) of sound and the other [objects] exist as distinct from the collection of their own respective qualities residing in earth and the other elements. These *tanmātras* are born from the *ahaṅkāra* characterized by *tamas*.
Likewise, in the *Mṛgendra*: "Sound, touch, form, and taste... (l2).

And smell is the fifth [tanmātra]. These tanmātras are permeated by the qualities (guṇas); they are designated by the term "tanmātra" because they are distinct from the categories of luminosity (prakāśa), activity (karma), and inertia (tamas).

From those subtle forms, which are causal in nature—the mere measures (mātrās) of sound and the rest—there arise, respectively, the five gross elements: ether, air, fire, water, and earth, which possess gross forms. ||10||
From his supreme knowledge, while the Kevalins remain established, Śiva—

having made certain lords of mantras similar to those whose yoga has reached its fruition, as well as other gurus who are pure and whose limbs are subtle, capable of dissolution in the stainless, pure path— and having likewise fashioned the Rudras as the guardians of the cities of the body, ordains them as his disciples.

Having thus demonstrated the arising of the thirty-six principles (*tattva*), he speaks in order to describe Ananta and the others who reside therein: "From knowledge" [means] Śiva. Here, by the word "Śiva," the venerable Sadāśiva is meant, who resides in the principle of Sadāśiva (*sadāśivatattva*) and is endowed with the thirty-eight digits (*kalā*) associated with the five Brahmās, due to his engagement in the fivefold cosmic functions such as creation and so forth. And it has been said regarding his body: *Note: The ellipsis at the beginning of the fragment indicates that the preceding portion of the text is missing.*

With the five mantras—Īśāna, Tatpuruṣa, Aghora, Vāmadeva, and Sadyojāta—which are employed for the five rites, [the deity] Sadāśiva is formed, beginning with the head and so forth; he is the Lord Sadāśiva, whose limbs are purified and who is equipped with the ornaments such as the *sakala* and others. Now, [one might ask], is he situated above the *Sadāśivatattva*?

In the scriptures, it is heard that [the Lord] is "the best among those possessing power" (*śaktimat*) in the principle of Power (*śakti-tattva*), which consists of subtle sound (*sūkṣmanāda*); and in the principle of Śiva (*śiva-tattva*), he is "the Lord of Sound" (*dhvanipati*), thus indicating a distinction between the Lord and [Power]. How then can he be the venerable Sadāśiva (*sadāśiva-bhaṭṭāraka*) residing in the principle of Sadāśiva? To this, the following is the resolution: through the metaphorical application of different functions, there is a distinction of the Lord just as there is a distinction of powers; however, because there is no ultimate distinction [in essence], he is indeed the venerable Śiva himself, [who is also] Power.

It has been stated that there is no other lord of the principle of Śiva; however, [it is said]: "But in this scripture, the distinction of lords [is established] through the metaphorical designation of a distinction in functions, like the distinction of powers (*śakti*), arising from the distinction of their respective stations. This is known from the realization among the *kevalins* that karma has been utterly destroyed, yet they remain associated with the various *vijñānakalas*, who possess the bonds of *māyā*.
Since [the category] *para* is said to exist above and beyond the *māyā-tattva*, the state of *vijñāna-kalā* and *kalā* exists in the interval between *māyā* and *śuddhavidyā*.

Because it is stated that *para* is "above *māyā* and below *śuddhavidyā*, veiled by nothing but impurity" (*malamātrāvṛta*), the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*)— situated in the middle of *vijñāna-kalā* according to the varying degrees of the ripening of impurity— is [surrounded by] the eight lords of knowledge (*vidyeśvara*), beginning with Ananta, as well as the *anīśvara*s and *anīśvara-anīśvara*s.
And he says that he acts for those who dwell in reality:

(l5) "resembling the application of the ripening of impurities"—that is, by way of the application of the ripening of impurities, through the connection with the gradations of the ripening of impurities—[he acts] for those who are similar to himself, being of a form slightly inferior or equal [to his own], [and for] the seven crores of great mantras. (l6)

He establishes certain lords of the mantras, such as Ananteśvara and others, who are joined with powers like Vāmā and accompanied by their respective portions of *adhikāra-mala*, within the principle (*tattva*) of the Lord of the Pure Path (*śuddhādhva-bhūteśvara*), existing in the relationship of the impeller and the impelled. As it is said in the *Mṛgendra*: "Therein, first, for those individual souls (*aṇu*) who are fit [for liberation], he creates the desired group, joined with powers such as Vāmā and surrounded by seventy million [attendants]; among them is Ananta."
And likewise Sūkṣma,
Śivottama, Ekanetra, Ekarudra, Trimūrti, Amitadyuti, Śrīkaṇṭha, and Śikhaṇḍin— the lords of the lords of the kings of kings—
even though they possess the yoga of omniscience and other qualities, they remain subject to command due to a trace of impurity.

"Thus, the mantras situated below are distinguished from one another"—so it is explained in its commentary by the venerable Narāyaṇakaṇṭha: "In this world, there are kings such as Indra and the other [world-protectors];

their kings are the hundred Rudras; and these are the lords and masters even of the lords of those [Rudras], such as Maṇḍalī and the rest; thus they are called Viśveśvaras (Lords of All). 'Distinguished from one another' means that those situated above are superior to those situated below."

It has been stated that they are distinguished, and it has also been said: "For whoever is superior in quality compared to another is considered to be above him. He renders the mantras—the seven crores of great mantras—distinct from one another;
and it is said that at the time of creation, there were mantras numbering seven crores.

Because of the state of emanation within the pure path (*śuddhādhvan*), that which is connected to *māyā* establishes the abodes of the worlds of Pure Knowledge (*śuddhavidyā*). At the conclusion of their term of office, the Supreme Lord himself—without requiring the presiding over them through the form of a Guru—grants them grace. And it is said in the *Tattvasaṃgraha*: "In this world created [by him], he grants grace to those men who have attained the purpose of the mantras brought forth by Śiva, even without [the Guru]."

The Supreme Lord, having assumed the form of the Teacher (deśika), exercises his sovereignty over the other [levels] up to Īśa; and having invested the entire path of Māyā with its three and a half crores [of mantras], together with their respective authorities, at the time of withdrawal, He presides over the form of the Guru and bestows grace. And it has been said:

Having exercised authority throughout the entire path while depending on the body of the practitioner for half of it, at the end of its persistence—[the state] "with the twenty [principles] of Śiva" means together with the Mantreśvaras such as the hundred Rudras and others; "not impure" refers to the impure path (*aśuddhādhvan*); "Lord" refers to Ananteśvara, because Ananteśvara is the agent (*kartṛ*) in the impure path; [he dissolves] the *layakalās*, that is, the *pralayākalas*.

Having fashioned the eighteen Rudras and the hundred-and-eight Rudras—possessing subtle bodies composed of *kalā* and the other [tattvas] and having subtle limbs—the meaning is that he has created them; the meaning is that he makes these the Lords of Mantras (*mantreśvara*) for the purpose of protecting the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*). And it is said:
"Then, manifested by Ananta and the others, because they are the binders of the Lords, [he creates] those whose bodies are begun by *kalā* and the rest... (p. 34a, l. 1–2).

The meaning is that he ordains— the hundred and eighteen remaining ones, who reside within the city of the body, who are joined with the eight cities [the subtle elements], and who are distinguished by the Self mentioned previously— namely Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Indra, and the others; he ordains them in *bhava*, the cycle of existence bound by karma, creating them as lords of the worlds within the cosmic egg (*aṇḍa*).
Likewise, in the *Mṛgendra*, it is stated: "The Lord, having entered even those world-rulers who possess *añjana*—from whom all this [universe arises] and whose power is bound by karma...

In the commentary (*vṛtti*) on that, Nārāyaṇakaṇṭha says: "...the Supreme Lord, having presided over others such as Brahmā and the rest, beginning with the circle-chiefs (*maṇḍalīprabhṛti*). This has been explained by Aghoraśivācārya in his *Tattvaprakāśadīpikā*.

Regarding the phrase "beginning with Brahmā" (*brahmaprabhṛtīn*), there are verses stating that Viṣṇu and others [are included]; other Prādhānika mantras, such as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and so forth, are supreme and accompanied by their respective adjuncts (*sāñjana*), and they reside within the cosmic egg (*aṇḍamadhyastha*). ||11||

O Śambhu, that which, through its effects such as *śakti* and the rest— consisting of subtle and gross sounds, points (*bindu*), and letters— the illusory power (*māyī*) of the world manifests itself as its own primordial sound (*nāda*) and as the crooked one (*kuṭilā*) by means of its *kalās*; and which, having cast people into [the cycle of existence], reveals their impurity (*mala*) in a single location along with their individual consciousnesses— that indeed is the power of command (*niyoga-śakti*).

Having first grasped the power of the agent (*kartṛśakti*), [the author] says that *kalā* is precisely the power of action (*kriyāśakti*) inherent in Śiva, which brings forth the entire universe produced from the power of *kuṇḍalinī* as its material cause. Regarding the term "subtle" (*sūkṣma*): it refers to the subtle and gross resonance (*nināda*).
Having blocked one's own ears with the tips of the thumbs and having made the sound (*ke*) [resonate], whatever sound one hears is *nāda*, which consists of the form of resonance (*dhvani*).
And it is said: having covered the two ears of the practitioner with the two thumbs...

(p34b, l1) ...thereafter he hears that sound which has a resonance like the thundering of clouds. The *bindu* is the locus of the arising and dissolution of the *kalās*, beginning with the cessation of vowels (*svara*) and consonants (*varṇa*). And it is said:
"Because from it proceeds the creation consisting of vowels, consonants, and *kalās*, and into it [all] is dissolved again; therefore... (p34b, l2)

"Bindu is so called"—this refers to the syllable of the script (*lipi*). Each [syllable] exists in two forms, subtle and gross; thus it is said that [the object] "goes to" those *nāda*, *bindu*, and *lipi* scripts, meaning by way of the essential natures of *nāda*, *bindu*, and *lipi*. Regarding the phrase "by the effects beginning with Śakti" (*śaktyādi-kāryaiḥ*): here, by the word "Śakti," the Kuṇḍalinī power known as Mahāmāyā is meant. By her "initial effects" (*ādikāryaiḥ*), that is, by the first-born effects such as *nāda* and the rest, [it is manifested] through Śakti.

Sound (*nāda*) in the form of resonance (*dhvani*) is the first agitation; the point (*bindu*) produced from that sound, consisting of internal discourse (*sañjalpa*), is the second agitation; and the phoneme (*varṇa*) produced from the point is the third agitation. And it has been said: "From power (*śakti*) comes sound (*nāda*), then the point (*bindu*), then the syllable (*akṣara*), and from that the Mother (*mātṛkā*)."

Likewise, (l5) that [is found] in the Three Jewels; and through the penetration of sound, this is a mass of sounds, a cloudless [expanse]; and this mass of sounds arises from the *bindu*, and the *bindu* from the *nāda*. This [nāda] is the cause of the pure paths, beginning with the *anāhata*. Thus, here (l6):

The distinction is that in the pure path (*śuddhādhvan*) the effects are subtle, such as *nāda* and so forth, whereas in the impure path (*aśuddhādhvan*) the effects are gross, such as *sthūlanāda* and so forth. Just as it has been stated that the power of Kuṇḍalinī, following *māyā* and *karman*, produces effects in the form of *nāda* and the rest, here [it is understood that] those known as *nāda*, *bindu*, and *varṇa* are the primary effects of the power of *parabindu*. Among these, [the first] belongs to the *kāryabindu*.

There are two states, gross and subtle, which, according to their respective functions, are called *vaikharī* (the intermediate) and *paśyantī* (the subtle). As it has been said: "That [reality] is the Bindu, known as the Supreme Nāda; Nāda is the cause of Bindu, syllables, and forms. Its four modes of activity (*vṛtti*)—namely *vaikharī*, that called *madhyamā*, *paśyantī*, and the one designated as *sūkṣmā*—pervade all things. In this regard:
The *vaikharī* [speech] consists of the perception of phonemes (*varṇa*). There are eight places of articulation for phonemes:

the chest, the throat, the head, the root of the tongue, the teeth, the nose, the lips, and the palate. When the wind is obstructed at these places of origin of the phonemes, that which subsequently assumes the form of the phonemes—[arising] from the upward movement of the two breaths...

That very [speech] which, flowing outward, is uttered for another as a pot or the like, and is graspable by the ear and verbal in nature, is *vaikharī*. That which precedes it is *madhyamā*, which remains in a state of extreme subtlety.

And it is said in the *Ratnatraya*: "In that regard, *vaikharī* is graspable by the ear and expresses the meaning; when the breath is held in the [articulatory] places, it assumes the form of phonemes."

This [articulation] is generally the basis for the maintenance of life for speakers; it is the intermediate state of grossness of the *kāryabindu*, perceived solely by the middle intellect (*madhyamā buddhi*),
and therefore consists of internal utterance, not reaching the path of the ear.

Consisting of the sequence of phonemes (*varṇa*), with a slight upward movement of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), that Speech which proceeds in such a manner is called the Intermediate (*madhyamā*). It is said to be the effect of the Visionary (*paśyantī*), and it is described as following the sequence of phonemes derived solely from the intellect (*buddhi*); however, being of the nature of internal discourse, it does not reach the ear. Transcending the activity of the vital breath, it exists under the name "Intermediate," according to the *Kāryabindu*.
The first stage is that [speech] which, like the down of a chick within the fluid of a peacock’s egg,

is devoid of all sequential order due to the non-differentiation of the phonemes residing in the word; and because of this very absence of the manifestation of all qualifiers, it shines forth by itself as speech whose object is not yet determined.

They perceive the subtle transformation; as it has been said: "The phonemes, withdrawn from all sides into an undifferentiated state, manifesting by themselves like the fluid within a peacock’s egg—this is what they perceive. The subtle [state] known as *nāda* is devoid of all specific qualities;
it is the very nature of the object, the internal illuminator of speech, and it abides for a long time. That is called the subtle, and as it has been said regarding its own nature:

"Light alone is the internal, subtle, and imperishable speech"—this indeed is the supreme bondage for those dwelling on the pure path (*śuddhādhvan*). Those who perceive this through discernment (*viveka*), having abandoned the agency of creation and so forth characterized by being an object of action, become equal to the sun. As it has been said:

In that [state] wherein the true nature has been perceived, one's eligibility for [transmigration] is revoked. Furthermore, it is that very [power] which, until liberation, does not release even the *pralayākalas* from their subtle bodies, but rather causes them to pass from one womb to another. As for the sixteen *kalās*, they consist of the five organs of action, the five organs of knowledge, the mind (*manas*), and the ego (*ahaṅkāra*).

The fourteen faculties of intellect and knowledge, together with the two powers of speech, constitute the sixteen digits (*kalā*) which are the instruments (*karaṇa*) of men. And it has been said: "In terms of their distinction as instruments, there are fourteen within one's own consciousness;

however, due to the division of the two powers of speech, they are traditionally recorded as being fully sixteen. For this very reason, among these sixteen digits, the sixteenth digit called *sūkṣmā*—which is synonymous with *śakti*—is the supreme bondage.

Thus it has been said regarding the Puruṣa consisting of sixteen digits: "They call her herself immortal. In this way, the manifestation of the effects beginning with *nāda* pertaining to the mobile world has been demonstrated. Now, the manifestation of the effects beginning with *nāda* pertaining to the immobile world is being demonstrated, because it has been stated that "the world, both mobile and immobile, is presided over by *nāda*. Here, since *nāda* has arisen from the power of Mahāmāyā, this constitutes the first expansion, which consists of the worlds (*bhuvana*). Therefore...

The worlds of Nāda and Kalā, beginning with Indhikā and ending within the Śiva-tattva, are described here. Among these, the five beginning with Indhikā—namely Indhikā, Dīpikā, Rocikā, and Ūrdhvagā—are mentioned; and by the term "Bindu," the four worlds of the Bindu-kalā are meant, namely Nivṛtti, Pratiṣṭhā, Vidyā, and Śānti, which arise from the Bindu. (l3–l4)

The inclusion of these [worlds] within the principle of Śakti is due to their subtle nature, which consists in their existence as the power (*śakti*) of the Supreme Bindu— the material cause of the worlds of Nāda and Kalā— and their gross nature, which consists in their manifestation in the form of the worlds themselves.

The subtlety of the worlds beginning with Nivṛtti, which abide as included within the principle of Śakti, is due to their being the means for the soul's experience of the body, the senses, and objects.
The grossness of the elements such as earth, which are the perceptions of the *kalās* beginning with *nivṛtti*, is thus [the world].

Through the effects beginning with *śakti*, the threefold nature of *māyā*—beginning with *māyā* itself—is the world consisting of the moving and the stationary; for it has been said: "And *māyā* is indeed remembered as being threefold. Alternatively, [it is so] through the effects beginning with *śakti*.

In this context, by the word "power" (*śakti*), the principle of power (*śakti-tattva*) is meant; by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the principles of Sadāśiva and the others are meant. Within the principle of power, there are respectively the subtle *nāda* and *bindu*, and within the principle of Sadāśiva, the gross *nāda* and *bindu*. In the principle of Īśvara, there are the subtle *lipis* (phonemes) joined with Ananteśvara and the others;
in the principle of Vidyā, there are the gross *lipis* joined with the seventy million great mantras (*mahāmantra*) in their *vaikarī* form.

The collection of twenty-eight tantras beginning with the *Kāmika* exists. And it is said: "Nāda, Bindu, Sakala, and that which is called Sadākhya—these are established upon the Tattva; furthermore, the Vidyeśas, the Mantras, and the Vidyās are within Īśa; thus [they are] called Vidyā. In this way, the entire world belonging to Māyā is [contained within] the innate nature of Nāda, which is the root. Because she exists in the form of a sprout having emerged from the Kanda, the Kuṇḍalinī-śakti is "Kuṭilā" (crooked). Her form is crooked because she stands in the shape of a sprout, having arisen from the Kanda.

By the use of the word "and" (*ca*), it is understood that [Kuṇḍalinī] is also presided over by the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*) inherent in Śiva; otherwise, being insentient in nature, Kuṇḍalinī would lack the status of being a substratum. Furthermore, that Kuṇḍalinī is the power of Śambhu, for she is described as being pure yet consisting of an insentient essence.
Likewise, in the *Kālottara*: "That which is Kuṇḍalinī is conjoined with the Moon, Fire, and Sun."

She should be known as residing in the region of the heart in the form of a sprout (*aṅkura*). For, because she is the substratum (*ādhāra*) for the impure sprouts of the world and the material cause (*upādāna*) for the pure ones, she is the foundation of the entire universe;

thus, the comparison to a "sprout" as her support is appropriate. This very power of support (*ādhāra-śakti*) has been explained at length in the *Āgamas* as being "crooked" (*kuṭilā*), presided over by the power of Śiva.
And so it has been said in the *Brahmāṇḍa-purāṇa*:

"The power (*śakti*) that is the support of the universe is Śiva’s own; she is the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*), the cause of the agitation of the world. She perpetually unfolds within all beings, within all principles (*tattva*), and within all seeds—that power is the sprout."

Having emerged from the milk ocean after revolving the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa), she remained there; then, having again burst through the egg, she stood like a sprout from a six-rooted plant. Beginning with the state of water (aptatva) and extending up to the end of the embryo (garbha), these [elements] have arisen.

The state of water is to be known as the seed-vessel; fire is the cause of its swelling; wind is its impeller; and for the sake of its function, space is fashioned, while the subtle elements (tanmātrāṇi) appear as sprouts, and the cavities are the sense organs.

And: "The ego-maker (*ahaṅkṛt*), situated in the center of all, possessing vitality and being the cause of growth—thus it perpetually nourishes the sprout, which is the cause of everything. Such is the Kuṇḍalinī power;
together with the five digits (*kalā*) beginning with Nivṛtti, she supports the entire universe, being without support herself.

In that same way, it sustains the people, beginning with Ananta and Īśvara, because it is the cause of the production of their bodies and so forth. And it is said: "The source of the Mantras is the supreme, eternal Kuṇḍalinī, which is insentient; she is the material cause of the bodies of the Vidyās, the Vidyeśvaras, and the Ātman-s.
Above Māyā is Mahāmāyā, the cause of all causes. Māyā, the possessor of Māyā (Māyin), and Māyā itself—these are traditionally known as the threefold Māyā. [Also] Īśvara and Sādākhya."

And because she is crooked and sustains the path, there is enjoyment (*bhoga*) within the power (*śakti*) on the pure upper path (*māyordhva-śuddhādhvan*). Its enjoyers are the Mantras, Mantreśvaras, and others who dwell in the worlds (*bhuvana*) of Vidyā and the Lords of Knowledge (*vidyeśvara*);
they have transformed into the forms of the means of attainment, the body, the senses, and their objects.

From that [kalā] comes the path of kalā (kalādhvan), and from that, the material cause of those [kalās] is the power Kuṇḍalinī. If it is asked how the production of kalās can occur without the intended fruit [of liberation], [the answer is]:

the production of the kalās is for the purpose of bestowing authority (adhikāra) upon those named Vidyā, Vidyeśvara, and so forth; otherwise, they would lack the authority regarding objects such as grace (anugraha). Just as Pradhāna is the material cause of Mahat and the rest, and Māyā is the cause of attachment (rāga) and the like, so too [is Kuṇḍalinī].

(17) Kuṇḍalinī is established as the cause of the kalās, such as *nivṛtti* and the rest. For those souls whose innate impurity has not yet been destroyed, whose knowledge is obscured by the karma of manifold births,
and for whom the process of emanation has been set in motion by the power of *māyā*, pleasure and pain arise due to their being enveloped by impurity.

Anticipating the objection that there is no experience [of the fruits of action], he states that there must be something which effects even a slight removal of the impure obscuration; thus, there is the establishment of the *kalā-tattva*, whose nature is agency characterized by the relationship between the fruit of action and its enjoyer, and the state of being an enjoyer. He says: "Cast forth" (*kṣiptā*)—because Ananteśvara is the agent with respect to the impure path (*aśuddhādhvan*), while Śambhu—that is, Śiva—is the agent with respect to the pure path (*śuddhādhvan*).

Since the subtle elements (*bhūta*), the *kalās*, the *rāgas*, and so forth, are measured by the *bindu* and the *mātrā*, therein— because it has been stated that "Śiva is the agent on the path of impure karma, while Ananta is the Lord on the pure [path]"— [one might ask]: "But since the *kalā* is insentient and agency is a property of the sentient, how can there be the production of the power of agency?"

He says that *kalā* has become manifest. It is characterized by the power of *niyoga* (determination), presided over by the power of concealment (*tirodhāna-śakti*) which is of the nature of Śiva’s will; for this very reason, it brings forth the power of agency (*kartṛ-śakti*).

This well-known *kalā* "measures" (hence its name *kalā*), meaning it manifests a limited capacity for action. It [operates] upon those whose consciousness is bound by the veil of ignorance, manifesting the beginningless impurity (*mala*) in a single location within that one [consciousness].
Just as, having been cast upon dry land and having dispelled [the darkness],

a lamp illuminates the various objects by removing the darkness from one region within a great darkness that covers everything; in the same way, the *kalās* illuminate by removing a portion of the impurity that covers everything.
The meaning is "it acts.

This has been stated in the *Mṛgendra*: "By that [power], which is like a lamp, the pure [power] then illuminates a single portion of the individual soul's consciousness, having pierced through the dense darkness"—thus, the power of agency previously existing within the self [is manifested].

He manifests— that is, he partially reveals— the power of agency (*kartṛśakti*), which is the nature of independent knowledge and action, existing within the self from the very beginning but obscured by impurity (*mala*). Having made that power oriented toward procreation, Ananteśvara created the *tattva* called *kalā*, which is the instrument that favors the power of agency.

Thus, in the *Mṛgendra*: "The agentive power of the individual soul (*aṇu*) is eternal and pervasive like the power of Īśvara; it does not shine forth with respect to objects because it is obscured by *tamas*. Following that, Hara, having agitated *māyā*, creates the principle called *kalā*, which is luminous (*taijasa*) and the supreme limb for [the soul's] activity. (12)

Knowledge residing within the self, having manifested itself, first impels men; then, the *vidyā* (intellect), endowed with the power of agency, brings about the cognition directed toward the objects of the senses located in the field of experience (*kṣetra*).

Furthermore, passion (*rāga*), which arises from the excellence of the [intellect] and follows after the Buddhist-like [momentary] destruction, generates a longing for enjoyment among men who possess clear vision, even though all objects have been known here.
This occurs through the instrumentality of that [intellect] which has become the material cause (*upādāna*) of the power of agency.

He states that there exists the principle of *vidyā* which serves as the instrument for the manifestation of the knowledge of objects. [Objection: But has it not been said that *kalā* alone is the illuminator of knowledge by piercing the impurity (*mala*) in a single location? How then is *vidyā* established? [Response: Even though it is established that *kalā* alone is the illuminator of knowledge, it is not capable of manifesting the entire range of objects without the most effective instrument (*sādhakatama*).

The meaning is that it is to be accepted as knowledge (*vidyā*). It is called *vidyā* because by means of it the entire range of objects (*viṣaya-jāta*) exists [for the subject] and is known. [It refers to] human beings who are already endowed with the power of agency (*kartṛ-śakti*), that is, accompanied by the power of agency existing from before;
[it refers to them] as being bound by nature, [and] as being internalized within the self due to being veiled by impurity (*mala*) residing in each individual self.

The meaning is that even though it exists, it remains as if non-existent; having manifested—that is, made manifest—the knowledge whose nature consists in the capacity for the thorough comprehension of objects, and having removed, by means of its own activity, the impurity-obscuration characterized by the incapacity of the power of knowledge to grasp objects, it illuminates the entire range of objects. This is the sense.

Thus, in the *Tattvaprakāśa*: "Having pierced through the veil by means of its own activity, this power called 'knowledge' reveals the multitude of objects; it is the supreme instrument of the Self. Now, since the Self is the substratum for the manifestation of consciousness, it is designated by the term "intellectual cognition" (*buddhibodha*);
therefore, in the apprehension of objects, the intellect and so forth alone exist as the instruments.

Anticipating the objection that knowledge (*vidyā*) is established as something distinct from that [ignorance], he states: first, regarding ignorance, the intellect (*buddhi*) is that which manifests the external objects through the senses conjoined with the mind, thereby manifesting the power of cognition of the self;

thus, since the objects of knowledge and the intellect are different, knowledge is established as distinct from the intellect. This is expressed by the term "Lord of the Senses" (*akṣeśa*); for if knowledge is the cause of the awakening of the intellect, it is said to be distinct from that [intellect].

"Within the range of the senses" (*akṣaga*) means that which has come within the scope of the senses (*akṣa*). "The lord of the senses" (*akṣāṇām īśaḥ*) refers to the mind (*manas*), [meaning] that which is connected to the mind—that is, that which is in close proximity to the mind—belonging to those [objects] that have entered the range of the senses (*akṣāṇām*), namely the sense-faculties (*jñānendriya*) and the action-faculties (*karmendriya*). "Range" (*gocara*) refers to their respective objects.

External objects cause the intellect (*buddhi*)—which, through its connection with the mind (*manas*), possesses the sense organs capable of grasping objects—to grasp them; that is, it becomes the grasper. Thus, in the *Mṛgendra* [Tantra]... (l6)

"Having accepted as the object of the instrument employed by the person those objects within the range of the senses, which are impelled by the atomic power of consciousness manifested through knowledge, [the mind] is 'knowledge'; other than that is 'ignorance'.

This is the intended meaning here: just as the instrument consisting of the eyes and so forth is the grasper of form and other objects when the mind stands as its manifester (*vyañjaka*), what further need is there for another manifester called "intellect" (*buddhi*)?
The purpose [of this] is that the accomplishment of various effects occurs through the sense organs presided over by the mind alone.

This being so, just as it is established that there exists a cognition (*buddhi*) which grasps external objects, it follows by connection that there likewise exists a *vidyā* which grasps that cognition. Even though such a reality of *vidyā* exists, [one acts] through a cognition that has become a source of misfortune.

(... ) He asks: what is the purpose? He says: "Internal" (*āntarī*). Knowledge (*vidyā*) is internal because it is the primary instrument for the manifestation of the Self's cognition; whereas the intellect (*buddhi*) and so forth are external. Thus, having set aside the notion that [knowledge] is the object of experience (*bhogyā*) consisting of pleasure and the like—which would be the case when explaining [the verse] as "then this knowledge would be the instrument, but the intellect would be the instrument for the grasping of objects"—(l2) [it follows that... (l3).
