The Blessed One Aghoraśivācārya has explained that since the intellect (*buddhi*) is incapable of apprehending the Self—which has attained the status of being the object to be grasped—as an instrument, therefore, in order to grasp it, *vidyā* serves as the instrument; thus, the accomplishment of *vidyā* is established. By means of the power of knowledge manifested through *vidyā*, even for those selves who have perceived their objects, regarding the objects of enjoyment...

Because there is no activity in the absence of desire, he states that there exists a state of passion (*rāgatattva*) which generates that desire. Regarding the phrase "from the Buddhist" (*bauddhāt*): according to the view of some, [this passion] arises from the qualities (*guṇa*) of the Buddhist—that is, from the qualities pertaining to sense objects—and is distinct from other elemental passions; it is born from the quality associated with the intellect (*buddhi*), due to dispassion (*vairāgya*). Now...

The view of others is that [the attachment] arises from the quality of the relationship with an object of Brahman, such as honey, sandalwood, or butter; in order to refute that, it is stated [in the verse] "other than the qualities derived from the objects of the Buddha" (*bauddhādvaiṣayikācca guṇataḥ aparaḥ*). Furthermore, if it is accepted that passion consists of the intellect (*buddhi*) characterized by detachment (*vairāgya*), then [it follows that] the intellect—(l8)

Since it has been stated that [the intellect] is, in brief, the object of enjoyment because it takes on the form of objects and consists of pleasure and so forth, and because the intellect— having transformed itself into the form of an object—

is of the nature of the enjoyed, it lacks the capacity to generate a desire for what is enjoyed. Therefore, there must be something else, namely passion (*rāga*), which is the cause of desire, which pertains to the enjoyer, and which produces the act of enjoying for those who enjoy.

If passion were established as something other than a quality of the intellect (*buddhi*), then, if passion were indeed a quality of the object, it would follow that everyone would possess passion merely through the proximity of external objects such as saffron, sandalwood, and women; thus, no one would ever be free from passion. Therefore, [passion is not a quality of the object].

It follows that there would be a defect in the nature [of the object]. Thus, it is established that the passion residing in the enjoyer (*bhoktṛ*) which generates desire is distinct from the quality of the object; it is a passion directed toward a specific object of enjoyment, such as deer-flesh and the like. Now, one might argue: "Let passion in the form of a deluder reside in *māyā* itself—what is the need for another passion here? To this it is said: *Māyā* does not possess the power to delude directly, but rather through its effects; therefore, there is no fault.

In this regard, within our own Śaiva Siddhānta, passion (*rāga*) is of such a nature that it is capable of producing [reactions] toward objects even while they exist. When one is engaged in enjoyment (*bhoga*), which proceeds in the form of pleasure, pain, and so forth—characterized by a feeling attached to the object of enjoyment—one thinks, "I am happy," "I am suffering," or "I am miserable. Regarding this, it has been said for those who possess clear vision through knowledge (*vidyā*): "The experience of enjoyment for a person is characterized by pleasure, pain, and the like."

For those humans whose knowledge has been rendered like a wooden board (*rkataṭī*) by their connection with the blazing [world], it is indeed passion that causes them to be colored; but not so for the stainless Lords of Knowledge (*vidyeśvara*s), who have realized all objects and whose vision is directed toward all external things such as sandalwood paste and the like.

It leads [the soul] toward the knowledge of what is false; it brings [it] forth—this is the function of the reality of passion (*rāga*). Thus, in the venerable *Mṛgendra*: "One whose power of vision has been manifested by that [passion], who has seen the object, and who is pervaded and perfumed by it, does not abandon that passion; therefore the Lord created it. Being colored by that [passion], even while touching an impure object of enjoyment, he takes it up; yet, while enjoying it, he does not fall into aversion."

Time (*kāla*), which discerns the past and the present, arose in the beginning from the power (*śakti*) of the Lord of the three worlds; it quickly casts down the person (*pums*) through the calculation of consciousness and the like. Furthermore, destiny (*niyati*)—known as the regulator of agriculture and other such activities—is the command of the Lord for men who are subject to His authority, ensuring they experience the fruits of their own accumulated karma.

By its power, it stands as the restrainer of Śambhu. The production of bodies—beginning with the stages of the embryo, the drop, the bubble, and so forth, through childhood, youth, and the rest—occurs solely by the force of *kāla* (time).

Thus, [the principle of] *kalā* exists even prior to *vidyā*, *rāga*, and the others. [Objection: If *kalā* indeed precedes *kāla* and the other principles, then why is it not mentioned immediately after *māyā*, rather than after *rāga*?

In this regard, the meaning is as follows: since the selves (*ātman*) are indeed uninterrupted, it is for the purpose of making known that time is conceived only with respect to those [selves] who possess the equal sensations produced by the three sheaths (*kañcuka*), beginning with *kalā*, as previously described; therefore, it is logical that Time (*kāla*) is mentioned immediately after Passion (*rāga*).

Likewise, in the *Tattvaprakāśa*, it is stated: "She, consisting of various powers, first generates the *tattva* of Time (*kāla*) alone. In the commentary on that work by the venerable Aghoraśivācārya, he says: "Now, in the *Śrīmataṅga* and other texts, its recitation is heard immediately after *kalā*, *vidyā*, and *rāga*. This is true; however, by this [statement], the sequence of their respective engagement with those [powers] has been shown for this very [tattva of time]. Here...

Thus, it has been explained that there is no contradiction in [the view that] this is the order of emanation (*sṛṣṭikrama*). According to the opinion of some, time is eternal because the insentient time—which is presided over by the power (*śakti*) of the Lord, the Supreme God—cannot function without being presided over by a conscious being. This is their position. (p. 40b, l. 1)

To refute this [position], he says: "Transformed by the divisions of past, present, and future. "Past" (*bhūta*) refers to elapsed time; "present" (*bhavat*) refers to current time; and "future" (*vibhāvin*) refers to coming time.
Thus, the meaning is that if time were sentient, it would be subject to transformation—that is, it would undergo change—by way of these three forms such as the past and so forth.
Since it would be manifold due to its threefold nature as past and so on, its impermanence would be established, like that of a jar or similar objects. This is the intended sense regarding time.

He states what the effect of time (*kāla*), acting as the agent in the manner previously described, is: (l3) "Because of the reckoning of the cognition of rapid opposition, 'rapid' refers to a swift period of time, such as remaining for a *muhūrta* or remaining for a *prahara*, and so forth; 'prolonged' refers to a long period of time, such as remaining for one day or staying for two days, and so forth. By the word "and so forth" (l4), [other durations are included].

Time, beginning with the year, arises from the reckoning—that is, the calculation—of their awakening and knowledge. Through this reckoning, by means of durations such as *truṭi* and *lava*, there occurs the sequence of the embryo (*kalala-lava-budbuda*), childhood, youth, and so forth.

When that [development] is to be accomplished, the connection of the person (*pums*) with a body follows; for one whose nature is bound by impurity (*mala*), it "throws," "projects," or "subjugates" him—this is the meaning.
And it has been said that the object of cognitions such as "moment" (*truṭi*) is time,

which arises from *māyā*. By the power of the fruits of karma previously acquired by the selves, whatever pleasure, pain, and so forth is to be experienced at whatever age, at whatever time, and in whatever place— [it is time that determines this].

In that very context, he states that there exists a reality called *niyati* (destiny), which ensures that one will be fed neither less nor more. Regarding the phrase "at the time of eating" (*bhuktau*), this means that at the initial stage, prior to [the present], when there is the absence of *niyati* regarding the enjoyment— the consumption of the fruits of pleasure and pain— of those actions acquired by oneself through one's own activities (actions whose nature is merit and demerit performed by oneself), then others might even enjoy the fruits of actions acquired by someone else.
He speaks by way of a simile:
just as the command (*ājñā*) of kings is the very power called "regulator" (*niyāmika*) for men— that is, for human beings— over the fruits produced from agricultural work and the like,
by virtue of its capacity known as "restraining" (*niyamana*), so too is the command that brings all people under control [the regulator].

The sense is that in the absence of royal policy (*rājanīya*), enemies carry off the fruits produced by agricultural and other such labors; just as the command of kings makes the fruits produced by various actions belong to their respective performers, so too does this power of necessity (*niyati-śakti*) of Śambhu, which consists of the nature of constraint, remain. The word "even" (*api*) is used to indicate that action itself lacks the capacity to regulate [the result], [since it is regulated] merely by the production of its fruit.
[Objection: Since its purpose has been fulfilled, does not the capacity of karma to produce a fruit also constitute its regulating power? [Response:

If that is so, then just as karma becomes capable of accomplishing the human goal when it operates together with the body, senses, and so forth—which are themselves engaged in their respective functions for the sake of producing the fruit—so too [does it operate] in the accomplishment of its own effect.

There is no fault in [the view] that karma is the regulator [of experience] while depending upon the principle of necessity (*niyati*), for otherwise there would be the undesirable consequence of the non-existence of all principles (*tattva*).

As it is said in the *Mṛgendra*: "Now, since that [power] accomplishes the goals of man while depending on the body and so forth, let it therefore be the regulator of karma while depending on necessity. (14)

When the self is here conjoined with these five [elements] and endowed with the state of being an enjoyer, it attains the condition of a person (*puruṣatva*) at the end of reality; through the removal of the impurity consisting of the *piṇḍa*, it becomes purified. First, the state of being an enjoyer is the object of activity for the self that has previously entered [into bondage], for the sake of its experience. (Section Heading: The Self with the Five)

Prakṛti is the substratum for the transformations such as the *guṇas* and the means for their realization. It is said [in verse 2]: "The *puruṣa-tattva* is so designated because of the union with the state of manhood (*puṃstva*) of the individual soul (*aṇu*), which is augmented by the five categories beginning with *kalā*, produced from *māyā*—which is stirred by the infinite [power]—and through its connection with the state of being a person.
Here, in this Śaiva Siddhānta, when—at which time—by these five previously mentioned [categories], namely *kalā*, *vidyā*, *rāga*, *kāla*, and *niyati*...
At that very time, [the soul] was bound— by Anantanātha, it is implied— and for that very reason,

the self became endowed with the state of being an enjoyer (*bhoktṛtva*), accompanied by the condition of being an enjoyer. Because of the impurity called *puṃstva*— which is precisely the conjunction with the five principles beginning with *kalā* and ending with *niyati*—
[the soul undergoes] initiation for the sake of purification from that impurity.

For the purpose of purification, by means of counting—through the exposition that from the end of one principle (*tatva*) to the middle of the next there are twenty-five principles, [making] the Puruṣa one single principle—he attains the state of being the Puruṣa-principle, known as the *tatpuruṣa*-principle. (L5) The word "iti" is employed as a negation in order to make known that, in the ultimate sense, there is an absence of a principle for the Self; for this very reason, the Puruṣa-principle possesses the status of being the support of the worlds (*bhuvana*).

"It is not tenable" refers to the persistence of the worlds taught under the *puruṣatattva* within the *rāgatattva*. In this verse, by virtue of the semantic force established by the word "when" (*yadā*), the indication is that the soul's state as a male (*puṃstva*) occurs precisely when it is bound by *kalā* and the other [principles]; thus, it is from the time of its bondage—

It has been made known that in the prior time, masculinity (*puṃstva*) does not exist; for this very reason, it has been made known that masculinity belongs to the *sakala* alone, and not to the *vijñānākala* or *pralayākala*.

Thus it was stated [in the verse]: "From that very [state], masculinity arose as the basis for the cognition of a person" (*puṃpratyayanibandhana*). On the occasion of explaining this verse, the venerable Nārāyaṇakaṇṭha stated that "the basis for the cognition of a person" means the cause for the perception of a person (*puṃpratītihetuḥ*).

By this, the distinction of the *rudrāṇu* residing within the womb of Māyā from those inhabitants of the worlds has been stated; it has been explained according to the previously mentioned method [of the categories] beginning with *kalā*, on the grounds that [the former] lacks the cognition of being a person (*puṃpratyaya*).

Because of being bound, the Self attains the state of being an enjoyer; thus he says that there exists a reality such as *prakṛti* for the sake of enjoyment. Regarding the phrase "the state of being an enjoyer": first, for the Self who has entered [into bondage] by means of the five preceding principles beginning with *kalā*, there is an initial engagement with an object of effort—that is, the state of being an enjoyer becomes the object of its exertion. The sense is that from the very binding by *kalā* and the other principles, the activity of the Self toward the state of being an enjoyer arises first. Regarding the state of being an enjoyer...
For the sake of the experience of the active self— meaning for the purpose of experiencing pleasure and so forth—

*prakṛti* is the foundational cause (*āśrayakāraṇa*) of the principles that serve as the means of experience, namely the transformations such as the *guṇas* and other categories, which are the effects of the *guṇa-tattva* and so on.
The meaning is that *prakṛti* knows pleasure and so forth through the collection of principles produced by *prakṛti*, beginning with the *guṇas* and *buddhi*.

Thus, in the *Kiraṇa*: "From Śiva, through the *samaya* [tradition], there is the connection of that impure [soul] with *kalā*. His capacity being empowered by that [kalā], and his range of experience made manifest by *vidyā*, *rāga* also [functions] through the act of coloring [the soul].

And *pradhāna*, in the form of the *guṇas*, along with the instruments such as the intellect (*buddhi*), [function] because of the connection [with the soul]; thus the bound soul (*paśu*) perceives. Then, due to the conjunction with *niyati*, he is constrained even regarding what has been acquired by himself."
Even time would become time [only] through association with that [reality]. ||15||

The manifestation of lightness and so forth from *sattva* and the other [guṇas], as well as support, exclusion, weightiness, and restriction—these are the functions (*vṛtti*) of the secondary (*gauṇa*) [nature] when mixed with the animal [element]. (l7) That increase of the person (*puruṣa*), produced by the instruments of the void (*khāti*), is comprehensive, capable of being experienced, luminous, determinative regarding the object, accompanied by conviction, and directed toward existence.
[The author] states the effect of the principle of primordial nature (*prakṛti-tattva*): "from *sattva* and the others," etc. (l8)

The manifestation of the qualities of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas* as lightness—that is, their manifestation in a subtle form through lightness—and their intermingling: just as gold exists in the form of functional power (*kriyāśakti*) as ornaments such as bracelets and crowns, so too the principle of primordial nature (*prakṛti-tattva*), existing in the form of power (*śaktyātman*), becomes the generator of its own effect, which is the *guṇa*. This is the meaning. Now, [an objection]: [Note: The provided text ends abruptly with "nanu" (now/if), indicating the beginning of an objection or a transition to a new point.]

It should be understood that the word *atha* is employed as a statement of doubt (*śaṅkā*) for the purpose of refuting the view of those who hold that the qualities (*guṇa*), such as *sattva* and the rest, are themselves the primordial nature (*prakṛti*). For indeed, since the qualities are non-conscious (*acetana*) and manifold, they must—like jars and other objects—exist in a state of division by way of being caused; therefore, the primordial nature must be distinct from the qualities of *sattva* and the rest.

Just as it is established that the constituent parts of effects such as jars must necessarily have a division within their substrate consisting of earth, so too the constituent parts of the *guṇas*—sattva and the rest—must necessarily have a division within some substrate. Thus, he states that the *prakṛti*-principle itself stands as the substrate: "It is the supporter of sattva and the rest; it also stands as the support."

He states the function of the *guṇas* and *tattvas*: "Exclusion" (*vyāvṛtti*) [is the function]. (l5) "Vr" means covering; "vi" means gone away; thus, *vyāvṛtti* is the removal of covering, which is illumination. This is the function of *sattva*. "Gau" means weight; "gurutā" means heaviness, which is activity. This is the function of *rajas*, for activity is the heaviness of [the state of] being active. Thus it is secondary (*gauṇa*). (l6)

By means of its application (*prayoga*), in the sense of denoting activity (*vyāpāra*), it is said that "the qualities are to be honored" (*gauravyāḥ*). It is well known from worldly usage and speech that the activity of the Great One (*mahābhāra*) proceeds in the form of a burden;

thus, the rule (*niyama*) is regulated. "Rule" (*niyama*) means that which is restrained or brought to cessation; it is a contraction, the function of darkness (*tamas*). The particle *ca* has the purpose of collecting [qualities] such as stability (*sthairya*) not explicitly mentioned. For this very reason, [there is] illumination (*prakāśa*)—

The three functions (*vṛtti*), consisting of the restriction of activity, have been described as belonging to *sattva* and the other qualities (*rajas* and *tamas*) respectively. However, there are other functions as well; as it is stated in the venerable *Mataṅga*: "Stability, fortitude, constancy, dexterity, straightforwardness, and likewise lightness... (p. 43a, l. 1).

Contentment, straightforwardness, purity, perseverance, as well as mindfulness, devotion to satisfaction, forbearance, compassion, generosity, constant mercy, and eagerness— these are declared to be the functions of *sattva*. Cruelty, intoxication, energy accompanied by pride,
stubbornness, mercilessness, divisiveness, and hypocrisy— these are to be understood as the functions of *rajas* in this scripture of the Supreme Lord.

Discontent, dullness, dejection, malice, constant harshness toward the guru, sleep, sloth, intoxication, laziness, suppression, and that which is delusion—these are known as the functions of *tamas*. It is established that these exist in all births. This is the secondary *guṇa-tattva*, which is mixed and combined with the bondage of the bound soul (*paśu*).

The reality of the qualities such as *sattva* and so forth exists pervasively within the self by means of the subtle body; it should be understood that, because of the particle *ca* used for the purpose of an unstated conjunction, this [nature] is secondary (*gauṇa*) and is endowed with the capacity to produce pleasure, pain, and delusion.

Likewise, in the *Tattvaprakāśa*, it is stated: "From the unmanifest (*avyakta*), the principle of the qualities (*guṇatattva*) arises, which consists here of the forms of manifestation, activity, and restriction—namely *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*, as well as pleasure, pain, and delusion.

This describes the effect of the principle of intellect (*buddhitattva*). Regarding the use of the word "that" (*tat*) in the term "intellect" (*buddhi*), the use of the relative pronoun "which" (*yat*) should be understood here: "the intellect which [belongs] to the person (*puruṣa*) by means of the *kalā*s and so forth."
Regarding the phrase "of the bound self by means of the instruments such as space" (l7):

"space and so forth" refers to ether and the other elements; "instruments" refers to the organs of perception. The intention is this: the intellect (*buddhi*), accompanied by these means, is the "comprehender," meaning it is fully capable of producing the cognition of objects. (p43b, l1)

The self is conjoined with the intellect (*buddhi*), the intellect with the senses, and the senses with their objects; thus, the production of knowledge occurs. The meaning is that the self, accompanied by the intellect and the rest, grasps the cognition of objects. For this very reason, the self is said to be the "appropriator" (*saṃgrāhikā*) of the cognition of objects through the intellect. If it is only the objects that are the things to be enjoyed (*bhogya*), how can the self be called the "enjoyer" (*bhoktṛ*)? [This refers to] regarding the objects.

Because it possesses the form of a reflection, the intellect (*buddhi*) has the nature of being an object of experience; thus it is called the "experiencer of objects" (*bhogyakā*). Regarding the sense-objects (*viṣaya*), the "shining ones" (*bhāsvanti*) are the eyes and other organs (*cakṣurādīndriyāṇi*), which are "radiant" (*nibhāni*) because they manifest due to their faultlessness, and which "determine" (*adhyavasāyikā*) the shining substances.

By means of the instruments of perception such as the eyes, the intellect (*buddhi*) is established through a determinative cognition (*adhyavasāya*) consisting of the certainty: "This is indeed silver, not mother-of-pearl. The word "and" (*ca*) serves to include unmentioned qualities such as *sattva*. By this, it is shown that [the intellect] consists of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*; as it is stated in the *Tattvaprakāśa*: "The intellect, due to its threefold nature of the *guṇas*, takes the form of the determination of objects; and here, she (the intellect) is likewise [of that nature]."

The threefold [nature] according to its qualities (*guṇa*) follows from previous karma; thus, the eightfold nature of existence consists of the qualities of the intellect (*buddhi*) known as dharma, knowledge, dispassion, and sovereignty—these are called the states of the *sāttvika* being—and likewise adharma, ignorance, ... [and so forth].

The absence of dispassion and the absence of mastery are states characterized by *tamas*. The absence of dispassion is a state characterized by *rajas*. Thus, these eight states—dharma and the rest—exist within the intellect (*buddhi*) in the form of latent impressions (*vāsanā*).

They are called "states" (*bhāva*) because they "manifest" (*bhāvayanti*) or reveal the subtle body (*liṅga*), which is the mark of the Self. For it has been said: "Since they manifest the subtle body, they are known as 'states' (*bhāva*)."

The meaning is as follows: those very factors, such as dharma and the rest, which have arisen together with the fifty conditions beginning with the divine (*divya*) and the perfected (*siddhi*), having reached a state of excellence, assume a coarse form and enter into the state of being objects of experience; thus they are called "conditions" (*pratyaya*).

As it has been said: "They cause the *kṣetrajña* to perceive; therefore they are known as *pratyayas*. Thus, there are eight *siddhis*, nine *tuṣṭis*, twenty-eight *śaktis*, and five varieties of the errors of the intellect (*buddhiviparyaya*).
In this way, there are fifty *pratyayas*; their names and characteristics are to be understood from the *Mataṅgapārameśvara* and other such works. Such is the nature of that intellect (*buddhi*).
Likewise, in the *Mṛgendra*, [it is said]:

"Thereafter, the principle of intellect (*buddhitattva*), characterized by the cognition of various objects, is the supreme object of experience for the self, refined by the meanings to be explained hereafter. (16) From it, the vital breaths (*marutaḥ*) residing in the body of men move; through their exertion, the creative power (*kṛtiḥ*), which consists of the grasping of *sattva* and the other qualities, produces indeed the determination (*vyavasāya*) of the sense organs.

The mind (*manas*), which is characterized by desire, is the instrument for engagement with sense objects; it is mobile, swift, and constantly forms volitions that produce attention. [The author] now describes the threefold function of the principle of egoity (*ahaṅkāratattva*) as agitation, pride, and the life-force (*jīvana*).

"They act" refers to the subject (*grāhaka*) which consists of the conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*) "I am the subject. By this, pride (*garva*) is indicated; for the "I" is distinct from the effects of the intellect (*buddhi*), whose nature consists of the reflective awareness of the object (*grāhya*). The meaning is that *ahaṅkāra* is pride, being the cause of the reflective awareness of the subject, as in "I know the cloth," and so forth, due to the intensity (*samrambha*) present in such a subject.

What is called *samrambha* (impulse) consists of egoity (*ahaṅkārika*) and has the nature of effort (*prayatnātmaka*). As it has been said, "Impulse is a function of the ego," that impulse arises through the power of action directed toward objects such as jars, which is based upon the causal power residing in those very jars and other things; for this reason, [it is so].

The meaning is that it has been stated, "Perform activity itself through exertion," because activity is preceded by effort (*prayatna*). This very exertion is said to be of the nature of life, since it is the cause for the movement of the internal wind consisting of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and so forth; this is expressed by the words beginning with "since" (*yataḥ*), [meaning] perform the impelling and drawing in of the wind without [external] effort.

Because it has been stated thus: from the exertion consisting of effort on the part of persons—that is, of the selves—the vital airs (*marut*) residing within the bodies, which have the body as their abode, [arise];
these are known by the names prāṇa, apāna, udāna, vyāna, and samāna.

The five winds (pañcavāyavaḥ) move about and perform their respective functions. Although the five winds, beginning with *prāṇa*, are mentioned by distinct names due to their individual functions, these names are not ultimate (*pāramārthika*), because there is no difference in their nature as wind. Thus it is said in the *Mṛgendra*: "But those [winds], *prāṇa*, *apāna*, and so forth, are ninefold due to the diversity of their functions."

By "praised" (*stuta*), what are the functions of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and so forth being referred to? Among those, the fourfold functions of the *prāṇa* are stated primarily. (p45a, l1) One function is the upward movement of the wind residing in the body as far as the "twelve-finger space" (*dvādaśānta*) outside the body; another is life itself, for when the *prāṇa* exists in the world, the body [remains]. (l2)

It is said that "it lives" because the nature of the intellect (*buddhi*), when examined, consists of fourfold functions: the act of deliberation (*vimarśa*), the instrument of impulsion, and the two instruments of strength. Thus, in the *Mṛgendra-tantra* it is stated: "That which is called 'life' (*jīvana*) is the application of its functional states (*vṛtti*). That which is the intellect (*mati*) of men, which searches for objects as if through delusion—that [intellect], while performing [this function], is called 'vital breath' (*prāṇa*), or rather, 'vital breath' [is so named] due to its connection with life."
The function of *apāna*, however,

is the downward conveyance of feces, urine, and semen— which arise immediately after the state of digestion of the food and water that have been eaten and drunk by the digestive fire (*jāṭharāgni*). This has been stated accordingly.

One who performs the removal (*apanayana*) of what has been eaten, drunk, excrement, urine, and semen is not excluded from the term "prāṇa" by those who perceive the truth; however, the function of *samāna* is the equal distribution throughout the body of the essence of the food and drink that has been consumed. As it has been said: "Because it performs the equal distribution of food and drink on all sides, it is called *samāna*."
The function of vyāna, however, is the emaciation of the body by way of causing an imbalance in food, drink, and so forth, which leads to the provocation of diseases.
Likewise, in the Śrī Kālottara: "Vyāna also pervades the limbs; vyāna..."

Because it causes the provocation of diseases and brings about the destruction of pleasure through its pervasion, it is called *vyāna*. As for the function of *udāna*, it has been stated that it is the process by which the speaker, preceded by the effort of the desire to speak (*vivakṣā*), differentiates the sound—which is of the nature of a quality—within the space inside the body across various locations such as the throat and so forth, and thereby effects the production of phonemes (*varṇa*) together with the organ of speech (*vāgindriya*). And it is said: [l. 2]

That [vital air] by which, preceded by the intention to speak and effort, the sound possessing the quality of the space within the chest is made into articulate phonemes (varṇa) with the assistance of the organ of speech is called *udāna* in this body; thus it is stated elsewhere as well: "The sound (*nāda*) originating from ether and air, emerging from the body, reaches the mouth; being differentiated in various locations, it attains the state of phonemes (*varṇa*), and that which is [thus produced] is 'sound' (*śabda*)."

Likewise, in the *Kālottara*: "The wind named Udāna causes the lower lip, mouth, eyes, and limbs to quiver; it agitates the vital points (*marmāṇi*). By the word "beginning with *sattva*" (*satvādi*), it refers to those whose nature consists of the qualities of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*; by the word "etc.
(*ādi*), it includes the *taijasa*, *vaikṛta*, *bhauta*, and so forth.

Egoity (*ahaṅkṛti*) is apprehended as having a threefold form through its three types of effects previously mentioned—pride and so forth; thus, the existence of egoity (*ahaṅkāra*) is established. [Now] he states the effect of the mind (*manas*):

"Of the senses" (*akṣāṇām*). It is the instrument for the activity—which consists of the operation of engaging—in the objects such as sound and so forth, of the ten external sense organs, which are the means of experience for the experiencer, the self (*ātman*).

The term *sādhakatama* means that even when there is contact between the self (*ātman*), the sense organ (*indriya*), and the object (*artha*), the external sense organs do not function toward their objects without the superintendence (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of the mind (*manas*) by the self; this refers to a thing whose nature is sweet, fragrant, and soft.

When a soft sound is being savored, the mind—due to its swift movement together with the sense faculties that grasp those respective objects—possesses the capacity to produce five cognitions simultaneously through subtle actions that are imperceptible, like the piercing of a hundred lotus petals; thus he says: "It has the nature of moving swiftly among objects that shift rapidly."

Likewise, as stated in the *Mṛgendra*: "The mind is the initiator of the gods, moving swiftly, and characterized by volition. When the mind is moved swiftly and simultaneously toward various sense-faculties, then there is cognition of the objects of those respective faculties; when it is not moved swiftly, then there is cognition of only a single faculty and no other, as in the case of the experience of form.

At any given time, there is no simultaneous experience of touch or taste; rather, that cognition arises sequentially due to the non-simultaneity of the senses and their engagement in succession. Nevertheless, it appears as if occurring simultaneously because of its rapid movement, as it has been said:
"I know the other," and because of such statements. Thus, the mind, whose nature is desire, is always and at all times the producer of focused attention (*avadhāna*).

Attention is one-pointedness; it performs—that is, produces—the mental volition (*saṅkalpa*) which is its generator. What is it that generates attention for the mind? Because its function consists of volition, this [mind] is distinct from both the intellect (*buddhi*) and the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*).

The intellect (*buddhi*) and the ego (*ahaṅkāra*), because they consist of action and lack the nature of cognition, are the causes for the activity of the grasped and the grasper; thus is the proof of the mind (*manas*). And that mind is said in the venerable *Mataṅga* to have a twofold function through internal mental action and through the operation of presiding over the external senses: "That mind has a twofold function; it is the means for the experiencer and the experience. Externally..."

Since it always acts as the instrument for the sense organs through its own appropriate function, and because it repeatedly effects the capacity of the senses by means of a volition residing within itself, that which exists internally is therefore called the internal organ, the mind (*manas*).
Intellect (*buddhi*) and ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*) are also internal organs.
Likewise, in the *Tattvasaṃgraha* it is stated: "The internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) is threefold, to be designated as mind (*citta*), ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*), and intellect (*buddhi*). (17)

The group of five beginning with the ear—the members of the physical body—perform their function for the sake of the mind by means of the power of following the state of being an agent, through the cognition of their respective objects: sound, touch, form, and so forth. The group beginning with speech, situated within the body, performs its own specific task—speech, grasping, and so on—which is attained by the mind, due to the influence of the transformation of prior karma.

It bestows a fivefold [nature] upon the human being. Now, desiring to explain the operation of the ten external organs, he first states the operation of the five organs of cognition (*jñānendriya*). "The first is hearing" (*śrotrādyam*): this is a component of the body (*vigraha*), meaning it is the primary limb of the body, a constituent part. It is "endowed with the mind" (*samanaska*), which means it is conjoined with the mind as a property of consciousness. This group consists of five.

Regarding the sense-objects of hearing and so forth—namely those known as the ear, skin, eye, tongue, and nose—it is not the case that the cavity of the ear or other such locations possesses the capacity to apprehend sound and the rest; rather, he states that this is the power of the sense-organ (*indriya*) which, acting as the agent, resides therein. (L6) "By the force of following the state of being the agent" means by the force of following the mere presence of the sense-organ existing as the agent in the apprehension of sound and so forth.
Because of the capacity for following [the object],

it is observed that in cases such as deafness, where there is an absence of sensory power, there is an absence of the apprehension of sound and so forth; for one's own ears and other senses have their respective objects— namely, sound, touch, form, and so on—
as their sequential objects of perception, such as sound (*ninada*).

Sound has the nature of being touched and so forth; by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), light and the like are included, while by the word "and so forth" [in the second instance], taste and smell are grasped. Does the self not perform the cognitions—that is, the acts of apprehension—of these? It produces the cognition of objects, because the ears and other senses are respectively engaged in the apprehension of sound and the rest, and because there is an absence of apprehension of other forms such as color. Thus, the specific engagement with each respective object is established.

Likewise, in the *Tattvaprakāśa*, the function (*vyāpāra*) of speech and the other [organs] is declared to be their sequential grasping. Thus, he describes the function of the organs of action (*karmendriya*) with the words "beginning with speech" (*vāgādyam*). This group of five, beginning with speech—namely speech, hand, foot, and so on—is situated in the body (*dehasaṃstha*), existing within the physical frame, and is attained by the mind (*cittāpta*), being conjoined with the internal organ (*manas*). It is fivefold (*pañcavidha*).

The [organs] called anus and genitals, by virtue of the reversal of previous karma— that is, by virtue of the inversion of merit and demerit acquired in a prior birth— are observed to lack speech and movement, as in the case of the mute and the lame due to the power of sinful karma.

Their respective objects (*viṣaya*), which are to be grasped in their own order, are speech, grasping, movement, excretion, and sexual pleasure, belonging respectively to their own [faculties] such as speech and so forth.
Speech is addressing; "taking" means the act of seizing.

Having first accepted that which is joined with going and so forth by means of the preceding word, [the senses] indeed perform—that is, accomplish—their own respective functions within their own domains. In this context, the repetition of the word *sva* (own/self) is for the sake of those who understand the meaning of words (*vāgvidinām*).

It should be understood that this was stated for the purpose of refuting the position that the organs of action do not exist; otherwise, since the word "own" (*sva*) was already used in the phrase "one's own objects such as speech and grasping," the repetition of the word "own" would be redundant. This is because it is observed that actions are performed by all the instruments, such as speech and so forth; therefore, the existence of the organs of action is established. If this is so, then [the movement of] the creeper-like eyebrows—
Since throbbing and so forth are actions, one might argue that other instruments must be postulated for them,

which would lead to the undesirable consequence of an infinite number of organs of action; however, this is not the case, because the organs of action are admitted to pervade the entire body due to their functioning both at a distance and in close proximity.

The activity of the eyebrows, eyes, and so forth belongs to the powers of their respective sense organs, not because of a specific presiding presence in those locations; thus it is said: "Know that [the range] of the gods is remote, while that of those whose nature is action is near. (18) That which remains as the subtle element (*tanmātra*), joined with one additional quality such as sound and so on, is called by its previous name preceded by 'ra' (e.g., *ākāśa*, etc.), and it is fivefold as the substratum of the elements (*bhūta*). Among these, the element is earth (*dharā*).

The water and other elements, each possessing five qualities, are deficient [in their respective subsequent qualities] by one; these constitute the activities of the array of the five elements known as Earth and the Planets. Of sound, touch, form, taste, and smell, which are the causes of space and the other elements, there is for each a subtle element consisting of sound alone.

The subtle element of sound (*śabda-tanmātra*) is endowed with the quality of sound; the subtle element of touch (*sparśa-tanmātra*) is endowed with the qualities of subtle sound and touch; the subtle element of form (*rūpa-tanmātra*) is endowed with the qualities of subtle sound, touch, and form; the subtle element of taste (*rasa-tanmātra*) is endowed with the qualities of subtle sound, touch, form, and taste; and the subtle element of smell (*gandha-tanmātra*) is endowed with the qualities of subtle sound, touch, form, taste, and smell. Thus, these subtle forms are endowed with qualities increasing by one in each successive stage.

He states that the five subtle elements (*tanmātra*) are established as the causes of the five gross elements: "The *tanmātra* consists of sound and so forth, each with one additional [quality]. Here, "sound and so forth" refers to sound, touch, form, taste, and smell;
"each with one additional" means [the subsequent element possesses] that same [quality] plus one more.

The meaning is that it is endowed with qualities (*guṇa*) increasing by one at a time—that is, possessed of one, two, three, four, or five [qualities]. For example, sound has [qualities such as] "pot" or "jar"; touch has [qualities such as] "cold" or "hot"; form has [qualities such as] "white" and so forth; taste has [qualities such as] "sweet" and so forth;
smell is of six kinds, namely "fragrant" and "unfragrant. The word *hi* indicates that although it is thus endowed and accompanied by such qualities, nevertheless (*tathāpi*).

The meaning is that although it is endowed with subtle elemental qualities (*sūkṣmabhūtaguṇa*), it remains possessed of the remaining qualities—that is, the qualities such as sound (*śabdādiguṇa*)—just like the form of a tree existing within a seed; it is endowed with unmanifest qualities. However, by means of the word "but" (*tu*), which serves to illuminate a specific distinction, [the text refers] to the previously mentioned sense organs, beginning with the ear (*śrotra*).
It is stated that the subtle elements (tanmātras), such as sound and the rest, exist in a subordinate state by virtue of having both gross and subtle forms.

Likewise, in the *Mataṅga* [Tantra] it is established that "the subtle elements here are like pots, and like the wind of the great elements," meaning that the fivefold subtle element consists of five types, beginning with the subtle element of sound (*śabdatanmātra*). He states that the subtle elements of sound and the rest possess names such as "Rava" and so forth: "That subtle element of sound and the rest has a name preceded by 'Rava'."

It has been explained. It is proclaimed by names preceded by "rava" (*l4*), just as for sound there are names such as *rava*, *dhvani*, and *nināda*; for touch, which takes the form of cold, heat, and so forth; for taste, which consists of white, black, red, and so on, as well as sweet, bitter, astringent, and so forth;
and for smell, which consists of fragrant, foul, and so forth (*l5*).

He asks: what is produced by this act of assigning names to gross forms? He says: "The support of the elements," which means that which exists as the substratum within the elements beginning with space (*ākāśa*), respectively. The five elements are space, sound, water, and earth. He asks: how many qualities do these possess, and what is their function? Regarding this, among the elements beginning with space, the earth element (*dharā*) is endowed with five qualities.

Water and the others—namely water, fire, air, and space—are each accompanied by five qualities known as smell, taste, form, touch, and sound; yet, respectively, they are individually deprived of one quality, being devoid [of the preceding ones] and possessing only [the remaining] qualities of taste, form, touch, and sound, in that order.
Water, for instance, is endowed with the qualities of taste, form, touch, and sound.

Fire is endowed with the qualities of form, touch, and sound; wind is endowed with the qualities of touch and sound; and space is endowed with the single quality of sound. By this, those who deny [the existence of qualities] by claiming that sound is the only quality of space while wind and the others possess no such quality are refuted; for thus, in space, there is an echo.
The sound "śaka-śaka" is heard in the wind, indicating its vibration;
the sound "dhamadhamā" in fire indicates its blazing; the sound "phala-phala" in water indicates its flow; and the sound "ghaṭa-ghaṭa" in earth indicates its solidity.
These sounds of the wind and other elements arise through their mutual impact.

Immediately upon arising, echoes are heard in the sky that possess the same coloration as their respective original sounds. Likewise, in the case of the king of beasts (the lion), the five elements—space, wind, fire, water, and earth—possess qualities that increase by one in each successive order; they have functions such as providing space and so forth. Just as the qualities of sweetness, heat, wetness, and hardness are perceived in honey, fire, water, and the earth respectively, so too do the qualities of sound, wind, and the rest exist within the ether (*vyoman*), sharing its own nature.
"Partaking of echoes" refers to the five qualities in the earth element (*pṛthivī*):

namely, sound in the form of jars, pots, and so forth; touch that is neither hot nor cold; various colors such as white, red, black, and so on; taste consisting of pungent, sour, salty, bitter, sweet, and astringent; and fragrance in the form of both pleasant and unpleasant odors.

In water there are four qualities: the sound such as *chalachala* and so forth; the quality of coldness in its form of touch; whiteness in its form of color; and sweetness in its taste. In fire there are three qualities: the sound such as *dhama-dhama* and so forth; heat in its form of touch; and luminosity in its form of color. In wind there are two qualities: the touch that is neither cold nor hot; and the sound such as *śaka-śaka* and so forth.

In space, sound is the sole quality, as is the case with sound itself, which is merely an echo. And it is said in the *Mṛgendra*: "This [quality of] sound exists in the five elements; touch exists in four elements: neither cold nor hot in earth and wind; cold and hot in water and fire; radiant in fire; and white in water."

On earth, color is manifold, beginning with white and so forth; taste exists in three [elements], while on earth it is water, being sweet and of six kinds. Smell is considered by the wise to be both non-fragrant and fragrant on earth. Thus, the functions of the elements—earth and the rest—are grasping, cooking, arranging, and providing space. The remainder is that these functions arise in their respective order through those [elements] such as earth: "grasping" (dharaṇa) is the function of the earth due to its solidity; "grasping" (graha) is... [the function of water].

Coalescence is the act of bringing together into a mass or forming a lump due to the quality of cohesion; this is the function of water. Cooking is the act of making something cooked due to heat; this is the function of fire. Arrangement is the joining of parts due to motion; this is the function of air. Space [provides] room.

Because it is partless and has the nature of a void, the function of space is to provide a locus for other elements. And it has been said: "The functions of wind, space, fire, water, and earth are, respectively, movement, providing space, digestion, cohesion, and support. (19)
Although it consists of progressively higher levels, it is pure because it brings about awakening; yet, due to the bondage of delusion, it is impure through inversion.

Even though it is pure by virtue of its spiritual nature (*pums-tva*), it remains superior. These very principles (*tattvas*), joined with the Lords of the Worlds (*bhuvaneśas*) who act as their assistants, abide within the selves; and these [principles], being turbid, are fully capable of bestowing external enjoyments.

Having thus described the principles (*tattvas*) beginning with Śiva and ending with Earth, he states that they possess a threefold nature—pure, pure-impure, and impure. Regarding the word "above" (*ūrdhva*):
the "upper path" (*ūrdhvādhvā*) consists precisely of the upper principles, those existing above the principle of *māyā*.
Furthermore, the entire path (*sakala evādhvā*), comprising the five principles from Pure Knowledge (*śuddhavidyā*) up to Śiva, exists there as the means of awakening for the selves situated therein.

It is pure because it generates the knowledge of omniscience, omnipotence, and so forth; for the sake of providing enjoyment (*bhoga*) to those whose nature is the pure reality (*śuddhatattva*), it has as its material cause the *bindu* which has been agitated by direct perception (*sākṣātkāra*) through Paramaśiva. For this very reason, the *vijñānakevalas* have transcended the bonds such as *kalā* and have utterly destroyed the fetters of karma.

Ananteśa and the others, though possessing residual *adhikāra-mala* (the impurity of office), exist as those who have not yet attained the splendor of Śiva; and it has been said that all the lords of the worlds of the pure path (*śuddhādhvan*) are supported by Him. From the knot (*granthi*), which is the *māyā-tattva*, there exists below—in the lower portion—the path (*adhvan*) consisting of the principles (*tattva*) beginning with *kalā* and ending with *kṣiti*, which is rich in delusion (*moha*).

The cause for the engagement of the cognition of permanence, purity, pleasure, and self with respect to what is actually impermanent, impure, suffering, and non-self is that [cognition] which has arisen from *māyā*; because of its superiority over [ordinary] wealth and so forth, it is "impure" (*aśuci*) due to its being an impure state of manhood, and it is "supreme" (*para*) because it exists above the principle of the *puruṣa*.

The path (*adhvan*), which consists of the essential nature of the categories (*kalā*) beginning with *rāga* and ending with *tattva*, is "pure" (*śuddha*) because of the removal of error (*viparyaya-hati*)—that is, through the abandonment of error whose power has been crushed by time (*kala*). It is "pure" in the sense that error is partially abandoned due to [the soul's] limited knowledge and limited agency; the word "also" (*api*) implies that it is also "impure. Impurity, however, pertains to the souls (*ātman*) who possess the true body (*saddhātṛṇām*) by way of the subtle body (*sūkṣmadeha*).
Because they produce pleasure, pain, and delusion,

the principles beginning with *prakṛti* and ending with the earth are indeed impure realities (*aśuddhatattva*) by their very nature, due to their possession of the qualities such as *sattva* and because they intensely produce pleasure, pain, and delusion. Thus he says, "the principles" (*tattvāni*), meaning that these created principles remain until the time of the great dissolution (*mahāsaṃhāra*).

Together with the lords of those worlds who have become their companions—those lords (*īśāna*) being the masters of the various worlds situated within the respective *tattvas*, which serve as the means (*sādhanas*) for the sake of enjoyment (*bhoga*)—and joined by them, [the soul] possesses its own [powers], such as the *vijñānākala* and others. The impurity (*mala*) intensely bestows external enjoyment; by the word "external" (*bahiḥ*), internal enjoyment is excluded, thus it is called "external enjoyment."

The twofold nature of enjoyment (*bhoga*) has been indicated: because Śiva himself is the direct agent in bestowing enjoyment, the enjoyment arising from the pure principles (*śuddhatattva*) is internal enjoyment; because [the deity] acts through Ananta and others as the agent, the enjoyment arising from the impure principles (*aśuddhatattva*) is external enjoyment.

For those who enjoy internal objects of experience, liberation occurs at the conclusion of that enjoyment. And it has been said: "For those established in a position of authority (*adhikāra*), impurity (*mala*) is the obstacle; by means of that [impurity], there would be enjoyment of the pure path (*śuddhādhvan*). When maturation (*pāka*) occurs, there is the destruction of that impurity; when the impurity of authority is destroyed, there is liberation, which is the supreme, imperishable state. For those who enjoy external objects of experience, [liberation occurs] after the internal enjoyment.
Liberation.

Thus, it was stated by the venerable Aghoraśivācārya in the *Pañcāvaraṇastava*: "And those who, desiring the enjoyments arising from the pure worlds here, worship you with various modes of sacrifice—to them [you grant these]."

"You grant enjoyments to those who practice for the sake of the Supreme Lord, and immediately thereafter, liberation. These principles (*tattvas*), beginning with earth (*kṣiti*) and ending with Śiva, persist and exist from the time of dissolution until the Great Dissolution (*mahāpralaya*);
precisely because they abide [thus], they are called "principles" (*tattvas*).

Likewise, in the *Tattvaprakāśa*: "That which remains until the dissolution [of the world] and bestows experience upon all beings—that is declared here to be a *tattva*, not a *tattva* such as the body, a jar, or the like."

They recite that the reality of earth (*kṣmā-tattva*) extends for a hundred *koṭis* of *yojanas*, starting from the waters up to the end of the *gauṇa*; by multiplying that [measure] according to the sequence of the principles (*prakṛti*), it likewise extends from the *māyā* down to *sadāśiva*, which is ten thousand times a hundred [the previous measure]. (l4)

Beyond that, extending for a hundred *lakṣas*, is Śiva, the ender of power (*śaktyantaka*), who possesses immeasurable majesty and is the presiding deity of the *bindu*. He states the measurements in *yojanas* for the principles (*tattvas*) beginning with earth: "The principle of earth" (*kṣmātatvam*) means the earth-principle (*pṛthvītatva*) is one hundred crore *yojanas*. Starting from the water-principle (*aptatva*), the meaning is that the water-principle is as previously described. They recite [the sequence] up to the end of the qualities (*gauṇāntakam*), which is the limit of the quality-principle (*guṇatattva*).

Ten times ten is the number; by multiplying that— that is, by increasing the measure of the earth-element, which consists of one hundred koṭis of yojanas— one arrives at the measure in yojanas for each successive element, beginning with the water-element and ending with the quality-elements.

For example, if one hundred million *yojanas* of the dimension of the earth-element are made into a single place, and that single-place dimension of one hundred million *yojanas* is increased tenfold, it becomes ten times the dimension of the water-element as the second place. In the same way, if it is multiplied further, it becomes the third place and so on, such as fire and the rest, starting from one hundred and so forth; for instance:

The nature of water is ten times that of the earth-nature; the meaning is that its dimension is ten places [of zeros], namely one thousand million (*sahasrakoṭi*) *yojanas*. In the same way, the number should be calculated for what follows: the nature of fire is ten times that of the water-nature, which is one hundred places; wind is ten times that of fire, which is one thousand places; and [space is] ten times that of wind... [l2]

Space (*ākāśa*) has the quality (*guṇa*) as its place; egoity (*ahaṅkāra*), being ten times that of space, has ten thousand (*daśasahasra*) as its place; intellect (*buddhi*), being ten times that of egoity, has one hundred thousand (*lakṣa*) as its place;
the principle of the qualities (*guṇatattva*), being ten times that of intellect, has ten million (*koṭi*) as its place.

Thus, from one up to one hundred million, the numerical value of the places of the *koṭi* has been established. He states the measure of the principles beginning with *prakṛti* up to the end of the *guṇatattva*: "In the same way" (*tathā*) means just as [previously described].

Starting from the reality of the earth element, which measures one hundred koṭis of yojanas, up to the reality of the qualities (*guṇa-tattva*), there is an increase by a factor of ten; likewise, starting from primordial nature (*prakṛti*)— from the reality of primordial nature up to the end of *māyā*, that is, the reality of *māyā*— there is an increase by a factor of one hundred.

The effect (*kārya*) is to be placed at the hundredth position because it causes increase; according to the principle of multiplication (*guṇana*), the Nature (*prakṛti*) is a hundredfold [of the effect], and its place is the lotus (*padma*). Passion (*rāga*) is a hundredfold of Nature, and its place is the *nikharva* lotus. Necessity (*niyati*) is a hundredfold of passion, and its place is the great lake-lotus (*mahāsaroja*). Knowledge (*vidyā*) is a hundredfold of necessity, and its place is the great conch (*mahāśaṅkha*). Artistic power (*kalā*) is a hundredfold of knowledge.

The time at that station of the Great Ocean is a hundredfold the time of *kalā*. That indeed is the station of *parārtha*; in this manner, the calculation should be carried out from one up to the station of *parārtha*, extending as far as Sadāśiva—from above the *māyā-tattva* up to the *sadāśiva-tattva*, [the time] increases by a thousandfold from each thousand.

The meaning is that the measure of the *māyā*-tattva, increased by a factor of one thousand, constitutes the measure of the *śuddhavidyā*-tattva. When the measure of *śuddhavidyā* is increased by one thousand, it becomes the measure of the *īśvara*-tattva; when that measure is increased by one thousand, it becomes the measure of the *sadāśiva*-tattva. Above that *sadāśiva*-tattva, extending up to the end of *śakti*—
Up to the limit of the Śakti-tattva,

when the measure of the Sadāśiva-tattva is increased by one hundred thousand (lakṣa), the measure of the Śakti-tattva becomes one yojana; it remains pervading as the pervader and the pervaded in the upper region situated above the Śakti-tattva.

The meaning is that Sadāśiva possesses immeasurable wealth (*ameyavibhava*) and indefinable power (*aparicchedyasāmarthya*), such that he cannot be established by means of measurement through numbers and the like, as being "this much" or "of such a count.

He is the presiding lord (*adhiṣṭhāyaka*) even over the *bindu*, serving as its locus (*adhiṣṭhānasthānabhūta*). And it has been said: "This *bindu* belongs to Śakti; it is pervaded by Śiva and not by anyone else. (L4)
Likewise, in the Mataṅga [Tantra] it is said: "From that earth, which measures one *yojana*, water is ten times greater;
from water, fire; from fire, wind; from wind, this space (*ākāśa*); and in this *Pārameśvara* scripture, from space comes the ego-principle (*ahaṅkāra*), and beyond that—"

O Sage, it should be known that the Great (Mahat) is beyond the Great; the triad of qualities (guṇas) is one hundred times superior [to Mahat]. The principle called Pradhāna consists of the three qualities, and the remaining principles taught in the scripture are each said to be a hundred times superior to the preceding one. The principles ending with Māyā are thus [calculated], but above them, by a thousandfold [increase], one reaches up to the principle of Sadāśiva; beyond that, it is by a hundred-thousandfold (lakṣa).
The group of four, ending with Śakti, is established; beyond that is the object of knowledge, which is Śiva.

(21) When the streams [of emanation] consist of various principles (tattvas) in subtle forms for each individual, serving as the substrates for all worlds and objects of experience produced by Māyā, He then employs those men for the sake of their maintenance; yet He is not perceived by them. (2)

Śiva provides the means for the attainment of one's own purpose through the body, the worlds, and enjoyments. He states that for each individual (*puruṣa*), there are many effects of *māyā*, consisting of subtle bodies and worlds. Regarding the phrase "of the streams" (*srotasām*) and "for each person" (*pratipuṃsaḥ*): because the word *puṃsaḥ* is used in the singular to denote a class, it refers to every individual. [He provides the means] by means of the principles (*tattvas*)—beginning with *kalā* and ending with *kṣiti*—which constitute the nature of the subtle body.
Illusions and those born of illusion,
streams and stations of many kinds and various sorts— meaning the subtle bodies and gross bodies, the dwelling places of all selves, [constituting] the subtle and gross bodies of all selves. (l4–l5)

Because of its twofold nature, it serves as the substratum for all worlds that are to be experienced by the self; "of all" (nikhilānām) means of every [being]. These are "objects of experience" (bhogyāni), meaning they are fit to be enjoyed either as lords of those respective worlds or as inhabitants of those respective worlds. It should be understood that the status of being a lord of a world belongs to Kālāgnirudra and others, while the status of inhabiting those worlds belongs to their retinues and the rest.

The streams born of Māyā, which consist of various types and have as their objects the *sakala* souls, are [constituted] by the principles (*tatva*) that serve as the substrata for the worlds— beginning with the *kalā*s and ending with the earth— which constitute the respective foundations of those worlds.
These are the manyfold currents belonging to the *sakala* selves.

For the Pralayākalas, there exist numerous unmanifest bodies and unmanifest worlds contained within Māyā; for the Sakalas and Vijñānakalas, there exist bodies and worlds produced by Mahāmāyā. At that time—when those ontological worlds created by [the Lord] exist, namely the principles from Kalā down to Earth which constitute the causes of the bodies—at that very moment...

He states that at the time of creation and so forth, [the Lord], having joined the souls—which are essentially Śiva—to their connection with bodies and the like, performs the fivefold activity beginning with creation. Regarding the word *sthityai* ("for the sake of maintenance"): it means by those selves who are presided over (*adhiṣṭhitaiḥ*) by Śiva, that is to say, impelled by Him; by them, He is characterized (*lakṣitaḥ*) as "our" [Lord].

The meaning is that Śiva, though present within the self as the inner impeller (*preraka*), is not perceived because he is veiled by impurity (*mala*). For the sake of attaining his own purpose—that is, for the selves to attain the goal of their own activity—he [acts] through *bhoga* (experience), which consists of pleasure and pain, by means of instruments that serve as the practitioner's methods: namely, bodies (*tanu*), deities (*deva*)—so called because they illuminate (*dyotana*) the divine—and worlds (*bhuvana*).
Because of the manifestation of external objects,

he— through the sense organs, the entities such as the eight principles beginning with *dharma*, and the worlds beginning with the Fire of Time (*kālāgni*)— binds those men whose souls are fettered by impurity, joining them to that [manifestation] for the sake of their continued existence.

By this, the emanation (*sṛṣṭi*) of Śiva through the instruments such as the body is described. Emanation consists of the production of the worlds (*bhuvana*), the production of souls (*ātman*) connected to those worlds, and the production of bodies; that emanation is twofold: the direct [emanation] by Śiva and the production of the worlds by means of the *bindu*, which serves as the material cause (*upādāna*).

[The Lord performs] the creation of the *baindava* bodies for the inhabitants of those worlds, such as Ananta and others; the creation of the worlds produced by Ānanda and others; and the creation of the subtle, essential *bhauvana* bodies for the souls dwelling therein. (22) [Furthermore,] through the favoring of the fetters (*pāśa*), there is the enjoyment of objects of experience by the persons according to their respective fitness; and by bestowing power upon them, the Lord’s function is their protection. However, they dissolve through transformation.

(14) At the time [of dissolution], those principles exist in reverse order within Māyā and even beyond it, by the command of Mahāmāyā-niśā. He describes the activity of concealment (*tirobhāva*) and so forth: "By the fetters" (*pāśa*), because of the grasping of the fetters. (15)

Because of the grasping of the bonds (*pāśas*) such as impurity (*mala*) and so forth— by means of establishing a relationship through the thought, "this is this person's bond" and "this is that person's bond"— just as [the Lord acts] toward the *vijñānākala*s with respect to impurity alone,

toward the *pralayākala*s with respect to impurity and karma, and toward the *sakala*s with respect to impurity, *māyā*, and karma; thus, in accordance with each respective bond, He acts in conformity with the object of experience (*bhogya*).

The meaning of *tirobhāva* (concealment) is the bestowing of enjoyment upon the selves (*ātman*) by providing them with the objects suitable for consumption; it is the act of concealing the knowledge of the true nature of the selves according to the degree of their bondage (*pāśa*), and then granting them the enjoyment of objects corresponding to that [state]. It is the act of favoring [them] through concealment.

Śiva [is present] within the bodies of Brahmā and others as one possessing limited knowledge (*kiñcijjña*) according to gradations, because it has been stated thus. By bestowing His power upon individual souls (*puṃsām ātmanām*), that is, by bestowing power for the enjoyment of objects of experience (*bhogyavastuviṣayabhoga-saṃbhojane*) therein— just as in the production of objects of experience— (l3)

Likewise, the capacity for stabilization is primarily the Lord Śiva’s function of preservation (*sthitikṛtya*). This means that the preservation of the entire universe—which has been restrained by the power of the Lord—is the establishment of each thing in its own respective domain. He describes the function of withdrawal (*saṃhārakṛtya*): "They dissolve" refers to the two forms [of withdrawal], namely the Great Withdrawal (*mahāsaṃhāra*) and the Intermediate Withdrawal (*avāntarasaṃhāra*), occurring at the appointed time.

At the time of dissolution, the principles beginning with Śiva, which had arisen in the order of emanation (*sṛṣṭikrama*), undergo transformation in reverse order, starting from the principle of Earth (*pṛthivī*). This occurs through a modification of *prakṛti*, like a change of state, rather than a loss of its essential nature.
Here, [regarding] Earth and the others...

The *ahaṅkāra*, known as *pariṇāma*, *bhautika*, *vaikārika*, and *taijasa*, is, in due order, the material cause (*prakṛti*) of the pentad beginning with smell. *Ahaṅkāra* is the material cause through transformation (*pariṇāma*). Its material cause is the transformation of the *guṇas*. The material cause of that is the Unmanifest (*avyakta*). Attachment (*rāga*) and Knowledge (*vidyā*) are its transformations; their material cause is the principle of *kalā*.
Masculinity, time, necessity, limited agency, and transformation—of these, Māyā is the primordial nature (*prakṛti*).

Thus, one should understand the relationship between nature and its manifestations within the principle of Māyā. Because [an entity] arises from that very source, it dissolves back into that same source through internal absorption; this remains true even beyond [the manifest world].

The paths of Māyā and the principles beginning with Śuddhavidyā— namely, Śuddhavidyā [dissolves] into the principle of Īśvara, Īśvara into Sadāśiva, Sadāśiva into Śakti, Śakti into the principle of Śiva which consists of the state beyond Śānti situated at the summit of the Śāntikalā,
and Śiva into the Bindu which is the material cause and the essence of Mahāmāyā— all dissolve in due order by the command of Īśa, that is, by the command of Śiva.

By the command of the Lord who is dependent on Māyā, [the elements] dissolve; thus it has been said by Aghoraśivācārya: "Earth [dissolves] into smell, water into taste, fire into form, wind into touch, and ether into sound."

Furthermore, these subtle elements (tanmātras) dissolve into the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra) of the tamasic type; the organs of action (karmākṣas) along with death (maraṇa) dissolve into that of the rājasa type; and [the organs of action] together with the organs of perception (buddhīndriyas) dissolve into that of the sāttvika type. That [sāttvika ego] dissolves into the intellect (buddhi), and that [intellect] dissolves into the qualities (guṇas). That multitude of qualities goes to dissolution into the Manifest (vyakta). Then, attachment (rāga), ignorance (avidyā), limited agency (kalā), and personhood (puṃstva)—namely, time (kāla), necessity (niyati), limited agency (kalā), and illusion (māyā)—all go to dissolution into Māyā.
The Lord of Knowledge (Vidyeśa), that region, that power, and intelligence—this is Śiva, the Bindu. ||23||

When thousands of years, yugas, and oceans—measured by a thousand suns among the divine [years]—have passed below, there is the dissolution (*laya*) of that very [universe] whose domain is the three worlds.

Even when its creations have reached the state of a *parārdha*, there is a dissolution here; from this, it dissolves again into the manifest (*vyakta*), and likewise, upon further creations, there is a dissolution of this [universe] along with the qualities (*guṇa*) and so forth into the *granthi* and the *bindu*. The conclusion of *prakṛti* is the intermediate [dissolution].

"Saṃhārajāla" refers to the conclusion of Māyā; "saṃhārakāla" refers to the enumeration of the time of dissolution. Regarding "among the gods," in the years associated with the gods, three hundred and sixty human days constitute one year for humans; such a measure of a year constitutes one day for the gods. In this manner, [the cycle] measures three hundred and sixty [such days].

One year of the gods is calculated in this manner. Within that very year, there are the *yugas*—the *abdhis* (oceans) of years consisting of twelve thousand years, comprising the four ages (*yugas*) of Kṛta, Tretā, Dvāpara, and Kali, each lasting one thousand years of the sun. Herein the meaning is as follows: the measure of the four *yugas*, when joined with twelve thousand divine years, constitutes [one cycle]; therein, the Kṛta-yuga...

O Deva, four thousand years is its measure; the period of twilight (sandhyā) is eight hundred years in measure. The measure of the Kṛta Yuga, as applied to the years of the twilight period, is four thousand and eight hundred years of the Devas; [the Tretā Yuga is]—(l8)— *Note: The text fragment provided ends with "tretā" and lacks the full description for that yuga.*

The duration of the *tretā* age is three thousand divine years; its *sandhyāṃśa* is six hundred [years], so that the total measure of the *tretā*, including its *sandhyāṃśa*, is three thousand six hundred years. The *dvāpara* age is two thousand divine years;

its *sandhyāṃśa* is four hundred [years], so that the total measure of the *dvāpara*, including its *sandhyāṃśa*, is two thousand four hundred years. The *kali* age is one thousand divine years; its *sandhyāṃśa* is two hundred [years].
The measure of the Kali age, including its transitional periods (*sandhyāṃśa*), is one thousand two hundred years;

likewise, the measure of the four ages (*caturyuga*) together with their transitional periods is twelve thousand divine years. And it is said: "The wise know the Kṛta age to consist of four thousand years."
Beyond that, each of the other ages, beginning with Tretā, consists of a *sandhyā* and a *sandhyāṃśa*.

Thus, it is stated in the Sūta-saṃhitā: "O Brahmins, a divine cycle of four ages (*caturyuga*) is said to consist of twelve thousand years. Of these, the Kṛta-yuga comprises four thousand [years], and its *sandhyā* and *sandhyāṃśa* are said to be eight hundred more [than that]. Tretā consists of three thousand [years]..."

The Kṛta [Yuga] is proclaimed by the gods; half of that is said to be the Tretā, and half of that is called the Kali. In sequence, the Sandhyā and the Sandhyāṃśa are each deprived of a fourth part. Thus, those [periods] of the Kṛta Yuga are one hundred, two hundred, and ten [respectively].

The *saṃdhyā* and its related *saṃdhyāṃśa* each consist of two hundred [years]. This same calculation should be applied to the *tretā*-yuga and the others as well. When the measure of such a *caturyuga* is calculated by the number of human years, its total duration is seen to be one thousand divine years; when reckoned by the human count, this results in three hundred and sixty thousand years. Thus...
The measure of the Kṛtayuga is seventeen lakhs and twenty-eight thousand years; the measure of the Tretāyuga is twelve lakhs and ninety-six thousand years;
the measure of the Dvāparayuga is eight lakhs and sixty-four thousand years; and the measure of the Kaliyuga is four lakhs and thirty-two thousand years. Such are the measures of the four yugas.
The measure [of time] is thirty-four lakhs and twenty thousand years by human calculation; when thousands of such calculated cycles of the four ages have passed,
the dissolution of the realm of the three worlds— the inhabitants of the three worlds who abide therein— is declared.

Even during the creations—that is, the emanations—of those very beings who are the objects of creation within the three worlds, throughout thousands of cycles of the four ages (*caturyuga*), such is the duration of the time of creation.

Here, for Brahmā residing in the midst of the golden egg, the duration of his day is up to a thousand cycles of the four ages, and his night is of equal duration. During that period of his day, while the creation of the inhabitants of the three worlds is taking place...

The period up until the end of the day is the time of Brahmā’s state of waking, because it is the time of the waking state of Brahmā; during his night, it is the time of the destruction of the people of the three worlds, because it is the time of Brahmā’s state of sleep. And it is said:
"Engaged in their own respective activities... (l6)
The lifespan of each of these Indras is said to be seventy-one *yugas*. By those fourteen Śakras, one day of the Lotus-born [Brahmā] is completed;

such is the duration of the existence of these three worlds in brief. O Great Sage, the night of Brahmā is of equal length, during which the darkness of the three worlds reaches its dissolution at the onset of that state known as the dawn of the Mahākalpa.

Brahmā too, having risen from his bed with a mind characterized by necessity and compassion, [creates] the world again through the power of Rudra’s Śakti. (56a, l1) Having stated the duration of Brahmā’s day in order to express the calculation of the intermediate period (*avāntarakāla*), he speaks here of the calculation of the time for the dissolution of the dispersed world, which culminates in the principle of Prakṛti.
If three hundred and sixty days of Brahmā constitute a year of Brahmā, then when the Brahmā-year has reached and passed through the number of *parārdhas* that will be stated later,
[the dissolution occurs].
Dissolution (*vilaya*), which is withdrawal (*saṃhāra*), is said to extend up to the manifest (*vyakta*) and terminate at the principle of primordial nature (*prakṛti*).

Likewise, in the *Mṛgendra*: "At the end of a thousand cycles of four yugas, there is the day of Brahmā; his night is of equal duration. By this reckoning, let it be [the same] for a *parārdha*. Dissolution extends up to the manifest, while the principles beginning with primordial nature are suspended. From this cause, which is the principle of primordial nature, [there occurs] again... of this [world].

The meaning is that during the creations— that is, the emanations— of everything from the qualities (guṇas) down to earth, as well as the measure of the period of dissolution lasting up to the limit of the number of a *parārdha*, followed immediately by the period of creation;
this is the "great dissolution" (*mahāsaṃhāra*).

He states the calculation of time: in the *Māyā-tattva* and in the *bindu*, which is the material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*) of all things, there is dissolution (*laya*), that is, the withdrawal (*saṃhāra*). The duration of the persistence of *prakṛti* and the other principles is one *parārtha*;

however, the period of withdrawal is half a *parārtha*. Thus, the duration of creation and withdrawal is measured by two half-*parārthas*. During that time, there occurs a cycle of the creation and withdrawal of *prakṛti* and the rest; [this constitutes] one *parārtha*.

(18) When [the categories] have reached their enumeration, dissolution occurs in *māyā* by way of the sequence beginning with *prakṛti*; dissolution occurs in the *bindu* by way of the sequence beginning with *śuddhavidyā*. As it is said in the *Mṛgendra*: "Thus, of the creations beginning with the *guṇas*, [dissolution occurs] in the supreme [state]. (p56b, l1)

The cause of the qualities (*guṇa*) is *kalā*, which consists of the arts and illusion (*māyā*); it turns away from its own office (*svādhikāra*). Upon its cessation, those gods who hold office also cease; for their office—consisting of creation, maintenance, and so forth—is dependent upon that [power]. Thus, among the twenty principal ones beginning with Mantreśa, the desired state is the reality (*tattva*) that always consumes *vidyā*. That is the *bindu*, the lunar [nature], and the resonance (*dhvani*).
The power that is intent upon mere names is itself called Hara by those who desire power. ||24||

One, ten, a hundred, a thousand, ten thousand (*ayuta*), a hundred thousand (*lakṣa*), a million (*prapūrvāyuta*), ten million (*koṭi*), a hundred million (*abaśadaka*), a billion (*padaka*), ten billion (*adhaḥ*), a hundred billion (*kharva*), a trillion (*nikharva*), ten trillion (*bṛnda*), a quadrillion (*mahāsaroja*), a quintillion (*apara*), a sextillion (*śaṅkha*), a septillion (*samudra*), an octillion (*antima*), a nonillion (*madhya*), and a decillion (*parārdha*)—the wise know these as the numerical designations. From one up to the end of the *parārdha*, there are twenty places of enumeration; thus he says, "one," and so forth.

A single place is a unit; a row (*paṅkti*) is either the number ten or everything is to be multiplied by multiplying by ten successively.
