Thus, the second place is not explicitly called "row" (*paṅkti*) [in the text], but having made the second [place] a hundred by multiplying it tenfold, the third place is the number hundred; if that is multiplied tenfold, it is a thousand, which is the fourth place; ten thousand is an *ayuta*.

The fifth place is the number *saṅkhyāka*; if that is multiplied by ten, it is *lakṣa*, the sixth place, which is the number of one hundred thousand (*śatasahasra*). *Prāyuta*—meaning *pra*-preceded *ayuta*, or *prayuta*—is ten lakṣas; this is the seventh place. If that is multiplied by ten, it is *koṭi*, the number of one million (*śatalakṣa*); this is the eighth place. If that is multiplied by ten, it is *arbuda*, the ninth place. If that is multiplied by ten, it is *padmaka*.

The tenth place is that multiplied by ten, [which is] *kharva*; the eleventh place is that multiplied by ten, [which is] *nikharva*; the twelfth place is that multiplied by ten, [which is] *bunda*; the thirteenth place is that multiplied by ten, [which is] *mahāsaroja*;
the fourteenth place is another *śākha*—meaning *śaṅkha*, which is *mahāśaṅkha*; if *mahāsaroja* is multiplied by ten, it is *śaṅkha*.
The fifteenth place is ten times that, which is *mahāśaṅkha*; the sixteenth place is ten times that, which is *samudra*; the seventeenth place is ten times that, which is the final *mahāsamudra*;
the eighteenth place is ten times that, which is *madhyama*; the nineteenth place is ten times that, known as *parārdha*; and the twentieth place is [ten times that], O wise ones.

Those who know the scriptures of the Śiva-āgamas understand the calculation of the Mīmāṃsakas in this way and speak thus: (25) At the time of dissolution, the lords of the worlds—Hari below and Brahmā, who likewise reach that state—along with those who possess higher knowledge, at that very moment and in the future, enter into the state of *kalā*. Those who are devoid of their own station by the will [of the Lord] during the ripening of the *ṛk* [mantra], O Śarva... (l. 2)

By Your grace, they shall be liberated; even those others who bestow their own stations are themselves surpassed by You, the Supreme. He says that at the time of dissolution, the lords of the worlds, beginning with Kālāgni and including the hundred Rudras and others, remain resorting to three forms. Thus, in the "Destruction"—that is, during both the intermediate dissolution (*madhyapralaya*) and the great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*)—the lords of the worlds, such as the hundred Rudras and others, [remain].

Hari, Viṣṇu, and Brahmā, the four-faced one— those who reach them, departing at the time of dissolution, attain the state of *vijñānākala*, that is, they go to the attainment of the nature of the *vijñānākala*. By this, the time of the great dissolution (*mahāsaṃhāra*) is indicated.

And because it is stated that the withdrawal up to the principle of Māyā—beginning from the attainment of the *kalā* of limited agency (*vijñānākala*) and ending with Māyā—is called the "Great Withdrawal" (*mahāsaṃhāra*). However, in the intermediate dissolution (*madhyapralaya*), the Lords of the Worlds (*bhuvaneśvaras*) remain within Prakṛti; having subtle bodies composed of the principles starting from Earth up to *kalā* while abiding in Prakṛti in the form of Śakti, they preside over the individual souls (*aṇus*) residing in the worlds by means of their own power.

Thus they remain. Likewise, at that time, the hundred Rudras, the two lords Vīra and Śrīkaṇṭha, and the two primary guardians, having pervaded with their power the subtle world, the subtle bodies, and the conscious beings abiding in primordial nature (prakṛti), stand [there].

They remain until the time [of dissolution], which lasts as long as the end of their sleep; thus, being impelled by Rudras such as Ananta at the time [of creation], they again begin intermediate creations and exercise their respective authority over their own worlds.

And it is said: "In Śiva, those designated as lords of the maṇḍalas, beginning with the eight mantras, having produced creation at the time [of manifestation], exercise their own authority. But in the Great Dissolution (mahāsaṃhāra)...

Existing within Māyā in the form of potentiality (*śakti*), those who hold authority over that [Māyā]—along with the Lords of the Worlds (*bhuvaneśvara*) residing in the worlds beginning with Prakṛti—are joined with an extremely subtle body; having ceased their worldly activities, they attain the nature of *Vijñānākala*. Among them...

He says that those whose impurities (*mala*) have reached maturation at the time of the Great Dissolution (*mahāsaṃhārakāla*) become liberated. At that very time— the time characterized by the Great Dissolution— prior even to the actual moment of dissolution, those Lords of the Worlds (*bhuvaneśvara*), their impurities having matured, being devoid of desire for their own station, [attain liberation] through the grace of Śarva, the Supreme Lord.

(15) Because they bestow supreme liberation, those who are liberated become truly liberated; others also [become liberated] due to the absence of the ripening of impurities. Others, endowed with the desire for their own state, [attain] their own state within Māyā through Śakti. (16)

Those who, established in their own abodes in the form of *rūpa*, maintain [the world], are the infinite ones (*ananta* and others) presiding over the pure path (*śuddhādhvan*). They sustain that very nature of Śiva, which is the ultimate liberation (*kaivalya*) for each respective [soul].
By this, the act of grace (*anugrahakṛtya*) performed by Śiva is indicated. ||26||

For the rest of those whose minds are weary, for the ripening of the series of their karma, and for the manifestation of the power of illusion and speech, Śambhu performs the great dissolution (*mahāsaṃhṛti*). When the fettered beings (*paśu*) remain, that stainless one, together with his power (*śakti*), again brings about [the world] for the enjoyment of souls.
Thus he says that Śiva performs the great dissolution solely for the sake of the purpose of Nature (*prakṛti*) regarding the selves: "For the rest," and so forth.

For the sake of the repose of those who are subject to existence— namely, transmigrating beings who wander upon the path of *bhava* and are therefore weary-minded and distressed in mind— for the purpose of resting by abiding in ease within the withdrawal (*saṃhāra*), where there is no birth or death.
The meaning is: for the sake of avoiding the various births of *saṃsāra*. Furthermore, for the ripening—that is, the digestion—of the accumulation of karma acquired over many lifetimes;

that is to say, for the transformation of the fruits produced by karma, since there is no experience [of them] during the dissolution (*saṃhāra*). Furthermore, for the production of the power of illusory speech (*māyāvāg*); that is, of illusory words, incessantly...

For the sake of generating power— that is, for the production of the capacity to effect creation once again— of Māyā and Bindu, which have had their powers diminished by the continuous succession of producing numerous effects such as bodies, organs, and worlds, and which serve as the material causes for the impure and pure paths; Śambhu, the Supreme Lord who is devoted to the welfare of all beings, [acts].

He brings about and performs the "Great Withdrawal" (*mahāsaṃhṛti*) and the "Great Cycle" (*mahāsaṃsāra*); however, the "Intermediate Withdrawal" (*avāntarasaṃhāra*) occurs [at intervals] beginning with Ananta, which is the meaning. Likewise, in the *Tattvaprakāśa*: "The Lord, out of compassion, effects the Great Withdrawal of all beings who are exhausted by the [process of] withdrawal, for their very rest. Thus, because at the time of the Great Withdrawal there is the non-existence of all [entities], it is eternal.

(18) He asks: "Who are those who remain? [The answer is: All bound souls (*paśu*) because of their connection with impurity (*mala*); the one endowed with power (*saśakti*) is Śambhu, whose powers of knowledge and action are inherently united and who is free from beginningless impurity.

*Śambhu* is the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*), so called because he brings about (*bhāvayati*) *śam*, which is bliss in the form of the impeller (*preryatā*). By the word "and" (*ca*) here, the *mala* (impurity) of the liberated souls (*muktātman*) is included—those who, by virtue of not being veiled by the *nādi*s, are endowed with eternity and omnipresence. The two types of *māyā* and the *bindu*—meaning the two substrata (*upādāna*) of the impure and pure worlds—are what remain; they are the "residues" (*śeṣitāḥ*), meaning they exist as eternal entities. This is because they consist of latent impressions (*vāsanā*).

For, since liberation would not be possible for souls if there were an absence of the experience of the fruits of their established karma, [the Lord] performs the activity of creation and so forth once again for the sake of experiencing the fruits of karma; thus he says: "And therefore, immediately after the withdrawal [of the world], out of compassion (*dayā*) and mercy (*kṛpā*), for the sake of the persons, the souls..."

"For the sake of enjoyment" means for the sake of experiencing the fruits of previously accumulated karma; "again afterwards" means he performs the fivefold activity beginning with creation. The meaning is that, having brought about the destruction of karma through experience, he performs the activities of creation and so forth once more in order to liberate the bound souls (*paśu*). As it is said in the *Kiraṇa*: "The karma pertaining to many births is burnt away by the individual souls (*aṇu*) like a seed."

That by which even the future is restrained—this indeed is called "enjoyment" (*bhoga*). Thus, in the context of reabsorption (*saṃhāra*), there is the statement regarding the three principles (*tattva*) as being eternal, beginning with Śambhu: "Śambhu, Puruṣa, and Māyā are eternal and all-pervading;
and [Puruṣa] is endowed with the power of agency even while asleep."
In the realm of transformations, the triad of the principles remains ever awake. ||27||
[The Jñānapāda is completed.]
The *Kriyāpāda* is now declared.

May there be success through the compassionate glance of the Lord of Kālahasti, together with the venerable Jñānāmbā. Oṃ, may there be auspiciousness! In the Root [Tantra], having been ripened by Time, the primordial Power falls upon the best of men. In this world, the fault of non-attainment arises; for one who desires the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*), there is the worship of the lower [levels]. That which follows it is his [attainment] through the office of the Hotṛ priest.

Having severed the bonds by means of his power, he leads [the disciple] to the state of Śiva, manifesting his inherent Śiva-nature; thus, the bestower of initiation should perform this ritual practice which effects the destruction of the fetters of the limbs.

(13) Having thus described the thirty-six principles (*tattva*) as distinguished by the *jñānapāda*, he now commences the *kriyāpāda*. Within that, wishing to explain the nature of initiation (*dīkṣā*), and since initiation—by virtue of being the ripening of impurity (*mala*)—is preceded by the descent of power (*śaktipāta*), he first states the investigation of the descent of power. [He says: "In the root," meaning in the *Mūla*[-tantra].

(15) When that which is beginningless and pure has, by some specific time, reached the state of being ripened— that is, having matured— just as [the eye is affected] by cataracts and the like, by [that] time... (16)

In the same way, ripening (*pāka*) occurs; because impurity is a substance, ripening is possible after a lapse of time, and thus it is said to be "ripened by time. However, the specific time for this maturation is the form of the equal distribution of *karman*, which consists of the nature of merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*). Herein the meaning is as follows: at whatever time there is an equilibrium of *karman*— [p. 60a] ...

(1) It occurs that at that very time there is the cause for the ripening of impurities; because of the absence of equality in karma, it must be said that one becomes deficient and another becomes superior.
When deficiency and superiority exist... (2)

Between two *karman*s—one consisting of merit (*dharma*) and the other consisting of demerit (*adharma*)—whichever one consists of merit or demerit that is more abundant is the stronger; it first becomes the provider of experience (*bhogada*).

Once that *karman* has ceased after giving its experience, the other may subsequently become the provider of experience. It is not the case that they are equal; therefore, when there is equality, that which provides the experience belongs to that [specific] self.
How does this occur? And it has been said:

"That which is the prior, greater portion of karma is the giver of experience; the other, however, [gives experience] when there is equality. But how is that experience produced when there is equality? If, even when there is equality... (l5)

[If] both [powers] were to grant enjoyment through karma, then at that time the self would experience the fruits of heaven and hell simultaneously; since it is not so, it is established that there is no enjoyment beyond that [karma]. From the ripening of impurity (*mala*), the primordial power—the power of concealment (*tirodhāna-śakti*)—falls upon the Supreme Person (*narapara*). Now, it was stated that "the power falls," yet [it cannot truly fall] because it is all-pervasive everywhere.

Since it is impossible for that which is all-pervading to fall from its location because it is inherently capable [of remaining there], the impossibility of the descent of power (*śaktipāta*) follows; to this, the following is the rebuttal: the application of words to objects is both primary (*mukhya*) and secondary (*gauṇī*).
[The rest of the sentence is missing.]

Therefore, in this case, the application of the word is figurative through its power (*śakti*), not primary. Just as in common worldly usage, when it is said, "This man's gaze has fallen upon this woman," one does not see the gaze actually detached from that man and falling onto the woman; rather, here, by the mere connection between the seer and the seen, the gaze is said to have "fallen" through metaphorical usage.

Just as the application of words is explained [in that case], so too here, with respect to this person, the incapacity for a relation— due to the relationship characterized by the benefactor and the beneficiary— has fallen away; thus it is stated metaphorically [that...].
But since this is said in a primary sense, there is no fault.

Likewise, in the *Kiraṇa* [Tantra], the figurative application (*upacāra*) of words is observed here, as in: "The Person (*puruṣa*), though all-pervading (*vibhu*) and eternal (*nitya*), is destroyed and has attained the state of Śiva. The meaning of this is as follows: although the Person is eternal, he is figuratively said to have met his destruction or been "killed" upon the fall of the body; likewise, although he is all-pervading (*vibhu*).

Just as it is said that a specific individual has met destruction through the figurative application [of the term], so too should it be understood that the descent of power (*śaktipāta*) is likewise spoken of by way of metaphor. Now, let this [descent of power] be metaphorical for the time being... (l2)

What can this formless [sound] do to the self? What does the self do after its falling? Just as in the world, for some object, a fall occurs in two places... (l3) ...there will be a calamity by the command of Meru; this falling sound, though formless, causes fear among the inhabitants of that village... (l4)

It has been seen [as follows]: because prior to the descent of power (*śaktipāta*), worldly enjoyment alone is considered supreme happiness; therefore, once the eye of knowledge has opened through the descent of power and so forth, one perceives the worthlessness of saṃsāra and attains a teacher who bestows his own state and is skilled in removing the fear of existence. And it is said: "May that pair which causes both the fall and fear not suddenly befall us..."
by that very [power], one perceives the Self as the Teacher; keeping this very meaning in mind, he asks: "How is it known that the descent of power (*śaktipāta*) has occurred for him?
and thus he states the sign of the descent of power: "In this regard, the power... (17)

Because the *śaktipāda* [descent of power] is difficult to discern for the bodiless *vijñānākala* and *pralayākala*, it is taught that it is the object of the embodied *sakala* self, stating: "The path itself is the reality... (p61b, l1). The underlying sense is that this applies to the *sakala* because he is common [to all], whereas the *vijñānākala* and *pralayākala* are without a substratum (*nirādhāra*) in this state of existence.
[In] the present...

(l2) the desire to abandon [the cycle of] existence, the desire for the highest good, the desire for liberation, the worship of the excellent gurus, [and] from the Supreme Lord [comes] the excellent [knowledge] of those who possess the knowledge of the uninterrupted tradition of the most eminent gurus... (l3)

The meaning is "namely. Devotion (*bhajanam*) means serving through [acts such as] desiring to hear [the teachings] and so forth. This is the intended sense: at this time, having reflected, "Who am I? What indeed is greater than suffering upon suffering?", for every person seeking liberation, there arises from their actual state a realization of one's true nature (*svarūpa-vijñāna*), characterized by longing and other such signs, which [arises] from worldly knowledge. That is it.

When the worship of the Guru arises for the sake of knowing one's own true nature (*svarūpa*), then that power (*śakti*) is said to have "fallen. And it has been said: "For those embodied beings, even if the power falls, it does not fall for the sake of worldly conduct (*vṛtti*)."

Their characteristic signs are an eagerness for liberation, aversion toward worldly existence, devotion to the devotees of Śiva, and faith in the ritual injunctions of His teaching. By this it is meant that [these signs] are stable;

they are stated here for the sake of disciples who possess even coarse intellects. When the power of the Lord [as darkness] acts as an obstructer, yet its intensity is slightly diminished, these signs appear in embodied beings.
"Self-nature consciousness is [that which is taught]...

thus it is said; and the characteristics of the excellent Guru are stated in the Āgamas: "One who is skilled in the meaning of the Vidyāpāda, who has mastered the sequence of the Kriyāpāda, who has practiced the Yogapāda, and who follows the Caryāpāda—[such a one is the teacher of] the Śiva-śāstra."

"The other is eternally intent on worship and the fire-sacrifice. Regarding that, the Lord (īśa)—the Supreme Lord Śiva—resides within that Guru as the nature of the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*), because no one other than Śiva possesses the capacity for the specific function of binding (*pāśa*). The meaning is that it is Śiva alone who, having taken the mere teacher (*ācārya*) as his locus or substratum, is the liberator from bonds. And it has been said: "Having assumed the form of the teacher..."

One who has been struck by the fourth descent of power (*śaktipāta*) is graced by the Blessed Lord; he alone [graces] all others as well. For this very reason, it is established that the excellent Guru is the very nature of Śiva.
And it has been said: "He who is the Guru is declared to be Śiva; he who is Śiva is the Guru."

The Guru is remembered as either Śiva himself or as Śiva abiding in the form of Vidyā; as is Śiva, so is Vidyā, and so is the Guru. Through the worship of Śiva, Vidyā, and the Guru, the fruit is equal. For he is the embodiment of all deities, and the Guru is composed of all mantras. Therefore, in every way, one should bear his command upon one's head. For the sake of knowing his true nature, [one should go] to the presence of the Guru.

For the disciple who has departed from the bonds, by means of the power of the mantra-based initiation (*māntrī-dīkṣā*)— preceded by the *kaṇḍa* and *maṇḍala* rites— which effects the cutting of the knots in the thread of the bonds through the agency of the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*) acting as a scissor upon its own nature, [the impurity of] *mala*, *māyā*, and *karman* [is removed].

Having performed the act of bestowing [the state], it is said that the power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*) resides in the agent, just as the fetters [are dissolved]. She is the supreme, subtle, and ultimate awakener of mantras for the agent. [In the case] of the most excellent teacher, that state of Śiva (*śivatva*), which is the very nature of Śiva, is fully manifested and clearly shown; here, the term "Śiva," used in its general sense, refers to the state of Śiva (*śivapada*).

According to the descent of power (*śaktipāta*)—whether mild or otherwise—he leads [the soul] to, that is, causes it to attain, the station or state of the Rudras, the Mantreśas, the Vidyeśas, or of Śiva. And it has been said: "[They become] partakers of the state of Rudra, Mantreśa, Pati, or Īśāna."

They become [disciples]. He who, having relied upon a Guru, bestows the initiation of consciousness (*cid-dīkṣā*) during the state of stability—that disciple, purified by such initiation, is called by the names Samayin, Putraka, and Sādhaka. [He should practice] the conduct of the rule (*samayācāra*), which causes the destruction of the limbs of bondage; "limb" refers to that which constitutes the daily and occasional rites, while "destruction of bondage" refers to the conduct of the rule that effects the dissolution of the bonds of impurity (*mala*) and so forth.

One should practice the conduct prescribed by one's own established doctrine and maintain it through performance; however, for those who have received initiation with seed (*sabījadīkṣita*), in the event of a transgression of the rules of conduct (*samayācāra*),
there is the penance for falsehood (*anṛtaprāyaścitta*).

Because one attains the state of a *piśāca*, it is said: "By violating the conduct of the *samaya*, one goes to the state of a Śaiva *piśāca*. Furthermore, the conduct of the *samaya* as taught in the *Āgamas* is as follows:

[omitted] ... for the practitioner (*sādhaka*), especially, it is declared by the command of Śiva to be performed constantly and in due order throughout one's life: bathing, worship, recitation (*japa*), meditation (*dhyāna*), and fifthly, the fire-oblation (*homa*).

In this manner, [the limb] is proclaimed again as being always [present]... on the eighth and the fourteenth days of both fortnights, at the end of the fifteenth day, at the moment of a solar transit (*saṃkrānti*), during the southern course of the sun (*dakṣiṇāyana*), when a month is pierced [by an intercalary day], when there is an excess of days, at the beginnings of the *ṣaḍaśīti* periods, and likewise during eclipses of the sun and moon; and in the *cāturmāsya* period as well, the vow and the recitation (*japa*) and other rites shall be twofold.

One should eat only a measured amount of sacrificial food on the eighth and fourteenth lunar days, and never eat [at those times]. Thus has the obligatory component been stated; now the occasional component is being described: initiation (*dīkṣā*) and consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*).

The occasional (*naimittika*) [rite] is to be known as...; the constant (*nitya*), the occasional, and the optional (*kāmya*)—these three have been declared for the teacher (*ācārya*), and the Guru likewise must perform these three. Furthermore, the exposition (*vyākhyāna*) must be performed by the instructor (*deśika*). The constant [practice]... according to one's own scripture, together with the six-faced [deity] as taught in the *Śāstra*, is thus proclaimed for both the initiate (*samayin*) and the spiritual son (*putraka*). One should perform what is prescribed in one’s own *Śāstra* and should not cause another’s *Śāstra* to be performed, nor should one revile it. The reason... [is that]... (p63b, l1).

One should not step over the shadow of the *liṅga*, nor that of one who possesses the eightfold [attainments], nor of a teacher, nor of a practitioner (*sādhaka*). One initiated by Śiva (*śivadīkṣita*) should not give away the remains of offerings (*nirmālya*).
Worship of Śiva and the Guru must be performed as long as one lives. One should never pass by a *liṅga* whose top is bare; such are the rules of conduct (*samayācāra*).
"By those seeking the welfare of Pālani... Śiva," thus [it is said]. (Ka) 1.
And she, perfected through her own lineage and birth...

(l3) ...performing even a fraction [of the rite] with great effort, having atoned for that [fault], at the end, with her mind fixed on Śiva, she attained the state of Śiva; having pervaded the entire world and become supreme, equal to Śiva, she was not surpassed by him... (l4)

The love for Śaṅkara, which is the sovereign of all and filled solely with its own bliss, remains [within him]. Thus, one who has been consecrated by the initiation of Śiva and observes the conduct of the rules attains the state of Śiva at the end of the body; so it is said: "By one's own tradition" (*svāmnāya*) means the practice established through the knowledge of one's own tradition. One's own tradition (*svāmnāya*) is the tantra of one's own established doctrine, such as the *Kāmika* and others; by the knowledge of that...

Because it is an instruction on the Dharma, this is established as "the Dharma" through the cognition prescribed by the established tenets; thus, it is determined that this practice— the performance of obligatory (*nitya*) and occasional (*naimittika*) rites and so forth— is complete, free from omissions whether performed intentionally or unintentionally.

One should act in such a way as it ought to be, performing [it] by means of its actual practice; the word "and" (*ca*) is intended to indicate the performance of what is prescribed in the Vedas and other scriptures, for that performance is stated in the *Āgamas*. Likewise, in the [section on] the *kāraṇa*... (l8)

Whatever may occur during the performance of duties established by the Śruti, Smṛti, and other sources—whether in obligatory acts, in purification, bathing, or sipping water; in the twilight worship, or in the offering of libations; in rites such as the study of the Vedas and their purificatory ceremonies, or even in the Soma sacrifice and the like; in the sacraments beginning with conception, or in cremation and the ancestral śrāddha rites; or even in the performance of the Aṣṭakā festival.

Whether it be the obligatory (*nitya*) or occasional (*naimittika*) rites, or whatever is prescribed for the twice-born in the performance of Vedic sacrifices and the like— all that must indeed be performed; however, Śaiva practice need not necessarily be performed, provided that [whatever is done] does not conflict with Śaiva ritual action.
"If there is a contradiction, one should abandon [the former], but one must not abandon the Śaiva; rather, everything Vedic should be accepted in accordance with the Śaiva words.

Likewise, in the *Mohaśūrottara*: "The Vedas, Smṛtis, Purāṇas, and so forth are teachers of dharma through the Āgamas; the Śaiva word is both general and particular, indeed specific. This is the practice of the Śrutis and the practice of the Śaivas.

This has been stated specifically for those initiated according to the worldly path (*lokadharmī*), and not for those initiated according to the Śiva-path (*śivadharmin*) who follow the Vedic tradition; for them, the performance of Śaiva rites alone is mandatory,
having abandoned worldly [practices].

Because it is stated that "the Cāraśivadharmiṇī [is the path]," and because of the statement, "The root of the Śivadharmiṇ is the locus of the fruits of Śiva-dharma," the injunction "having first performed the Vedic [rites], one should thereafter practice the Śaiva [rites]" refers to those who follow the worldly path (*lokadharmin*). However, another, whose nature is dispassionate and who is turned away from worldly objects, may perform the Brāhmi [rite] or may not perform it.

"Exclusively Śaiva by necessity" (l8)—this statement refers to the subject matter [of the specific ritual]. However, regarding the performance of the Vedic *sandhyā*, there is an optional statement based on personal choice. But the other [type of person], whose nature is dispassionate (*virāga*) and who is primarily intent upon worldly matters, is [described as] *bhau*...

In the same way, the lifelong celibate (*naiṣṭhika*) should perform [the rites] for the sake of Brahman, whether previously [done] or not; however, [the rites] of Śiva must be practiced according to the rules, because it is said: "They are to be observed by those striving with effort. Regarding their violation, there is a distinction between intentional and unintentional:

here, the intentional (*sakāma*) is a transgression committed out of one's own will, while the unintentional (*akāma*) occurs due to being under the control of others, such as gods and so forth. And it is said: "Due to a god, illness, delusion, or through fear of kings, thieves, and the like—by these..."

Non-desire [for action] arises from the remaining defects; however, desire is to be understood as the absence of knowledge regarding the scriptures and so forth—namely, the lack of understanding that "this action must be performed in this manner. By its expiation—that is, by the expiation of that lapse in conduct—...

The meaning is that this expiation (*prāyaścitta*) is the performance of the scriptural injunctions for the purpose of fulfilling the requirement of this omission; "wealthy" (*āḍhya*) means prosperous, which is to say, endowed with the means for expiation. Thus it is said:

"Expiation must be performed as prescribed in the scriptures and taught by the Guru; otherwise, his initiation (*dīkṣā*), the ritual section (*karmakāṇḍa*), and his final state at the end—when life comes to its conclusion—will be fruitless."

With the mind fixed on Śiva, as stated in the first verse, one should— by means of the recitation of the *prāsāda* mantra— imagine oneself as the nature of the *nāda* residing in the *mūlādhāra*, through the process of abandoning the lords who are the causes, such as Brahmā and the others, starting from the locations of the heart and so forth;
[this occurs] by means of the piercing of the *brahmarandhra* (or *rudrarandhra*).

With his mind established in the state of immovability as Śiva—by means of the contemplation of piercing the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*) and by means of the contemplation of union with Paraśiva residing at the "end of the twelve" (*dvādaśānta*)—he dies, that is, his vital breaths have departed.
Thus it is stated in the *Triśatikālottara* (p. 65a, l. 1):
Having assumed the lotus posture (*padmāsana*) or whatever position is comfortable, and having fixed the mind upon the crown of the head, one should slowly recite the Lord (*Hara*) with the mind.
Having drawn [the breath] from the external strength while remaining composed, O Rudra...

(l2) ...one should cause it to run toward the tip of Kuṇḍalinī, which has the luster of a debt (*ṛṇaprabha*). Then, having performed the *hitkā* sound, one should worship and project the wind of Skanda.

Having pressed the [channel] situated in the ear upward... (l3) by that [means], it has gone to the *svastika*; above that is Sadāśiva, and above him is the pervasive *nāda*. Having abandoned the *bindu-nāda* above that, one should then follow the *śakti*.
Having abandoned the *śakti*, one should go to the end, to supreme Śiva. (l4)

"The cause by which [the soul] does not arise again in any state of existence—this, O son, is what is called *pratijñāna*; thus, O one of good vows, the *utkrānti* has been briefly explained to you. Such is the practice of meditation upon Time (*kāla-dhyāna*) at the end of life for one who is incapable [of other means]. All of this must be performed on behalf of that incapable person by a teacher or others.
Likewise, at the time of the departure [of the soul], one should recite—especially the Śiva-mantra or the five-syllabled mantra (*pañcākṣara*)—well-joined to the vicinity of the ear;

all this should be performed by either the preceptor (*deśika*) or another. The "final sacrifice" (*antyayāga*) is the consecration (*saṃskāra*) prescribed for the body of one who has departed [from life].

The *antyeṣṭi* (final rite); therefore, having obtained the state of Śiva through that which is final (*antyā*), he has attained it. Now, [an objection]: it is not tenable that the state of Śiva comes from the final sacrifice (*antyayāga*), because the state of Śiva was already attained previously at the time of initiation (*dīkṣā*) through the severing of the bonds (*pāśaccheda*). To this, the following is the resolution: [it applies] to one who, in the period immediately following initiation, has committed a lapse in the conduct of the rules (*samayācāra*) arising from ignorance, and who, due to that very ignorance, has not performed the expiation (*prāyaścitta*).

Keeping in mind that for one who has been initiated (*dīkṣita*), the final sacrifice (*antyeṣṭi*) must be performed for the sake of purification, it is stated in the Āgamas: "Therefore, for those who properly perform the daily rites (*nitya*) and so forth, the final sacrifice should be performed using only the Śiva-fire, omitting the final sacrifice accompanied by [ordinary] purification."

However, for those who have failed in their proper conduct (*samācāra*), it is stated that the reality is not attained and the final rite (*antyeṣṭi*) must be performed with purification. Likewise, in the *Kāmika*: "Whether they be teachers (*ācārya*), practitioners (*sādhaka*), spiritual sons (*putraka*), or those established in the observance (*samayin*), when their final rites are to be performed by the initiated, these three—beginning with the teacher—if they are devoid of proper conduct and do not perform penance..."
And for those who have died, having properly performed the funeral rites (*antyeṣṭi-karman*)—

having correctly carried out the daily and other obligatory rituals (*nityādi-karman*) while avoiding what is prohibited— and for those who are thus free from negligence, it is said that there is a "mere funeral rite" (*kevalāntyeṣṭi*) even apart from the purification of the elements (*tattva-śuddhi*). This is because [it is taught] that the attainment of Śiva follows for one whose self (*ātman*) has been [thus] purified.

He speaks of the moment (*kṣaṇa*): by way of pervasion (*vyāpti*), that is, by way of being the pervader (*vyāpakatva*)—through the absence of such qualities as being a limited knower of only a portion of the universe—and through the attainment of omniscience (*sarvajñatva*) and so forth, he is one who has attained knowledge of the creator of the entire universe.
By this [it is shown that] he possesses qualities such as omniscience (*p66a, l1*). [These qualities are:
omniscience, contentment, beginninglessness, sovereignty, eternal unimpaired power, and infinite power. For this very reason, he is equal to Paramaśiva.

"Having a form equal to Paramaśiva"—by this it is indicated that [his] knowledge is eternally pure; for, as stated by those with the vision of bound souls (*paśu*), due to their connection with fetters (*pāśa*), they lack equality with Paramaśiva. And it has been said in other Tantras: [omission].

The knowledge derived from the authoritative scripture (*āptavākyāgama*) proclaimed by the omniscient Supreme Śiva is alone the cause of the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*). And it is said in the *Raurava*:
"For the sake of the enjoyment and liberation of bound souls (*paśu*), the Authoritative One [acted]...
when he uttered the authoritative word, that authoritative word is the scripture (*āgama*)."
And likewise, in the *Vāyupurāṇa*, in the dialogue between Upamanyu and Kṛṣṇa, it is stated that the knowledge taught in the Śivāgama is indeed the supreme knowledge:

"This Śivāgama was spoken by Śiva, the venerable Śrīkaṇṭha, to Śivā; out of compassion for those who take refuge in Śiva, it is the means for attaining the highest good. Thus, while there is equality between the liberated souls and Śiva, [the text continues] regarding Śiva...

To the question "What is the distinction?", he says: although [the individual soul] is capable—by virtue of its equality with Śiva—in performing the fivefold acts (*pañcakṛtya*), it is not a sovereign lord (*īśitā*) over creation, maintenance, withdrawal, concealment, and grace; for these are the desired powers of lordship (*iṣṭaiśvaryāṇi*). (l7) Therein, the state of being a non-lord (*anīśitā*) exists. The creation, maintenance, destruction, concealment, and liberation of the world—this alone is the object of knowledge, which is the fruit of the entire range of causal factors (*kāraka*).
Based on the statement of the *Hitivacana*, even ignorance [is established] solely by His grace as the attainment of one's own true nature (*svarūpalābha*).

The intention is that the beginninglessness of Śiva has already been stated. He is filled with his own singular bliss; he is the self-existent Lord, primarily full of natural bliss, surrounded by all the liberated ones—that is to say, together with them.

The meaning is that by virtue of this equality with Paraśiva, there exist many liberated souls (*muktātmānaḥ*). "Delight in Śaṅkara" means satisfaction equal to that of Śiva; he "abides" or remains [in that state], signifying that through this there is no returning to rebirth and so forth.

By the boon granted by the Goddess (Dyo-dita-varayā), the Siddha shines at the summit in the *Mṛgendra* Śaiva [tantra]. In the creation of the liberated, the Lord is superior to the other male [liberated] beings, having supported all misfortunes of the universe by his own splendor, [the splendor] of all the Lords.
"But it is always mixed," [it is said]. ||2||

Afflicted by the long duration of the great afflictions of existence and by pains that ripen with extreme intensity, he has no desire for even the slightest inquiry as to "when will there be liberation from Śambhu? Therefore, O Śicinvaka, draw me out from this belly; may you have the power to unite me here with the incomparable state of Śiva.

Having reached this abode of impurity, one whose bonds are severed and who is divested of his own limited body attains the state of Śiva immediately. First, through the descent of power (*śaktipāta*) that brings about the cessation of the ripening of intense impurity, one receives the initiation for immediate liberation (*sadyonirvāṇadīkṣā*). Having [previously] released those belonging to all categories of objects, now, when the impurity of the *vijñānākala*, *pralayākala*, and *sakala* has reached its most intense ripening, through the most intense descent of power, they attain the state of Śiva immediately. Immediately...

He says "exceedingly" (*atyartham*) by way of introducing the initiation into *nirvāṇa*. (.... In the middle, when there is an exceedingly great, ultimate, intense ripening, or even more intense ripening—the word "and" (*ca*) is for the purpose of [indicating] an even more intense descent of power (*śaktipāta*). Now, [one might ask]: "Is it not the case that the descent of power occurs when there is equality of karma in one who is a locus of pure being (*sattva-pralaya*...)? For the *vijñānākala*, karma ends with speech; he is [therefore... (l2)"

How is it so? As for what was said—that for one who has transcended the stage of consciousness (*vijñānākala*) there is no karma—that means he lacks that which is merely a magical instrument (*māyīyakaraṇa*). Is it not the case, then, that there is a total exhaustion of all phenomena (*dharma*)? Therefore, it is simply the fruit of some prior karma. For him, the state of having transcended consciousness (*vijñānākala-avasthā*) is the cause; and even for that [state], because it is like a sudden flash of light, it is indeed powerful in its manifestation. Due to his possession of a subtle body (*sūkṣmaśarīrin*), karma is difficult to perceive.

It should be understood that equality [of all beings] exists due to the cause of the descent of power (*śaktipāta*). Otherwise, because there would be no descent of power for one who is devoid of consciousness (*vijñāna*), there would be an absence of initiation (*dīkṣā*); and due to the absence of initiation, there would be an absence of liberation.
Initiation alone liberates [the soul] upward into the state of Śiva.

Since it has been stated that "it also leads one to the abode," and because it is said that "initiation occurs through the descent of power" (śaktipāta), [the text continues]: "Afflicted by the length of the great suffering of existence. Here, "existence" (bhava) refers to saṃsāra; its "great suffering" (mahākleśa) is a great disease.

Afflicted by the "length" (dairghya) of that [suffering], he is pained. For this very reason, he reflects: "At what time, at which moment, will my liberation from Śambhu, the Great Lord (Maheśvara), come to pass? Thus he contemplates.

Reflecting on this very point, he is indifferent—devoid of desire—for the maintenance of his own body (*svadehadhāraṇe*) within his own form; for among these three kinds of selves, what man or what power whatsoever here in these worlds during our time could [liberate] me from this saṃsāra? Thus... in this world... [he remains].
Having reflected and considered that Śambhu is capable of uniting [the soul] with the state of Śiva— the station of Śiva which is free from all inequality—
and having attained this Śambhu who is able to deliver one from saṃsāra,

(l2) being one whose entire fetter has been severed and who is devoid of his own body, he goes and departs at that very moment, immediately after the cutting of the fetters and the abandonment of his body.

In this context, it should be understood that what has been stated primarily concerns those who have attained the state of Śiva immediately through the descent of an extremely intense *śaktipāta*— namely, the *vijñānākala*s and *pralayākala*s; however, for the *sakala*s, it applies generally, as does [the statement] regarding the *vijñānākala*s and *pralayākala*s.

Because the body is the object of enjoyment for the karma that has already begun to bear fruit (*prārabdha-karma*), the descent of power (*śaktipāta*) occurs for some with a slow or slower intensity, and for others with a sharp or sharper intensity, according to the intended gradations of time and the equilibrium of karma.
Thus, due to the manifold nature of the descent of power, the attainment of Śiva-hood for all [souls] is indeed common [to all].

Likewise, because it has been stated that the Lord bestows grace upon all through the descent of power (*śaktipāta*) by assuming the form of a teacher—just as the illustrious Varuṇaśiva did—[he acts] in the fourth [way]. ||3||

Some, having been ripened by [the guru] beginning with Mandara, and having obtained a remnant of memory regarding the time and portion [of their practice], through the worship of the *liṅga* and so forth, [attain] the state of the fallen...
(l7) ...and those who, having joined the Raudra and Aiśa levels with worldly [practices], sacrifice to the Lords after death and become satisfied in this world, their seed...
(p68a, l1) ...they attain Śiva-hood directly by the teachers of the worlds. Now, for all [these], according to the division of the stages of power (*śaktipāta*)... (l2)

He states that by means of the ritual procedures for initiation (*dīkṣā*) such as the *samaya* [initiation] and others, the levels of Rudra and so forth are attained: "By the dull and so forth. When there is maturation—due to the darkness of impurity (*mala*)—by means of the dull, very dull, and very intense [degrees], the descent of power (*śaktipāta*) occurs as dull and so forth. Now, regarding the signs of the dull and other descents of power:
the sign of the very intense descent of power is the falling of the body immediately after initiation; the sign of the intense descent of power is fainting immediately after initiation.

For one whose descent of power (*śaktipāta*) is mild, there is trembling of the body after initiation; for one whose descent of power is mild in relation to the body, there is horripilation after initiation. And it has been said: "With respect to the fruit of destiny which is equal [for all], there is intensity [of descent] as fourfold—intense, mild, very mild, and [extremely mild]; [the signs are] immediate fainting, trembling, and horripilation, respectively. (l4–l5)

Having thus understood the descent of power (*śaktipāta*) as being mild (*manda*) and so forth, the various types of initiation (*dīkṣā*) should be performed: for one who is very mild (*mandatara*), the initiation of observance (*samayadīkṣā*) should be performed; for the mild, the specific initiation (*viśiṣṭadīkṣā*); for the intense (*tīvra*), immediate liberation (*sadyonirvāṇā*); and for the very intense (*tīvratara*), immediate liberation.

[The initiation] for the mild should be performed by the Guru from a mild location, according to the descent of power, because the disciple deserves grace. Thus, the fetter (*pāśa*) is also called *vrātī* and *vratarāc*.

Regarding the distinction of exhaustion: when cessation occurs immediately, that very [intensity] is considered "more intense" (*tīvratarā*), because it has been stated that for a person who does not live [to see the result], there is a different [kind of intensity] which effects the purification of bonds (*pāśaviśodhikā*). Now, if it is asked: "Since signs such as the falling of the body are to be known after initiation (*dīkṣā*), how are they to be known prior to initiation?"—thus it was said by the Guru.

By means of knowledge of one's own capacity and by observing the external actions of the disciple, [the signs] are to be known through knowledge; otherwise, a fault arises for the guru, and there is a loss of the disciple’s accomplishments (*siddhi*) and so forth. And it has been said: "Wherever the descent of power (*śaktipāta*) has fallen, there accomplishment (*siddhi*) arises. [But] without [that], there is no wisdom, no conduct of Śiva, no liberation, nor the [other] accomplishments. Therefore, having observed the signs of the descent of power, [one should proceed] further by means of knowledge.

Or else, by means of ritual action (*kriyā*), the teacher should purify the disciples; he who performs [this] elsewhere [is one who... (l2) ...the evil-minded one perishes. Therefore, in every way, one should examine the teacher and the disciples; having placed the superior in inferior [tasks] and the lowly in superior rites, even those who are drawn away or beaten may fall into despair. They are fit for stability... (l3) ...[and so forth].

Among the Śūdras who are eligible for the rite of Śiva-initiation (*śivasamskārakarma*), some—being progressively slower and more dull-witted than others—receive from the Guru the initiation known as *samaya*, which is the purification called *samaya*. Those who are even more dull-witted receive an initiation characterized by a certain specific feature within that *samaya*-purification. For those who are merely dull enough to require only the *samaya* [initiation], having first performed the *samaya*-purification, the specific purification is then carried out.
For the purpose of indicating that it is a duty (*kārya*),

[the word] "the remaining" (*śiṣṭām*) contains the pronoun *tat*. Therefore, because one has the exclusive entitlement (*adhikāra*) to the obligatory rites (*nityakarman*) through the worship of the Liṅga and so forth, one is bound by the obligatory duties— namely, the prescribed worship of Śiva, bathing, the twilight prayers (*saṃdhyā-vandana*), recitation (*japa*), and the daily fire-ritual (*agnikārya*)— for as long as life lasts.

The remainder of the meaning is as follows: having performed the worship of Śiva and other rites, those who have abandoned their bodies—the *samayins* and the *viśiṣṭasamayins*—attain, respectively, the *raudra* state connected with Rudra and the *aiśa* state connected with Īśvara.

Thus it has been stated by Varuṇaśiva: "Where there is yoga in the state of Rudra, and where there is yoga in the state of Īśvara, but where there is no cutting of the topknot (*śikhāccheda*), that is the initiation of the *samayin*."
[The teacher] says, "I desire [to initiate you]. In the *Kāmika*: "There is fitness for the daily ritual (*nityakarman*) for one who has not undergone the cutting of the topknot (*śikhāccheda*).

Those who are endowed with an intense descent of power (*tīvraśaktipāta*), who were previously purified by the two specific initiatory consecrations (*samaya-viśeṣasaṃskāra*), and who were subsequently joined to the worldly [initiation] and the initiation of liberation (*nirvāṇadīkṣā*)... [the rest follows].

Those virtuous ones, through the excellent worship of the Lord—the Supreme Sovereign—by performing proper rites such as adoration, and having performed [these] until the end of their lives, attain in the world of purity, at the conclusion of their existence, the enjoyments situated in that pure realm. Having been initiated by the Maruts (the gods), who are born of the worlds and possessed of wisdom, out of dispassion—that is, due to the absence of desire for enjoyment—they directly and perceptibly attain the state of Śiva. And it has been said:

Purified by initiation, those born into the maṇḍala of Gaṇapati and the Guru, having attained perfection from the Siddhas through this succession of the solar maṇḍala, shall possess bodies free from disease. Having enjoyed pleasures for a very long time accompanied by hosts of celestial nymphs, their longing subsided, they become partakers of the sovereignty of the state of Supreme Śiva. 4.

One who, having received initiation into the domain of the auspicious state (*śivapada*)—which is free from various deficiencies—and thereafter practices the mixed conduct (*caryāmiśra*) with devotion, yet falls into transgression regarding it, goes at the end to the attainment of a flesh-eater (*kravyāda*). Even if he were equal to one who has performed a hundred [sacrifices], he shall eat [flesh] at the end, [and his face]... (l5)

Those who are deficient in their observances (*samaya*), have fallen from their commitments, or are full of doubt, lead [themselves to ruin]. One who is endowed with a perfect initiation (*dīkṣā*) and performs the observances and other rites without obstacle reaches the state of Śiva, even if he practices unintentionally.

One who is eloquent and has performed the required penance goes to the state of Śiva immediately after attaining the state of a *piśāca*. For those whose initiation is deficient, the state of Śiva is never attained.
He says that it is possible: "Various... (l7) ... "The person who... (l7) ... "various, free from deficiency. By the word "deficiency," the lack of the components of initiation (*dīkṣā*) is meant;
and that [lack] pertains to the person for whom the descent of power (*śaktipāta*) is very slight, regarding [his attainment of] *nirvāṇa*... (l8)

And [there is] the omission of mantras, rituals, and the arts (*kalā*). Thus, having obtained initiation (*dīkṣā*) which is free from such various defects and is directed toward the feet of Śiva— indeed, that which leads to the attainment of the feet of Śiva—
and having gone [to the teacher],

one should perform the conduct (*caryā*) consisting of the obligatory and occasional rites prescribed by the rule (*samaya*), with devotion to the Supreme Lord (*Parameśvara*) and with the understanding that "the performance of worship is for the sake of [attaining] the Lord."

He practices and performs the observance of the rules of conduct (*samayānuṣṭhānācaraṇa*); he proceeds and goes toward the specific state of Śiva-ness. Its violation is the abandonment of the rules of conduct and so forth.
For one who has abandoned the practice of the rules intentionally and for whom no penance has been performed, there is the rite of the final oblation (*antyeṣṭikarman*).
It should be understood that the word "iti" has been used for the purpose of indicating that [the purification occurs] through the abandonment of the convention established by the intellect.

For if purification were to occur through the final sacrifice (*antyeṣṭi*) after one has performed the penance prescribed by the intellect, there would follow the undesirable consequence of rendering the scriptures on penance (*prāyaścitta-śāstra*) meaningless; furthermore, this is because it would contradict the scriptural injunction stating that one becomes a *piśāca* by transgressing the convention. Therefore, by transgressing the convention...

He says that there is the attainment of the state of a *piśāca*: at the end, at the time of the relinquishing of life, through the pervasion by a flesh-eater (*kravyāda*), being equal to a hundred [years]—that is, having forgotten the years by way of a count of a hundred—he remains as such for the duration of a hundred years. (l5–l6)

And the meaning is that one attains the state [of Śiva]. And it has been said: "Due to the transgression of the rule (*samaya*), the state of being a flesh-eater (*kravyāda*) is declared for a hundred years. Through eating—that is, through communal feasting—at the end, at the conclusion, one attains the state of Śiva. Even those possessed of deficiencies—deficiency in initiation (*dīkṣā*) being the omission of its primary and secondary limbs; accompanied by that, yet not deficient in initiation in every respect—the mere deficiency...

Because it is logical that even for those who have received the initiation into isolation (*kaivalya-dīkṣā*), the state of Śiva exists through the performance of the rules of conduct (*samaya-ācāra*); this should be understood because the performance of the rules prevents deficiency. And it has been said:
"Those who are established in initiation and knowledge..."

Devoted to the worship of the *liṅga*, they go to the abode of Hara, which brings the bliss of all sovereign powers; O Goddess, those who have fallen from their commitment (*samaya*), who have strayed from proper conduct, and who harbor doubts while performing virtuous deeds, nevertheless go to Śiva and thereafter ascend, being gazed upon by Śrīkaṇṭha. Thus it is said. Those who have fallen from their commitment, who have strayed from proper conduct, and who are full of doubt while the performance of good deeds is being carried out—[they too attain this].

"By whom has it been seen whether the fruit arising from the collection of purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) performed through ritual action exists or does not exist?"—by this [question], the meaning is that those who construct that [body] are in doubt; because of their doubt regarding the fruit of action, they lack a decisive cognition when performing the practice. Those who [have received] initiation... (l5)

Those who are joined with doubts regarding deficiencies, time, and conduct do not attain the principle of Śiva (śivatattva); they do not go [there], but rather remain within the cycles of worldly existence (saṃsāra)—this is the meaning. ||5||

If one brings this mantra— which has six parts, whose support is the Īśa [cakra] at the beginning of the bud-like apertures of the mouth, and which enters the fourth abode— in sequence, and sprinkles it twice with the nectar of its grace, then at the end, she proceeds to her desired goal.

The wise Manu has declared that for those who have been initiated as previously described, for the teachers who practice the Niṣkala-prāsāda [mantra], the mantra "Namaḥ Śivāya" along with the Tāra [Om] is to be recited for Śambhu.

He states that there is an intermediate state consisting of the nature of the splendor of Paraśiva. Regarding the word "mantra": here, because it is primary in the Śivasiddhāntas, the term "mantra" refers to the Prāsāda-mantra.
The intended [subject] is the resonance (*nāda*) of the palace...
the mantra which has arisen from Paraśiva; from *nāda* comes the *bindu*, from the *bindu* the primordial vowel, and from that all the phonemes (*varṇa*) have arisen—such is the sequence.
Likewise, in the *Kāmika*: "Resonance is said to be the low tone (*mandra*). It is that... (p70b, l1–l2).

Sound (*nāda*) is born from the Supreme; from that sound, the Bindu is produced; from the Bindu arises the first vowel (*ā*). From that [vowel] come two pairs of vowels; through their divisions, there are fourteen vowels.

The sixteen known as the "living ones" (*jīva*), beginning with *ka*, are the path of the body; in number they are thirty-four, and these indeed are the consonants (*vyañjana*). By them alone is the scripture composed.

Distinguished by the higher and the lower, the nine sections are indeed called *nāda*, containing within them the fifty seed-syllables (*bīja*). The word "mantra" is derived from two roots: in the sense of "knowing" (*manutve*) and "protecting" (*bodhane* / *rakṣaṇe*). Contemplation (*mananam*) is the meditation upon Supreme Śiva;
that Śiva is one's own self (*svādhyāya*).

The meaning of the word *mantra* is that which provides protection from the ocean of *saṃsāra* for all living beings who are not disciplined. For this very reason, the palace-mantra (*prāsāda-mantra*) is to be meditated upon; and it has been said: "Because it involves the contemplation (*manana*) of all the deities and because it provides protection (*trāṇa*) through the grace of the Lord, it is called a *mantra* due to its nature of possessing both contemplation and protection. By means of this [mantra], the six-syllable limbs, beginning with the heart, are joined with the long vowels.
The Niṣkala Prāsāda is indicated [here].

Since the Supreme Lord has as His body the syllables of the five Brahmans beginning with Īśāna, the Prāsāda that denotes Him is also possessed of parts (sakala). Therefore, in the Sakala Prāsāda, [the worship is performed] with the syllables of the limbs of Brahmā.

This chapter is composed by mixing [the two]. The Niṣkala-prāsāda chapter consists of the very same initial syllables. Likewise, in the venerable Kālottara: "The supreme Niṣkala mantra is Śiva himself, Sadāśiva manifest, bestowing enjoyment and liberation upon men, the all-pervasive Lord accompanied by the five limbs. Since it is devoid of the Netra-mantra, its status as having five limbs is appropriate; yet how can the Prāsāda [mantra] here be said to be "accompanied by the five limbs"?

If it is argued that this [mantra] possesses six syllables (*ṣaṭkala*), the rebuttal is as follows: because the cause— the letter *ha*— is situated above both the eye (*netra*) and the palace (*prāsāda*), and because it has been stated that the eye is the root which, having been included within the mantra,
is accompanied by the five limbs (*pañcāṅga*).

The expansion of the *prāsāda* into six syllables is indeed appropriate; for this very reason, those desiring liberation should meditate upon the *niṣkala-prāsāda* alone, because it has been said: "The short [form] burns away sins, while the long one bestows liberation. It is the support for the bud-like cavity of the mouth (*āsya-randhra-mukula*). By the word *adra*, the location of the drop (*bindu*) situated in the middle of the forehead is expressed. *Randhra*...

The term *mukula* refers to the *brahmarandhra*, meaning the lotus-bud situated at each respective location beginning with the heart. By the word *ādi*, the locations beginning with the *śakti* situated above the *brahmarandhra* are indicated. In these locations, [one should contemplate] the support (*ādhāra*) as the locus of the presiding presence (*adhiṣṭhāna*).

The meaning is that [the practitioner] should contemplate [this] according to his own capacity among those [states]. The *aiśam* (lordly) *dhāma* (abode), belonging to Paraśiva, is the fourth (*turya*) state situated at the location of the *dvādaśānta*.

By means of the sequence of abandoning the causal principles (*kāraṇa*) beginning with the directions, and by abandoning the locations beginning with the heart (*hṛdaya*), through the grace of that Paraśiva, by means of a long-lasting contemplative intellect (*bhāvanā-buddhi*), [one attains] the great boon all at once.

Entering together with the supreme Śiva-tejas, [the practitioner] should meditate upon the previously mentioned mantra; this is the remainder [of the instruction]. By this, the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*) is described. Thus, every day, by means of the nectar of the moon, [one should contemplate] the partless power (*niṣkalaśakti*) situated above the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*).

Sprinkled with the flowing nectar-essence—meaning drenched and consecrated both internally and externally—they proceed to, or go toward, their desired abodes in the worlds purified by the wind; at the end, that is, upon the conclusion of their enjoyment, they reach—that is the ellipsis—the splendor (*mahaḥ*) belonging to Paraśiva. For him, Śambhu, there is the excellent mantra *namaḥ śivāya* for the virtuous.

For the great-souled ones who have been initiated, that which is to be recited (*japya*)—accompanied by the *sāvara* [syllable] and the *oṃkāra*—is fit to be recited because it bestows supreme liberation; thus, the meaning here is that it is fit to be recited by one initiated into the Śiva-mantra. However, as for the *prāsāda* [mantra]...
"By means of recitation, all seven [types of] residual doubts [are removed]," according to the scripture. ||6||

He who utters the Root-syllable (*mūlāṇu*) up to its place of dissolution—having agitated the Śakti, the cause of the universe, which has flowed forth—he is purified by the streams of the flood of nectar [issuing] from that, until the end of the vital breath (*prāṇa*). (l7) By means of immersion in the center, he quickly reaches his own body through the channel; having emerged externally, he floats here within those internal stations. This is the mental bath (*mānasa-snāna*), which provides nourishment. He [the author] now describes the procedure for the mental bath for those who have been initiated. (p72a, l1)

Regarding the term *mūlāṇu*: the "root" (*mūla*) is the *mūlādhāra*. Therein resides the *aṇumantra*, which is the *prasāda* [mantra] ending at the point of dissolution (*layanānta*). This "point of dissolution" refers to the *dvādaśānta* (the twelve-finger space). For this very reason, it is well-known in the Āgamas that the nature of the *mūlāṇu* consists of its utterance (*uccāra*), beginning from the *mūlādhāra* up to the *dvādaśānta* according to the sequence of pronunciation. [This extends] through the heart, throat, palate, the middle of the eyebrows, and ending at the *brahmarandhra*, [corresponding to the stages of] Brahmā, Acyuta, Rudra, Īśvara, and Sadāśiva.

The "place" (*sthāna*) consists of the *mātṛkā* beginning with the letter *a*, which is to be abandoned by means of the sequential abandonment [of phonemes]. It is the location of the four *kalās*, beginning with *Śakti*, situated above the *brahmarandhra* and presided over by *Anāhata-Śiva*.
That is the twelve-finger space (*dvādaśānta*), which constitutes the seventh place ending with *unmanī*.

The meaning is that the initiated one who utters the root-atom (*mūlāṇu*)— which is presided over by Paraśiva and extends thus up to the point of dissolution— contemplates himself as having become one with Paraśiva through the sequence of uttering the root-mantra. (l5) Having "agitated" the cause from the "people"— that is, having caused the agitation of the Power (*śakti*) which is the material cause of the world, namely the Crooked Power (*kuṭilāśakti*)— he states the capacity for such agitation.

"Having restrained the vital breaths and remained" means having performed *prāṇāyāma* and remained; "by the streams of the flood of nectar flowing forth from that," meaning by the currents of the mass of nectar flowing from the agitated *śakti*, [he remains] in the midst, within the abundant waters of nectar.

One's own body [is purified] by smelling [the breath], from immersion, and from bathing; for this very reason, the burning of the body by the fire of yoga prior to that immersion is indicated by the statement:

"One should burn the body with the fire of yoga from the soles of the feet to the head. Having emerged externally through the *brahmanāḍī*, one places the self in the locations such as the heart, having immersed the body through the process of emanation (*sṛṣṭikrama*) via the channel.
The meaning is that he should settle [the mind] in this way. Thus, daily engaged in meditation, he floats, submerges, and causes to submerge within this gross body;
this mental [element], which is nourishing and serves as the means of immersion for the body, [is what is meant].
This is known as "bathing.

Likewise, in the sequence of ritual action (*kriyākrama*), while uttering the root mantra ending with *nādānta*, one should gradually contemplate oneself as being externally consecrated by streams of abundant nectar flowing from the agitated power (*kṣubdhaśakti*) that drenches one's own body and mind. (Verse 3)
Therefore, bathing should be performed in all circumstances. ||7||

One should meditate upon one's own body as a banyan tree (*nyagrodha*) with roots above: sown with the seeds of the elements, fashioned by Hari and Brahmā, having its own sprouts as its foundation, rooted in karma, auspicious, with time and the like as its pith, possessing sense-objects as its leaves, with the void (*kha*) and other elements as its branches and sub-branches, bearing flowers in the form of all states of being (*bhāva*), yielding excellent fruit that is yet concealed, to be enjoyed by the bird-like individual soul (*puruṣa*), and having its branches hanging downward toward the essence of sense-objects.

Now, he describes the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*) through the meditation on one's own body in the form of a banyan tree, beginning with the words "one's own body" (*svadeham*). Just as in the world, from a seed cast into a field there arises the production of sprouts and so forth—

Just as a gross form in the shape of a tree is seen gradually [emerging from a seed], so too he shows the nature of the body as being like a seed; this is stated with reference to the gross body, [meaning] it is the seed of the elements.
Likewise, in the *Siddhāntadīpikā*: "This gross body, which is the locus of pride regarding caste, family, and so forth, is a composite (*samavāya*) of earth, water, fire, air, ether, and the rest;
it is the seed of the senses, conjoined with the portions of the subtle elements. (p. 73a, l. 1)

It is well known that what is sown in a field arises in the form of a body. By means of the subtle and gross bodies, the seed is the *āṇavamala* (the innate impurity), and the field is *māyā*, consisting of the impurities (*mala*), *māyā*, and *kalā*. Because even the trees that are the bodies have been cast off [by the soul], it is "created by Hari and Vidhi"—meaning that because Brahmā is the agent of creation, the field is created; and because Viṣṇu is the agent of preservation, it is protected.
Just as a seed, through the processes of creation and preservation,
arises in the form of a sprout with karma as its root, and just as a tree, properly entering the earth at its root, comes to possess the forms of trunk and branches,
so too [does it arise] in accordance with the merit and demerit accumulated in previous births.

The body of a Brāhmaṇa and so forth; the sharpness of the senses; and that which carries fixed lifespan and determined enjoyment—thus is established the root-nature of karma. It is to be understood that in the subsequent time, the essence of the principles such as the future time (*bhaviṣyatkālādi*) remains, like the trunk and other parts of a tree. By the word "etc. (*ādi*), passion (*rāga*), sap (*niryūṣa*), the individual soul (*puruṣajīva*), and the great body of primordial nature (*prakṛtyādimahākāya*) are included, residing within the petals of the sense-objects (*viṣayadala*).
The sense objects such as sound,

which have descended into the receptacles of the sense objects such as sound, consist of the branches and sub-branches of the elements beginning with space; the organs of action and the organs of cognition themselves are, respectively, the branches and sub-branches—
the great branches and the small branches.

One should contemplate one's own body as being thus constituted: it is joined with the fifty previously mentioned emotional states (*bhāva*) which are its blossoms; these very *bhāvas* constitute all its flowers, which yield excellent fruit when matured. This fruit consists of the results of intellect, determination, and volition, fit to be enjoyed by the male bird [the individual soul]. It is a substance to be relished by the birds of the senses, possessing roots above and branches below—namely, those that extend downward—and is endowed with such a structure.
[In the case] of Nyagrodha [and so forth], one should meditate on it in the form of a banyan tree. ||8||

Reciting the *sāma* and other mantras through the pair of half-inhalations (*kumbhāpūraka*) and half-exhalations (*rekaka*), and accompanied by the sequence of qualities residing in the [elements] beginning with earth (*bhūḥ*) and joined with the application of the petals and so forth, he burns the sheath (*kośa*). By removing that ash, he becomes pure; not due to the absence of enjoyment, but being possessed of a mantra-body flooded by power (*śakti*), he should perform worship in the heart through the burning and flooding of the body and so forth.

Regarding the statement that one should perform mental worship after having established this [practice], he says "kumbha" and so forth. Here, the term *kumbhaka* (retention) was previously mentioned in order to avoid violating the meter; the sense is that because of the absence of *pūraka* (inhalation), it would have been impossible to prescribe *kumbhaka* alone. Thus, by the sequence of performance, there is half [of each] of *pūraka*, *kumbhaka*, and *recaka*.

By "pairs" (*yugalaiḥ*) is meant by the first half and the second half of the [verses] beginning with *pūraka*; however, the prior and posterior halves are to be understood according to time (*kāla*). For the time of *pūraka* and the others is threefold:
superior, middling, and inferior.

By way of division: having covered the knee-circle (*jānumaṇḍala*) with the hand to the extent of one *mātrā*, [the time] consisting of three snaps of the fingers (*choṭikā*) covering the knee-circle for one *mātrā* would be the *mātrā*; because it has been stated that [this is] preceded by three snaps of the fingers and so forth, the time called *tāla* consists of twelve such *mātrās*. For it has been stated that a *tāla* consists of twelve circumferences of the knee; thus, with twelve *tālas*, there is the *prāṇāyāma* of the youngest [level].
With twenty-four [counts] it is middling; with forty-eight it is superior.
Likewise, in the *Sarvajñānottara*, it is stated: "Twelve *tālas* should be known as the lowest *prāṇāyāma*; the middling is twenty-four *arccas*, and the best should be double that."
Prāṇāyāma consists of the aggregate of inhalation (*pūraka*), retention (*kumbhaka*), and exhalation (*recaka*).

Among these, inhalation lasts for twelve *mātrās*, as does the retention and the [exhalation] that follows; this is declared to be the "minor" (*kanīyasa*) prāṇāyāma, because it is stated that its duration is precisely twelve *mātrās*.

One view is that the time for each of the exhalation (*recaka*), inhalation (*pūraka*), and retention (*kumbhaka*) is equal. Likewise, in the *Kāmika*: "The middle [duration] is considered to be twice twelve *mātrās*, and the superior duration is three times [twelve]; this applies to each of the exhalations and so forth. Therefore, for the previously mentioned inferior breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*) measured by twelve *tālas*, the time for each of the inhalation, retention, and exhalation— [...is as follows:]... The measure of four *tālas* was thus produced. In this manner, over the course of time, the measure of the first half of the *yāma*-filling [breath] for the youngest [measure] was known to be two *tālas*; likewise, the measure of the latter half of the *kumbhaka* and *recaka* in their respective first and latter halves [was known].

In this very manner, the measure should be applied to the medium and superior [levels] as well; by means of that temporal measure, the duration of the inhalations (*pūraka*), retentions (*kumbhaka*), and exhalations (*recaka*) for the preceding and succeeding halves should be understood according to their sequence.

Thus, while reciting the *hlādi* mantras according to the measure of the preceding and succeeding halves of the aforementioned inhalations and so forth, here the letters *la*, *va*, *ra*, and *ha* are the seed-syllables (*bīja*) of earth and the other elements, respectively.

Likewise, in the [section on] the cause: earth and so forth are the seeds of the [syllables] *la* and so on, with a measure of half a *kāra*. Thus, the letter *la* joined with the heart-seed (*hṛdbīja*) and the bindu is the seed-syllable of the Nivṛtti-kalā. The letters *va-ra-ha-ka*, joined respectively with the seed-syllables of the Head, Crest, and Armor, are the [seeds of] Pratiṣṭhā and Śānti... [and so forth].

Nivṛtti is to be known as earth, born from the seeds of the kalās beyond Śānti; Pratiṣṭhā is said to be water; Vidyā consists of the seeds of fire; and Vāyu is proclaimed as Śānti. Since it is stated that "Śāntyatītā shall be space" (L4), [the elements] beginning with earth possess the qualities situated therein. The qualities existing (*sthita*) in the elements beginning with earth—namely earth, water, fire, air, and space—are possessed of a sequential order of stability (*sthiti*).
Smell, taste, form, touch, and sound—these are their [respective] abodes.

The stability of the elements, beginning with earth, consists of five, four, three, two, and one in number. Reciting them in such a way as to be joined with that sequence—that is, accompanied by the corresponding numbers—one should understand that earth possesses five qualities.

The meaning is that one should recite [the mantra] five times mentally for the sake of destruction. The recitation of the mantras for water and the other elements should be performed according to the number of their respective qualities. Regarding the phrase "endowed with the non-connection of leaves and so forth": this refers to the absence of connection (*ayoga*), that is, the lack of relation, between the coarse—such as leaves, flowers, and fruits—and the subtle, such as colors and so on. In this context, the intention is as follows: [this applies to] the *pūraka*...

Reciting five times the seed-syllable of the *nivṛtti-kalā* with the first half-verse for the destruction of the five qualities of the earth, one should meditate upon that tree as his own body, devoid of coarse leaves, flowers, fruits, and so forth; then, with the second half-verse, [one should recite] the seed-syllable of the *pratijñā-kalā* for the destruction of the four qualities of water during the *pūraka* [breath-retention].

Reciting [the mantra] four times, one should visualize it as endowed with fine leaves, flowers, and fruits; from the meditation on the remaining form as dry, by the burning away of the ashes and their removal... by the destruction of the root of the hell and the reduction to ashes, by the removal of those ashes and their casting in the ten directions while reciting the seed-syllable of the *vidyā-kalā* three times, for the destruction of the qualities of the elephant in the forest.

One should contemplate that [the body] is dried up by the Kālāgni fire arising from the big toe of the right foot during the first half of the *kumbhaka* (retention), and burnt during the second half. Then, during the first half of the *recaka* (exhalation), while uttering the seed-syllable of the *śāntikalā* twice for the twofold destruction of the wind (*vāyu*), one should cause it to become ashes and dissolve into the ten directions.
Thus purified, one is no longer subject to worldly enjoyments (*bhoga*).

The Vedic usage "vanāt śuddho nabhaḥ" (from the forest, pure as the sky) refers to the meditation on the stainless ether (*nirmalākāśa*). By means of the supreme *recaka* (exhalation), for the sake of destroying the qualities of the ether one by one, while reciting the seed-syllable of the *śāntyatīta-kalā* once, one should meditate upon the stainless ether, which has the color of pure crystal. Now, since the ether is formless, it is impossible for it to be the object of meditation; how then can it be "pure"?
It was stated [previously] that [the practice begins with] meditation (*bhāvanā*);

this is now explained: because the sky possesses a formal nature (*mūrtatva*) by way of the forms of the constellations and so forth existing within the interval between heaven and earth, it is the very essence of the object of meditation (*dhyeya*) through its conditioned form (*aupādhikākāra*). Therefore, those constellations...

Regarding the phrase "the direction" (*dīśā hi*), it has been stated that because space (*ākāśa*) possesses a stainless form, it exists as the very nature of that which is to be meditated upon; thus it is said, "pure space through meditation.

Likewise, in the *Niśvāsakārikā*: "One should contemplate the supreme void (*vyoman*), which is devoid of qualities, beyond the realm of the senses, free from planets and stars, and resembling pure crystal. By means of power—that is, the Supreme Power (*parā-śakti*)—with a thick stream of nectar flowing forth.

Having meditated upon the circle of power (*śaktimaṇḍala*) at the *dvādaśānta*— which is [complete with] its six aspects and consists of abundant nectar— one should, preceded by the *prāsāda* mantra, using the power ending in *vauṣaṭ* and through exhalation (*recaka*), [cause it to flow] via the path of emanation; then, by means of streams of abundant nectar flowing forth and entering the openings of all the channels (*nāḍī*), [one should perform the sprinkling].

Having bathed his entire body, both external and internal, and being endowed with the form of the mantra, he should perform worship—namely, the worship of Śiva—in the heart, within the lotus of the heart, having placed his body according to its proper order by means of the root-mantras, the Brahma-aṅgas, and the thirty-eight kalās. (9) May there be [protection] for you from Īśa, Aghora, Maheśvara, Tatpuruṣa, and Sadyojāta; from the Rudras, the Ghoras, and the Veda-crested ones; and from the stains, the stains, and the stainless ones, through the Vāmadeva mantra.
Indeed, [the syllables] *mo*, *ca*, *mi*, *mo* (15),

*tri*, *ṇī*, *tma*, *ṃ*, *va*, *dvi*, *ta*, *ya*, *ma*, *vi*, *ka*, *laṃ*, *sa*, *dyam*, *an*, *tre*, *kalā*, *nāṃ*, *pañcābdhiṃ*, *cāṣṭa*, *viśvo*, *pyahiḥ*— thus, according to their respective order, there are thirty-eight [syllables], including the eight [additional ones].

He states the sequence of mantras for the deposition of the thirty-eight kalās: "Īśa," etc. The deposition of the thirty-eight kalās is twofold, distinguished by being with power (*saśaktika*) or without power (*viśaktika*).
