The sequence of the deposition with power is: "Īśānaḥ sarvavidyānāṃ, śaśinyai namaḥ. (l7)

Śaśinī should have her head upward, and Aṅgadā should have her head facing east; this is the sequence of ritual action as stated in the *Kriyākramadyotikā*. Regarding the placement (*nyāsa*) prescribed by that method, in the case of the mantra for Īśāna (*īśe īśānamantre*), the word "nandvebhyām" is the genitive plural. Having first uttered that in its dual form up to the end of the suffix *-ān*, one should then utter the power (*śakti*) beginning with Śaśinī; this is what is taught.

The intended meaning is as follows: among the five [deities] beginning with Īśāna and Śaśin, first one should perform the recitation while satiating Īśāna—the Lord of all vidyās and the Lord of all beings—with the utterance "dviram tarpayantaṃ";
immediately thereafter, the kalās beginning with Śaśin are to be joined.

The word *bhū* should be understood to apply even further on; thus, *haḥ* refers to the Lord of Brahman (*brahmādhipati*), the overlord of Brahman, which is said to extend as far as *brahma* and as far as the utterance [of the mantra]. Immediately after that, one should join *iṣṭāyai namaḥ*, extending up to *astu śivo me*.
*Oṃ* extends up to *sadāśivoṃ*. In this way, the pronunciation of each syllable for the five parts of the *Īśāna-kalā* should be understood. He.
Thus, by means of the single syllable:

*iti* ending with *tatpuruṣāya vidmahe*, *hi* ending with *mahādevāya dhīmahi*, *dra* ending with *tanno rudra*, and *yām* ending with *pracodayāt*; [these correspond] to *nare* and *puruṣa*, which constitute the four parts of the *Tatpuruṣa*.

It is declared that [the mantra] ends with "bhyaḥ" twice; [the first part] ends with "aghorebhyaḥ," then [the second part] ends with "ghorebhyaḥ," [the third part] ends with "rutighorāḥ," [the fourth part] ends with "bhyaḥ," [the fifth part] ends with "ghoratarebhyaḥ," [the sixth part] ends with "śarva," [the seventh part] ends with "sarva," [the eighth part] ends with "bhyaḥ," [the ninth part] ends with "rudra," [the tenth part] ends with "namaste rudra," [the eleventh part] ends with "bhyaḥ," [the twelfth part] ends with "rūpebhyaḥ," and [the thirteenth part] ends with "śivebhyaḥ. And [it is said]: "O you who are terrible... [The rest is illegible].
By means of the Aghora mantra, thus [is formed] the eightfold Aghora-kalā. The four *makāras* are: "Salutation to Vāmadeva," "Salutation to Jyeṣṭha," "Salutation to Rudra," and "Salutation to Kāla";
these are taken as ending with the four *makāras*. [The syllable] *la*.

"Ma" up to "kala," "Namaḥ to the Vikaraṇa"—[this is the first]; "ma" up to "la," "Namaḥ to the Vikaraṇa"—[this is the second]; ending with "la," "ma" up to "bala," "Namaḥ to the Pramathana"—[this is the third]; ending with "ma," "ma" up to "sarvabhūtadamana," "Namaḥ"—[this is the fourth];
with the Vāmadeva mantra, "ma" up to "manas," "ma" up to "unmanas," "Namaḥ"—[this is the fifth]. Thus, there are thirteen kalās of Vāmadeva, ending with "ma."

The first [mantra] is taken as ending with *sadyojātaṃ prapadyāmi*, ending with *mā* [in] *sadyojātāya vai namaḥ*, ending with *ve*, ending again with *bhave*, and ending with *anādibhave*. The second [mantra] is taken as ending with *māṃ* [in] *bhajasva mām*, and there too, one [mantra] is prescribed as ending with *bhava* and *śaśinyai namaḥ*.

The meaning is that the *nyāsa* is "with powers" (*saśaktīka*). The *nyāsa* beginning with "Obeisance to Kevalaśaśinī" and so forth is "without powers" (*viśaktika*). He states the number and sequence of the *kalās*: five for Īśāna; four for Tatpuruṣa; eight for Aghora; thirteen for Vāmadeva; and eight for Sadyojāta.

The eight digits (*kalā*) of Sadyojāta make thirty-eight in total, as stated respectively. It is said: the five digits of Īśāna; the four digits of Pūṣan; the eight digits of Aghora; the thirteen of Vāmadeva; and the eight digits of Sadyojāta.
Thus, it is traditionally taught that there are thirty-eight digits (kalās). ||10||

The head, the five faces, then the two [parts] in the heart and throat, along with the navel and the belly, the back, the chest, the private parts, the pair of thighs, and the pair of knees—[these constitute] the eight kalās of Sadyojāta for all vidyās; salutation to Śaśinī. (In the left margin: *mava...ṣikaṃ māntaṃ udbhavāvāya namaḥ* ... thus in the Sadyomantra, the eight kalās of Sadyojāta; *ala...* thus...)

The back, the two sides, the pair of feet and hands, the nose, and the crown of the head are the locations for the thirty-eight *kalās* in the formation of Śiva’s body. He describes the locations of the thirty-eight *kalās*: [the head]... (l2)

The "heads" (*mūrdhānaḥ*) are the five [parts] beginning with the upper, eastern, southern, northern, and western cranial regions. These are the locations (*sthānāni*) and faces (*vaktrāṇi*, *mukhāni*) of the five *kalās* of Īśāna:
the east, south, north, and west [belonging to] the four *kalās* of Tatpuruṣa.

Regarding the word "now" (*atha*), since it has been stated that the Puruṣa possesses four *kalās*, there is an absence of an upper face; for this very reason, Aghoraśivācārya [states]: "Salutation to the unmanifest *kalā*."

Thus, "upward-facing" has been explained. (l4) The heart is the region below the throat; the throat; the two shoulders; the right and left arms; on the head, the nose; the belly is the low-lying area surrounding the abdomen; the lower abdomen is the region below the navel; the back (–) is the posterior part of the spine; the chest (–) (l5).

The region below the heart— these indeed are the locations for the eight parts of Aghora: the secret organ (*guhya*), the anus (*guda*), the penis (*śiśna*), the phallus (*liṅga*), the pair of thighs (*ūruyuga*)—

the pair of right and left thighs— furthermore, the pair of knees (*jānuyugma*), the joint situated in the middle above the shanks (*jaṅghordhvamadhyasthitasandhisthāna*), the right and left shanks (*dakṣavāmajaṅghe*) which are the regions below the knees, and the right and left sides of the back (*dvispṛk pṛṣṭhapārśvapradeśa*).

At the waist, the place for binding the thread; the two sides below the right and left armpits, or the regions extending to the hips—these are the locations of the thirteen kalās of Vāmadeva. The two feet, the right and left; the pair of hands, the right and left;
the nose; the crown of the head; and the arms.

The two staffs on the right and left [shoulders] are for the purpose of forming the body of Śiva and generating a physical form equal to that of Śiva; the locations for the thirty-six *kalās* (including the eight) should be as follows—this is the meaning of what has been stated. And it is said: "Īśāna is fivefold:

on the head and on the four faces, with the fifth [face] by means of the *praṇava* itself. Then one should place the *kalā* of Aghora in the heart, and [the remaining ones] on the throat, the secret parts (*guhya*), the navel, the two testicles, the back, and the chest."

One should place the *vāmadeva*-kalā in the secret organ, the penis, as well as the thighs, knees, shanks, buttocks, hips, and sides; then, the *sadyojāta*-kalā is to be joined to the feet, hands, nose, head, and the two arms. Thus [it is said]. (11)

O Lord of the Heart, seated upon the throne of the Great Illusion manifested by the mind, You are to be meditated upon in the form of a lamp-flame; O Supreme Śiva who dwells in the steady consciousness, [I offer] beautiful flowers, the sentiment of devotion, forgiveness as the water for the guest-offering (*arghya*), and water for anointing. (L5) In the vessel of the vital breath (*prāṇa*)... [in the vessel] of the mind, this very ego-sense (*ahaṅkṛti*) is the supreme incense consisting of the subtle body (*liṅga*). True sense-objects that bring about perfect satisfaction, such as fragrance and the rest, are the lamps.
The [elements] beginning with earth;

the mirror, fan, hymns, and so forth, along with the drinking of wine and other offerings; the offering of food (*naivedya*) performed by oneself with focused devotion; when one is joined with the subtle body (*sūkṣmāṅga*), then the recitation (*jāpa*) occurs through the sound (*nāda*) itself.

[He] requested [this] from his kinsman. With a pair of verses, he describes the method of internal sacrifice (*antaryajana*). Regarding the phrase "in the heart-lotus," the worship of Śiva is of two kinds, distinguished as external and internal.
Among these, first, for those possessing spiritual knowledge (*ādhyātmajñānin*), there is internal sacrifice;

for them, external worship is not prescribed because of the risk of faults arising from the procurement of flowers and other offerings. For those who perform ritual actions (*kriyāvat*), external worship is ordained. And it has been said: "Sacrifice is declared to be twofold: external and internal."
Regarding the distinction: one should worship [Śiva] with non-violence (*ahiṃsā*) and so forth.

Since the injury to substances (*dravyahiṃsā*) performed in various [external rites] must not be committed, Śiva—who resides within the limbs [of the practitioner]—is always to be worshipped by those who perform ritual actions (*kriyāvat*) with flowers and other offerings. Thus, for those who practice external worship, there is no possibility of fault in gathering flowers and such items.

And it has been said: "Just as there is no transgression for one who gathers flowers and the like from a garden for the sake of the king's enjoyment, so too the one who takes flowers for the sake of worshipping the Lord incurs no fault. Even by those devoted to external worship, internal sacrifice (*antaryajana*) must be performed through the disposition of the mind; for without internal sacrifice, external worship is not perfected. Thus it was said: "First, the internal sacrifice..."

Having performed the external ritual, one should then practice [the internal]; for that *jyotirliṅga* which resides within the heart is itself worshipped externally. Therefore, the internal sacrifice (*antaryāga*) must first be performed; it is said here that he who performs the external sacrifice without having performed the mental sacrifice (*mānasayāga*) exerts himself in vain—such is the teaching of the scripture.

"Accumulation" refers to the heart-lotus; the word "natural" is to be understood as the ellipsis. In the world, a lotus is seen to have arisen from a bulb (*kanda*); likewise, it should be known that here too, it has emerged from a bulb. And so it has been said: "The location of the bulb for human beings is nine finger-breadths from the middle of the body. It is four finger-breadths in height and likewise in width. Its shape is like an egg, and it is thick."

It should be known that from that *kanda* arises the heart-lotus, complete with its pericarp (*karṇikā*). Within the pericarp of that heart-lotus, which is conjoined with the Sun, Moon, and Fire, Ananta, Sadāśiva,
and Paraśiva abide by their very nature.

Likewise, in the *Niśvāsakārikā*: "The heart of all embodied beings resembles the flower of the plantain tree (*kadalī*). In its center resides a lotus with eight petals and a pericarp. The heart is one span (*vitasti*) in measure, while the lotus is four finger-breadths;
the stalk of the lotus, extending up to nine finger-breadths, is situated above the navel and possesses nine openings."
Surrounded on all sides by thorns, from the pericarp-tips of which the size of a thumb-joint [emerges], there shall be a pericarp with filaments;

in the center of that [pericarp] is the Moon, in the center of the Moon is Fire, and in the center of that is Maheśvara. Within Sadāśiva is Maheśa, and beyond even him is Śiva. Thus, this worship of Śiva in the heart-lotus, established by its very nature, is the most excellent of all for everyone when performed mentally.

In the heart-lotus, upon the seat situated above the power of Kuṇḍalinī— which exists by virtue of the essential nature of Mahāmāyā, which has been cultivated through mental cognition and established by meditation— and which possesses a lion-throne existing above that, [the following] is spoken regarding the state of Mahāmāyā as it is to be described.

The meaning is that [the practice] is accompanied by the seat (*āsana*) and meditation (*dhyāna*), beginning with the power of speech (*vādā-dhāra-śakti*) and ending with the power of the [supreme] energy (*śakti-paryanta*). Regarding the statement "Kuṇḍalī resides naturally in the heart-lotus" within the context of the three powers to be accomplished (*sādhya-triśakti*): although the primordial Kuṇḍalinī is joined with the Moon, Fire, and Sun, she is to be known as residing in the region of the heart in the form of a sprout; this refers to her position on that seat. She has the appearance of a lamp-flame, being equal to the blaze of a lamp. By this—
The nature of *nāda* has been illuminated. That *nāda* is the end;

it is the *haṃsa*, the Sadāśiva, residing within the bodies of all living beings. According to the statement, "He who says 'haṃsa, haṃsa' is indeed Sadāśiva," the utterance of the breath in the form of a lamp-flame is [perceived] by means of the ear and the thumb.

The sound that arises from conjunction is equal to the flame of a lamp's fire; it is designated as *nāda* (the primordial sound), which has been revealed as a wonder for the removal of the fetters of the bound soul (*paśu*). Thus is Paraśiva to be meditated upon.

He is to be invoked by means of the *mudrās* such as *āvāhana* (invocation) and others. "Bhāva" refers to the purification of the mind. By the word "bhāva," the eight flowers—beginning with non-violence (*ahiṃsā*) and including well-prepared flowers and excellent blossoms—are indicated.

Since it is stated that "non-violence is one flower, [the restraint of] the senses is another, the flower of patience, the flower of compassion, the supreme measured flower of knowledge, the flower of austerity, the flower of truth, and the eighth is the flower of intention"— therefore, among these eight flowers, patience alone, as it has arisen in the midst of them, constitutes the *arghya*, the water for the feet (*pādya*), and the water for sipping (*ācamana*).

"Forgiveness alone"—this is the ellipsis. "Water" means bathing water; the meaning is that one should perform the consecration (*abhiṣeka*) with water that has the nature of nectar (*amṛta*), in the form of abundant nectar overflowing from the agitated power (*kṣubdha-śakti*). (L4) "The intellect" (*dhīḥ*)—meaning the understanding (*buddhiḥ*) whose nature is certainty and which is pure like the self—is the "ointment" (*lepa*), the unguent such as saffron, camphor, sandalwood, and so forth, in the mind.

In the vessel—the vessel consisting of *maṇi* (mind) marked by the syllable *Aṅkāra*—the vital breath (*prāṇavāyu*) is the fire (*anala*). Egoity (*ahaṅkṛti*), which is pride (*garva*), is this very supreme incense; it is the ritual for the best incense. As it has been said: "The fire is the vital breath, the mind is the vessel, and the crest of the incense-flame is pride. This is the son born of wisdom (*dhīmānātmaja*). Consciousness (*cit*) is the intellect (*buddhi*), which is one's own nature (*svarūpa*) because it illuminates all objects (*sarvārthaprakāśakatvāt*). Thus is the state (*padavī*).

The lamp; the objects of the six sense-fields, which are of the nature of the aforementioned things to be enjoyed; the excellent means of realization (*sādhakatama*), which are the most effective instruments for complete fulfillment; the [five] qualities beginning with odor—namely odor, taste, form, touch, and sound.

By the word "odor" (*gandha*), a substance possessing an extreme fragrance is indicated. By "taste," that which has become delicious is indicated; by "form," that which has become captivating; by "touch," that which has become subtle and smooth; and by "sound," a substance possessing a pleasant resonance is indicated. The elements beginning with earth—the earth, water, fire, air, and space.

By this, the five offerings (*pañcopacāra*) are [explained]: subtle [offerings] such as [incense], mirrors, fans, hymns, and so forth; the knowledge [of these]; water fit for drinking; and even water and the like are offerings by way of association (*saṃbandhopacāra*), while the mirror and so forth are offerings by way of association with fire (*agnisaṃbandhopacāra*). The fan is [an offering] of air (*vāyu*).

The offering of fans such as palm-leaf whisks for the purpose of movement is a metaphorical association with air; hymns of praise and the like are a metaphorical association with space; the offering of food (*naivedya*) through the presentation of these items is a metaphorical association with earth. All of this previously mentioned is perceived directly by one endowed with a subtle body through the power of yoga.
However, for one devoid of the power of yoga who possesses only a gross body, everything must be performed through the mind. Thus he says: "When [one] is deprived of the subtle body..."

At that time, being devoid of the subtle body (*sūkṣmaśarīra*), he would be endowed with the mental cultivation of the *samana* [breath]... for one who possesses the subtle body, there is the mantra consisting of sound (*nādātmaka-mantra*) which arises spontaneously by itself through the sound (*nāda*) that has arisen of its own accord.

That recitation which has arisen spontaneously from the *mūlādhāra*—that is, the mental utterance of the mantra—is what constitutes *japa*. One should perform the *japa* as it arises from the navel through the mental visualization of the gross body. 12.

Having thus worshipped the fire as well, one should perform the oblation by means of the previously mentioned yoga, using the *iḍā* [vessel] and the *sruva* [ladle] for that which resides in its place, and the *suṣumnā* [vessel] with the *sudhā* mantra until the end of the full offering (*pūrṇāhuti*). Having completed the sacrifice, having respectfully asked the Lord for forgiveness, and at the end being free from mental constructs, one should enter into *samādhi*, merged in the supreme state. This is the mental fire-ritual of Śiva, which is *samādhi*.

And he said: "In the fire" means that by the previously mentioned yoga—that is, by the previously mentioned connection—one should contemplate the place of oblation in the self-established navel-pit (*nābhikuṇḍa*);

the meaning is "by way of that connection. "In the fire" means in the navel-pit, in the perfected Śiva-fire (*siddhaśivāgni*) invoked according to the prescribed rite. "Thus also, having worshipped," means having performed the worship of Śiva just as it was performed in the location of the heart; one should then perform the *homa*, the oblation.

One should perform [the rite]. The meaning is: having visualized the *iḍā* channel in the form of a *sruva* ladle—[the channel] located at that place [of the heart], which exists in the position of the *bindu*—one should offer an oblation (*homa*) with the clarified butter of nectar flowing from the *bindu* drawn in by inhalation (*pūraka*), in a number such as one hundred and eight.

Having performed [the rites] at the end, at the conclusion of the numbered oblations (*saṃkhyāhoma*), he—having meditated upon the *suṣumnā* channel as the sacrificial ladle (*sruc*) and the sacrificial hall (*srugāgāra*)—performed the ritual procedure of the oblation up to the final offering (*pūrṇāhuti*). Having offered [this] out of great reverence, he asked the Lord for forgiveness; then, having completed everything for the deity worshipped within, he concluded with the final act of dedication at the end.

"Always devoid of objective existence" means being free from the nature of the forms of Sadāśiva and so forth, that is, having the nature of the *niṣkala* (undivided). "Dissolved in the supreme state" means merged therein at the *dvādaśānta*. "Samādhi" [refers to] being of a single form throughout the twelve locations, beginning with *mālādhāra*, up to the *dvādaśānta*.
Meditation on Śiva is *samādhi*; one should attain, that is, go toward, the *samādhi* of that very nature. And it has been said: "Then, until midday, one should remain established in *samādhi*.

One should join the mind and the vital breath (*prāṇa*) with the *liṅga* consisting of the light of knowledge, blazing like the autumnal moon, situated between the eyebrows. Absorbed in that, the yogi who has arisen as that [very essence] should gradually lead the consciousness into emptiness. When the consciousness has perished, there is the bliss of pure consciousness (*cidānanda*)."
The supreme samādhi is said to arise spontaneously... [the jewel]...

[of] qualities... I have thus described the seat of Śiva, which is to be worn and meditated upon as the foremost, below the lotus, and above, extending to the end of Śiva; it is inlaid with gems and is the portion that transcends all paths.
[The pedestal] called the *Saṃyutaśivajñāna* [is] the state of the power of action (*kriyāśakti*), accompanied by the stalk of the portion that transcends all paths.

Having thus described the internal worship and so forth, ending with the meditation on peace, he now speaks of external worship of Śiva as being supported by a *liṅga*, because the *liṅga* alone is conducive to the highest good. "With the Lord, the Unstruck," [the Guru says]: in one's own form, or in an image, or in the seat of knowledge (*vidyāpīṭha*), or in fire, water, or on a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*).

Whether the *liṅga* is fixed or mobile, worship performed when its presence (*sannidhi*) has been established is the best among these; for it is stated that [worship] is performed upon a *liṅga* possessing the aforementioned characteristics. Therefore, according to the scriptural injunction, "one should practice the propitiation of the *liṅga* with constant effort," he speaks of those who possess the Lord (*seśān*).
Thus, the lords of the regions (*arikopariseśāḥ*) are those accompanied by Īśvara.

The meaning is that she is presided over by Śiva. [She is] the Support Power (*ādhāra-śakti*) who assumes a form that is pervasive and manifests as the locus; the meaning is that the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*) inherent in Śiva itself is the form of the support. It was stated previously that she is to be worshipped within the pedestal of the *liṅga*, in the lower portion, upon the Tortoise Stone (*kūrma-śilā*).
Seated upon the tortoise-stone below, her body white as the ocean of milk,
with the form of a seed-sprout upon her crown, she bestows boons and fearlessness.

[She is] the Śakti Kriyā, holding a noose and a goad, whose form is the foundation. Alternatively, "together with Īśāna" means accompanied by Īśvara; she has emerged from the *kanda* like a sprout, and having again burst through the cosmic egg, she stands from the *kanda* like a sprout because of her [nature as] that [foundation]. Above that, upon the supporting Śakti, are the knots beginning with Earth and ending with the principles (*tattva*) such as the elements and so forth; below the knot is the principle of Māyā.

The "region" (*pradeśa*) here refers to the sequence: the earth-element in the form of the *kanda* [root-tuber]; the water-element as the sprinkler; the cause in the state of rising is the wind, which is of the nature of an impeller; space for the sake of growth; the five subtle elements (*tanmātra*), such as odor, in the form of the sprout;
the ten sense organs in the form of apertures; the principle of ego (*ahaṅkāratattva*) as the cause of the intellect (*buddhi*); and the intellect (*buddhi*).

The four principles ending with *guṇa*, *prakṛti*, *puruṣa*, and *anta* (the Unmanifest), which consist of the forms of *dharma*, *jñāna*, *vairāgya*, and *aiśvarya*, are shaped like lions and constitute the feet. The four principles ending with *rāga*, *niyati*, *vidyā*, and *kalā*—consisting of *adharma*, *ajñāna*, *avairāgya*, and *anaiśvarya*—are situated above the feet and constitute the limbs. The principle of *kāla* is the form of the stalk (*nāla*). The place where the stalk and the petals join is the *māyā*-principle, located within the mantra.

The principle of Māyā is the lower covering; the principle of Śuddhavidyā is the upper covering. Śuddhavidyā is the upper lotus—the lotus in the form of a full-blown flower situated above the principle of Māyā, inlaid with lotuses ending at Śiva, and pervaded by the lotuses concluding with the principle of Śiva. It is of such a nature.

The *pīṭha* is the seat of Śiva. Herein is the sequence: it is joined with the eight petals of the eight Lords of Knowledge (*vidyeśvara*), contains within its womb the fifty seed-syllables (*bīja*), and possesses a yellow pericarp endowed with sixty-four filaments.

Regarding this, "the fifty seed-syllables" refers precisely to the fifty phonemes beginning with the letter *a* and ending with the letter *kṣ*. As for the phrase "endowed with sixty-four filaments," it is as follows:

The five groups of five consonants beginning with *ka* and ending with *ma*, along with *ya-ra-la-va-śa-ṣa-sa-ha*, each joined with the vowel *a* and the nasal bindu (*m*), when uttered, constitute the sixty-four filaments. These are said to be located at the tips of the filaments starting from the east, and together with the nine powers in the center, they are situated upon the tips of the petals.

In the tips of the pericarp [petals] (*karṇikāgra*)... [there are] the solar, lunar, and fiery mandalas, with their respective presiding deities Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra. In the center of the pericarp is the *śakti*-mandala, whose presiding deity is Īśvara. Above that, one should contemplate Śiva, who pervades everything from the earth-mandala up to the end [of the series]. This is because it has been stated that "the seat of the Supreme Lord (*parameṣṭhin*) extends from *śakti* down to the end of *śakti*."

It consists of the *liṅga* known as Śivajñāna, which is endowed with the preeminent portion (*adhikabhāga*) of all the paths (*sarvādhvan*). [Regarding] the six paths (*ṣaḍadhvan*) of all the paths: the "preeminent portion" (*adhikaśreṣṭhabhāga*) refers to the portions designated as Rudra, Viṣṇu, and Brahmā. That which is conjoined with, or measured by, these is the *liṅga* consisting of Śivajñāna—the Śiva-liṅga composed of the power of knowledge (*jñānaśaktimaya*). It is the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*) for Śiva’s state of having the power of knowledge as his body.

It is well known that it is the very power whose nature is knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*), which inheres in Śiva, that is metaphorically designated by the term "form" (*mūrti*); thus it is stated in the *Mataṅgaparameśvara*: "Now, the locus of the Lord consists of His own powers and rays. Likewise, in the *Varuṇapaddhati*: "The installation (*pratiṣṭhā*) is the ritual union of the pedestal with the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*) within the *liṅga* whose nature is the power of knowledge; and that [installation] is fivefold."

The pedestal (*pīṭha*), which serves as the support for the *liṅga*, should be conceived here as consisting of the power of action (*kriyāśakti*) and having the nature of the power of action; it is joined with the stalk (*nāla*) representing the portion exceeding all time-periods (*sarvādhva*), and is accompanied by the "cow's mouth" (*gomukha*) joined with the portions of Rudra, Viṣṇu, and Brahmā, who are the most excellent among those named after the six paths (*ṣaḍadhvan*).
Here, [the portions] of Rudra and Viṣṇu...

The method of joining the six paths (*ṣaḍadhva-yojanā*) for the portions of Brahmā is now demonstrated. Having conceived the *liṅga* as consisting of three sections: in the upper portion belonging to Rudra is the *kalā* Beyond-Peace (*śāntyatīta*); in the portion belonging to Viṣṇu is the *kalā* of Peace (*śānti*); and in the portion belonging to Brahmā are the five *kalās*: Knowledge (*vidyā*), Illusion (*māyā*), and Cessation (*nivṛtti*). [Thus] is the placement of the five *kalās*. [The first two] belong to the principle of Śiva-Śakti within the *kalā* Beyond-Peace; the [remaining] two belong to the *kalā* of Peace.

The three principles—Sadāśiva, Īśvara, and Śuddhavidyā—are in Virūḍhā; the seven principles known as Māyā, Kalā, Kāla, Vidyā, Niyati, Rāga, and Puruṣa are in Pratiṣṭhā; and [the principles] Prakṛti, Buddhi, Ahaṅkāra, Manas, Śrotra, Tvak, Cakṣus, Jihvā, Nāsā, Vāk, Pāṇi, Pāda, Pāyu, Udara, Upastha, Śabda, and Sparśa [are in Nivṛtti].

Form, taste, smell, [touch, sound], fire, and water. Upon the cessation of the twenty-three principles (*tattva*), there is the single principle of earth (*pārthiva-tattva*). This is the deposition of the principles (*tattva-nyāsa*). In the Śāntyatītā [kalā], there are fifteen worlds, beginning with Anāśrita and ending with Nivṛtti. In the Śānti-kalā, there are eighteen worlds, beginning with Sadāśiva and ending with Vāmā. In the Vidyā [kalā], there are twenty-seven worlds, beginning with Aṅguṣṭhamātra and ending with Vāmā. In the Pratiṣṭhā [kalā]...
There are fifty-six worlds from Śrīkaṇṭha to Amareśa in Nivṛtti; [from] Bhadrakālī...

(l3) there are one hundred and eight worlds. Thus, she has declared that in the Path of the five Kalās, there are two hundred and twenty-four worlds. In the month of Śāntyatītā, there are fifteen cities, and likewise Anāśrita. (l4)

The Lords are infinite: Vyomarūpinī, Vyāpinī, and Ūrdhvā; likewise Mlocikā, Rocikā, Dīpikā, Indhikā, Śāntyatītā, Śāntikā, Vidyā, Pratiṣṭhā, and Nivṛtti are thus remembered. Within the Kalā known as Śāntikā, there are eighteen cities: Sadāśiva, Śikhaṇḍin, Śrīkaṇṭha, and Trimūrtika.
Ekarudra, as well as Ekanetra, are likewise remembered;
Śivottama, Sūkṣma, and the one named Ananta; Manonmanī should be known, as well as Sarvabhūtadamanī, Balapramathinī, and Vikariṇī, and also Kalavikaraṇī.

Kālī, as well as Parā, Raudraśreṣṭhā, and Vāmā, will be described in due order within the Vidyā. Beyond that, the twenty-seven worlds are considered to be of the size of a thumb. These [lords] are Īśāna, Kapiṅgala, Udbhava, Bhava, the greatly resplendent Vāmadeva, Śikhaṇḍin, Kali, Pañcāntaka, Śūraka, Piṅga, and Jyotis.
Saṃvarta, Krodha, [Kāla-]śiva, as well as Anantājña, and likewise Vāmadeva of great splendor; Śikheda, Umāpati, Pracaṇḍaka, Ekavīra, as well as Īśākṣa, Bhava, Ugra, Bhīmaka, and Vāma... [etc.]

...In the section on the *Pratiṣṭhā*, however, I shall explain [the following]: Śrīkaṇṭha and the others... there are fifty-six cities. One should know that Śrīkaṇṭha and Dyau are likewise [there], as well as Kaumāra, Vaiṣṇava, Brāhma, the two Bhairavas, Kṛta, and Brāhmya. Regarding Praje... (l2)
And likewise Aindraka, and the Gandharva should be known; that which is named Yakṣa-Rākṣasa should be known as Paiśāca, and is remembered as Sthaleśvara.

Sthūleśvara is Śaṅkha, and Karṇa is remembered as Kālāñjana. Maṇḍapa is at Ramākoṭi, and Daśaṇḍa is at Gala... [l3] ...[omitted] ...is proclaimed by the name Rasa; Svarṇākṣa is another, and Bhadrakaṇṭha is Gokarṇa, remembered as Mahābala. [In] Avimukta...

Rudrakoṭi known as Vastrapādaka, Bhīmeśvara, Mahendra, Aṭṭa, and Bhāsa thereafter; likewise Vimalēśa is proclaimed, [and] Nakha... (l4) ...Nākhalas, as well as Kurukṣetra and Gayā, and that which is designated Bhairava; Kedāra, Mahākāla, and likewise Madhyameśa; Āmrātaka, Jalpeśa, and Śrīśaila as another; Hari, Rudra as proclaimed, and Lākūlīśa is remembered; Bhā... (l5) ...[is proclaimed].

Vīrabhūti, likewise Ḍiṇḍimuṇḍi, as well as Auṣadhi, Puṣkara, and Naimiśa; furthermore, there is the one known as Prabhāsa, and the one remembered as Amareśa. In the [tattva of] Nivṛtti, however, there is the city subordinate to Kalā, numbering one hundred and eight.
Bhadrakālī is thus proclaimed, and likewise Vīrabhadra; Trilocana, [................], Nabhas, and another; Vibhāva is thus proclaimed, and Saṃvāhi as well.
The Lord of the Thirty-three is thus proclaimed, and the Three-eyed One is likewise remembered; Gaṇādhyakṣa...

Śambhu, Daṃṣṭrin, and Vartika; Phaṇīndra and Udumbari are proclaimed, as well as Agrasana and Mārutāśana; those known as Krodhana and Ananta, and Vṛṣasāra is likewise remembered; Vṛṣa, Bali, Priya, and Bhūtapāla are thus proclaimed.

Jyeṣṭha and Śarva are likewise declared to be the lords of the gods (*sureśau*) for one who has reached the further shore of the Vedas; Jñānabhuk is likewise declared, as is the other, Sarvajña. Īśa and Vidyādhipa are to be known as those who grant desired grace; and separately, Ratna... is likewise declared. [The remainder of the line is illegible]. Lakṣmīdhṛk is likewise declared, and he is remembered as Jaṭādhara. He shall likewise be Saumyadarśa, Dhānya, and Rūpavān.

Nidhīśa is likewise proclaimed, as is Meghavāhana; Kapardin is also proclaimed, and [he] would be Pañcāntaka. He is remembered as Kṣayāntaka; Tīkṣṇa, Sūkṣma, Vāyuvega, Laghu, and Śīghra are celebrated;
Sunāda, Meghanāda, and Jalāntaka are remembered; and Dīrghabāhu is proclaimed.

Likewise, the other is called Śveta and Śvetadhā, known as Mahābala; he is renowned as Pāśahasta, and likewise there is Atibala. Bala and Daṃṣṭra are to be known, as well as Lohita and Dhūmaka; Virūpākṣa... (l3) ...and Pha is remembered as Bhayānaka. Krūradṛṣṭi, Hantā, Māraṇa, and Nirṛti are likewise mentioned; Dharma is proclaimed, and another Dharma follows after him.

Līyokta, Tathāprokta, Saṃyokta, and the next, Kartṛsaṃjña; Vidhātṛ, Tathāca, Hara, Mṛttika, Yāmyakṣaya, Antaka, and he who is remembered as Bhasmāntaka; Babhru, Tathāprokta, Ardahana, Jvalaka, Hara, Ghātaka, Piṅgala, and Hutāśana—these are the fires. (l5)

Rudra, likewise the one known as Tridaśādhipa, Pinākin, Śāstṛ, Avyaya, Vibhūtika, the one celebrated as Pramardana, and another, Vajradeha; indeed, Buddha, Aja, Kavālīśa, Rudra, and Vaiṣṇava; Brahmā, Hāṭaka, and Kūśmāṇḍa—these, together with Kalāgni, are declared to be the one hundred and eight cities (*pura*). Thus it is.

I have clearly declared, in due order, that there are two hundred and twenty-four worlds belonging to the five kalās. Within the Śiva-tattva, ten worlds beginning with Anāśrita are situated; in the Śakti-tattva, the world of Śāntyatīta and the Dīpa are declared;
and within the Sadāśiva-tattva, one world, Sadāśiva, is declared.

The eight worlds beginning with Śikhaṇḍin are in the principle (tattva) named Īśvara; the nine worlds beginning with Manonmanī are in that called Śuddhavidyā; the eight cities beginning with Aṅguṣṭhamātra are recorded as being in the principle named Māyā. In the principle named Kāla, there are Śikheda and Ekavīra; and in Kalā, Piṅga and Jyotis clearly exist.

In the principle known as Vidyā, there are nine [mantras]: Aṣṭāṅguli... and Para. In the principle known as Māyā, Śikhā and Ekavīra are recorded. In the principle known as Kāla, Pañcāntaka and Śiras would exist. In Kalā, Phaṭkāra clearly manifests. (l. 2) Jyoti is thus considered in the principle known as Vidyā. Saṃvarta and Krodheśa exist in the principle of Niyati. There is one world beginning with Śiva; in Rāga, there are five.

The single hero is established in the six worlds within the principle (*tattva*) of *puruṣa*. The eight worlds beginning with Śrīkaṇṭha are established in *prakṛti*. Furthermore, the eight worlds beginning with Brāhmī clearly exist in the *buddhi* [principle]. And in the principle of *ahaṅkāra*, there is that which is known as Sthaleśvara, extending from Anādi to Ghrāṇa.

In the group of six, Sthūleśvara resides. In the group of five, however, Śaṅkukarṇa resides. Within the principle (tattva) of the organs of action, there are the worlds beginning with Kālāñjana and ending with Chagalaṇḍa.

In the group of five, from sound up to smell, Pañcakeśa clearly resides. Starting from Sthāṇu, there is a group of eight worlds situated in space; in the wind, there is a group of eight worlds beginning with Bhīmeśvara.

The eight worlds beginning with Bhairava are established in the principle of fire (*tejastattva*); the group of eight worlds beginning with Lakulīśa is situated in the principle of fire; there shall be one hundred and eight worlds beginning with Bhadrakālī located in water; likewise, in the principle of earth (*pṛthvītattva*), other [worlds] are proclaimed, starting from the letter *ma* up to the *visarga* in the state beyond peace (*śāntyatītā*).

The sixteen vowels are for *śānti*; *ka*, *kha*, and *ga* are for *vidyā*; the seven *mātṛkā*s beginning with *gha* and ending with *jña* are for *pratiṣṭhā*; and the twenty-three syllables beginning with *ṭa* and ending with *ha*, together with the single syllable *kṣa*, are for the *nivṛtti-kalā*. This is the assignment of syllables (*varṇanyāsa*). As for the assignment of words (*padanyāsa*), it is twofold: the path of eighty-one words through the division of word-extractions as in the fourth [chapter], and likewise in the assignment of the paths (*adhvanyāsa*).

It has been taught that in the *kalā* beyond peace (*śāntyatītā*), beginning from the "Pervasive Sky" (*vyomavyāpin*) and ending with "Oṃ," there are clearly eleven words; indeed, in the peaceful body (*śāntikāya*), they exist starting from "Meditation-Food" (*dhyānāhāra*) up to "Pervasive One, Pervasive One" (*vyāpin vyāpin*). In the *kalā* called Knowledge (*vidyā*), [the sequence is as follows]... (l2)

There are twenty words for *pratiṣṭhā*; from the word *arūpya* onwards, up to the word *maheśvara*, there are twenty-one words clearly stated in their proper sequence. From the word *mahādeva* onwards, there is a distribution of twenty-eight words in the *nivṛtti-kalā*. Thus has the sequence of the placement (*nyāsa*) of the eighty-one words been explained; or else, the placement of the words may be done in another manner.

It is prescribed that there are ninety-four words in sequence; here too, in the Śāntyatītā [kalā], there are twenty-one words, and in the Vidyā [kalā], starting from *vyāpin* and ending with the word *śarva*,
there are thirty-two words in the Pratiṣṭhā [kalā].

By means of the expansion of the words, beginning with "bhava bhava" and ending with the word "oṃ," twenty-eight words are [contained] in the Nivṛtti [kalā]. Furthermore, the extraction of eighty-one words is stated first:
(l6) the first word is traditionally known as the single syllable "oṃ"; then "vyomavyāpine," "vyomarūpāya," and "sarvavyāpine"—thus [these] consist of five syllables.

The three-word mantra *śivāya* is considered to consist of three syllables; likewise, *anantāya* is declared to be a two-word mantra of four syllables. *Anāthāya* is likewise taught as a two-word mantra of four syllables; *anāśritāya* is considered a five-syllable mantra, and *dhruvāya* is considered a three-syllable mantra. Furthermore, *śāśvatāya* is indeed a four-syllable word; [and] *yogāya* consists of eight syllables.

The word for the one who rests upon the seat (*pīṭha*) is likewise eternal; the yogin [should] always... and indeed cause [it] to be taken away. The two feet are said to be threefold, endowed with five syllables. *Tat* and *thau*, *namaḥ śivāya*—this is the six-syllabled [mantra]. ... to the source of all, the five... Śiva... the word for the head of Īśāna is known as the six-syllabled one. The word for the face of Tatpuruṣa would be seven syllables.

To the Aghora-heart (aghora-hṛdayāya)—(l2)—this shall consist of seven syllables; the phrase "to the secret Vāmadeva" (vāmadeva-guhyāya) is considered to be seven syllables; and the phrase "to the Sadyojāta-form" (sadyo-jāta-mūrtaye) shall also be seven syllables: *oṃ namo*—(l3).
The word *vaṃ* shall consist of five syllables; the word *guhyātiguhyāya* is traditionally known as having six syllables. The second word, *goptre*, is likewise proclaimed;

the word *anidhanāya* is traditionally known as having five syllables. The word *nidhanāya* is endowed with four syllables; the word *sarvayogādhikṛtāya* shall consist of eight syllables; and the word *jyotirūpāya* consists of five syllables.

The eight-syllable phrase "smṛtaṃ parameśvaraparāya" should be [the first]; the eight-syllable phrase "acetana acetane ca" should be [the second]; then the word "vyomin," then the word "vyomin," and likewise the two words "vyāpin" and "vyāpin. These are the two [final] words.

The two [syllables] *mleyau* are endowed with four phonemes (*catur-arṇa*). The two-word phrases *arūpin arūpin* and *prathama prathama* should be understood as being endowed with six syllables each. After that, the word *tejas tejas* and likewise the word *jyotis jyotis*—both these word-pairs should be understood as being endowed with four phonemes. After the word *arūpa*, then after that the word *anagni*, and after that the word *adhūma*.

After that, "Abhasma" is proclaimed; likewise, the three-syllable "Anāde" is taught as the fifth word. Then there is the various word "Nānā," followed by "Dhūdhū" and again "Dhūdhū. This should be understood as a two-word [phrase] endowed with four syllables. The word "Oṃ Bhūḥ" is proclaimed as being endowed with two syllables, and then the word "Bhuvana."

Afterwards, *oṃ suvaśca*; following that, the two-word [phrase] should be known as being endowed with three syllables. The word *anidhana* is said to be endowed with four syllables. The word *nidhana* is said to be endowed with three syllables. After that, the word *nidhabhaveti* is endowed with five syllables. Afterwards, the word *śiva* and likewise the word *śarva*—these two words should be known as being endowed with two syllables each.

Endowed [with these], the station of the Supreme Self (*paramātmapada*) follows; thereafter, the station of Maheśvara, as well as the station of Mahādeva, is proclaimed. This three-word [mantra] consists of four syllables (*caturvarṇaka*). With the addition of the word *sadbhāveśvara*, it becomes five-syllabled (*pañcākṣara*).
The station of Great Splendor (*mahāteja*) is proclaimed to be endowed with four syllables.

The word *yogādhipate* is endowed with five syllables; after that, the word *muñca muñca* is endowed with four syllables. The first word is known as being six syllables long. The word *śarva śarva* is said to be endowed with four syllables. After that, the word *bhava-bhava* and likewise the word *bhavodbhava*—these two words should be understood as each being endowed with four syllables.

The phrase "bestower of happiness upon all beings" (*sarvabhūtasukhaprada*) consists of eight syllables. The phrase "causing the presence of all" (*sarvasāṃnidhyakara*) is considered to consist of seven syllables. The phrase "the supreme state of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra" (*brahmaviṣṇurudraparapada*) consists of eight syllables. [The terms] *anarcitā*, *anarcitā*, *asaṃskṛtā*, and *saṃsnatā* [follow], as does [the word] *pūrva*.

First, the three groups of eight syllables are remembered: after the word *sākṣi*, the word *sākṣi* [is repeated]; likewise, the two-word phrase *turu turu* is to be known as endowed with four syllables. After the two-word phrase *pataṅga pataṅga*, there is the six-syllable [phrase] (*sal8*).

After *piṅga piṅga*, there is the word *pakṣa*, and after that, the word *pakṣa*; likewise, the word *jñāna*, the word *jñāna*, and after that, the word *śabda*, the word *śabda*; and likewise the word *sūkṣma*, the word *sūkṣma*.

It should be known as having four feet and being endowed with four oceans. (l9) [The word] *veti*... [the word] *sarva* likewise follows; it should be understood as having two feet and being endowed with two syllables. Following that, the word *sarvada* is proclaimed to have three syllables. *Oṃ namaḥ*... (p85b, l1)

The five-syllable *pada* is [the mantra] ending in *namaḥ*; the eight-syllable *pada* is considered to be *namaśśivāya*. Others proclaim the single-syllable *pada* to be simply *oṃ*. Thus has the extraction (*uddhāra*) of the eighty-one *padas* been declared. Now, the extraction of the external [mantra] is being described; in the extraction of the eighty-one *padas*, there are ninety-four [syllables], beginning from the *oṃkāra-pada* up to the *dhyānāhāra-pada*.

Regarding the thirteen words [in] *sure*... (*l3*), just as after the word *dhyānāhāra* there is the single word *modi*, [one should] arrange [the next] with two syllables as *namaḥ*; after that, one should arrange [the next] with three syllables as *śivāya*;
after that, [one should arrange the next]... (*l4*).

The word *namaḥ* should be placed [there], and likewise, beginning from the "Secret of Secrets" (*guhyādiguhyam*), there are twenty words for the sequence starting with *dhūrdhva*. Thus, in the eighty-one squares, as follows:

above the square of *dhūrdhva*, there is one *oṃ*; then by the single syllable *bhūḥ*, there should be no further word above that; one word *oṃ* is prescribed; then the word *bhuvaḥ*; then one word *oṃ* is prescribed.
Then, from "suvacche" [pada], there is the *anidhana* pada;
and up to the limit of the *sarvadā* pada, thirty-two padas are proclaimed. Just as in the twenty-one padas, after the *sarvadā* pada, the single pada "oṃ" is traditionally taught with two syllables.

"Na meya," "Śivāya," and then the three-syllable [mantra]; then the single word "Oṃ" is proclaimed, followed by the word "Namaḥ. The word "Namaḥ" is proclaimed, then the word "Śivāya," and likewise with the single syllable "Oṃ. This is considered the extraction of the ninety-fourth [syllable], and it is indeed declared in the Āgamas that both [parts] have been made into two words.

The placement (*nyāsa*) of two numbers and two words [is as follows]: ... (p86a, l1) having performed [the placement], one should effect the placement with one [word] in the middle of the two words of the number two. For the *kalā* Beyond Peace (*śāntyatītā*), the mantras are those of Śiva, Īśāna, and Astra. In the *kalā* of Peace (*śānti*), the mantras are Tatpuruṣa and Kavaca. In the *kalā* of Knowledge (*vidyā*), [the mantras are] Śikhā and Aghora. In the *kalā* of Establishment (*pratiṣṭhā*)...
The head and the two left [hands] are in the Nivṛtti-kalā; the Sadyojāta and Hṛdaya mantras—such is the sequence for the nyāsa of the six paths (ṣaḍadhvan). ||14||

With his mind fixed on his own support (*svādhāra*), that is, the *mūlādhāra*, consisting of the power (*śakti*) of the *śivamantra* through the act of giving, and having uttered the mantra according to the sequence of the Lord of the Radiant Parts (*dīptikalā-īśvara*) by means of the measure (*mātrā*), he should lead [the consciousness] into the beautiful *añjali* and, having attained a state of oneness with Supreme Śiva (*paraśiva*), he should then place the great *mahont* upon the target— the resonance of the bell located at the forehead and the flower. "On his own support" means with the mind fixed on the *svādhāra*, the *mūlādhāra*.

"Having attained the mind" means that the mind is first engaged in the meditation upon the *mūlādhāra*. "Consisting of the power (*śakti*) of the *śivamanu*" means having a nature endowed with the efficacy (*sāmarthya*) of the root-mantra (*mūlamantra*) of the *śivamanu*. By the performance of the recitation (*japa*) of the *prāsāda* mantra, he speaks thus;

the meaning is that he is skilled in performing the ritual action. "The measures (*mātrā*) [are] the movement into the lords of the radiant parts" refers to the measures: the letters *a*, *u*, *m*, the *bindu*, and the *nāda*.

The locations of these [energies] are, in order, the heart, throat, palate, the space between the eyebrows, and the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*). The meaning is that from these measures (*mātrā*), the radiances (*dīptayaḥ*) shine forth; they are born from them, namely the digits (*kalā*) beginning with Vijayā:
Vijayā, Saumyā, Aṅguṣṭhajā, Dhṛti, Mardanā, Bandhinī, Mocanī, Māyā, and Mohinī.

Thus, the sixteen digits (*kalā*) born from the letter *A* reside in the heart: Bodhinī, Gulmā, Manoramā, Dīptā, Sudīptā, Homakārikā, Sādhūmā, Piṅgalā, Pītā, Vāruṇī, Śīghragā, Calā, Śaśāṅkā, Suprabhā, Kevalā, Jñānā, Mokṣadā, and Pārā. Furthermore, the sixteen digits born from the letter *U* reside in the throat: Śravaṇī, Śrāvaṇī, Jalpakarī, Ghrāṇavartinī, Suśabdā, [and so forth].
And Vāhinī, O Pārvatī, is above the mind; likewise, Prabhāvā shall appoint Ratopavāhinī in the directions.

Following the path of the ancestors, she perceives the paths of the earth and the non-earth. Having filled [them] by binding the vital breaths, she is well-pierced, established in wealth, smoke-colored, and incense-like—thus is the fourfold [manifestation].

The [kalās] residing in the palate, born from the syllable *ma*, are Nivṛtti, Pratiṣṭhā, Vidya, and Śānti; these four kalās reside in the forehead and are born from the *bindu*. Indhikā, Dīpikā, Rocikā, Mocikā, Ūrdhvagā, Vyāpinī, Vyomā, Anantā, Nāthā, and Anāśritā—these ten are born from the *nāda* and reside in the *brahmarandhra*; they are the lords (*īśvarāḥ*) of these kalās in their respective order.

Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśvara, and Sadāśiva—of these lords... (l4) ...by means of the gift and acceptance of the path of sequential renunciation (*kramatyāgamārga*), [the teacher]—the word "teacher" (*ācārya*) being understood from the context—should utter the mantra. With joined palms (*añjali*), that is, a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*), for whom? For the head (*kāntakaṃ kasya*); "of the head" (*śirasyaḥ* = *śirasaḥ*), meaning the location of the *brahmarandhra*. At its end... (l5)

They consider that the seventh station is the form of the twelve-finger space (*dvādaśānta*); having led [the deity] there, the tradition regarding the sequence of invocation (*āvāhana*) is indicated. Holding the first handful of flowers at the *mūlādhāra*, one leads it upward in succession;

having stayed for a short time in the region of the heart, one performs the abandonment of Brahmā by means of the abandonment of the letter *A* of the root mantra, and then stays at the location of the throat.

By abandoning the letter *u*, one performs the abandonment of Viṣṇu; staying above that in the place of the palate (*tālusthāna*), by abandoning the letter *m*, one performs the abandonment of Rudra; staying above that in the middle of the eyebrows, by abandoning the *bindu*, one performs the abandonment of Īśvara. Staying above that in the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*), by abandoning the *nāda*, one performs the abandonment of Sadāśiva; above that, at the end of the twelve (*dvādaśānta*).

Having remained [in that state], with the thought "I am he," one should contemplate the Supreme Śiva who is beyond thought, the Supreme Śiva established as the object of meditation; having contemplated this second nature through the realization of oneness, then immediately after that contemplation, while lowering the handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*) toward the space between the eyebrows, one should remain for a short time.
Then, by means of drawing [the breath] into the space between the eyebrows—[which is] the forehead of Gaṇārāda, sounding like the ringing of a bell—one should [focus on] the *nāda*.

One should reflect that some degree of "possessing all parts" (*sakalatva*) has been described by way of its own nature (*svarūpeṇa*). Then, one should place—that is, invoke—the splendor (*tejaḥ*) which resides in the flower, specifically the splendor [contained] within the handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*) held at the region of the heart; such is the form of the light.
One should place this within the *liṅga* and so forth, whether they be the *lakṣya-liṅga* or an image, and within the lotus of the heart.
(L3) One should invoke it.

Thus, in the venerable *Parākhyatantra*: "Having thus conceived the body of Śakti, one should manifest within it the Supreme Cause—the supreme, eternal, and constant [reality] whose nature is knowledge, bliss, and happiness;

which is all-pervading among all principles (*tattva*); immeasurable and incomparable; devoid of the relationship between the signified and the signifier; beyond the sphere of speech and mind; and specifically partless (*niṣkala*) within the whole (*sakala*). This indeed is the supreme invocation (*parāvāhana*)."

"Because of the restraint by the Śiva-mantra," it is said; and [it is further stated]: "One should mentally contemplate, within the space between the eyebrows, the form of Śiva as the mantra, who is endowed with Bindu and Nāda, accompanied by the final *s* (sānta), joined with the ritual action of the mantra, the partless (*niṣkala*) supreme seed-syllable, which ends in the state of *unmanā*.
Having contemplated him, whose appearance is like the orb of the moon, [one should place him] in a handful of flowers."
Having brought it back by means of the āvāhinī [mudrā], one should establish it in the heart by means of the sthāpinī [mudrā]. ||15||

The mudrās of invocation (*āvāhana*), stabilization (*sthāpana*), presence (*sannidhāna*), confinement (*nirodhana*), piercing (*avakuṇḍana*), and satisfaction (*saṃtoṣa*), as well as the water for the feet (*pādya*), the water for sipping (*ācamana*), the offering of honor (*arghya*), and the presentation of flowers—these are considered the ten recollections (*saṃsmṛti*). He states the ten consecrations beginning with invocation: "invocation," etc. Here, "invocation" means that by this Śiva-mantra, [the deity] is invoked; he is summoned... (l. 8)

Thus ends the invocation (*āvāhana*). Now, an objection is raised: by this [invocation], the non-pervasiveness (*avyāpakatva*) of Śiva is indicated everywhere; for how can there be an invocation of a pervasive entity? The sense is that since it already exists everywhere, [an invocation is redundant]. In the world, one calls for that which is not present [in a certain place]; likewise here too, the invocation of Śiva is performed as if he were not present, and thus the non-pervasiveness of Śiva would follow. But Śiva is indeed pervasive. Therefore...

If it is argued that [the rite of] invocation does not occur [in all cases], because the rite of invocation exists in all Āgamas, then for this very reason, the absence of the pervader (*vyāpakābhāva*) would necessarily follow regarding the rite of invocation; such is the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*). This is the intended meaning: just as fire, which resides everywhere within wood, is made manifest by friction in one particular spot, so too here, [the object] which resides everywhere is [manifested] by means of a substance... (l. 3).

The statement "only [the deity] is made present" serves to dispel the objection regarding [the deity's] omnipresence. And it has been said: "Just as fire situated from root to tip is manifested in a tree, so too the manifestation of consciousness, which is omnipresent, is not [merely] established in one place. Here, "invocation" (*āvāhana*) refers to the activity of the mind, and that consists of a particular, unsurpassed degree of faith; its expression is performed together with the recitation of the root mantra.

Invocation (*āhvāna*) is the act of making [the deity] present and facing [the practitioner]. And it has been said: "That which makes the Lord of Gods, Sadāśiva—who is all-pervading and tranquil—face [the practitioner], that is called invocation. Furthermore, that invocation is of two kinds: at the time of consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*), there is one type of invocation, which consists of the manifestation of consciousness (*citprakāśa*), preceded by the ritual placement of the vital principle (*jīvanyāsa*) within the *liṅga* and other objects.

Regarding the second [form of] invocation (*āvāhana*), which consists of making [the deity] face [the worshipper] at the time of daily worship: that facing is performed specifically toward the *Īśāna* face situated above the midst of the five faces. And it has been said: "One should designate that direction in which the door is located as the East; therein, the *Tatpuruṣa* face and the upper [face] shall be facing [toward the worshipper]. However, [the offering] should be given to the upper face."
Regarding the phrase "in front of oneself and in front of another," *sthāpana* (installation) means that which is established therein.

Because it is said by the wise: "The Lord, the ocean of compassion, has established himself in the *liṅga* and other supports for the sake of favoring me; the fixing of the mental disposition through the text is *sthāpana*, as it is the settling [of the deity] there with devotion," it is therefore called *sannidhāna* (proximity), because he is present there.

The meaning is as follows: "cessation" (*nirodhana*) refers to the state of being oriented toward a succession of graces, characterized by the relationship between the one to be favored and the one who favors, between the worshiped and the worshiper; it is that which is brought to an end.

It signifies a specific form of prayer: "O Blessed Supreme Śiva, become intent upon bestowing grace within that [state] which consists of You. This injunction in the form of a prayer is a quality of the virtuous, even for those whose impurities have ripened.

The concealment (*avakuṇṭhana*) is the cessation of the manifestation of individual beings (*satvavyakti*). O Śiva, it is the direct manifestation [of Śiva] among His devotees; it is called "concealment" because it effects their cessation [of worldly existence]. The placement of the heart-mantras and other mantras in the locations of the heart and so forth of Śiva is, according to some, the "encasement in armor" (*kavacaveṣṭana*); [this is] the *saudha-mudrā*, the *dhenu-mudrā*... [etc. (l4).

By this mudrā, the process of *amṛtīkaraṇa* (the rite of immortalization) is illuminated; and it has been said: One should place the white heart-mantra on the heart, the yellow one on the head, the red crest-mantra on the crest, and the black armor-mantra on the body. One should place the weapon-mantra, which has the brilliance of fire, upon the various weapons. Having offered a flower consecrated with the root-mantra onto the head of the deity, one should meditate on the single face of Śiva, [visualizing] the limbs together with the possessor of the limbs. This is the *amṛtīkaraṇa*.

"One should perform [the ritual] with the *dhenumudrā* for the mantras"—by this term "mudrā," the *āvāhana* (invocation) and other mudrās are indicated. The word *mudrā* is derived from two roots: from *mṛd* (to soften/delight) and *hṛṣ* (to rejoice), and from *drava* (flowing). It refers to that which delights the gods (*surāṇām*) and flows (*dravaṇāt*) toward the gods; thus it is called *mudrā*. And it has been said: "It brings joy to the gods and likewise drives away the asuras; because of its delighting and its flowing..."
(…) is proclaimed as the *drati* [mudrā]. Having formed the *añjali* with the hands, by joining the thumb to the root joint of the ring finger, it is the *vāhinī*.
This same [mudrā], when placed face down with the thumbs joined and the hands raised together, is the *garbhāṅguṣṭha-aji*.
Having formed two fists and extended the index fingers, by moving them in a circular shape, it is the *avakuṇṭhana-mudrā*. [It is formed] when the fingers are interlaced with one another.
The middle finger [is placed] between the little finger and the ring finger, and the index finger [is positioned] like the breast of a woman; this is the *saudha-mudrā*. (l.

2) Water for washing the feet should be offered to the two feet with the root mantra ending in *namaḥ* while forming the *hṛdaya-mudrā*. Water for sipping (*ācamana*) should be offered to the five faces with the mantra ending in *svadhā*. The *arghya* offering should be given to the five heads with the mantra ending in *svāhā*.
[The materials for] taking up flowers include *dūrvā* grass, flowers, unbroken rice (*akṣata*), and so forth. (l. 3)

One should offer the gift with the word *vauṣaṭ* at the end. And it is said: one should present the water for the feet (*pādya*) with both hands facing forward; the water for sipping (*ācamana*) likewise into the mouths; and similarly the respectful offering (*arghya*), consisting of *dūrvā* grass, flowers, unbroken rice, and so forth, into the five [faces] including the head. Afterwards, following the worldly conventions, one should perform the fourfold presentation—namely, salutation (*namaskāra*), *svadhā*, *svāhā*, and *vauṣaṭ*—accompanied by the respective seed-syllables (*jāti*) from the heart-mantra. Having thus completed these rites, one should present the offerings. Thus are the consecrations.
The *saṃskāras* are exactly ten, denoting the number ten. And it has been said:

having performed the invocation (*āvāhana*), installation (*sthāpana*), bringing into proximity (*sānnidhya*), confinement (*sannirodhana*), and the ritual of making [the deity] whole (*sakalīkaraṇa*), followed by the veiling (*avakuṇṭhana*), one consecrates the water for the feet (*pādya*), the water for sipping (*ācamana*), and the respectful offering (*arghya*) with flowers.
These ten, beginning with Śaṅkara, are the primary ones in the form of the *elā*.
It should be understood that this was stated for the purpose of making it known that the formative forces (saṃskāras) are other than those which constitute its members. ||16||

Fragrance, roots, fruits, tubers, flowers, food, and so forth are considered terrestrial; water, milk, cloth, and the like are aqueous; curd and such are held to be fiery; [substances such as] sandals, ornaments, and so on are airy; and likewise incense, the fan, the bell, and the sound of song constitute the offerings. These five types of offerings are for Śiva. All the offerings made to Śiva are comprised within this collection of five offerings.

He says that the perception of the elements is not fully accomplished [by these alone]. Regarding "fragrance" (*gandha*): fragrance such as *śrīcandana*; roots such as *hrībera* and so forth; fruits such as mangoes (*cūta*) and so forth;

tubers such as *sūraṇa* and so forth; flowers such as *musuma* and so forth; leaves and the like; food and the like; as well as soups, cakes, and so forth—these are the services (*upacāra*) being performed. That which pertains to the earth (*pārthiva*), meaning connected with the earth, is water (*vāri*), liquid (*udaka*), milk (*payaḥ*), or cow’s milk (*kṣīra*). Water derived from the element of water (*āpya*) includes cloth such as silk (*kauśeya*) and the like, as well as curd (*dadhi*) and so forth.

The meaning is that it is connected with what is desired, great, and endowed with radiance. "Jewel" (*maṇi*) refers to the nine kinds of gems; "oil for lamps and so forth" (*dīpāditaila*) refers to lamps and the like; "lamps, ornaments, and so forth" refers to items made of gold, silver, and the like; "fiery" (*āgneya*) means connected with fire, such as incense (*dhūpa*) containing resin and other substances;

"chowrie" (*cāmara*) refers to the wind associated with chowries, fans, and the like; "resounding with the sound of bells and song" refers to the ringing of bells and singing; and "drums" (*muraja*) refers to [the sounds of] drums and so forth.

In this manner, there is a long and intense connection with space regarding Śiva, in the context of the worship of Śiva, consisting of the five types of offerings (*pañcopacāra*). As it has been said: The *pārthiva* [offering] consists of scents, flowers, and so forth, as well as bulbs, roots, fruits, and the like; the *argha* [offering] consists of water, milk, wine, curd, ghee, cloth, and so on.

The *āgneya* [offering] consists of gold, jewels, lamps, ornaments, and the like; the *vāyavya* [offering] consists of the chowrie, the parasol, the fan, bulbs, roots, fruits, and the like, as well as the *argha* [offering] of water, milk, and cloth.

Curd, cow urine, and so forth belong to the fire element (*āgneya*); gold, jewels, lamps, ornaments, and so forth belong to the wind element (*vāyavya*); the fly-whisk, incense, the fan, and the sound of the wind belong to the ether element (*nābhasa*);
song, instrumental music, the bell, and the sound of the Vedas and so forth—these [are the five]... (the five offerings).
Thus have the *cāras* been described by those who know the treatises. ||17||

From the *nāda* arisen at one's own base (*svādhāra*) on the path of Śiva, there are the [twelve] suns beginning with *medhā*. Having recognized those presiding deities situated in their respective places as being merely a fraction (*kalā*) of that state, and having brought about dissolution beyond that, drawing [the breath] with the fingers... (l7) ...and the collection of moments (*kṣaṇikara*) one by one, having performed the recitation mentally and then inaudibly (*upāṃśu*), one should offer the mantra of Śiva—the deity who is the form of the recitation—into the God. Now, he states the rule for recitation (*japadhi*) beginning with "svādhāra": [The text continues: "From the *nāda* arisen at one's own base... and so forth. This refers to the twelve *ādityas* (suns), such as *Medhā*, which reside upon the path of Śiva starting from the *svādhāra*. One should contemplate these presiding deities established in their respective locations as being of the nature of a mere *kalā*. Then, effecting dissolution into that supreme state, drawing [the breath] with the fingers... (l7) ...and the multitude of moments (*kṣaṇikara*) individually, having performed the recitation first mentally and then inaudibly, one should offer the mantra of Śiva—who is the very form of the recitation—to the Divine. Thus, he explains the procedure for recitation starting with the words "svādhāra."

From the *nāda* arisen at the *svādhāra*— that is, from the *nāda* produced at the *mūlādhāra*, meaning from the syllable *haṃ* which expresses that [state]— there is the journey toward the partless Śiva (*niṣkala-śiva*) on the path of Śiva (*śivapatha*). The "twelve suns" beginning with *medhā* refer to the twelve *kalās* (energies), of which *medhā* is the *oṃkāra* and the first among them.
The syllables Oṃ, E, U, I, A, Ū, Ai, Au, and the letter A ending in the Visarga—these indeed are called mantras. [They are] established in these [places]: Au, E...

(l2) ...established in these, the lords of the five letters beginning with Au, who are situated below them. Alternatively, they reside in the locations of the heart, throat, palate, the space between the eyebrows, and the aperture of Brahmā.

Having contemplated that these lords— Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and Sadāśiva— who abide in their respective order within the syllables *a*, *u*, [and *m*], and in the states of the moon and the sound (*nāda*), have undergone dissolution and have reached the state of absorption; then, from that supreme place situated at the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*)...

Having meditated upon Paraśiva, who resides at the *dvādaśānta* existing above [the head], for the purpose of attaining the state of mind that has entered into Him; the "collection of senses" (*akṣanikara*) refers to the multitude of *rudrākṣa* beads present on the rosary. This characteristic is stated in the *Āgama*:

"As a rosary of beads (*akṣasūtra*) consisting of one hundred and eight [beads] is always considered the best; half of that is declared the middling, and half of that again is regarded as the inferior, when made of *rudrākṣa* for the sake of the Great Form (*mahāmūrti*)."
The supreme bestower of liberation...
(l6) It should be made with one face, three faces, four faces, five faces, or six faces; therefore, one should avoid those that are mixed. A face should be placed upon a face; the root...

That which remains the size of an *dhātrī* fruit is the best; that drawn from a large jujube (*badara*) is the middle; and that the size of a chickpea (*caṇaka*) is the lowest. It is said that [the thread] should be made with fresh butter-fiber as before, auspiciously... (l8)... However, the knotting should be done either as the *sāvitra*, the one called *brahma*, or the one called *meru*, which has a knot above the knot; it must not be transgressed. Alternatively, it should be made with twenty-seven [threads].
And it is said: "With twenty-seven beads, on five faces...

one should fashion a rosary in the shape of a cow’s tail ring. From the middle of the fingers, pulling each bead one by one—one toward the middle finger—for the sake of enjoyment (*bhukti*) via the downward path;
for the sake of liberation (*mukti*), upward via the upper path. And it is said: for enjoyment, [the movement is] in the direction of creation..."

One should pull the rosary by means of the thumb; one should pull it for the sake of liberation slowly along the upward path. The mantra-practitioner must not overstep the *meru*; by overstepping it, he incurs a fault.
Rosaries that lack a *meru* should be made separately... [lacuna].

The remainder [of the instruction] is that one should pull [the beads] with the thumb and the index finger. And it is said: "While reciting the mantra, [one should hold the bead] positioned on the middle finger with the thumb and the index finger."
One should gradually reduce it by one *kṣama* at a time. Then, for me... [in] the abode...

(l4) ...the turning of the earth; one hundred and eight [recitations] are to be chanted, as well as a thousand and half [of that], and not an indefinite number, nor wandering [the mind], nor even with delay—having thus chanted mentally, the meaning is that the recitation is for the cultivation of the mind... (l5)

(…) by merely moving the lips while hearing for oneself, it is *upāṃśu*. And it has been said: "That which is performed with the mind alone through the restraint of the movement of the vital breath (*prāṇavṛtti*) is mental (*mānasa*); that which is recited by merely moving the lips is proclaimed as *upāṃśu*. (l6) That which is audible to those listening and is known to produce sound is to be understood as *sāttvika*; the second is *rājasa*; and that which is clearly articulated is declared to be *tāmasa*. *Tāmasa* [is the third].

Having thus recited the *śivamanu*, the *śivamantra*—[which is] of a fierce nature—he should offer that recitation performed by himself to the God. He should perform the offering; the manner of offering is as follows: having placed the rosary in the palm of his right hand, having worshipped it with the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*) and protected it with the armor (*kavaca*) and weapon (*astra*) mantras, having placed it in His [the deity’s] hand, [he should place it] in the region of his heart...

Having placed the ground between his feet and knelt down, he should recite the verse beginning with "guhyātiguhyam," and then offer the water for the arghya with his cupped hands into the hand of Śiva—which is always held in the boon-granting gesture—saying: "Accept this recitation for Śiva, svāhā. ||18||
By Nemi...

(p90b, l1), while dwelling in the fire, joined with the eighteen purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) known as the *vāṣṭa*, they worship the fire born of the planets, beginning with the *bindu*. Having entered that fire of Śiva—which has arisen from the command (*ājñā*) of Vāgīśvarī—by means of this channel (*nāḍī*), [they worship] within their own heart as before, in the Supreme. (p90b, l2)

Having resorted to Śiva, and having well-accumulated the path of fire in the upward space of the sky, one should consume [the oblation] with ghee and sesame seeds; then, having placed the *śakti* in the *sruk* and Śambhu in the *sruva* within oneself, while reciting the mantra, one should stir the nectar of the *śakti*. Then, as it flows forth through the channel (*nāḍī*), the practitioner of immortality, having performed the filling of the *sruk* according to the prescribed method, should slowly perform the full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) for the completion of the fire-rite procedure. He describes this sequence of the fire-rite in a pair of verses. On the day... (the rest of the verse is not provided).
The rims (*nemi*) are at the [distance of] two fire-dwellings (*vahni-vasati*); the girdles (*mekhalā*) are at the center of the navel-pit (*nābhi-kuṇḍa*).

The inner region, being fashioned like a lotus with a measurement of half a pit (*kuṇḍārdha*), is to be made the "womb of the pit" (*kuṇḍayoni*); this is the remainder [of the sense]. Thus, provided with rims and a navel, [the fire-altar] reaches the rims and the navel;
having thus prepared it, at the fire-dwelling of one cubit (*hasta*)—that is, measuring one cubit—[one should proceed].

In the *kuṇḍa*, endowed with the eighteen-fold consecrations (*saṃskāra*)— that is, joined with the specific rites performed for the purpose of purifying the *kuṇḍa*— namely, inspection (*nirīkṣaṇa*), sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*), striking (*tāḍana*), and the measurement of the ground (*bhūpramāṇa*) in the *kuṇḍa*; [it is] endowed with the eighteen-fold consecrations— meaning joined with the specific rites performed for the purpose of purifying the *kuṇḍa*— [beginning with] inspection...

Indeed, the eighteen purificatory rites (saṃskāras) are: sprinkling, striking, pouring water over, digging, scattering [seeds], filling, leveling, moistening, pounding, sweeping, smearing with cow-dung, fashioning the image out of clay, encircling it with three threads, worshipping the image fashioned from clay, drawing four lines, making it possessed of a face, and ending with the four feet. Is this not so? [The sense organ] akṣa...

Regarding the term *pāṭa*, one consecration (*saṃskāra*) is not prescribed; therefore, how can there be a rule that there are eighteen? Some, having subsumed the consecration called *kalāmayābhyarcana* within the consecration called *kalāmayakalpanā*, assert that there are eighteen consecrations including the *akṣavāṭa*. However, by the former teachers who know our own tradition, the consecration called *rakṣapāṭa* was not accepted among the eighteen consecrations.

The manner of non-acceptance [of the site] is established simply from the sequence of the readings in the words of the former teachers. For example: "One should perform the inspection of the pit (*kuṇḍa*), the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*), and the striking with *kuśa* grass using the weapon-mantra (*astramantra*); the sprinkling is held to be performed with the armor-mantra (*varman*). One should also effect the removal of the excavated earth with the sword, its filling, and its leveling; the draining [of impurities] should be done with the armor-mantra..."

One should perform the sweeping, the smearing, the fashioning of the forms of the *kalās*, the encircling with three threads, and the sprinkling with the *varman* [mantra]; then, with the *hṛdaya* [mantra], one should draw three lines.

(L3) One should make one [line] facing east with *kuśa* grass using the *śiva-astreṇa* [mantra], or else there is a reversal of those [lines]. The making of the faces is with the *astra* [mantra], and with the *darbhas* and the *hṛdaya* [mantra], [one makes] the crossroads—thus it is stated in the *Somaśambhu-paddhati*. However, here, after stating the consecration of the fashioning of the forms of the *kalās*, [the author] speaks of the consecration of the encircling with three threads.
Immediately following that, the consecration (*saṃskāra*) consisting of the worship of the armor (*varman*) is prescribed.

For this very reason, it is indicated that the worship of the *kalās* is a separate consecration; for if it were a separate consecration, one would have stated the worship of the *kalās* immediately after the consecration of the conceptualization of the form of the *kalās*. Furthermore, because it is a separate consecration... [text fragment] ...because it is a separate consecration.
Immediately after the conceptualization of the form of the *kalā* within the *bhāva*, the worship of the *kalā* is a separate consecration (*saṃskāra*).
Because it is a separate consecration, it is made known that the consecration of the axle-pin (*akṣapāṭa*) is accepted as being among the eighteen consecrations.
Likewise, (l7)

In the *Jñānaratnāvalī* as well, the sequential recitation is as follows: having gazed with the eye and the *saṃpradāya*, the wise one should sprinkle [the site], strike it with his own *ātman*, and sprinkle it again with the *varma* mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*. He should perform the excavation and leveling with the *astra* mantra, the sprinkling with the *hṛdaya* mantra, and then the pounding with the *hetu* mantra. He should perform the sweeping and the smearing with the *kavaca* mantra.

The *kalās*, beginning with Śāntyatītā and the others, should be deposited starting from the center and proceeding eastward. One should encircle [the area] with three lines drawn in a subtle manner; then, having joined the [deity] consisting of the *kalās* to the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), one should perform the worship. Three lines facing east should be made.

With the *cottarānana* mantra, one should fashion a vajra-shape with three blades of *kuśa* grass; with the heart-mantra (*hṛdaya*), a fourfold [shape] should be made. From two *kuśa* blades with tips bent downwards, the eighteen purifications (*saṃskāra*) are briefly declared for the knot. For the stringing of the beads (*akṣapāṭa*), [one should act]... above, one should place the *kuśa* blades with the armor-mantra (*kavaca*). "Stringing of the beads" (*akṣapāṭa*) refers to the veil (*tiraskaraṇī*) or the cloth (*śāṭī*). Now, why has the purification of the stringing of the beads not been accepted even by the teachers?

If it is accepted that the consecration of the curtain is performed because the *tiraskariṇī* (curtain) of Akṣapāṭa was fashioned for the purpose of concealing Vāgīśvarī and Vāgīśvara, then when the eighteen consecrations of the pavilion (*maṇṭapa*) are being performed, [one must likewise perform] the consecration of the curtain there in that pavilion for the purpose of concealment.

Because it is impossible to perform [all of them], the inclusion of the *akṣapāṭa* consecration among the eighteen consecrations is unestablished and not accepted; rather, the remainder is that one must perform the invocation of Vāgīśvarī and Vāgīśvara within the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*). [The fire] is produced from the *araṇi*, from the house of a twice-born, and so forth.

*Araṇi* refers to a specific type of tree such as the *aśvattha*; "twice-born" refers to a member of a Brahmin lineage; by the word "and so forth," one's own home, sun-crystals (*sūryakānta*), and others are included—[the fire] produced from these is [taken] from the *araṇi*.

Having brought fire from a sun-crystal (*sūryakānta*) or from a brahmin’s house into an earthen vessel—or [from elsewhere]—according to the sequence of ritual procedures, one should observe the superior, middling, and inferior qualities of the sun-crystals respectively.
Likewise, regarding the cause: that which arises from a sun-crystal is the best, while that produced from wood is [inferior].

It would be the middle [state]. It is proclaimed that "the fire born from the form of the *śrotriya* consists of the portion of the maiden. Thus, there is a unification of the fire beginning with the *bindu*, and it has attained a state of oneness with the *gavi* and the fire.
Likewise, in the *Jñānaratnāvalī*: "The consciousness [is] by the seed-syllable of fire; it is to be consumed by the heart. (l. 8)

Taking [the seed-syllable] with the *hāramudrā*, one should join it with the *bindu* by means of inhalation (*pūraka*). Then, having effected its unification with the fire at either the heart or the navel through the practice of breath-retention (*kumbhaka*), one leads it outward by exhalation (*recaka*) into the blazing fire.

Thus, it is generated in Vāgīśī, who is called *Śayodit*, and produced within the goddess Vāgīśvarī. By this, the purificatory rites (*saṃskāras*) beginning with conception (*garbhādhāna*) are indicated.
