For the *saṃskāra* of conception (*garbhādhāna*), worship should be performed in the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) preceded by the recollection of Sadyojāta-Śiva. Having worshipped with [the mantra] beginning with "Sadyojāta," one should offer three oblations (*āhuti*) with sesame seeds using the Heart-mantra ending in *svāhā*. Thus it is stated in the *Ṣaṭsahasrasūka*: "He who, having placed [the seed] in the fire like a seed, [worships] Sadyojāta..."

Recalling Śiva with the *Sadyojāta* mantra and worshipping Him with the *Hṛdaya* mantra while offering three oblations with the *Dilā* mantras—in the *Puṃsavana* and other rites as well, worship must be performed preceded by the recollection of Śiva through the *Vāmadeva* and other mantras; this is to be understood from what is stated in the *Ṣaṭsahasraka*.
Or, the *Sīmantonnayana* consists of the assumption of the [divine] face and limbs, beginning from the head, by means of the *Śikhā* mantra.

Thus it is stated in the *Mṛgendra-tantra* by the venerable Nārāyaṇakaṇṭha in his commentary (*vṛtti*): "Immediately thereafter, regarding the manner of worship, it is said that his body should be produced by means of the thirty-eight *kalās*, or else [by means of] the aggregate. One should bring about that body by way of its being the form of Īśāna on the head, Tatpuruṣa as the face, Aghora as the heart, Vāmadeva as the secret organ, and Sadyojāta as the feet. This refers to the parting of the hair (*sīmantonnayana*).

By the phrase "Śivāgni," it is indicated that the naming ceremony (*nāmakaraṇa*) is to be performed, for it has been stated: "The naming and the ritual act (*nāmakarma*) must be performed; the fire is to be named 'Śivāgni' for the sake of accomplishing the remaining sacraments (*saṃskāra*); afterwards, one should cause the full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) to be offered. Alternatively, the naming should be performed by means of the principles (*tattva*) of Ātman, Vidyā, and Śiva. And it is said: "Or else, O Guha, one should cause the fire to be made 'Śivāgni' in another way, offering the full oblation three times with [the mantras] called Ātman, Vidyā, and Śiva."
One should cause [the fire] to blaze; thus the Śiva-fire is born.

By that, [he] is "devoid of all conditioned factors" (*sarvasaṃskāravarjita*). Because it consists of the splendor associated with Śiva, it is "sinless" (*anagha*) and its nature is merit; by this, the prayer is illuminated. And it has been said: "O Fire, you are the splendor of the Lord, for you are the supreme purifier (*pāvamāna*); therefore, in your heart-lotus..."

The meaning is as follows: having established [the deity] with the thought "I satisfy [him]," one should enter through the channel (*nāḍī*)—having entered into the interior of the body by means of the central channel in the form of the *suṣumṇā*—and then contemplate one's own self, thinking "I have entered. When that fire within one's own heart has been worshipped in the Supreme Śiva as previously described, [one should contemplate] the radiant form situated above the end of the crooked power (*kuṭilā-śakti*), beginning from the foundational power (*ādhāra-śakti*).

Having resolved [upon the form], having invoked Śiva into the image, and having meditated upon Him— consecrated by the rites beginning with installation (*sthāpana*), accompanied by the thirty-eight *kalās*, joined with either one enclosure or five enclosures according to the influence of the substrate and limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), and endowed with a reddish hue— (l4).

The meaning is that one should worship. Having emerged from the body of the fire—that is, having gone outside—and first having joined the faces of Śiva and Agni with their mouths turned upward, [one worships] the upward-turned faces beginning with Īśāna. By this, there is the joining of the faces through the flow of the face, the unification of the faces; [this occurs] by means of the wind that has reached the south-west (niṛti) through a single utterance of the five faces, and [the wind] that has reached the north-east (īśāna).

With a continuous or interrupted stream of ghee oblations, having offered the clarified butter into the western mouth of the fire-eater while facing north with the left hand, and into the northern mouth with the right hand— by means of a person of manifold forms facing upward—
with the mantra of Īśāna, using either single ghee oblations or three.

The "Vāruṇa" [rite] is described as the joining of the faces; one should offer five oblations of clarified butter (*ājya*) as follows: with the *vāmā* and *aghora* [mantras], one should offer clarified butter from the *sruva* ladle into those two mouths;
with the *ghora* and *tatpuruṣa* [mantras], one should offer clarified butter into that pair of faces;
and with the *puruṣa* and *īśāna* [mantras], one should offer clarified butter into the pair of faces, and also into the northern face.
One should offer clarified butter (*ājya*) into that mouth, which expresses Śiva; one oblation is prescribed for the mouth, or three oblations for the joining of the mouths.
Thus the joining of the mouths has been described, and now the unification of the faces is explained:

one should likewise pour a stream of ghee from the five mouths beginning with Sadyojāta. Starting from the southeast corner and proceeding to the northwest corner, and starting from the southwest corner...
With an uninterrupted stream of clarified butter (*ājya*), one should effect the unification of the faces beginning with Sadyojāta and ending at the Rudra-corner (*rudrakoṇa*).
However, the unification of the face with the corresponding face should be performed in the sequence starting from Īśāna.

Thus, in the *Kālottara*: "In the pouring and joining of the faces, one should begin with the face; from the west up to Īśāna, the 'pouring of the faces' (*vaktrābhighāra*) is performed through the yoga of oblations of one's own mantras."

(……………) (l4) This is the supreme illumination of the faces. One should arrange [the offerings] above these two with the Śiva-mantra and the Īśa-mantra; likewise, for the pair of Vāma and Sadyojāta, one should arrange the path there by offering one oblation each with the Puruṣa and Aghora mantras. (l5)

"One should cause a single oblation to be offered through two faces; the joining of the faces is said to occur through the application of five oblations. Alternatively, the sprinkling (abhighāra) should be performed in the sequence beginning with Īśāna. And it is said:

"In the joining of the faces and the sprinkling, one should perform it with the [mantras] Sadyojāta and the others, or later with Īśāna and the others, having understood the unity of the face through ritual action. However, in the daily rite (nityakarman), [it is performed] at the face of Sadyojāta.

Having visualized the inclusion of the remaining faces within that [central] face, one should visualize that face as being the measure of the *kuṇḍa*; this is the "unification of the faces" (*vaktraikīkaraṇa*) according to the *Kālottara*. Furthermore, it is stated in the *Siddhāntaśekhara* that "the performance of daily rites (*nityakarman*) is beneficial in this western face," and likewise regarding the daily rites for disciples and the consecration (*saṃskāra*) in the [face] called *samapāṇi*.

"One should meditate on the other [faces] as being contained within the face of Sadyojāta. Thus, in the western [direction], one should perform the purification of the disciple and carry out the daily fire-oblation (*nityahoma*).
According to Somaśambhu, however, regarding the unification of the faces of Puruṣa, Aghora, and Vāmadeva:
having joined that [face] in the place of Tatpuruṣa and Īśāna, one should join that Īśāna in the place of the triad beginning with Tatpuruṣa. This is likewise stated in the *Vaktrābhiṣeka-sandhāna*.
One should perform [the rite] with the *Sadyojāta* and other [faces of Śiva].

Having understood the ritual action for the northeast (*aiśāna*)... [p93b, l1] ...having meditated upon the desired action, one should direct it toward the south-east (*āgneyī*). That primary action should be performed facing upward; its mouth should be directed toward that location, moving upwards.
The faces should be internalized, and that [mandala] is of the same measure as the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*). [p93b, l2] ...

Having discerned the inclusion [of all] within the nine [faces], one should contemplate that the bestowal of the fruits spoken by each respective face resides in the Īśāna face; for among the other faces, the Īśāna face is preeminent as the bestower of the fruits of all desires. Thus, it is said that although there is but one [deity], she is the bestower of fruits through many forms (*bahurūpā*), because of the context in which the tongue of Īśāna is described in the *Bahurūpā* [Tantra].

Likewise, in the *Kāmika*, it is proclaimed that the tongue of Bahurūpeśa is the locus of the tongue. Thus, by means of the unification of the faces, once the upward-facing face has been established, one should perform the unification of the contact and application of the nectar upon the tongues of all [the deities], beginning with Hiraṇyā. And it is said: "One should perform the kindling of the tongues by offering oblations one by one, using the letters from *ya* to *ha*, excluding the letter *ra*, with the letter *ra* conjoined with the sixth vowel (*ū*)."

"Having joined each pair together, one should lead them into dissolution in the middle. This means that when the fire has been properly joined with its upward-facing mouth—that is, when the joining of the upper face of the fire and the upper face [of the vessel] has been performed—one should offer oblations of ghee and sesame seeds. Regarding the eighteen refinements (*saṃskāra*) of the ghee, it has been stated by the Teachers as follows: "The four [refinements] beginning with inspection (*vīkṣaṇa*), the threefold circling of the fire, heating, placing upon the fire, taking down, causing to overflow, and pouring back."

Likewise, after the illumination of the *nīrājana* rite for the [deity] who has become thus, and after purifying the protective vessel (*rakṣā-kuṇḍana*), one should perform the recollection of the eighteen [offerings] with clarified butter (*ghṛta*) preceded by the mantra; then it shall become nectar. Having meditated upon the clarified butter as consisting of nectar, one need not further purify the ghee or the oil;
by casting a drop from the heart-mantra (*hṛdaya*), [it is purified].

Having poured the filtered fragrance [into the vessel], and having placed Śakti in the *sruk* ladle and Śambhu in the *sruva* spoon—likewise, as stated in the *Kāmika*: "Having taken the *sruk* and *sruva*, sprinkled them with water using a cloth, and enveloped them with the *kavaca* mantra; having heated their ends or whirled the tips over the fire, [one places] the tips of the *darbha* grass... (l9)

Having touched [the base] and rotated [the ladle] in the middle, and having rotated again from the middle, one should touch the base with the base; then, having performed the ritual placement (*vinyāsa*) of the three principles (*tattva*) upon those two, one should place Śakti on the *sruk* and Śambhu on the *sruva*.

Having worshipped them, one should place them to the right of the Master upon *darbha* grass and worship them with the Heart-mantra. From the beginning of the resonance (*nāda*) to the end of the resonance...

While reciting the mantra, [one should offer] the nectar of power (*śaktyamṛta*) from the skull-cup (*kapāla*) with clarified butter, while contemplating it as the nectar of immortality (*amṛtabhāvanayā*).

The meaning is that one should perform—that is, carry out—the completion of the ritual procedure of the fire-oblation (*homavidhi*), namely the *pūrṇāhuti* (the full oblation), which is of a complete nature, slowly and with an unbroken stream using the *sruk* ladle. Herein, the sequence for the *pūrṇāhuti* is as follows: with the *sruva* spoon... (line 3).

Having filled the *sruk* with clarified butter (*ājya*), holding the *sruva* with its opening facing upward, and placing it with its opening downward upon that [opening of the *sruk*], having placed a flower on the tip of the *sruk*, and having grasped the bases of the *sruk* and *sruva* with both hands joined in the *śaṅkha-sannibhā* mudrā—
grasping the upper part of their bases with the right hand and the rear part of their bases with the left— and having risen together with the *saṃpāta*.

With his body straightened, fixing his gaze on the base and tip of the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles at his own navel, and uttering the root mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ* with a final *pluta* vowel, he gradually leads the base of the *sruk* and *sruva* to the left breast; while recollecting that the stream of clarified butter issuing from the place of the drop is a stream of nectar, [he pours it] in a stream the thickness of a barley grain.

One should offer the entire clarified butter into the fire in an uninterrupted stream; this is the procedure for the *pūrṇāhuti* (final oblation). And it is said: having filled the *sruc* with ghee and placed the *sruva* face-down upon its tip, having fixed a flower there like a conch-shell [mudrā], holding the *sruc* and *sruva* with both hands, placing their bases at the center of the navel, and rising up, one should stand with body straight and mind concentrated, reciting the root mantra—this is the explicit [instruction].

Uttering the mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*, filling the sacrificial ladle (*sruca*) with clarified butter by means of the rays of the nectar of the *bindu* that have emerged from the aperture of the crown, one should offer the full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) into the fire of Śiva. ||20||

For the attainment of gold, with honey; for the perfection of cattle, with cow’s milk; for prosperity, with clarified butter; for fortune, with sugar; for fame, let the straight-acting [priest] offer [oblations]; for the increase of internal [wealth], when there is [the presence of] cloth; for pervasion, with rice grains; for immediate purpose, with parched grain; for clothing, with *sumbha* flowers; for garments, with lotuses; for a lord of the earth, with blue lotuses... (p94b, l2)

[The bride] should offer oblations day after day with dolls (*puttalī*) and other such objects made of clay, using syllables beginning with *sā*, *di*, *na*, *hi*, *ra*, *ga*, and *ja*, for the sake of moving the bedstead, for the prevention of drought, and for the increase of wealth.

[She should offer] with *ṛpipetaiḥ* (?). With a pair [of verses], he states the visible fruit of the optional oblation (*kāmyahoma*): "With gold" (*svarṇa*)—that is, with honey (*madhu*), meaning honey from bees—and with ghee (*ghṛta*), she should offer for the attainment of gold, that is, for the purpose of acquiring wealth; thus the connection is made.

With cow’s milk (*gavyapayasā*)—that is, with cow’s milk—for the sake of accomplishment; with clarified butter (*sarpiṣā*)—that is, with cow-ghee—for the sake of cattle; with sugar (*śarkarayā*) for the sake of prosperity (*lakṣmyai*), that is, for the sake of accomplishing the attainment of sons and other riches; with curd (*dadhnā*) for the sake of fame, that is, for the sake of accomplishing renown; [with] yogurt-curd (*dadhnā*) for the sake of all aims, that is, for the sake of all divine aims—one should offer.

One should perform the *homa* with *antardhāna* [mantras] for the sake of internal prosperity; with sesame seeds (*tila*) for the attainment of wealth; with rice grains (*taṇḍula*) for the acquisition of materials; with parched grain (*lāja*) for immediate fame; with *sāśvārijai* [seeds] for the sake of auspiciousness;
with *kusumbha* flowers together with buffalo ghee for the sake of clothing; and with lotuses (*padma*) so that one may behold a king or sovereign—thus they are connected.
O King, with blue lotuses (*utpala*) [he honors] the king’s wives;
with white lotuses (*kairava*), the ministers of the kings; and with fuel-sticks (*samidh*) from the *aśvattha*, *palāśa*, *udumbara*, and *vaṭa* trees, the castes beginning with the [Brahmin] face.

One should bring under control—that is, subjugate—the classes of Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras by means of effigies made of flour, dolls fashioned from rice-flour, and female figures made of cooked rice; this should be done day after day until success is attained. (p95a, l1) … One should offer oblations of *śīra* fruit for the purpose of subjugation; such is the connection [of the text]. During a time of drought, the practitioner (*mantrin*) should offer oblations with sea salt (*loṇa*), employing the appropriate mantra for that purpose.
For the sake of sustenance, one should cross a river with the mind;
[having crossed], one should act as follows. ||22||

Initiation (*dīkṣā*) is of two kinds: the worldly (*laukikī*), which consists of the material and the ascetic (*bhautika-naiṣṭhikī*), and the other, which belongs to one whose nature is Śiva (*śivadharmiṇi*).

Of these, the first is called "with seed" (*sabījā*), capable [of yielding results] in the case of those possessing supreme power; likewise, the one called "seedless" (*nirbījakā*) is for others. When a person possesses intense suffering, [the seedless initiation] brings about immediate [liberation].
She bestows nirvāṇa, is seedless, and is purified by the conduct of her own *samaya*;

she abides in devotion, is the dissolution of consciousness, and is without support for the *pralayākala* and *sakala*. She has Śiva alone as her support, who is the self of all; yet she does not arise from the body nor from the nature of Śiva himself.

He explains [the nature of] initiation (*dīkṣā*) by means of a pair of distinct etymologies. Regarding the word *dīkṣā*: the syllable *dī* has the sense of "giving" (*dāna*), and *kṣā* has the sense of "destruction" (*kṣaya*). There is "giving" through the bestowal of the state of Śiva, and "destruction" through the effecting of the destruction of the three bonds (*pāśatraya*). First, it departed from the mouth of the Supreme Lord.

The *kriyādīkṣā* is so called because it brings about the realization of the fruit consisting of both worldly enjoyment (*bhukti*) and liberation (*mukti*) as intended by the people who are its listeners— beginning from the lords of knowledge (*vidyeśvara*s) down to gods, sages, and humans—

and because it effects the destruction of the bonds (*pāśa*s) such as impurity (*mala*). Furthermore, that ritual action (*kriyā*) by which one’s nature as Śiva is manifested through the separation from the three bonds by means of the grace of Śiva is called *dīkṣā*, characterized by devotion and dispassion.
Elsewhere also it is said: "The true nature of knowledge is bestowed...

the latent impression of karma is removed by the threefold gift... for initiation (*dīkṣā*) is that which purifies the self. Thus, because it bestows both worldly enjoyment (*bhukti*) and liberation (*mukti*), it accomplishes two goals. First of all, he states that initiation is of two kinds. This is initiation... (p95b, l1)

The initiation (*dīkṣā*) accompanied by the bestowal of a name, which results in the attainment of various desired enjoyments, is the first; that [is] the *bhautikī* initiation, which subsequently bestows liberation.
Likewise, in the *Rurusaṃhitā*: "Initiation [purifies] the body... (l. 2).

Those born within the maṇḍala, whose bodies shine with the splendor of the maṇḍala produced by the Siddhas, having enjoyed pleasures for a very long time and being accompanied by throngs of celestial nymphs, their longing subsided, they become partakers of the sovereignty of the state of Supreme Śiva. These are the *bhavanasiddhas*...

(l3) ...established in mindfulness, that absolute liberation (*kaivalya*) is attained through that wealth [of yoga]. Belonging to those perpetual ascetics who have received the final initiation (*naiṣṭhikī-dīkṣā*) and are endowed with boundless austerity, they are the *naiṣṭhikas*.

Having avoided the stages of *niṣṭhī* and *gṛhapada*, and after observing the vows for a few days, [he becomes] one who is established in the stage of (*...*) (*l4*). It is said that the *naiṣṭhika* [vow] lasts until the fall of the body, while the *bhautikī* vow leads to liberation;
by the word "but" (*tu*), it is indicated that there is a distinction between the initiation (*dīkṣā*) of the *bhautika* and the *naiṣṭhika*. The *bhautikī* [vow] is dependent (*sāpekṣā*)... (*l5*)

The *sāpekṣā* [devotion] is that which depends on the material world; the *naiṣṭhikī* [devotion] is independent. The *sāpekṣā* is accompanied by dependence on the performance of conventions (*samaya*) and so forth, while the *nirapekṣā* is devoid of the performance of conventions and so forth.

And it has been said: "That which leads one to Śarva according to the conventions and so forth, consisting primarily of distinguished personal qualities, is called *sāpekṣā* by the wise; [that which is] incapable of conventions and so forth [is the other]."
Because she disregards those such as the elderly, the foolish, and children,

she is "indifferent" (*nirapekṣā*). By the word "but" (*tu*), it is further shown that *Śivadharmiṇī* alone is considered twofold— namely, *Bhautikī* and *Naiṣṭhikī*— and thus another opinion is transcended.

Likewise, in the *Siddhāntaśekhara*: "In the Śivadharma, there are two types: the worldly (*bhautikī*) and the ascetic (*naiṣṭhikī*). Among these, the first is called 'worldly' (*laukikī*); it consists of worldly duties such as those prescribed by the Vedas and so forth. Regarding the fruit for one who follows worldly duties (*lokadharmiṇī*), [the text] says: "(p96a, l1) It bestows the eightfold supernatural power (*aṣṭaguṇardhi*) above the body; after the fall of the body, it grants the abundance of the eight powers beginning with *aṇimā*, namely: *aṇimā*, *mahimā*, and *garimā*..."

Lightness (*laghimā*), as well as lordship (*īśitva*), mastery (*vaśitva*), attainment (*prāpti*), and the power of irresistible will (*prākāmya*)—these are the eight qualities (*guṇa*). [She] bestows excellent enjoyments in the desired world, that is, in the world of one's own choice; she perfectly grants enjoyment. In all the lands of enjoyment (*bhogabhūmi*), the portion of one's misdeeds remains here [in this world] until the body perishes; for the sake of [attaining] powers such as atomization (*aṇimā*) and so forth, that which is desired by the learned is called "possessing worldly characteristics" (*lokadharmiṇī*). Another is designated by the name "possessing Śiva-characteristics" (*śivadharmiṇī*).

When that *śivadharmiṇī* initiation has been performed, a human being who has abandoned both worldly and Vedic conduct becomes an enjoyer of Śiva (*śivabhuk*); he does not become merely the supreme Self. That initiation is called *śivadharmiṇī*.

The meaning is that immediately after the enjoyment of the fruits of the Śiva-dharma, there occurs the manifestation of attributes such as omniscience for the self; for it has been stated that "the root of one who possesses the Śiva-dharma is the support for the fruits of the Śiva-dharma. In that regard, first, for those possessing the Śiva-dharma who bear the *liṅga*, [there is] the cutting of the topknot (*śikhāccheda*), while for householders who possess the worldly dharma (*lokadharmin*), [there is the cutting of the beard].

The cutting of the topknot (*śikhāccheda*) has been stated to be twofold: the initiation of worldly nature (*laukikī dīkṣā*) and that of the nature of Śiva (*śivadharmiṇī*). It should be known that the initiation of worldly nature belongs to the householder, while for one who bears the [Śaiva] marks (*liṅgin*), it is the initiation of the nature of Śiva. Where there is no cutting of the topknot, that initiation is of worldly nature; the initiation associated with the cutting of the topknot is that of the nature of Śiva. Likewise, elsewhere it is said: "In the initiation of worldly nature, the Guru should not initiate householders."

In that same way, one should initiate those who possess the *śivadharmī* [nature] by means of the austerity-based initiation (*tapodhana*) accompanied by the cutting of the topknot (*śikhāccheda*). (L8) It should be understood that where there is no cutting of the topknot, it pertains to the *sālokadharmī*. Having caused the one possessing the *śivadharma* to ascend, one should unite him with the supreme state; upon the fall of the body, liberation shall occur. (The conduct of the observance... (P96b, L1)

(…) having superposed [the deity] upon the substratum (*dharmin*), one should effect the protection of its attributes within the creator of the world. For one whose devotion is fixed on Śiva, there is enjoyment (*bhoga*) in the reality of Sadāśiva; his dissolution (*laya*) is in the state beyond that, which is the primordial (…). (l2) Together with the name “seed of the Egg” (*aṇḍabīja*), the state of being a seed (is established). Because it is accompanied [by this], there is a dependence upon the performance of the rules of conduct (*samayācāra*), which serves as the means for the fruit ordained by initiation (*dīkṣā*).

The remainder [of the meaning] is that for those who possess the seed (*sabīja*) and are capable of performing the daily (*nitya*) and occasional (*naimittika*) purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*), the rite with seed (*sabījā*) must be performed.

Likewise, by Varuṇaśiva, it was proclaimed that for the wise who are capable, the rite with seed is prescribed; whereas for others who are incapable of the lifelong vow (*naiṣṭhikī*), [the rite without seed is intended].

Regarding those who are incapable of performing the observances (*samaya*) and other rites—such as children, the dull-witted, the elderly, and women—the initiation known as "seedless" (*nirbījā*), so called because it lacks the performance of such observances and rites, is intended for them; the meaning is that it bestows [liberation] even upon children and the like. For children, the very foolish, the elderly, women, those who enjoy [worldly pleasures], and those afflicted by disease, there is the seedless initiation in this world, which is devoid of the rules of conduct (*samayācāra*).
Because it has been stated thus: "Bāliśa" means a fool (*mūḍha*).

Regarding the term *bāla*, [the lexicon] *Nānārtha* states: "The words *bāla* and *bālikā* mean a fool. By the word "thus" (*tathā*), it is indicated that for even those such as the *bālas* who desire enjoyment on the pure path (*śuddhādhvan*), and likewise for those ascetics without limit who desire liberation, the *nirbīja[-samādhi]* must be performed. And it has been said: [ni... (l7)

However, for those who are incapable [of renunciation] but whose souls delight in enjoyment, one should first perform the initiation that purifies the *samayas* and so forth; then, effecting their dissolution into the supreme reality (*paratattva*), one should contemplate their enjoyments within the path of purification (*śuddhādhvan*). With devotion, they should always perform the worship of Śiva for as long as they live, as well as the worship of the teacher (*ācārya*) and of ascetics according to their ability. This has been stated even for those desiring liberation: "He whose karma has been burnt by the fire of initiation..."

The knower of reality (*jñānin*), having reached the state where bonds are severed by *māyā*, abides in the supreme, seedless (*nirbījā*) culmination within Śiva. For him, there is no need for observances (*niyama*), nor for external signs (*liṅga*), nor for visiting sacred fords (*tīrtha*) or shrines (*kṣetra*), nor for bodily mortifications (*dṛṇa*). Now, the seeded (*sabījā*) [initiation] is also considered to be of two kinds, according to the distinction between "with qualification" (*sādhikāra*) and "without qualification" (*niradhikāra*). Among these, that which is with qualification... (p97a, l2)

Because *dīkṣā* (initiation) bestows the qualification (*adhikāra*) for performing those respective rites such as *sthāpanā* (consecration) and so forth, whereas for the *samadhis* and the *putrakas*, it bestows the lack of qualification (*anadhikāra*) for performing those respective rites such as *dīkṣā* and *sthāpanā*. And it has been said: "It is with qualification (*sādhikārā*) [for the practitioner and the teacher], because through it there is qualification; since both [the *samadhi* and the *putraka*] lack qualification regarding the success of *dīkṣā* and *sthāpanā*, that [initiation] is considered to be without qualification (*niradhikāriṇī*). (L3)

Then he says that for those who are incapable [of the aforementioned practices], there are two ways: [the path] devoid of conventional conduct (*samayācāra*), which consists of seeds (*bīja*), and that which is immediate liberation (*sadyonirvāṇa*). [This state] exists—meaning it is present—in a man, a human being, who is devoted to the Lord (*īśabhakta*) and utterly detached, when the "sickness" of impurity has ripened and reached its final stage, and when [the fire] is not yet intensely blazing.

The *sadyonirvāṇa* initiation is that which purifies one's own conduct according to the rules (*samaya*) immediately after the initiation; it consists of the purification of the conduct prescribed for the obligatory (*nitya*), occasional (*naimittika*), and other rites through the application of seed-syllables (*bīja*). It grants liberation immediately upon the completion of the initiation—meaning that liberation is attained right then and there. The *asadyonirvāṇa* initiation, on the other hand, grants liberation only after the fall of the body once the *prārabdha* karma has been exhausted; this is its meaning.

Likewise, in the *Siddhāntaśekhara*: "Now, the seedless initiation (*nirbījakā dīkṣā*) is declared to be of two types. [The first] grants immediate liberation; the latter grants liberation after some time. By the former, the karma of those who are intensely detached—whether already begun, accumulated, or yet to come—is purified, and it grants immediate liberation. But by the latter, [the karma] of those whose karma has already begun is purified through experience and so forth..."
Immediately thereafter, [he says that] initiation (*dīkṣā*) is twofold—by way of being without support (*nirādhāra*) and having support (*sādhāra*)—so that it may grant liberation after a long time.
He states that [initiation] performed by Śiva himself among the souls who are *vijñānākala* and *pralayākala* is [the one without support]. (p97b, l1) ...

it is called "without locus" (*niradhikaraṇa*), "without foundation" (*niraṇa*), and "without support" (*nirādhāra*). That which has an office (*sādhikāra*) is "with support" (*sādhāra*). Support (*ādhāra*), locus (*adhikaraṇa*), substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*), and station (*sthāna*) are synonyms.

By that [reasoning], the meaning is as follows: since there is no possibility of efficacy through the *paraśiva* who is devoid of that substratum (*ādhāra*)—[the rest of the sentence is lost]—[it is because] the purpose [of initiation] cannot be achieved by the severance of the bonds (*pāśa*) such as *kalā* and the rest. And it has been said: "This initiation is thus divided into that which possesses a substratum and that which is devoid of a substratum; [without an *ācārya*,] the ritual action [cannot proceed]. (l. 3)

For them, [the initiation] of Śambhu... and of the *pralayākala* through the descent of intense power (*dīpra-śakti*) is an initiation devoid of commonality (*sādhāra-varjita*). By resorting to the form of the Guru, [the initiation] is performed through the descent of mild power (*manda-śakti*), and thus it is "with parts" (*sakalā*) and possesses commonality (*sasādhārā*). This refers specifically to the domain of the initiation with commonality (*sādhāra-dīkṣā*), which distinguishes it from the previously mentioned types of initiation. This fourfold initiation is "with commonality," as it is stated in the teaching of Śiva: "This is the initiation with commonality according to the Śiva-scripture."
The initiation (*dīkṣā*) and its purificatory rite (*saṃskāra*) pertain either to the body or to the caste (*jāti*).

[In order to remove doubt regarding this, he says: "And in this Śaiva Siddhānta, the purificatory rite of initiation is not prescribed for the body, as it is for the twice-born (*dvija*) in the Vedic tradition; nor is it prescribed merely on account of [caste] Brāhmaṇahood. Rather, [it pertains] to the Śaiva self (*śaivātman*)."

The initiation (*dīkṣā*) rite is prescribed for the purpose of establishing the Śiva-nature of the self (*ātman*), which has been thirsting since beginningless time; thus it is said [in the text] "of the Śaiva self.

The status of being a twice-born (*dvija*) according to the Veda is stated to belong to the body alone, and not to the self. Accordingly, one should interpret the words of the *Smṛti* that set forth the meaning of the *Śruti*: "The purification of the body is to be performed by means of sowing, sprinkling, and so forth, as well as by the *garbhādhāna* rites, the *jātakarma*, the *caula*, and the tying of the *mauñji* [girdle]," because the body is insentient (*jaḍa*).

Ritual consecration (*saṃskāra*) is not accepted [as the basis for caste] because, when a person belonging to a specific birth-group such as a Brāhmaṇa undergoes a ritual consecration, and having become endowed with that consecration, his sons and descendants are likewise considered consecrated by virtue of that [consecration]. Thus, since consecration is established by the world [as the cause], it is not accepted as being based on birth. Therefore, in this case... [text missing].

The initiation (*dīkṣā*) which is presided over by Śiva, acting through the Guru as the teacher of all embodied souls (*sakalātman*), is that which possesses a common substratum (*sādhārā*). The substratum is the teacher alone;

it is Śiva himself who, presiding over the form of the Guru, [performs] the initiation for all embodied souls... [the] purification (*saṃskāra*) intended for the removal of impurity (*mala*) is recognized as belonging to the body. And regarding the [question of] birth, it has been said: "The purification of a living being is not considered to belong to the birth nor to the body, if..."

When one member of a family is initiated, it follows that the rest of the family is also initiated; yet this does not apply to the *jāti* (the caste or species), because the body is considered to be insentient (*jaḍa*).

Śiva, who bestows grace upon all, declares that grace resides in the conscious nature (*cidrūpa*). Thus, it is stated in the *Kālottara*: "There is no purification of the body, nor of the *jāti*, nor of karma. The Self does not cause initiation for one whose throat is constricted by beginningless impurity."

Its cessation must be brought about by means of mantras, like the neutralization of the potency of poison. Initiation alone bestows liberation upon men, effecting the manifestation of consciousness within the unconscious. 24.

The time for initiation (*dīkṣā*) is during the rainy season, excluding the months of Pauṣa and Caitra; during festivals of the gods, on the *dvāmana* [day], at the sun’s passage into a new sign (*saṃkrānti*), at the equinoxes (*viṣuva*) and solstices (*ayana*), and during the festivals of initiation and purification (*pavitra*). It is auspicious on Mondays, Sundays, Wednesdays, Thursdays, Saturdays, and Fridays; and under the asterisms Maitra (Anurādhā), Ārka (Śravaṇa), Anila (Svātī), Saumya (Mṛgaśiras), Paitṛ (Maghā), Nirṛti (Mūla), Pūṣā (Puṣya), Śārdūla (Pūrvabhādrapadā), Īśvara (Ārdrā), Jyeṣṭhā, Rohiṇī, and the three Uttaras (Uttaraphalgunī, Uttarāṣāḍhā, Uttarabhādrapadā). It is also auspicious on Tuesdays and Sundays. This is the time for initiation.

He states the determination of the lunar mansions and so forth: "At the time" (kāle)—the remainder of the sentence being that initiation (*dīkṣā*) should be performed at a time excluding the rainy season (*vārṣika*), the month of Pauṣa, and the month of Caitra. The "rainy season" (*vārṣika*) consists of the two months beginning with Caitra, because, according to the sequence of spring, summer, rain, autumn, winter, and the cool season (*śiśira*), the rainy season occurs [in those months]; specifically, Śrāvaṇa and Bhādrapada. According to the sequence of spring, summer, autumn, winter, and the cool season, the two months beginning with Caitra constitute the seasons.
Regarding the phrase "are proclaimed": Pauṣa (the month of Puṣya) and Caitra are [recommended] for the rite of initiation (*dīkṣā*).
In the remaining eight months, initiation should be performed.
Likewise, in the *Siddhāntaśekhara*: "Initiation during the autumn season and in Vaiśākha bestows the most excellent fruit; initiation in Phālguna, Mārgaśīrṣa, and Jyeṣṭha is middling."

In the month of Āṣāḍha, [the obstruction] of the planets beginning with Jupiter (*jña*) should be performed. Starting from the corner of the path (*vīthikoṇa*), one should know that the center, measuring four squares, extends up to the outer corner.
There, in the eight arrays (*vyūha*) of the lords of the directions (*viśayeśvara*), Gaṇeśvara, Indra, and so forth, [the ritual should be done] in due order.

(…) *svastikas* should be made in the form of lotuses and water-lilies (*kuvalaya*). Likewise, regarding the arrangement of the *vajra* and other [weapons]: *svastikas* for the weapons such as the *vajra* and *śakti* [are placed]; for the weapon of the Lotus [deity], a lotus should be made on the four squares to the south from the northeast corner; from the southwest corner (…) (l3) on the four squares to the east, a water-lily should be made for the Wheel [deity]. On the four squares to the south from the northeast, a lotus should be made for Brahmā; from the southwest corner, on the four squares to the north…

A lotus is to be made for Viṣṇu; for Brahmā and Viṣṇu, as well as for the guardians of the directions beginning with Nirṛti and Īśāna, their positions are to be established on both sides of the door by means of equal units. On both sides of the door, starting from one unit of measurement, [the construction] extends from the cheeks and throat up to the side of the door, including the neck and its vicinity.

The work should be executed with the remaining words by those who are learned. The corner [of the mandala] consists of the two sides of the corners starting from the southeast. It is covered with petals of the color of the moon (white), and covered with petals of yellow color;

the pericarp (*karṇikā*) is yellow, and the filaments (*kesara*) are yellow. Starting from the upper part, they possess the luster of white, red, and gold, joined with stamens (*kiñjalka*) of white, red, and golden hue. The central lotus in the middle should be made; the ground is green.
The area between the petals should be made green in color.

The corner squares, representing the [faces] beginning with Dharma, possess white, red, yellow, and black colors. The body is variegated, consisting of various colors. The svastikas should be red in color.
The weapons at the gates, such as the pāśupata and others, are golden; the face-gate is [the face of] Tatpuruṣa and the others.
The door is accompanied by its own color; this is the specific characteristic of the primordial maṇḍala. It is described in the *Kiraṇa* as "the arrival of rays" (*kiraṇāgama*).
Likewise, in the *Kiraṇa*:
[omitted] (p99a, l1) "Or else, having divided eight hands—or indeed sixteen—into three parts, and each part again into eight, one should draw a lotus with four [parts]."

The *vidhikā* should be equal to those parts; for the purpose of the wave (*vīci*), first... (l2) ...the enclosure on the outside, and the doors, which are the measure of the lotus, one should fashion with that very same proportion. One should then fashion the neck (*kaṇṭha*) equal to one part, and likewise the cheek (*kapola*).
Having fashioned the area near the neck (*upakaṇṭha*) in the same way, the remainder is praised as being beautiful... (l3) ...so it is sung.
Having placed the sun [in its position], the first leaders, the fierce-faced ones situated upon blue lotuses, are to be worshipped as the Īśvaras in the eastern lotus.
The Lokanāthas are to be worshipped on the svastika, excluding the four parts. [The outer circle] bestows the collection of weapons... (l4) ...well-rounded according to the characteristics. ||50||

In a field divided into ninety-six squares by means of vowel-squares, there is a lotus in the center; outside of that, the body-lines and the paths are formed by eight [squares], then the directional lotuses by eight, the eight doors by [eight]...
(l5) ...by the squares situated between the elephants, the junctions by four, and then the elephants in the directions by the sages (seven), the doors by the internal [squares], and the path.
As before, there is a lotus in the eight directions with intervals of seven parts;

the doors are established in eight squares, and outside there is the worship of the enclosure wall and the world-protectors. Alternatively, there is a svastika in the eight directions made of two [squares], or a dot and a lotus;
the doors are formed by the inner [intervals], and the positions of Hari are according to the rule of the directions and the petals.

*Mṛgendrapura*. With a pair of verses, he describes a particular type of city layout and mandala. Regarding the phrase "in the field": when the accepted field has been divided into ninety-six parts and the lines for east and north have been laid out with ninety-seven squares each, one should construct a lotus consisting of sixteen squares in the center using the [sixteen] vowel-squares. (l8) ... (p99b, l1)

Outside the lotus, on the exterior, one should construct a *vīthikā* (procession path) with eight lines and eight squares on all sides; the remainder implies that the line-structure (*rekhāgātraka*) and the rows should be made starting with white lines and so forth.

Therein, by a measurement of three squares, one should respectively construct the four [elements] beginning with the white line, starting from the bottom (*yathākramaṃ śukla...*). With the remaining five squares, the *gātraka* and the *vīthikā* should be made in the four directions and the corners. Immediately after performing it thus below—

With eight [units], sixty-four squares multiplied by eight [and] eight (i.e., 64), lotuses with eight additional petals are to be made; by means of sixteen squares situated between the petals, with a width of two squares and an elevated edge of eight squares on both sides, two squares are for the purpose of the cheeks... (l. 4).

In each of the eight directions, eight doors should be made by means of two doorways [per direction]. Then, immediately after that, a series of walkways (vīthikā) should be constructed all around, consisting of four squares (pada) and provided with limbs such as white lines and so forth. In the eight directions, fifty-one lotuses should be made, multiplied by the seven sages (saptaguṇita); for here, the lotus is said to have a measurement of seven squares (sapta-pada-pramāṇa).
The central lotus situated between the eastern and western directions should be provided with an increase of the northern syllables;

the lotus situated between the southern and northern directions should be provided with an increase of the eastern syllables. By means of the syllables located in the center of the inner lotuses, [the arrangement] of the neck and its vicinity on both sides of the door [should be made]... [gaika].

Having set aside one part, the eight gates are to be made with one part; in the same way, it should be done at the northern gate as well. As before, the path should consist of four parts and be formed by seven [parts] each; there should be eight lotuses. The inner [spaces] should be formed by the middle parts, and the eight gates should be made [thereby]. After performing it thus on the outside...
The world-protectors stand upon eight squares;

[therein is] the worship of the weapons of Indra and the other gods, such as the thunderbolt (*vajra*). For the purpose of worship, a *svastika* should be made in the eight directions, or else it should be fashioned in the shape of a drop, a lotus, or a pair of lotuses, with the *svastika* and other [symbols] in the interior.

Outside the *stika* and other [enclosures], eight gates are to be constructed with the remaining words, measuring four squares each. The direction of Īśa and Palāśa is the path (*vīthī*) between the directions of Īśāna and Rākṣasa;
the place of Hari is, in due order, the place of Brahmā and Viṣṇu.
The directions of Astra, Īśāna, and Nairṛti serve as indicators. The place for the lotus is in the square to the south of Īśāna, and that of Cakṣas is in the square to the north of Niṛti.

The location for the two lotus petals is in the upper and lower regions respectively; this is the specific feature in the Brahmā-Viṣṇu-pūjanaya-maṇḍala. It is also stated in the Mṛgendrāgama: "The five groups [of deities] are in the great seat (*mahāpīṭha*), adorned with the gate of teeth; [therein are] Truth (*satya*) and Peace (*śama*). [The rest of the line is illegible.]

Having abandoned [the previous measurement] and established ninety-six [units], one should fashion the pedestal (*pīṭha*) and the lotus-petal [pedestal] as three parts; its width should be four units. One should worship the deities and perform the eightfold rite (*aṣṭaka*).
Having fashioned that characteristic here, it is said that the first [measurement] is by an eighth part in every direction.

From within that, there are thirty-two [units]; the doors are as before. One should arrange the *śobhā* ornaments wherever they appropriately fit. Likewise, [one should place] the faces of the world (*loka-bhaktra*) and the *namaḥ*.
[One should place] Satya, Īśa, Garuḍadhvaja, [and] Svāstra-mūla-ūrdhva... (100b, l1) ...

[with] the seventeen-fold [mantras] on both sides; one should invoke Gaurī-latā in the center with Vedic words, and in the intermediate directions with [ordinary] words, and place the lotuses of the elements. The liṅga, the cloth, the lake-lotus, the neck-lotus, and the pedestal [should be placed] in sequence on the right... (l2).

With many squares formed by the intersection of lines, there should be creeper-patterns; [this refers to] Gaurī’s specific type of creeper-design made with marked threads. With seventeen-fold—that is, with threads numbering seventeen—drawn from both sides, east and south, [and so on]...

west, having thus made the field consist of sixteen squares by means of the seventeen threads running east-west and north-south—the remainder being that—in the center, with four squares for the Veda, in the intermediate directions...

In the four directions from the center of the southeast [quarter], by means of four-syllable words designated by letters—specifically the letter *gha*, which represents the number four, or twice that measure—one should place or construct five lotuses, which are the "elemental lotuses" (*bhūtāmbuja*). [The phrase] "rain-clouds" (*varṣābhra*) refers to the number of syllables; thus, "four, six, earth" (*catuḥ-ṣaḍ-bhūri*) signifies four.

The letter *re* occurs twice, the letter *vi* once, the letter *kā* four times, and the letter *ṣa* six times. With these numbers of directional words (*dikpada*) located in the four directions starting from Indra and with the central word, one should—in due order—construct the *liṅga*, the silken lotus, and the throat-lotus, as well as the silken cloth; this is the remainder [of the sense]. By means of the corner-joined words, that is, the words placed in the four corners starting from Agni, there should be five-word [units] in the form of creepers. Thus it is.
The creeper (latā) is called *gaurilatā* because it causes one who has committed [an offense] to fall to the ground (*medinīpātanāt*); thus, it receives the name *gaurilatā*. ||53||
Having established the Rudra-padas in the field, one should fashion a white lotus in the center with Graha-padas; in the four corners, one should arrange eight squares.

In the Dīkṣāditya-padas, one should place Svastikas with the radiance of gold, and below them, Liṅgas and Pīṭhas. Having removed the remaining distinct colored powders, one obtains the incomparable and supreme Bhadra-maṇḍala, preceded by the Subhadra.
Thus he states the characteristics of the maṇḍala known as Subhadra.

Regarding the term "field" (*kṣetra*): having made the field into eleven squares by means of a twelve-squared line drawn toward the northeast from the Rudra-square (the center), one should construct a lotus—a white water-lily—situated in the middle of nine squares consisting of the planetary squares. In the four corners, [in the group of eight squares]—because the total number of squares in the collection of four corners is sixty-four, being eight times eight—one [square] per corner...

Sixteen squares have been produced; with those sixteen squares, one should fashion [the design] consisting of golden light, yellow in color, and in the form of a svastika. Alternatively, there is the reading "with eight squares in the four corners"; that is, with sixteen squares established in each of the four corners starting from the southeast (agni), one [should fashion] the svastika.

It may be thus: immediately thereafter, in the directions—specifically in the four directions beginning with Indra—in the twelve squares corresponding to the positions of the Sun, or in the three, one, and single squares, the *pīṭhas* and *liṅgas* should be fashioned according to the sequence of the *yudhā* [mantra]. The remainder—that which is to be left over—should be erased (*lopya*) so that it becomes a different color from the color of the *liṅga* made of distinct powder; it should be "incomparable" (*atula*), meaning devoid of equality, that is to say, excellent (*śreṣṭha*).
The meaning is that it comes to have the name "Supūrvabhadra-paramasubhadra-maṇḍala" and so forth. ||54||

When divided into thirty-two parts, there is a lotus in the center; with sixty-four [parts] it is outside that, and with three parts there is a pedestal (*pīṭhaka*); then with one [part] the green path (*vīthī*), and in the cardinal directions, the gate with two [parts] for the sages (*ṛṣi*), and on both sides with excellent speech [parts] joined by the syllable *vaṣaṭ*, the *liṅga* with the outer part, and the path (*vīthī*) is variegated—this is indeed the characteristic of the mandala of Umākānta. He states the characteristics of the Umākānta mandala.

"Thirty-two" means: having divided [the area] into thirty-two parts, and having divided it into thirty-two portions by means of thirty-three threads extending across the three directions, a lotus—meaning a *kamala*—should be made with sixty-four parts. Outside of that, meaning outside the lotus, a pedestal (*pīṭha*) should be made all around with three parts each. Four... (line 9)

*Kṣu* means a pathway (*vīthī*) joined with the body [of the mandala]. Then, after the construction of the pedestal (*pīṭha*), one should create a yellow-colored pathway there, near the pedestal. In the directions—in the four directions starting from Indra—one should construct it with fourteen squares, having a width of two squares for each pair of *ṛṣis* and reaching a height of seven squares, forming four gates on both sides of the entrance.

With speech [expressed] through excellent verses consisting of sixty-four syllables, the *liṅga* should be fashioned according to the previously mentioned sequence of the pedestal (*liṅgapīṭha*) and so forth, accompanied by sixty-four lines.
By means of an external line—that is, a single line situated outside the *liṅga*—the enclosure (*vīthi*) should be made.
The other part, which is of a different nature, is variegated; it is adorned with various colors such as white and others, and thus becomes the mandala of Umākānta.
There may be a *svastika* [pattern] starting from the northeast corner (*aiśāna-koṇa*) among the chosen squares;
in three squares, the central compartments and other squares are likewise [arranged] by means of four squares.
He states the definition of the *svastika-maṇḍala*: "There may be," etc. Among the chosen squares, that is, among the sixteen squares.

The word *iṣṭi* is a term denoting a Vedic sacrifice; likewise, there is a Smṛti statement in the Śruti: "On the sixteenth day one should perform the *iṣṭi*, on the fifteenth day the *madhyā-iṣṭi*, and on the fourteenth day the *jayantī-iṣṭi*; thus there shall be five or seven. When the sacrifice has been commenced in the bright fortnight (*pūrvapakṣa*), it is performed on the sixteenth day of the following fortnight (*uttarapakṣa*) because of the primacy of that [sixteenth] day. The word expressing the number sixteen refers to the *svastika* [diagram] formed by five lines running eastward and northward, consisting of sixteen squares.

"One should cause [it] to be made"— thus, by the power of the Lord, beginning from the southeast corner (*aiśa-koṇa*), across three squares up to the four squares situated in the middle of the east, and across the three squares at the mouth of the southeast corner, ending with the central square, one should [proceed] near the previously mentioned three squares, using the square located at the position of Nairṛti and Vāyu.

The meaning is "together. Having erased—that is, having wiped away—the four squares of the *veda*, and having performed the procedure as previously stated starting from the other squares and so forth, there shall be a *svastika*.
Starting from the southeast corner (*agnikoṇa*), in the southern direction, [one should proceed] with the square facing Nairṛti;

together with the middle square equal to that, there is a group of four squares. Starting from the southwest corner (*nirṛtikoṇa*), [one proceeds] with the three squares facing Vāyu, together with the middle square situated equal to those squares.

One should erase four squares. Starting from the corner facing the wind (the northwest), one should erase four squares consisting of the three preceding squares together with the middle square equal to them. When this is done, a svastika will be formed. 56.

When the field has been divided, one should place two additional parts from here toward the east; having set aside one part in the middle, one should leave it out. Having made the inner face of the half-moon with three parts, one should place two parts for the neck above, and a row of squares all around. One square is for the north, and one should place three for the south; the lotus is considered to be for Caṇḍa, and the axe for Caṇḍeśvara. For the purpose of worshipping Caṇḍeśvara, [one should draw] the lunar disc...
He states the definition: "In the field" means in a field that has been taken up and divided according to the Vedas, made into four squares by five lines drawn eastward and northward.

From this field divided into four (halves), one should place—that is, cause to be made—an additional portion in the eastern direction, measuring two squares; specifically, one part [of that] should be placed. Furthermore, the field divided into four (halves) [is to be treated] again in the eastern direction.
The meaning is that one should cause it to be made endowed with an excess of a row measuring one *pada*.

(l6) Then, after the construction of the additional *pada*s, leaving aside a central portion measuring two *pada*s, one should, together with the *adhipada*s—the additional *pada*s—construct the *antarmukha*, which is a mandala in the shape of a half-moon (*ardhendu*). (l7) Above.

Above the half-moon, there is a neck (*gala*) of two squares (*dvipada*) surrounding the exterior square. A row should be made in the north (*saumya*); one should cause the northern square to be circular (*vṛtta*), with a single square situated in the center. The meaning is that one should cause three [squares] each to be formed in the northern squares. In the south (*yama*), in the southern square, one should place—that is, cause—to be made—a lotus (*kamala*). For Caṇḍa, for Caṇḍeśvara, the *ṭaṅka*—the mandala known as the *ṭaṅka*—is prescribed.
This is the consensus regarding the fierce worship (*caṇḍapūjā*).

(57) Having placed the disciple upon a seat of *kuśa* grass within the western mandala, having sprinkled him from the feet upward, having struck him well, having gazed at him, having sprinkled him with ashes, having scraped [the area] below the navel with *kuśa* blades empowered by the weapon-mantra (*astra*), and having touched his heart, one should contemplate the placement of the mantra (*mantranyāsa*)... (l2)

The hands, with flowers placed upon them, should be grasped below in the *bandhana* [mudrā]. Having thus explained the procedure for the various types of mandalas, he now describes the ritual for initiation according to specific commitments (*samaya*) in five verses beginning with "the western door" (*pratyak-dvāraka*). Since it has been stated that this pertains to the mandala with the western door, the performance of the preliminary worship of the pavilion (*maṇṭapa*) is indicated first; namely, having constructed the pavilion according to the prescribed characteristics, and having performed the two daily rites, one should perform the evening twilight worship (*sāyantanī saṃdhyā*) in the late afternoon.

Having completed the special twilight rite (*viśeṣasandhyā*), and having performed the special twilight procedure consisting of the libation (*tarpaṇa*) with the root mantra and so forth for the Lords of Knowledge (*vidyeśvara*s), the Lords of the Principles (*tattvādhipa*s), and likewise [the others]— according to the *Mṛgendra*: "Then, having sipped water again, the supreme Guru [should offer it] with the tips of his fingers to the five beginning with Brahmā, to all the Vidyās, the Vidyeśvaras, and the Lords of the Principles."

(15) Meditating upon all [the deities] within the Kālāntamaṇḍala, one should satisfy them with their names in the dative case followed by "svāhā. Then, with the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*) hanging from the neck, one should [satisfy] Sanaka and the others, as well as Bhṛgu and the others, together with their lineages (*gotra*). (16)

He should satisfy the ancestors of the highest lineage through the root-path (*mūlamārga*), the spirits (*bhūta*s) and others through the joints of the limbs, the paternal ancestors together with their wives by the right-hand path (*apasavya*), as well as the grandfathers, the great-grandfathers, the teachers, the instructors, and other elders; likewise,
he should satisfy the brothers, friends, preceptors, maternal grandfathers, and maternal uncles by uttering their names preceded by *svadhā* and ending with *namaḥ*.

The worship of Śiva and Sūrya; the worship of the doors and the door-keepers (*dvārapāla*); [the performance of] the expulsion of obstacles (*vighnodvāsana*); thereafter, the purification of oneself preceded by the deposition of the thirty-eight *kalās* (*aṣṭatriṃśatkalānyāsa*); the invocation of Śiva into oneself; the unification with Śiva by means of the presiding Lord of the Maṇḍala; and the preparation of the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) with its water.

The sprinkling of the sacrificial pavilion (*yāgamaṇḍapa*), the scattering of the *vikira* offerings, the worship of the Lord of Sacrifice (*yāgeśvara*), the worship of the *Pāśupata* weapon in the *vardhanī* vessel, the issuing of Śiva’s command to the world-protectors (*lokapāla*), the circumambulation of the *vardhanī* and the *śivakumbha*, the presentation of the sword of knowledge (*jñānakhaḍga*), the performance of the worship of Vighneśa and the Guru, the invocation of Śiva who pervades all paths (*adhvan*) within the mandala, the performance of the fivefold enclosure worship (*pañcāvaraṇapūjā*), and the performance of the fire ritual (*agnikārya*).

The joining of the mouth of Śiva with the mouth of fire by means of the root mantra, the libation to Śiva, the performance of ten oblations for the wives of the Brahmāṅgas; (l3) the pacification of portents of place, portents of time, ill omens, and auspicious omens; the performance of oblations for the entrance of the disciple; the procedure for the *sthālīpāka* offering; the division into three portions;
and the granting of grace through prayer to Śiva—after all these actions have been performed in this manner, the Guru... (l4)

Having gone out from the pavilion facing north, he calls the disciples. At the western door of the pavilion—that is, the western door of the mandala—he establishes the disciple within a square mandala made of cow dung and strewn with *kuśa* grass, located outside that [door] and facing it, using the *astra-mantra*. This mandala is provided with *darbha* grass, flowers, unbroken rice (*akṣata*), and so forth, with the tips pointing north and east according to the orientation of the disciple's face, and is accompanied by the *praṇava* (the syllable *oṃ*) as its seat. [The disciple] is to be clothed in white garments and the like; this is the remainder [of the instruction].

And it is said: "There, having seated the disciple—who has bathed and fasted, who is clad in two white garments, who is a devotee of Śiva, who has been tested, and who desires worldly enjoyment—facing east;
and having seated him who desires liberation facing north with his body erect, [the teacher] himself stands facing east, situated to the right of the disciple; or [he may stand] facing north."

Having established [the deity] and remaining oneself facing north, starting from the feet and moving upward, one should sprinkle [the deity] with the mantra ending in *huṃ phaṭ* and perform the sprinkling with the *astra-mantra* for the purpose of bathing. Here, the sprinkling starting from the feet and ending at the head should be performed;
likewise, the sprinkling starting from the head and ending at the feet should also be understood as being done during the visualization.

Likewise, in the *Siddhāntaśekhara*: "From the head down to the feet, having sprinkled [the image] with the water for the *arghya* and the *prokṣaṇī* while reciting the *astra-mantra* ending in *huṃ phaṭ*, and having struck it well with the *patākā-mudrā* for the sake of purification through bathing; then, having struck it with ashes using the *astra-mantra*, having gazed at it with the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*), and having beheld it with the *prāsāda-mantra*... [and so on].

(....bha) Having sprinkled ashes upon the head for the purpose of the ash-bath with the *astra-mantra*, the four purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) known as *nirīkṣaṇa*, *prokṣaṇa*, *tāḍana*, and *abhyukṣaṇa* are prescribed here in reverse order; therefore, it should be understood that this pertains to those seeking liberation (*mumukṣu*). Likewise, in the *Mṛgendra-tantra*, there is a statement concerning those seeking liberation: "Having prepared a mandala in a portion [of the ground], having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*), having sprinkled the seat with the *praṇava*, having struck it, and having drawn [the lines] with water outside..."
Alternatively, it should be understood as having come down through the lineage of the Guru’s oral instructions (*gurusaṃpradāyakrama*).

For in the *Kriyākrama*, it is stated according to the sequence of visualization; and since it is prescribed in the *Jñānaratnāvalī* as being preceded by sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*), [the area] below the navel—meaning starting from the navel down to the feet—is [to be purified]. Having recited the *astra-mantra* over the *kuśa*-grass tips with the *astra-mantra*, [one uses] the roots of the *darbha* grass.

Having rolled [the grass] up, one should perform the tracing three times for the purpose of the Aghamarṣaṇa rite. Furthermore, beginning from the navel up to the region of the head, one should trace three times with the tips of *kuśa* grass using the Astra-mantra for the purpose of purification.
Thus, for one seeking liberation (*mumukṣu*), the tracing is performed as described;
for one seeking enjoyment (*bubhukṣu*), the tracing should be done above the navel first, and afterwards below the navel.

Likewise, in the *Siddhāntaśekhara*: "The practitioner of mantra should obtain those [blades of] kuśa grass for cleansing with the weapon-mantra (*astramantra*). For the removal of sin, he should mark three times above the navel with the tips of the kuśa and three times below the navel with the bases of the kuśa; subsequently, for the separation from sin, he should mark three times each with the tips of the kuśa using the weapon-mantra for cleansing above the navel, and with the bases of the kuśa for the *aghamarṣaṇa* rite below the navel."

The statement regarding the sequence of ritual action is: "First, for one who is material (*bhautika*), one should scrape below the navel; afterwards, for one who is resolute (*naiṣṭhika*), one should scrape above the navel. Having touched the heart with the *astra-mantra*—that is, having performed the touching at the region of the disciple's heart in order to generate all virtues—and having meditated thereon upon oneself in embodied form by means of the *mūrti-mantra*, one performs the *mantranyāsa* (the deposition of mantras) upon the body of that disciple, which consists of the binding of the eyes with a cloth [and the subsequent] deposition of mantras.

The *sakalīkaraṇa* (the act of making [the deity] complete) consists of the placement (*nyāsa*) of the *saṃhitā-mantras*, beginning either from the head or from the feet. Regarding the "binding of the eyes with a cloth" (*paṭākṣibandha*):

it means that the binding of the eyes should be performed with two white cloths made of cotton or similar material, which have been sprinkled with the *astra-mantra* and consecrated by reciting the *kavaca-mantra* and the root-mantra (*mūla-mantra*) over them while being blunted [of their power]; this is to be done with the *netra-mantra*, accompanied by the binding of the two eyes—this is the remainder [of the instruction].

Likewise, in the Kāmika [Tantra]: "Having performed the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa upon that disciple and having applied a blindfold, the preceptor—having consecrated it with the Astra-mantra, rendered blunt by the Varma-mantra, and purified by the Mūla-mantra—should cover him with a white cloth. This blindfolding is to be performed for the sake of those who lack understanding due to their sins; for it is said that one should bind them with the Netra-mantra so that sinners do not look elsewhere. [Then] the two flowers for the afflicted...
The preceptor, taking the two hands of the disciple—which have accepted the flowers with palms joined—in his own hands, should lead him into the pavilion. ||58||

Having gone to the south and standing at the front with eyes cast downward, [one performs] the removal of bonds (*bandhahāni*) for Śiva, the throwing of flowers (*puṣpakṣepa*), and then the subtle (*aṇu*)...

and the supreme (*para*) [initiation], as well as the entering (*saṃveśana*) and its maintenance (*dhṛti*). The purification concerning the self, the mantra, and the elements, the stability of the *manus*, the stationing of the banner, the lord, and the hand, and the jar of Śiva—this is what was stated again regarding the *varca* [rite]. Having gone to the south of the pavilion by way of circumambulation and having entered the front...

The arrangement is as follows: the deity should be positioned in front; to the right of the deity is the position for oneself, and to the right of oneself is the position for the disciple. In this matter, the arrangement should be made according to the order of the castes, beginning with the Brāhmaṇa, on one's own right and left sides.
As stated in the *Brahmaśambhupaddhati*: "One should stand to his right. (l7)

The Brāhmaṇa and Kṣatriya [should stand] on the left side, while the Vaiśya and Śūdra [stand] according to the rule for the Guru. Then, immediately after standing before the deity, one should perform the removal of the eye-bandage by taking off the cloth over the eyes. One view is that after having the disciple perform the throwing of flowers (*puṣpakṣepa*) by Śiva—that is, the scattering of flowers—one should remove the eye-bandage following the throwing of flowers; [another view is] having him enter and then having him perform the throwing of flowers.

Since it is stated in the *Kāmika* that "one should show [the mandala]," and because it is further stated here that "having brought [the disciple] there, one should look upon him with the eyes," and because it is stated in the *Kriyākrama* that "having removed the eye-cloth (*netrapaṭa*), one should have him cast a flower," the other position holds that the removal of the eye-cloth should be performed first, and the casting of the flower should be done immediately thereafter.

The naming ceremony should be performed using the *Īśāna* and other mantras, according to the sequence of the social classes (*varṇas*) beginning with the twice-born, ending with the name *Śivadevagaṇa*. When the flower falls upon the face of Īśāna of Śiva situated in the mandala, the name of a Brāhmaṇa should be made *Īśānaśiva*; for a Kṣatriya, [the name] *Īśade...* (l.
3); for a Vaiśya, *Īśagaṇa*; and for a Śūdra, *Īśagaṇa*. This applies when the flower falls upon the *Tatpuruṣa* face, following the sequence of the Brāhmaṇa and other classes.

The names Tatpuruṣa-Śiva, Tatpuruṣa-deva, and Tatpuruṣa-gaṇa should be assigned; likewise, when [the mantra] falls upon Aghora and the others, as well as upon the Heart (hṛdaya) and so forth, the names Hṛdaya-Śiva, Hṛdaya-deva, and Hṛdaya-gaṇa should be assigned. For women, the name should end with "Śakti"; thus, [the names are] Īśa-Śiva-Śakti, Īśa-deva-Śakti, and Īśa-gaṇa-Śakti.

Or [the names] Śakti, Īśa, Śivīśa, Devīśa, and Gaṇīśa. Likewise, in the Kāmika [Tantra]: "The name should be determined preceded by the place indicated by its fall, followed by the word 'Śivapāda' (the feet of Śiva). For a Brahmin, it ends with 'Śiva', 'Deva', or 'Gaṇa'; for Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, and so forth, as well as for women, [it ends with 'Pāda']. (6)"

Regarding the phrase "ending with the [initiation] by power" (*śaktyantasañjūka*): likewise, in the *Siddhāntaśekhara*, it is said: "By virtue of the falling of the flower, the preceptor (*ācārya*) shall duly bestow names upon those [disciples], beginning with the Brahmins, in their proper order; this is now being stated. When the flower falls on the head... (l7)

A Brahmin should be [named] Śaśiva...; the king is said to be Īśadeva, while the Vaiśya and the Śūdra class shall be [named accordingly]. These—Tatpuruṣa, Aghora, Vāmadeva, and Sadyojāta—are to be applied in sequence to the positions of the heart and the other limbs when the flower falls. For Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas, the teacher should give names ending in Śiva, Deva, Gaṇa, or Antaka, either according to his own will or otherwise. For Brahmins and Kṣatriyas, [the names] should end in Śiva, Deva, Gaṇa, or Antaka.

The names ending in *gaṇa* have been stated generally for Vaiśyas and Śūdras; likewise, in the root [text] (*mūla*), it is said that for the best of the twice-born they end in *vāntaka*, while for others they end in *gaṇa*. Prior to the lying down, the disciple should be seated facing the deity—the self of Śiva—on a maṇḍala provided with a seat of the syllable *praṇava* to the right of the Lord.

Then, having struck the disciple’s heart with the *astra* [mantra] using a flower—this is the ellipsis—one should perform the purification concerning the elements (*bhūta-śuddhi*) by means of the mantra for self-establishment (*ātma-sthāpana*). By means of the *ātma-sthāpana-saṃhāra-mudrā* and the *ātma-mantra*, one should perform the purification concerning the bestowal and protection of consciousness (*caitanya*) within the pericarp of that disciple’s heart-lotus by means of the *nivṛtti* and other mantras. This constitutes the purification of the elements, the immersion (*āplāvana*), the stabilization of the mantras, and the ritual of *sakalīkaraṇa*.

Regarding that: placing the hand of Īśa upon the head of the disciple means the teacher, having meditated on his own right hand as being of the nature of radiant energy (*tejas*), fashioning it into the "Hand of Śiva" (*śivahasta*), and reciting the root mantra up to its dissolution (*laya*), visualizes the removal of the entire collection of bonds (*pāśa*). Having placed [the hand] upon the head of the disciple while reciting the Śiva-mantra, he should perform the touching of all the limbs of that disciple.

Furthermore, later on, having obtained the Śiva-vessel from the fire, the Guru should cause the disciple to worship the image of Śiva contained within that vessel. While reciting the mantra into the disciple’s right ear, the Guru should cause the disciple to perform the worship of the deity with a garland and other offerings, as well as prostration; this is the meaning. For it has been stated: "While grasping the root-mantra, one should cause the flower to be offered to the deity in the ear. (59)

The placement [of the fire] within the southeast mandala of the pit; the placement of the channels with a blade of darbha grass below; the oblation with mantras upon the head; the offering of the *sampāta* [remnants];

one hundred root oblations; the recitation of the *Śaivamantra*; atonement (*niṣkṛti*) below; the worship of Vāgīśa in the fire-pit; the sprinkling and striking of the disciple; the internal movement; the piercing of the divisions of consciousness (*cidbheda*) upwards; [the movement] into the heart; and the binding of the directions of the fire in the southeast mandala of the pit.

The phrase "abiding in the maṇḍala endowed with the residual impressions" (*vāsanā-yukta-maṇḍale sthitiḥ*) indicates that by this [instruction], the Guru faces east while the disciple faces north. Furthermore, immediately after seating them, there is the placement of the channels (*nāḍī-sthiti*). Having consecrated the root of a *darbha* blade with the Root Mantra, one should place the tip of the *darbha* upon the junction of one's own calf, considering it to be on the disciple’s palm; or else, one should apply the tip of the *darbha* to the surface of the disciple’s palm and its root to one's own calf. And it has been said:

Having drawn out the disciple’s *piṅgalā* channel— which resembles the tip of a blade of *kuśa* grass, which has its root in his own body, and which is like a lotus fiber under the guise of *kuśa*— and having entered it through one’s own *iḍā* channel, one should contemplate the state of oneness; then,
having exited by means of the *recaka* breath while reciting the *Śiva-mantra*, one enters [the disciple] by means of the disciple’s *pūraka* breath.

Having exited by means of *recaka* (exhalation) and entered one's own heart by means of *pūraka* (inhalation), one should thus perform the union of the channels (*nāḍī-sandhāna*) and the abiding in the channels together with Śiva, who resides in the fire within the *kumbhaka* (retention) and the maṇḍala.

For the purpose of the union of the channels for the oblation (*homa*), one should offer three oblations with the root mantra (*mūla-mantra*). Upon the head of the disciple, one should perform the "pouring oblation" (*saṃpāta-havana*), which is the offering of the remnants along with the subtle mantras (*aṇu-mantras*). One hundred root oblations are offered with the root mantra for the sake of stabilizing the "hand of Śiva" (*śiva-hasta*). As for the oblations in the fire...

One hundred repetitions of the rite should be performed; furthermore, a *homa* sacrifice of one-tenth the number of the *brahmāṅga* mantras must be carried out, and the *pūrṇāhuti* offering should be prescribed. And it is said: for the sake of stability, one hundred and eight [repetitions] of the root mantra of the *śivahasta*, along with one-tenth the number of *brahmāṅga* mantras, together with clarified butter, constitute the completion (*pūrṇatā*).
This applies to the *śaiva-manu* consisting of the five Brahmās beginning with Śiva and the six... [etc. (l5).

"Utterance" (*ukti*) means pronunciation, that is to say, instruction. "Expiation" (*niṣkṛti*) refers to the performance of an expiatory oblation (*prāyaścittāhuti*) one hundred and eight times with the root mantra. Having caused the worship of Śiva to be performed, one should declare the duties to be observed. This concludes the procedure for the initiation into the rules (*samayadīkṣāvidhāna*). For the purpose of commencing the special initiation (*viśeṣadīkṣā*), one should perform the sacrifice and other rites as prescribed in the rules, including the entry of the disciple and the bestowing of the hand of Śiva (*śivahasta*). In the fire-pit (*kuṇḍa*) or the sacrificial fire (*agnikuṇḍa*), [one should worship] the Support Power (*ādhāraśakti*).

Having laid down the seat of Vāgīśvara and having prepared that seat, one should invoke Vāgīśvarī and Vāgīśvara upon it. As it has been stated, "O Agni," one should perform the worship of Vāgīśī, as well as the worship, adoration, and satiation of Vāgīśvarī and Vāgīśvara. This includes the sprinkling and striking of the disciple, and the entry [of the deity] within. The sprinkling of the disciple is performed with the Astra-mantra.

In that very context, the striking with a flower using the weapon-mantra ending in *huṃ phaṭ* constitutes the "internal entry. Following the striking, there is the path of differentiation from the path of the ritual action being performed; this is the path established through the differentiation of the upper consciousness (*ūrdhvacaitanya*). By this, the following meaning is established: piercing with the mantra consisting of the weapon-mantra ending in *huṃ phaṭ*, separation by means of the *jyeṣṭhā* [mudrā], and then drawing [the soul] forth by means of the self-mantra and the *aṅkuśa* mudrā.

One should lead the disciple to the *dvādaśānta*, where one performs the binding of the three knots—the form of which is difficult to perceive—and the contemplation of the individual soul (*jīva*) by means of the *ātma-mantra* and the *saṃhāra-mudrā*; then, one should gather [the soul] into the heart, that is, into one's own heart. 60.

For the purpose of establishing and purifying one’s own self, [there is] the oblation of the vision of one’s own sins through the seed-syllables and the extraction; then there is the oblation from the womb and even from the body born of that [womb], followed by the Rudrāṃśahoma, and then the wearing of the lineage-lord’s *yajñopavīta* and a hundred root-oblations. [This is] for the establishment and purification of one’s own self... (l. 3).

By means of inhalation (*pūraka*), one causes the consciousness of the disciple to enter into one’s own self; by means of retention (*kumbhaka*), one brings about a state of homogeneity with one’s own self, which is the stabilization of the self (*ātmasthāpana*); and by means of exhalation (*recanā*), while uttering the root mantra until its dissolution, one employs the *udbhavamudrā* together with the mantra of the self to [unite] the Lord of the Causes, beginning with Brahmā, [at the point] between the eyebrows. Following this, having brought [the deity] down to the space between the eyebrows by way of emanation (*sṛṣṭi*), the exit through the right channel is "exhalation" (*recanā*). After this external exhalation, outside...
