The state of Vāgīśī. Having meditated upon the union of those two with the *ātma-mantra*, [one performs] the casting [of the self] by Vāgīśvara... (l5) ...and the satisfaction through the purificatory rites beginning with conception (*garbhadhāna*). The oblation of the inspection of sins belonging to the self residing in the womb; the inspection of sins by means of the self existing within the womb of Vāgīśvarī... (l6)

When the *homa* is being performed for the purpose of purification (*saṃskāra*), then, by means of the smell of excrement and so forth present in the fire, one perceives the past sins committed, such as the killing of a Brahmin (*brahmahatyā*). It is said that once the rites beginning with conception (*garbhādhāna*) have been accomplished, during the *homa* performed with the *Śivāṇu* mantra, one should infer the disciple’s impurity from the signs arising from that fire: "If there is the smell of excrement, he is a stealer of land, a killer of a Brahmin, a violator of the Guru’s bed, or a drinker of liquor."

The killer of a guru, the killer of a cow, the destroyer of what has been done, O Kṛṣṇe, he whose thighs are submerged in stench, and the destroyer of the fetus and its sustainer—fire blazes at the murder of a woman, it trembles at the theft of gold; it bursts forth at the killing of a child, and becomes lusterless at the abortion of a fetus. When such signs as these appear, [one should perform] a thousand [recitations] by means of the multiformed one for the expiation of the sin.

(…) may I [be protected] by the ninefold self. Here, the Aghora mantra in its fragmentary form is the mantra for consuming sins, joined with the ninefold self—the Śiva mantra consisting of nine syllables—just as [the mantra]:

*śikhāṇḍārdhendu* (…) *viśvarūpaṃ śaśi* (…) (*p106b, l1*) (…) *vāyuḥ* accompanied by the sixth vowel, endowed with the moon-drop and the crest, adorned with two *phaṭ*s, beginning with *praṇava* and ending with *namaḥ*.

"Accompanied by the consumption of evil. Thus, for the sake of pacifying the defects arising from the body produced from charcoal, for the sake of pacifying the defects of the body, for the sake of warding off the defect of improper conduct (*āśācāra*), for the sake of warding off the defect of the womb, and for the sake of pacifying the defects of the body produced from the aforementioned seeds and so forth... (l. 3)

The rite should be performed with sesame seeds three times; for the enjoyment of the oblation, one should offer three oblations with the root mantra, saying: "O Lord, may the portion of Rudra reside within my self. Thus it is stated in the *Kāmika*: "O Blessed One, Supreme Lord, [may I become] a pure twice-born, purified from the defects of food and state of being, from the womb, the seed, and the body... O Lord, may the portion of Rudra descend; one should perform three oblations for the descent. 'By Your grace, O Lord, may this self become the portion of Rudra. So it is said.

"Causing the descent of a portion of Rudra" means the causing of the descent of fitness for the purpose of uniting the disciple's self within the womb of Śakti; thereafter, following the descent of the portion of Rudra, "wearing the birth-caste-thread" refers to the wearing of the *yajñopavīta* by those who have attained their respective castes.
The "lords of birth" (*jātīśāḥ*) are the primary [deities] of the twice-born and other classes, namely the *aṇus*, which are the mantras such as Tatpuruṣa and the rest. [One should... them.
(…) Those belonging to the various castes must wear sacrificial threads (*yajñasūtra*) or sacred threads (*yajñopavīta*), maintaining the number of strands prescribed for their own caste.

Likewise, in the *Kāmika*: “For the Brahmins and others, the mantras of Tatpuruṣa, Aghora, Vāma, and Īśāna [are used]. (l. 7) That sacred thread, made of cotton, triple-stranded, and twisted three times over, should be worn with the mantra prescribed for one’s own respective caste; however, for Śūdras, that thread consists of a single strand.

For Vaiśyas it should have two strands; for Kṣatriyas, however, three strands... (l8) ...having a number of [strands]... or seven, five, or nine threads for them. For the sake of strengthening the wearing of the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*), one hundred oblations of the root-mantras should be performed. The root-mantra... (l9)
One should perform the libation (tarpaṇa) for the principal deity one hundred and eight times, and for the limbs of Brahmā one-tenth of that number. ||61||

When the five purificatory rites (*pañcasaṃskṛti*) have been performed with oblations to the limbs of Brahmā, the prior union of the self becomes Śiva. In the heaven of Vāgīśī, there is the fulfillment of creation... [the removal of] obstruction in the fire and other elements. Through the observance of the rule (*samaya*) and the purity of conduct beginning with the rule, what has been done for the child and others makes one fit for the worship of Śiva, the knowledge of Śiva, and so forth. When the five purificatory rites have been performed with oblations to the limbs of Brahmā, [Vāgīśvarī... (p. 107a, l. 2).

(…) There is no obstruction. Regarding the oblation for the five purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) known as *puṃsavana*, *sīmantonnayana*, *jātakarman*, and *nāmakarman*, the [term] "Brahmāṅga" refers to the worship performed in due order for *garbhādhāna* and the others, preceded by the recollection of Śiva as Sadyojāta and the rest, using the five Brahmans—the mantras beginning with *sadyojāta*—and the oblations for the limbs (*aṅgāhuti*) with the five limbs. This consists of individual oblations for each of *garbhādhāna* and the others in their proper sequence, using the mantras of the heart (*hṛdaya*), head (*śiras*), crest (*śikhā*), armor (*kavaca*), and weapon (*astra*).

There are five [steps]. In the rite of parting the hair (*sīmantonnayana*), for the purpose of fashioning the face and limbs, one should perform the deposition of the thirty-eight *kalās* preceded by the deposition of the *praṇava* and the five *brahmans*, using the *śikhā-mantra*. For the sake of accomplishing the specific consecrations (*viśeṣasaṃskāra*), one should also offer the *pūrṇāhuti*.

Herein, having extracted the self residing in the womb from the womb of *māyā*, there is the application [of it] by causing it to attain the state of being the seed of Śiva within the womb of *śakti*. [... (l5)

The purification (*dhāna*) is the manifestation of one's own stainless qualities. The *puṃsavana* (the rite for generating a male) is that upward-leading movement which elevates [the self] above the worlds situated within the womb of *māyā*. That upward-leading movement is the *sīmantonnayana* (parting of the hair). O son, birth (*janana*) occurs right here in Śiva; the *jātakarman* (birth-rite) is the emergence of the principle of Śiva within oneself.

The naming (*nāmakaraṇa*) is the act of determining "this is indeed he" when [Śiva] has been produced within the self. And it is said: "Having extracted [the self] from the womb of *māyā*, its placement within the womb of Power (*śakti*), and its state as the seed of Śiva within the self..."

That which is called *garbhādhāna* (conception) is the manifestation of the qualities of the Self as masculinity (*puṃstva*). When that manifestation is stainless, it is *sīmanta* (the parting of the hair); whatever is the upward movement along the path, that indeed is to be known as *sīmantonnayana*. Birth is the state of being a son of Rudra; for this very reason, in the state of Śiva-ness, there is awakening and the proclamation of the name. For the child—the disciple—there is the prior union with the Self, as before, [leading to] the stainless Self... and... (l. 8).

(…) Here, one should perform [the rite]: having extracted the Self residing within the womb of Vāgīśvarī—who resembles the tip of a blazing fire—by means of the *saṃhāramudrā*, and having placed it within the heart-lotus of the previously [visualized] fire, one should bring about a state of identity through *kumbhaka* while uttering the root mantra up to its dissolution (*layānta*). Then, separating [the Self] from one's own Śiva-nature (…) and grasping it with the *hāramudrā*, one should lead it to the *dvādaśānta* by way of abandoning the causal deities beginning with Brahmā. There, for the sake of the disciple’s enjoyment, one should [place it] in the body of the disciple through the yoga of *recaka* using the *udbhavamudrā* and one’s own mantra.

"One should apply the mind" refers to the prior yoga of the self. [The creation] of Vāgīśvarī... (p107b, l1) preceded by the complete satisfaction of Vāgīśvarī and Īśvara, their dismissal (*visarjana*) must be performed. For the sake of fulfillment and expiation (*prāyaścitta*), having offered a thousand or half a thousand oblations with the *śruva* ladle using the root mantra, one should perform the full oblation (*pūrṇāhoma*). In the fire and so forth, in Śiva residing in the fire, [in the form of] a drop (*bindu*) residing in the staff (*daṇḍa*)... (l2)

When Śiva is present in the *kuṇḍa*, the disciple should cause the scattering of flowers and the worship with blossoms to be performed. Then, having offered worship to the Guru according to his capacity with materials and other offerings, he should prostrate before the Guru. Regarding the conduct of the observances (*samayācāra*) as prescribed by the scriptures and established doctrines: one should not, under any circumstances, revile or transgress against Śiva, the Śiva-scripture, the Śiva-fire, or the Guru—even their shadow. [One should also perform] the eating and giving away of the *nirmālya*.
One should abandon fasting (*laṅghana*) and perform worship of Śiva, the fire, and the Guru; this is the prescribed rule for life.

(L4) At the outset, regarding the purification of conduct such as the observances (*samaya*) for those who are unable to perform them—such as children, the elderly, the sick, and so forth—the oblation (*huta*) must be performed in numbers of a hundred and so on.
For example: [this applies] to all these aforementioned incapable persons, even in regard to the observances. (L5)

Having obtained the command of Śambhu, the Preceptor should then purify [the disciple] as follows: having worshipped the Supreme Lord in the mandala, the pitcher, and the fire; having worshipped and gratified Vidyeśvara, Gaṇeśāna, and the World-Protectors in due order within the fire; and having offered two hundred oblations with the Śiva-mantra and presented the final full oblation, he should address Śiva: "O Blessed One, this one is incapable of maintaining the proper conduct; therefore, by means of this oblation..."

Forgive all of that. Having made the hosts of Vidyeśvaras, Gaṇeśas, and the World-Protectors (lokapālas) witnesses, the preceptor, the most excellent of teachers, should cause him to be bound by the pledges (samayas). The Guru is capable of ensuring the performance of the conduct and observances of the pledges, such as the worship of Śiva and the knowledge of Śiva.
One who is fit shall become qualified for the worship of Śiva, the study of the Siddhāntas, and the hearing of mantras.

Likewise, in the Kāmika [Tantra] it is said: "Thus, one who is endowed with the purificatory rites of the *samaya* is fit for the worship of Śiva, for the fire-oblation (*homa*), for ritual adoration (*arcana*), for meditation (*dhyāna*), and even for the hearing of mantras...
and such a person attains the divine and fierce state (*pada*) of the Lord. Thereafter, O twice-born, he becomes eligible for the initiation into liberation (*nirvāṇadīkṣā*). (Kā 1.9–62)
The heart-mantra (*hṛnmanu*) arises from the earth-element (*kṣmātatva*); from the *praṇava*, the final [syllable]...

from the world [of fire], from Kāla and Kṛśānu, one hundred, eight, and two; from *gandha*, five qualities, and the object of smell (*gandhaviṣaya*). When [the breath] has ceased in the state of withdrawal (*nivṛtti*), the rule is that it moves through the pair of the vital breaths called *iḍā* and *piṅgalā*, and through the organs called the genitals and the nose.

Now, in order to explain the initiation into Nirvāṇa, he describes the procedure for the sequence of invoking the six paths (*ṣaḍadhvāvāhana*) by way of the process of withdrawal (*saṃhārakrama*). Regarding the word "earth" (*kṣmā*): the principle of earth (*kṣmātattva*) resides in *Nivṛtti*, that is, within the power (*kalā*) called Nivṛtti; thus the state of being earth comes into existence. One should establish the connection with "smara" and "dini. [The mantra] *aja*...
(l3) ...the Sadyojāta and Hṛdaya mantras, from the final *praṇava* among the eighty-one words.

Starting from the final existing word *oṃ*, there are twenty-eight words ending with the word *abhavat*. Now, one might ask: starting from the final quarter-verse (*pāda*) up to the word *mahādeva* (l4), how can there be twenty-eight words ending with a word? [The answer is: it is by counting the words ending with the [respective] quarters.

Likewise, in the *Varuṇapaddhati*: "From the final word up to the word *mahādeva*, in reverse order, the words of the *vyomavyāpin* [mantra] number twenty-eight. For this very reason, it should be understood that here, in the sequence for the placement (*nyāsa*) beginning with the words of the *vyomavyāpin*, the count of ninety-four words is prescribed; because they are prescribed as eighty-one words in the *Varuṇapaddhati*, there are two types [of recitation].

The "placement of the steps" (*padanyāsa*) is thus established. As for the detailed expansion of the path of the two types of steps, it has already been demonstrated at length in the commentary on the passage beginning with "connected to all portions of the path" (*sarvādhvāyikabhāgasaṃyukta*); it should be understood from that very place. (l7) Regarding the path of worlds (*bhuvanādhvan*), there are the worlds starting from the world of Kālāgni, which is born from the Fire of Time (*kālakṛśānu*), up to the end of Kālī, ending with the world of Bhadrakālī.
One hundred and eight [syllables] in the *alā* [alphabet]; the two seed-syllables are *a* and *la*.

(l8) Beginning from scent (*gandha*) as the first quality, there are five qualities known as scent, taste, form, touch, and sound. Scent is the object; *kṣo* is the syllable *kṣa*. Color is the color; the rule (*vidhi*) is Brahmā, the Lord of Causes. The two vital breaths, *prāṇa* and *apāna*, are the wind called *iḍā*. (p108b, l1)

Piṅgalā is that which is called the anus and the generative organ; the pair known as Iḍā and Piṅgalā refers to the two channels (nāḍīs). The generative organ (upastha) is the sense-organ called the nose.

One should remember these [deities] as being included within the *nivṛtti-kalā* and contemplate them thus. It has been said: "In the *vṛtti* [of Nivṛtti], there is the earthly element, and therein you alone and the worlds, ending with the worlds of Kālāgni; likewise, Bhadrakālī is associated with three. Herein are one hundred and eight."
The letter *kṣa* is indeed the phoneme itself. The words begin with *bhava* and extend as far as the final *oṃ*.

(L3) There are twenty-eight in number: *sadyojāta*, *hṛdaya*, and *śambara*; likewise the two seed-syllables (*bīja*) *al* and *au*; the channel (*nāḍī*) known as *indhā* and *paṅgala*; *prāṇa* and *apāna*;
as well as the nose (*ghrāṇa*) and the generative organ (*upastha*); and the sense-organ of air (*vāyvindriya*). The object (*viṣaya*) is smell (*gandha*) alone. (L4)

The five qualities beginning with sound; the earthly mandala is pale yellow, adamantine, firm, and heavy; it is quadrangular, measuring one billion yojanas in height, stable, associated with the waking state, and its presiding cause is the Lotus-Seated One (Brahmā). (L5) Visualizing all this as pure and resembling gold, the Guru should place the thread from the child's knees down to the feet. (63)
The path of reality (*tattvādhvan*) begins from the end of *prakṛti* down to the shore of the waters;

*pratiṣṭhā* extends up to Śrīkaṇṭha; the path of worlds (*bhuvanādhvan*) begins from Amareśa; Vāmadeva is the atom of the head (*śiraḥ-aṇu*); [the paths] extend up to Vyāpinī starting from the two feet of Śarva; the two channels, Gāndhārī and Madhyamā, are located at the palate and the anus respectively; and the qualities of the sense-objects (*śrutiguṇarasaka*) consist of giving and honor.

Hariśca states that the principles (*tattva*) and so forth are included within the *pratiṣṭhā-kalā*. Regarding the phrase "the principles": starting from *salila* (water), that is, beginning from the water-principle up to the end of *prakṛti*, the path of principles (*tattvādhvan*) consists of twenty-four in number. It exists within the *pratiṣṭhā* [kalā]... (l8).
The *pratiṣṭhā-kalā* consists of twenty-three phonemes, beginning with the letter *ṭa* and ending with *ha*, starting from the letter *ha*. From the world (*bhuvana*) of Amareśa...

The row consists of fifty-six worlds, beginning with the world of Śrīkaṇṭha and ending with the world of Śrīkaṇṭha... [the worlds] of ...ṇīka. Vāmadeva is the head-mantra; the mantra of Vāmadeva is the head-mantra. Starting from the two words of Śarva—namely, the two words "Śarva" and "Śarve"—[it extends] to Vyāpin... [to] Pinyā... (l. 2).

The thirty-two [channels] ending with the palate and the anus: by the word *tālu*, the tongue is meant. Since the palate lacks the status of a sense organ (*indriya*), the reading should be "the tongue and the anus" (*jihvā pāyu*). Both the letters *u* and *va* are two seeds. Gāndhārī is the central channel (*madhyamā-nāḍī*)...

(l3) ...and the Suṣumṇā channel is the quality of hearing. The four qualities known as taste, form, touch, and sound constitute the quality of taste; the object is that which possesses taste. [The qualities are] giving and honor; the upward-moving breath (*udāna*) and the equalizing breath (*samāna*).

Vāyu, Hari, Viṣṇu, and Kāraṇeśa—having spoken thus, one should then place [the mantras]. The nooses are endowed with the *pratiṣṭhā* kalā. (.... (l4) The principles (*tattvas*) beginning with *prakṛti* and ending with water, numbering twenty-three, and the worlds (*bhuvanas*) numbering fifty-six starting from Śrīkaṇṭha-Bhairava down to Amareśa—the end—consist of thirty-two locations (*padāni*). Vyāpin, Vyāpin. (l5)
The letters beginning with *ca* and ending with *ha*, starting from *pa* and ending with *śarva*, have been briefly declared here; they number twenty-three.

[The deities are] Vāmadeva, Śiras, and Raṇu. Likewise, the two seed-syllables (*bīja*), the two channels (*nāḍī*)—Gāndhārī and Sumnayā—the two vital breaths (*prāṇa*)—Samāna and Udāna—and the two organs, the tongue and the anus. The objects of the senses are taste, as well as sound, touch, form, and flavor. The principles (*tattva*) are these, and the seed-syllable of Varuṇa.

The true Guru should place [the elements] there upon the *pūrva-sūtra*, while meditating that all this— white, marked by a lotus, having the shape of a half-moon, stable, the son of Śītalā, joined with the sound of the syllable *gha*, extending for a thousand *yojanas* and a hundred [leagues], existing in the state of dream, the cause, bearing the banner of Garuḍa— is situated from the navel of the disciple down to his two knees. ||64||

[Māyātattva]... [the Puruṣa], and then the two [energies] whose forms are the crest [of the flame], from Jña down to Gha; Vāmā and the others, [measuring] only a thumb's breadth... [the path of words] which sustains the entire world, ending with the letter Ra; the two [paths] of space and sound, the elephant’s trunk, and the previous designation here is Nāga... [the two]... [those] called Form, having reached the objects of the senses; Rudra, Vidyā, and the Guṇas [are] the three women. He speaks of the principles beginning with Vidya, Kalā, Yāmala, Sūta, and Tattva, etc., starting with "Māyā. At the beginning...

In the first [section], there are seven principles (*tattva*), beginning from the principle called Puruṣa and ending with the principle of Māyā. Regarding the *śikhā* and *dhūmra* mantras: [the former] consists of seven syllables beginning with the letter *ña* and ending with the letter *dha*; [the latter] is the letter *sa*, which belongs to the *sarajagata* [group]. The letter *ra* is joined twice; this is the meaning. Starting from the world (*bhuvana*) called Vāmā and ending with Aṅguṣṭhamātra—beginning with the world named Vāmā and extending up to the world of Aṅguṣṭhamātra.

The collection of worlds. In the void (*vyomin*), beginning with *vyomin* and ending with the stars, up to the letter *au*, there is the path of twenty-one words. In the desert (*maru*) are two [letters], *ma* and *ra*. The two seed-syllables are the trunk, the neck, the tongue, and the hand; they are known as *pūṣan*, and the channel named *pūṣā* is twofold.

Here, in this *vidyā-kalā*, there are the mountain and the wind, the feet, the toes, and the organ of sight. It has reached the object called form (*rūpa*), and is designated by the name "form," accompanied by its respective objects.

The *vidyā-kalā* has entered into the three *guṇas*; Rudra is said to be the Lord of Causes (*kāraṇeśa*). And it is stated: "Then one should deposit the *vidyā-kalā* of the bond (*pāśa*) by means of mantra. One should deposit the twenty-seven principles (*tattva*), beginning with *māyā* and ending with *puruṣa*. One should deposit [the worlds] beginning from the world of the size of a thumb (*aṅguṣṭhamātra-bhuvana*) up to the end of the city of Yāma. Here, the worlds are twenty-seven in number. [The rest of the line: *padamoṃktaramā...*

(…) In the void, there is the sequence of steps in the void; and in the Vidyā, there are twenty-one steps. There are seven syllables beginning with *kha* and ending with *jña*. The two mantras *Ghora* and *Śikhā* are proclaimed specifically within the Vidyā. Furthermore, the seed-syllables are *mala*, *rau*, as well as *nāsa*, *pūṣā*, and *karjihvakā*. Likewise, *vyāna*, *nāga*, and *vāyu* are [assigned] to the organ of the feet. And form is the object.

The mandala of fire possesses the qualities of sound, touch, and form; it is red, burning in nature, and situated in a triangle. Its height is ten million times ten thousand *yojanas*. Rudradeva is its cause, and its state is that of deep sleep (*suṣuptikā*). One should deposit all of this there—the radiant, most excellent, and transitory [element]. From the heart down to the navel, one should [deposit it] in the disciple's body.

Vidyā, Īśvara, Sadāśiva, and the letters *ga*, *kha*, and *ka* [constitute] Śānti. In the Nṛvarma [system], the letters *nū* and *vā* represent the worlds beginning with Vāmākhya and ending with Sadāśiva; *tīśa* is the Lord (*adhipa*), and *bindu* and *yau* are the *dhyāna* [and other elements].
Yaśā is the mouth of the necklace (*hāra*) through its pervasion of the sky (*gagana-vyāpti*). Pūṣā is the root of the end. Regarding the sense organs (*sparśārā*), [the text says]:
"The hands, touch, and the skin of the hand are included within the Śānti-kalā. Thus he speaks. As for "Vidyā," Vidyā is the principle (*tattva*) of Śuddhavidyā, as well as Īśvara and Sadāśiva.

In this way, there are three principles (*tattva*): the *Īśvara* principle and the *Sadāśiva* principle. The letters *ga*, *kha*, and *ka* are to be meditated upon as the *Śāntikalā*; this is the remainder [of the sense]. Now, regarding my ninth [chapter], the *Tatpuruṣa-kavaca-mantra*: beginning with the world named *Vāmā* and ending with the final world of *Sadāśiva*, there are eighteen worlds starting from the world named *Vāmā* up to the world of *Sadāśiva*. The Supreme Lord (*Parameśvara*) is the sovereign (*adhipa*) of these, beginning with *Īśa*.

*Kāraṇeśvara* is the *bindu*. In the seed-syllable (*bīja*), there are the two *bindu*s and the two *ya*s. "Dhyānāhāramukha" refers to the twelve-word mantra beginning with *dhyānāhāra* and ending with *vyomavyāpin*, extending up to the end of the *vyomavyāpin*. [The two channels] *pūṣā* and *yaśas* are the two *sparśa* and *rāva* qualities; that is, the two qualities are touch and sound. *Kūrma* and *kṛkara* are the wind and the quality of touch. The object is touch; the hand and the skin are the organ of touch (*tvagindriya*). And it has been said:

One should place the three principles: Sadāśiva, Īśvara, Vidyā, and Śānti. Then one should place the eighteen cities beginning with Sadāśiva and ending with Vāmā, starting from Vyomavyāpin and extending as far as the words of the Dhyāna-hāra. These words are known to be sixteen in number, and the syllables are remembered as *ka*, *kha*, *ga*, and so on. In the seed-syllable consisting of the dot (*bindu*) and the letter *ya*, there are two mantras: the one for the face and the one for the armor. Thus it is complete.

To Pūṣan belong the *śānāḍī* [vein]; to Vāyu, the *kṛkara* and *kūrma* [veins]. The skin is said to belong to the sense-organ (*indriya*), and touch is indeed its object. The Vāyava-maṇḍala is black, flickering, hexagonal, and marked with six dots. Its two qualities are touch and sound. It measures one hundred thousand crores of *yojanas* in height; it is in the fourth state (*turyāvastha*), infinite, and one should install Īśvara as its cause. All of this is dark-colored.

One should meditate on the ploughs (*phāla*) up to the heart within the body of the child, there upon the cord of bonds (*pāśasūtra*). [The letters] ending with *abha* and the vowels (*svara*), from the world of *Nivṛtti* up to the city of *Anāśrita*, beginning with the first syllable *Tāra* (*Om*), the pair starting with *Ha*, the *Atītā* together with *Sadeśa*, *Kūhū*, *Śaṅkhinī*, *Devadhanañjaya*, and *Ravaguṇa*... [are to be placed].

In the *vāk* and *śrotra* [kalās], within the *śāntyatīta-kalā*, because the *tattvas* beginning with *ānava* are included therein, there is the *tattva*. Both *śakti* and *śiva* are the two *tattvas* known as the *śakti-tattva* and *śiva-tattva*; from the *visarga*—beginning with the *visarga* accompanied by the letter *a*—up to the end of the letter *a*, that is, up to the short vowel *a*.

The sixteen vowels; the three mantras beginning with Īśāna; the worlds of Nivṛtti, starting from the world called Nivṛtti up to the world called Anāśrita—these are the fifteen worlds (*pura*). The first is the primordial *tāraka* Oṃkāra, which is a single word (*pada*) joined with the pair of "good abodes" (*sunālayugala*), namely the two seed-syllables (*bīja*) known as Ha and Nāda. This is the Transcendent (*atītā*), meaning the state beyond tranquility (*śāntyātītā*). That region is Sadāśiva, the Lord of Causes (*kāraṇeśvara*).
The *kuhu* and *śaṅkhinī* are the two channels (*nāḍī*), namely Devadattā and Dhanañjayā.

Wind is sound, whose quality is sound. Sound alone is the object of sound. Speech and hearing refer to the organs of speech and hearing, and it has been said: "In the Śāntyatītā [kalā], there are two principles consisting respectively of Śakti and Śiva. Likewise, [the sequence] from the Unmanifested (*anāśrita*) down to Nivṛtti begins with Śakti.

Know that the sixteen worlds presided over by those [energies] are the syllable *praṇava* born of *nāda*, which is directly of the nature of Śiva. The sixteen phonemes beginning with *a* and ending with the *visarga* are proclaimed; the mantras of Śiva reside in the *īśāna* and *astra* [sections]. There are two seed-syllables (*bīja*), as well as the two *nādas*, *ha* and *au*; likewise, the channels (*nāḍī*) are *kuhū* and *śaṅkhinī*, and the two vital airs (*prāṇa*) are *devadatta* and *dhanañjaya*. And it has been declared therein: "He is indeed the agent."

One should meditate on Sadāśiva, from the crest-lock (*śikhā*) down to the *phala* [the end], as the entire white head. (67) The mantras are pervaded by the words of the *tṛnni* suffixes; the phonemes (*varṇas*) are pervaded by the feet [of the mantras]; those worlds (*bhuvanas*) are likewise pervaded by the phonemes; and these are pervaded by the principles (*tattvas*). Those which are called the impurity of karma (*karmamala*), delusion (*moha*), and worldly existence (*bhava*) are the pervaded (*vyāpya*); they too are pervaded by those [principles]. (68–69)

The pervasive meditations (*vyāpakabhāvanā*) here are the *kalās*; by means of them, these [entities] are beneficial. Having understood the relationship of the pervaded and the pervader (*vyāpyavyāpakabhāva*) through the six paths (*ṣaḍadhvan*), initiation (*dīkṣā*) should be performed.
To address the question of "which are the pervaded and which are the pervaders," he states the rule for the pervaded and the pervader:

(p111a, l1) In this regard, within the six paths, those categories (*padārtha*) that are capable of pervading their own respective categories according to the principle of the pervaded and the pervader are the "pervaded" (*vyāpya*); they [pervade] their own...
The meaning is that they are included within the categories (*padārtha*).

(l2) "Pervading" means that they abide by encompassing their own categories within themselves; they are the "pervaders. Thus, the remaining words—namely the words "pervading the sky" (*vyomavyāpi*)—refer to the "existences" (*bhāvanā*) which exist as the ontological reality of both the pervaded and the pervader. (l3)

The meanings [of the levels] are as follows: the lords, Īśāna and the others, are pervaded by the mantras; the mantras are the pervaded and the words are the pervaders. The words are pervaded by the syllables or phonemes (*varṇa*); the sense is that the words are the pervaded and the syllables are the pervaders. Those phonemes are pervaded by the worlds (*bhuvana*); the phonemes are the pervaded and the worlds are the pervaders. Those worlds are likewise pervaded by the principles (*tattva*), the thirty-six principles; the worlds are the pervaded.

The state of being pervaded belongs to the principles (*tattva*s), while these collections of principles possess pervasiveness. Having delineated karma—consisting of the merit and demerit of impelling *bhāva*-karma—one should consider the *mala* known as the *āṇava-mala*. Since it has been stated that "the deluding *māyā* is called the deluder because of the enjoyment of the sweetness of sense-objects," the entities (*bhava*) arise from these [principles].

The previously mentioned principles (*tattva*) and so forth that have arisen are the pervaded (*vyāpya*). Impurity (*mala*), karma, and *māyā* are the pervaders (*vyāpaka*). Because karma is the cause of pleasure and pain, certain objects manifest for its sake; because impurity is the cause of the subject’s instruments of experience, certain objects manifest for its sake; and because *māyā* is the cause of the body, senses, and objects, certain objects manifest for its sake.

He says that those impurities (*mala*) and so forth, which are the pervaders (*vyāpaka*) of the principles (*tattva*) and so on, become the pervaded (*vyāpya*). Here, within the six paths (*ṣaḍadhvan*), there exist the *kalās* such as Nivṛtti and the others, which abide in the relationship of pervader and pervaded; that is, they exist as both the pervaded and the pervader. Nivṛtti is the pervaded, while Pratiṣṭhā is the pervader; [and] Pratiṣṭhā is the pervaded.

Vidyā is the pervader of Vidyā and the pervaded by Śānti; Śānti is the pervader of Śānti and the pervaded by Śāntyatītā; and Śāntyatītā is the pervader of the universe and of impurity (*mala*) and so forth. Because they function as the pervaders and the pervaded of the universe and of impurity, they are called *kalās*. And it has been said: "Since they cause the universe to be differentiated (*kalayanti*), they are *kalās*. These powers (*śaktis*) are the fivefold divisions established within the Supreme Power (*parāśakti*). Just as, first, in the earthly principle (*pārthiva tattva*), the experience of karma (*karmabhoga*) is brought to cessation through *nivṛtti*.

The state of *nivṛtti* is to be understood as complete; now *pratiṣṭhā* is being described. Through the sequence of drinking the [nectar] of the beginningless reality (*anāditattva*)... the self, colored by passion for Śiva, is established in the *puruṣa* principle. This is to be known as the *pratiṣṭhā-kalā*. Thereafter, the *vidyā* principles are declared. By means of discernment, one knows the effects of *māyā*.

The stages of *vidyā* are as follows: That supreme *kalā* should be known as *vidyā*, whose nature consists of the power of knowledge (*jñāna-kalā*). It is that by which the authority of *mala* and *māyā* is brought to rest for the person; it is called the *kalā* of *śānti*. Being established in its own authority and bestowing its own state, it is the *kalā* of *śāntyatītā*, described by them as "the infinite awakening of *nirvāṇa*. By these *kalās*, the previously mentioned *mala* and the others are grasped and pervaded; thus, the state of being pervaded belongs to *mala* and the rest.

The sense is that the *kalās* possess pervasiveness; thus, the collection of girdles (*mekhalā*) is pervaded by the *bindu*—this is the ellipsis. (l4) It is pervaded by the power of *Hu*; the *Śakti* is pervaded by Śiva. And it has been said: "The pervasive one is completely pervaded by the names of the worlds and so forth along with the *bindu*; this Śiva is not pervaded by anything other than the *bindu-śakti*. If these *kalās* are established... (l5)
All [principles] beginning with *tattva* become stabilizers if they are purified; since they become purified when they are cleansed, it follows that *kalā* must also be purified.

For the sprinkling and striking of the disciple, [one should perform] the entry into the heart by means of the weapon-mantra (*astra-mantra*). Indeed, with the heart-mantra (*hṛdaya*), one should effect the extraction of the self, including its containment up to the end of the crest-mantra (*śikhā*). In the case of expulsion into one's own self, having entered through the nose-tip and placed [the self] in the heart, one should likewise draw it out; having thus grasped the self, one should expel it through the *piṅgalā* [channel] and place it within the *śakti*.
He describes the sequence for the placement (*nyāsa*) of the disciple’s consciousness upon the power of Śiva residing in the *pāśasūtra*. Regarding the word "disciple" (*śiṣya*):

even here, having performed the previously mentioned rites such as the offering of the sacrificial cake (*caru*) and the expiation (*prāyaścitta*) for the [defects in] the knowledge-mantras and so forth, and having carried out for the disciple the specific consecrations beginning with the entry into the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*) up to their conclusion, one should—after requesting the command of Śiva through the completion of the ritual acts ending with the satiation (*tarpaṇa*) and kindling (*dīpana*) of the root and other mantras for the purpose of performing the *nirvāṇa-dīkṣā*—[proceed].
For one standing in the southern maṇḍala of the Śiva-fire,

[the body] is sprinkled in due order with the root-mantra of the Weapon and Armor, tripled and then tripled again; having been worshipped, [the body] is bound by means of the Suṣumṇā-natured cord of bonds, starting from the crest-lock and extending down to the big toe of the right foot, while it remains within the physical body.

Because it performs the cutting and piercing of the bonds (*pāśas*), the body should be made of thread. And it has been said: "Those bonds are to be cut and pierced within the body by means of the thread's position; therefore, the body composed of thread must be meditated upon by the teacher... [l. 2] From the mantra of the weapon (*astra*): the sprinkling and striking of the disciple is to be performed with the weapon-mantra—this is the remainder [of the sense]. With the weapon-mantra ending in *huṃ phaṭ*, there is sprinkling at the heart with the tip of a blade of *kuśa* grass.
In that very place, a striking should be performed by means of the *huṃ* syllable through the exhaling breath (*recaka*).
Having restrained [the breath], its entry should be effected; the entry of that disciple should be made through the left channel (*vāmanāḍī*) by means of the filling breath (*āpūraka*) at the heart.

With the heart-mantra (*hṛd*), encapsulated by the heart-mantra and ending with the *sadyojāta-astro-huṃphaṭ* mantra, the lotus of the disciple’s heart should be slightly [pierced] by the *jyeṣṭhā* power.

The shaking and piercing [of the bonds] should be performed through the satisfaction of the self-nature of the ritual act; then, by means of the mantra joined with *sadyojāta* enclosed within the heart (*hṛtsampuṭita*), the drawing forth (*karṣaṇa*) should be performed with the *aṅkuśa* mudrā.

The remainder [of the procedure] is that one should perform the gathering (*saṅgraha*) up to the end of the crest (*śikhā*) and the extraction (*bahirnissāraṇa*). [At the end of the crest... (l5) "Up to the twelve-finger limit" (*dvādaśānte*) means having led the self as far as the limit of the twelve-fingers. "Gathering" (*saṅgraha*) means that the gathering of the self situated at the twelve-finger limit should be performed by means of the *ātman-mantra*.

The external expulsion: after [the disciple] has been gathered into one's own self at the midpoint between the eyebrows, his exit to the outside must be performed. Having caused him to enter by means of the wind in the left nostril located in one's own nose—having performed the entry and placed him in the heart—one should [unite him] with one's own self through breath-retention (*kumbhaka*) within one's own heart.

Having established [the mind] through the state of equanimity (*samarasibhāva*), having drawn that self upward by means of those [energies], and likewise having drawn it upward through the sequence of abandoning the causal deities beginning with Brahmā, having led it as far as the *dvādaśānta*, and having gathered one's own self there; then,

having brought the self to the middle of the eyebrows from the *dvādaśānta* via the *piṅgalā*— that is, by the exit of one’s own right channel— and having expelled it outward by means of the exhaling breath (*recaka*), [one should place it] within the *Śakti*.

When the pervasive Śiva-śakti is established according to the *Pūṣasūtra*, one should envelop the bonds (*pāśa*) such as impurity (*mala*) with the mantra whose essence ends in the letter *ma* (*māntātmamantra*), and then perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of that self. Following the placement, three oblations should be offered with the root mantra (*mūla*) for the sake of [the deity’s] presence (*sannidhāna*) and for the purpose of [establishing] the state of being the enjoyer (*bhoktṛtva*)... [and for] the bond of impurity equal to [the removal of] the cause of [bondage].

...one should offer oblations separately for each of the following, in order to bring about their presence within the thread: the noose of karma, which is variegated in color and has as its causes the body, the senses, and sense-objects, and which consists of white and black forms that are the causes of suffering; the noose of *māyā*, which is of a dark-grey hue; and the power of Śiva (*śivaśakti*), whose nature is the three qualities (*guṇas*) beginning with *tamas*. [Objection: But surely, that power of Śiva is stainless; how can it possibly take the form of a fetter (*pāśa*)? [Reply: True, but nevertheless—
Although not explicitly stated as that which is to be purified (*śodhya*) and the purifier (*śodhaka*), it is metaphorically designated as *sadipāśūti*. And it has been said regarding them:

"O Goddess, here Śivā is the power (*śakti*) that bestows grace upon all; yet, precisely because she follows after [the fettered] qualities (*dharma*), she is called a 'fetter' (*pāśa*). Thus, as previously mentioned, having joined the *nivṛtti* and other kalās—which contain the principles (*tattva*) and so forth—to the *pāśasūtra*, [one should] perfect... (l5).
Three oblations should not be offered. 66 (? 69?)

For one who has been joined to those wombs for the simultaneous attainment of conception, birth must be offered; and for the sake of the accumulation of one's own karma, its fruition, and dissolution, there is an oblation. In the stream of Māyā, in purification, and in the Root Principle (mūla-tattva), there is indeed an oblation for the concealment of the fetters, for their division, severance, and cutting by the weapon of Kalā. Now, for the Self...

He states the procedure for the fire-oblation (*homavidhāna*) for the sake of the purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*), beginning with conception (*garbhādhāna*), within Vahnivāgīśvarī. Regarding the phrase "of her" (*tasyāḥ*): first, as previously described, one should [visualize] the *nivṛttikalā*, which is joined with the principles (*tatva*) and so forth, and joined with the fourteen levels of existence from Brahmā down to the stationary beings, as well as the heavens and so forth, on the thread below the knees; [and] the *nivṛttikalā* ending in the dative case, enclosed by the heart-mantra (*hṛdayasampuṭita*).

Having visualized [the deity] with the *aṅkuśa-mudrā* and drawn her in with the *pūraka* [breath], having grasped her with the *sumbhaka* [mantra] and the *saṃhāra-mudrā*, and having placed her within the *ādhāra-śakti* situated in the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) by means of the *udbhava-mudrā* and the *recaka* [breath],

one should worship her. Then, having offered three oblations for the presence (*sannidhāna*) with the seed-syllable of the *nivṛtti-kalā* ending in *svāhā*, one should invoke Brahmā as its presiding deity, pray to him, and [visualize] the *nivṛtti-kalā* as all-pervasive.

Having invoked Vāgīśvarī and Vāgīśvara, one should offer three oblations for their presence. In the same way, having proceeded through the stages such as the *pratiṣṭhā*-kalā and so forth, one should perform the invocation and other rites for that Vāgīśvarī who pervades the *nivṛtti*-kalā, together with [the deities] beginning with Gata.

Is it not true that Vāgīśvarī exists within many wombs across various classes of beings? How then can her state of having many wombs be considered real while she is associated with only a single womb? Indeed, since the wombs ranging from stationary objects to others exist within the *nivṛtti*-kalā and the rest, it is entirely possible for Vāgīśvarī to possess many wombs by virtue of pervading each of those respective *kalās*. Having thus integrated [the disciple] as previously described—beginning with the striking of the disciple and so forth—and having gathered the Self into one's own heart...

Immediately after the installation, having led [the disciple] outward by means of the sequence of abandoning the causal principles beginning with Brahmā, and having visualized the union of the parents,

one should— by means of the *ātman-mantra*— simultaneously effect the union of the disciple’s self (*nuḥ*) in the form of multiple individual manifestations within all wombs at once; this occurs simultaneously and in a single instance across all wombs due to the diversity of the channels (*karṇa*).

"Female, male, and neuter," "beasts, birds, and so forth"—for the sake of obtaining a womb, that is, for the purpose of achieving conception, O Ātman, one should perform the *havana* or *homa* with the root mantra, saying, "Become joined with conception. For the sake of the birth of all embryos, the performance of the *homa* with the root mantra is prescribed. Since it is stated here that birth follows immediately after conception, the *puṃsavana* and *sīmantonnayana* rites must be performed.
When this has been made known: the *puṃsavana* rite is for the purpose of preventing [the birth of] a female or a neuter;

therefore, since the birth of a female or a neuter is here prohibited, the *puṃsavana* must be performed. Furthermore, the *sīmantonnayana* is performed to prevent [the child from having] such forms as being one-eyed, humpbacked, or lame, by means of its own specific ritual action.

By means of one’s own [wealth], for the sake of the accumulation—that is, the collection—of worldly and Vedic [objects] such as musical instruments, water-pipes, wells, and water-sheds, as well as the forty [types of] ritual actions, an oblation must be offered with the root [essence]; that which has been enjoyed through its experience, the enjoyment consisting of the sensation of pleasure and pain belonging to that action, an offering should be made with the root for the purpose of experiencing it; therefore, it is for the sake of enjoyment.

The reflection (*pratibimba*) in the great shadow is the consciousness (*cidvitti*) of the self, which is the cause for the exhaustion of the fruits of experience (*bhoga-karman*). Therefore, immediately after the enjoyment of dissolution (*laya-bhoga*), when there arises a recollection (*saṃsmṛti*) consisting of the determination of difference (*bhedādhyavasāya*) regarding the objects of enjoyment and the enjoyer, an oblation (*āhuti*) must be performed with the Root Mantra (*mūla*). And it has been said: "That state of consciousness (*cidvṛtta*) which is intensely devoted to the non-dual determination (*abhedādhyavasāya*) between the object of enjoyment and the enjoyer [is the means]."

"Yaścidvṛte mata iti. In the stream of *māyā*, for the purification of the worlds produced by *māyā*—so that there may not be a further pervasion (*vyāpti*) in these worlds already experienced by him—there is the purification of the streams. Half of that [offering] is an oblation with the root mantra (*mūla*). For the expiation (*niṣkṛti*), one should offer with the root mantra the impressions (*saṃskāra*) such as caste, lifespan, and experience. And in the *tattva*, it is for the sake of lightness, like a lotus from which the water has departed.

When each respective *kalā* has been purified, the oblation (*havana*) must be performed with the root mantra (*mūla*). And it is said: "Just as there is lightness in a water-bearing autumn cloud that has discharged its rain, so too is purification here prescribed for the reality (*tattva*) through the rite of the right-hand path. Regarding the fetters (*pāśas*)—namely, impurity (*mala*), *māyā*, and action (*karman*)—and the *kalās* beginning with *nivṛtti* which are conjoined with impurity, *māyā*, and action: in their concealment (*tirodhāna*), when the power of impurity is veiled, and in their division by means of the triad of fetters consisting of impurity, action, and *māyā*.

But the dissociation from the bond of concealment by the power of impurity (*mala-śakti-tirodhāna-pāśa-viśleṣaṇa*)— which is the state of being obscured (*tirobhāva*) characterized by auspiciousness— is here [the cause] due to the influence of the auxiliary factor (*sahakārī*). When the seed of experience (*bhoga-bīja-kalā*) is destroyed, because the activity of impurity (*mala-vṛtti*) lacks a cause, the dissociation of that [seed] from the bond with respect to the state of being an enjoyer (*bhoktṛtva*) is called "severance" (*cheda*), such as the [kalās] beginning with *nivṛtti*.

By the severing of the bonds (*pāśacchedena*)—the remainder being that it is a "scissors" (*kartarī*) empowered by the knowledge-power (*jñānaśakti*) consecrated seven times with the weapon-mantra (*astra*). And it has been said: "The scissors, which is the power of knowledge, severs all these bonds; it is supreme, subtle, and the highest binder of mantras. (Kālottara 1.8).
With the "weapon-mantra" (*hetinā*), such as *huṃ phaṭ* at the end, joined with the mantras of *nivṛtti* and the others, one should sever each respective boundary (*avadhi*). ||70||

Rubbing with both hands is the oblation; from the state [of the soul], the noose and sprouts [are offered]; in the rite of atonement, there is the contemplation of the one consciousness alone; for the purification of the subtle limbs, there is the offering of the eight white [substances] beginning with sound through the heart-mantra; for the Lord, there is the extraction of the *viṣva* and the *arghya*; the oblation to Vāgīśī and Īśa is performed in the heart by means of the heart-mantra, and the full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) is performed with the root-mantra. After the severing of the bonds, he describes the ritual actions such as rubbing.

"With the two hands" means: with the two hands, one should perform a rubbing with the *astra-mantra* ending in *huṃ phaṭ*; immediately after the rubbing, one should roll up the severed cord of the *pāśa*, place it on the tip of a ladle filled with ghee, and perform the oblation (*havana*) while reciting, "I offer the *pāśa* of the *nivṛtti-kalā*. After it has been cast downward, because the sprout of the *pāśa* no longer exists, one should again perform the oblation upon the sprout of the *pāśa* by means of the *astra-mantra* ending in *huṃ phaṭ*, according to the rule for expiation (*prāyaścitta*).

In the procedure for destroying defects arising from deficient or excessive ritual actions, eight oblations should be offered with the Astra-mantra. As it is said: "When auspicious rites are produced by deficient or excessive actions, one should offer eight expiatory oblations with the Heti-mantra for the sake of rectifying the loss. One should perform the meditation on the identity of consciousness (*cidaikya-manana*), conceiving of the consciousness as persisting even when the entire body is destroyed; [this applies] to all bodies generated by their respective karmas.

The meaning is that, although the self exists as distinct [in different bodies], the possibility of the unity of consciousness (*caitanya*) arises upon the destruction of each respective body. Regarding the purification of the subtle body (*sūkṣma-śarīra-śuddhi*), it is said for the sake of purifying the subtle body that the subtle body is constituted by the "eightfold city" (*puryaṣṭaka*). It is stated: "Sound, touch, form, taste, and smell as the fifth; intellect, mind, and ego—this is the body known as the eightfold city. [One should perform this] with the heart-mantra (*hṛdaya-mantra*) over the presiding deities.

In the sequence of the kalās beginning with *nivṛtti*, within the presiding deities Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśvara, and Sadāśiva, the offering of the white [substances] consisting of the eight [qualities] beginning with sound should be performed according to the order of Brahmā and the others; that is to say, with the heart-mantra, one should offer the white [substance] to Brahmā, saying: "O Brahmin, accept the white [substance] consisting of sound and touch. In the same way, [it is done] for Viṣṇu.

The offering of taste is made to Rudra; the offering of form is made to Īśvara; the offering of intellect and ego is made to Sadāśiva; and the offering of the mind is made to Sadāśiva. One should place the power of the bindu, which is the cause of sound and the other [objects of sense], upon Sadāśiva. And it is said: "One should place sound and touch upon Brahmā, and taste upon the Śrīvatsa-mark of Viṣṇu; one should abandon form and smell to Rudra, and abandon intellect and pride to Īśvara; and the mind, as well as sound and the rest, [should be offered] to the deity Sadāśiva."

One should abandon the causal power (*hetukī śakti*) there, according to the sequence [of the *bindu*...]. One must effect the extraction of the self (*ātmoddhṛti*) for the liberated soul who maintains [the state] from the multitude of bonds belonging to the *nivṛtti-kalā*. After the extraction, having placed [the soul] in one's own heart and led it to the *dvādaśānta*, one should perform the joining (*niyojana*) into the body of the disciple’s thread. For the purpose of nourishment (*āpyāyana*), [one uses] the *vauṣaṭ* [utterance] for the *arghya* water.

With the mantra, for the purpose of fixing the body within Rudra in the heart, one should perform a *ātma-homa* ending with the root-mantra (*mūla*). A final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) should be performed with the entire ritual action completed. Eighteen [purifications]—the eighteen purificatory rites (*saṃskāras*)—the Guru should perform upon the bound soul (*paśu*) for the destruction of the three impurities (*malas*) and for the satisfaction of Śiva. The self [is purified] through the striking and feeding of the self; this is his own performance.
For that [sacrifice], there is the authority over the [victim], its enjoyment, and its dissolution;

then, in this [rite], there is purification. Its purification consists of the concealment of its state as a bound soul (*paśutva*), the loosening and severing of the fetters (*pāśa*), and the burning of them. Regarding the performance of the rite in reverse order, one should maintain the sacrificial animal even while performing the *iṣṭi*; furthermore, all the intermediate consecrations (*saṃskāra*) are to be understood as being performed with the full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*).

The nature of separation (*viśleṣātmatā*) would be sufficient. Separation is for the sake of drawing forth; drawing forth is indeed for the sake of grasping; grasping is the cause of the world; the leading away of that which is fit for the depositing of the embryo is for the purpose of birth; and birth is for the purpose of qualification. Furthermore, qualification [is fulfilled] by means of the vow alone, and that which has become [realized] would be the cause of dissolution. And through the end of dissolution comes expiation (*niṣkṛti*); and expiation is for the purpose of disjunction, while disjunction is the cause of cutting off. It is precisely the two types of distraction (*vikṣepau*).

Even an interruption is a projection; its cause is that [projection], and by that very means it becomes full. (L5. Now, regarding "caused by a stream" and so forth: ||71|| When there is impairment through the ears and other senses, there would indeed arise the state of being a consumer of raw flesh associated with the lord of that [impairment]; thus, for the cessation of that, among those presiding deities, there is that which is pure, such as sound, touch, and so forth—namely, sound, touch, and so forth. (L6.)

[Objects] that are extremely subtle, or those that obstruct purification, should be offered for the sake of reaching the state of Śiva in the primary cause beginning with Brahmā, and this [offering] is for their satisfaction.

Regarding the five causes beginning with Brahmā, he states the cause consisting of sound, touch, and so forth, which is white (*śukla*): "By means of the ears and so forth. This means that when there is impairment—namely, impairment through the connection of each respective sense organ—with the ears and so forth, i.e., with the sense organs of hearing, sight, taste, and smell...

The impairment of the sense of hearing and the sense of touch results from the non-performance of prescribed duties and the performance of prohibited acts; this impairment of hearing and touch leads to rebirth in the wombs of Brahmarākṣasas and other such beings. The impairment of the sense of taste arises from smelling the intoxicants produced by Viṣṇu, Śakra, and Vyādaja, as well as from the impairment caused by the eyes of Rudra and Kravyāda.

The intellect (*buddhi*) and ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*) that bestow [the state of] *pluta* are the eaters of raw flesh (*kravyāda*) belonging to the portion of Īśvara; the corruption of the mind (*mano-vipluti*) bestows birth as an eater of raw flesh belonging to the portion of Sadāśiva. Thus it is said that being born as an eater of raw flesh occurs together with the *sthapatika*.

For that [state] is indeed darkened for them by sound, touch, and so forth, produced by the corruption of the sense of hearing and the sense of touch. "Together with the *sthapatika*" means together with its presiding deities, such as Brahmā and the others.
"Born from meat-eaters" means those who eat meat, such as Rākṣasas and others;

[may he be born] among them. Regarding the "Lord who is the cause of sound and so forth," this refers to the Lord produced by the distortion of the ears and other senses; "the toll of sound, touch, and so forth"—by the word "and so forth," the toll of taste and the rest is meant—this is "to be given," that is, fit to be offered. Now, [regarding] the earth... (l3)

(…) the acts of offering in Brahman; or rather, only the fragrance of one’s own qualities should be offered. To dispel the doubt as to how sound and touch—which are the pure principles (*tattva*) of earth and are the qualities of ether and air—can be offered in Brahman, (it is said:

(l4) (…) "having the form of sound, touch, and so forth" means having the form of sound, touch, etc.; "extremely subtle-bodied" (*tanutaratanugāḥ*) means extremely subtle-bodied (*tanu-tara-tanūḥ*), that is to say, the subtle body (*liṅgaśarīra*). That [body]...
Because it moves, they become increasingly subtle. And it has been said: "Sound, touch, form, taste, and smell as the fifth;

intellect, mind, and ego—this is declared to be the *puryaṣṭaka* (the eightfold city). Therefore, for the sake of purifying the *puryaṣṭaka*, these qualities such as sound and the rest—which constitute the *puryaṣṭaka*—are produced solely from the impairment of the sense organs, beginning with the ear. Thus...

In the purification [of the elements], during the purification of the principles (*tattva*) beginning with earth, those who are restrained become the restrainers. Therefore, for the sake of attaining the state of Śiva—that is, as a means to reach the state of Śiva—one should offer this white [substance] consisting of sound, touch, and so forth, for the satisfaction of Brahmā and the others; that is, for the purpose of satisfying Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśvara, and Sadāśiva, the causes beginning with Brahmā. In this context, however, the sound produced by the impairment of the sense of hearing and the touch...

The impairment of the skin-sense organ (*tvagindriya*) and the impairment of the feet, hands, anus, and genitals are included within the skin-sense organ because their object is touch (*sparśa*). Because their object is sound, both [the ears and the organs of speech] are included within hearing; thus, these two portions of Brahman are resolved in Brahman. Likewise, taste produced by the impairment of the sense of taste is resolved in Viṣṇu. And likewise, smell... [9]

Fame, as well as the objects of sound, form, and smell, are offered to Rudra. Likewise, the delusion of the intellect (*buddhi*) and the ego (*ahaṅkāra*), as well as the delusion of the mind (*manas*), are offered to Īśvara;
and even the power of the *bindu*, which is the cause of all modifications, is offered to Sadāśiva. And it has been said:
"The ear is Brahmī, the tongue is Vaiṣṇavī, the source of the sense of smell and sight is Raudrī, the root of pride and intellect is Aiśvarī, and Śivadevatā resides in the mind."

Touch, object, speech, action, [mind, intellect, ego, and mind-stuff]—these eight are established as such. Regarding the sounds, the wise say that there is a variety of phonemes therein, like a leaf. Having effected the severance of the bonds together with the three internal functions of the external objects, one should cause the deities to ascend.

Likewise, in the *Kālottara*: "One should abandon sound and touch in Brahmā; one should abandon taste in Keśava; one should abandon form in Rudra; one should abandon intellect and ego in Īśvara; having said 'mind' and 'bindu' in Śiva, one should say 'be Śiva' for the sake of liberation. (70)
In the *tattva* called Māyāntātmā, when the ritual procedure has been partially removed through the recitation of the *bhāṣya*,

there is the substitution (*sādeśa*) known as the end of *vidyā*. In the *tattva* of Manu-vikaloccāra, which is designated as *upāṃśu*, within the *śaiva* state ending in *śakti*, the meditation of the Guru indeed effects the destruction of the loss [of the self] in the mind.
From the movement of the mind, there should be hundreds of oblations directed toward Śiva and Manu.

(L5) [The author] states the rule for the fire-oblation (*homa*) with the root mantra for the purpose of purifying deficiencies in ritual action, mantras, and so forth, by means of the principles (*tattva*) known as Dīkṣā, Vidyā, and Śiva. Regarding "Māyā":
in the principle called Ātman ending with Māyā—that is, in the principle bearing the name that begins from the Earth-principle (*pṛthvī-tattva*) and concludes with the Māyā-principle—(L6)

The meaning is: [this occurs] within the *ātmatattva*, which pervades up to the end of the *māyātattva*. When there is a deficiency in the ritual oblation (*vidhihuti*), joined with an omission of the procedure (*kriyālopa*) due to the skipping of the sequence of the individual soul (*aṇu*), [the recitation] ends with the pronunciation of the root-mantra (*mūlamantra*) as explained in the commentary (*bhāṣya*). Because of its pronunciation joined with some slight audible sound, it is called "with a portion" (*sādeśākhyānta*); it culminates in the *vidyātman*, which bears the name Sadāśiva—that is, in the *tattva* ending with the appellation Sadāśiva—and [finally] in the *svarūpatattva* consisting of the *bindu*, known by the term "whispered" (*upāṃśu*) due to the deficient pronunciation of the mantra.

For the sake of purifying any deficiency in the utterance of the mantra, [one should perform] the contemplation (*bhāvanā*) of Guru Śiva within the mind (*mānase*), in the *Śivatattva* which pervades the *Śaktitattva*, at the end of the power of utterance conjoined with some degree of hearing from one's own internal perception (*prākṣusaṃjñāt*); this is the reflection upon the destruction of loss, the abandonment of... [line 9].

[This is] for the purpose of removing the fault of losing the contemplation (*bhāvanā*) of Śiva. From the mental utterance—that is, from the mental recitation of the contemplation—one should perform hundreds of oblations (*āhuti*) directed toward Śiva, meaning having Śiva-mantras as their object. For each of the principles beginning with the *ātmatattva*, one hundred oblations should be performed with the Śiva-mantra.

Likewise, in the Kāmika [Tantra] (p116a, l1), the supreme Guru, having contemplated that the *kalā* beyond peace (*śāntyatīta*) is dissolved into the principle of power (*śakti-tattva*), and having established the principle of the self (*ātma-tattva*) up to the limit of *māyā*, should first consider the principle of the self ending in the dative case, conjoined with its respective principle and the word "namaḥ," and combined with the *praṇava* (OM). Having thus meditated upon it and worshipped it in its presence for the sake of purifying any deficiency in the ritual procedure—

Having offered one hundred oblations with the Śiva-mantra ending in *svāhā* accompanied by sound, one becomes purified from the deficiency in the pronunciation of the mantra through the *vidyā-tattva* [offering] performed in a whisper (*upāṃśu*). Having established the *śiva-tattva*, one should mentally contemplate it up to the *śakti*. Having offered one hundred and eight oblations, the deficiency of one's own mind is said to be removed; one should then perform the cutting of the topknot (*śikhācchedana*) with the Śiva-mantra. (73)

The Guru, whose seat is the principles known as the Pure Path (*śuddhādhvan*) and so forth, the Earth (*vasudhā*), and the Drop (*bindu*); whose body and instruments are enriched by the *kalās* beginning with *nāda*; who is the sole-minded servant of Śarva;

whose instrument is the power of consciousness (*dhī*) situated within the *samanā* level; and who is the *unmanā* of the Pure Path principles—he himself, having meditated upon the Śaiva reality filled with the principles from *vidyā* up to the one called Śiva above, describes the contemplation of Śiva for the purpose of performing the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) at the end of initiation. (ll. 4–5)

"Pure Path" (*śuddhādhva*) means as follows: the ground of the sacrificial site (*yāgavasudhā*) consists of the principles (*tattva*) beginning with the Pure Path; the principles beginning with the Pure Path consist of the principle of Pure Knowledge (*śuddhavidyātattva*); and through the mental contemplation (*manobhāvanā*) of the sacrifice, the equality, and the ground of the sacrificial site, one should contemplate the nature of the principle of Pure Knowledge as the locus of sacrifice (*yāgasthāna*), [subsuming] the principles beginning with earth (*pṛthivyādi*). Seated upon the throne of the principle called the Bindu (*bindu*), there, on that ground of the sacrificial site—this is the meaning.

Seated upon the throne of reality named Bindu, [the practitioner] meditates on the body endowed with the digits (*kalā*) beginning with *indhikā* within the *nāda*; his external organs are joined to the body formed by the digits of *nāda* beginning with *indhikā*, while the internal digits beginning with Vyāpinī are joined to the external organs; with his mind fixed solely on Śarva, he performs the meditation on the Supreme Lord.

The Ācārya [is] power itself; *dhiḥ* is *buddhi*. "Ending with *samanā*" (*samanāntarālya*) means that which exists within the internal organ (*antarālya*), the internal instrument (*antaḥkaraṇa*); the meaning is the internal organ ending with the power of *samanā*. The Pure Path (*śuddhādhvan*)... by the three principles (*tatva*)—namely, the principle of *Śiva* situated above the principle of *Vidyā*, whose nature is the Self, and the principle of *Vidyā* whose nature is *Unmanā*—it is "filled" (*nicita*), pervaded, the Śaiva connection to Śiva.
Having meditated upon and contemplated Śiva as described,

and having performed the purification of the instruments (*karaṇaśuddhi*), one should unite [the soul] with Śiva. The Preceptor, established on a seat fashioned from the *bindu* at the stage of the *vidyā-tattva*, [should contemplate] Indhikā, Dīpikā, Rocikā, Mocikā,
and likewise Urdhvagāminī and Sūkṣmā.

The state of the Kṣatriya is remembered as the power of the seed (*bīja-śakti*), while the power of sound (*nāda-śakti*) is called *kalā*, O twice-born ones. The supreme teacher possesses a body externally constricted by these *kalās*.

Furthermore, there are Vyāpinī, Vyomarūpā, Anantā, Aparā, Anāthā, and Āśritā; with these [powers] externally joined with the instruments of action, the body is completely filled by the principle of the Self (*ātma-tattva*) and the mind. Thus ends verse 74.

Having placed the *srava* ladle filled with abundant clarified butter (*ājya*) upon the *sruk* offering-spoon, one should then, having raised [the body] with the mudrā called the conch (*śaṅkha*), meditate on the root of the *sruk* and the navel as being situated upon the path of the five supports (*pañcādhāra*).

One should contemplate Śakti in the two [parts], in the base, the jar, the tip of the handle, and the neck; and in the flow of the clarified butter, one should contemplate the face of Śiva consisting of the *sruk*.

He describes the invocation of Śakti and Śiva: "Filled with clarified butter" (ājyāḍhyām) means overflowing with ghee, that is, completely filled with clarified butter. "With the *srava* [ladle] held out" means having placed the *sruva* upon the opening of the *sruc* while it is turned face-downward. Having taken up the *sruva* by means of the mudrā called the conch (*śaṅkha*), which is shaped like a conch, the true Guru, rising from his eastern seat, [proceeds]... with the previously risen [breath].

The body has a previously elevated form; it is even in its descent, with feet standing evenly; the root of the *sṛṅ* (channel/root) is at the navel, and the root of the *sṛṅ* is held in the navel. And that which is the entire *dhvani* (sound/vibration) established in the five supports (*pañcādhāra*)—that which is the entire *dhvani* within the five substrata known as the mandala, fire, the jar, the disciple, and one's own self—and that collection of the six paths (*ṣaḍadhvan*) previously deposited in an identical manner in the five locations of Śiva.

Because it exists [priorly], the placement (*nyāsa*) of the six paths (*ṣaḍadhvan*) must first be performed everywhere. Now, having grasped the collection of sounds (*dhvanicaya*) abiding everywhere, one should invoke the emission (*sṛṣṭi*). Sadāśiva is established in the circle of witnesses for all rites; he is established in the *śivakumbha* as the protector of the sacrifice; and he is Sadāśiva residing in the fire as the locus of the oblation (*homa*).

For it has been stated: "The Lord who effects the release of the bonds of his disciples from the body of the *śikya*, the Lord who bestows grace, is established within my body; that Lord of five bases (*pañcādhikaraṇa*) is indeed I, Sadāśiva. Thus, [the parts are: the *sṛkkumbha* refers to the regions of the cheeks and neck;

the *sṛṅmūla* refers to the jars and so forth situated at the base of the horns; the *daṇḍa* is the staff of circular form; and the *agra* is the knob (*gaṇḍika*), because the word *kha* denotes space (*ākāśa*).
"Bila" means a sacrificial altar (*vedi*) provided with a cavity. "Gravakaṇṭha" [refers to] these...
in the remaining parts, one should recollect—that is, contemplate—all [of them] according to the sequence of the digits (*kalā*) beginning with Nivṛtti.

Likewise, in the *Mṛgendra*: "Having placed the path upon the ladle (*sruk*), [one contemplates] the neck, the shoulder, and the handle of the pitcher, and the altar, the neck, and the mouth-parts, according to the divisions beginning with Nivṛtti"—thus, at the mouth of the ladle.

Since the invocation of Śiva has been performed, one should keep in mind the prescribed six locations. In the *ājyasaraṇī*, the path for the flow of clarified butter, one should contemplate the *śakti*. In the mouth—that is, the opening of the sacrificial ladle (*sruk*)—one should contemplate Śiva, who consists of the ladle and whose nature is the ladle itself. One should [contemplate] the Lord who pervades all paths, following the movement of the ladle.
The meaning is "one should remember," because it has been stated that Sadāśiva is the mass of power (śaktipiṇḍa) by means of the designations *sṛk* and *sṛva*. ||75||

Through the union of the disciple’s own mind with the recollection [of the Self], the *prāṇava* arises from the non-mentation of the *nāda*. By means of the *viṣuva* of the channels through the upward utterance from the three *kandas* and the very severing of the knots, the *nāḍī-viṣuva* occurs from the emergence of the *nāda* in their center. Having abandoned the six, there is the *praśānta-viṣuva* of the initial *kalās*; its dissolution is in the *Śakti*, in the seventh. That sound of the *Śakti* resounds only upwards; it is that which is known as the *kalā* of the *Śakti*, the seventh moon.

By means of the *truṭis* [of time], the end of the mind of Śakti is threefold. Within that *prāṇa*, there is another [division] consisting of the *parāpara* and *para* [states]; that which is called Time (*kāla*) is the Supreme (*para*), known as the *tattva*, the flow of the equinox (*viṣuva*), the station of Paraśiva, which effects the manifestation of consciousness (*cid-vyakti*). (L7) Now, with a verse in the *yuga* meter, he describes the meditation at the time of the *pūrṇāhuti* [offering], regarding the sevenfold division of the equinoxes, which corresponds to the number of the *prāṇa*, the *mantra*, the *nāḍī*, the *praśānta-śakti*, and the *kāla-tattva*. He says: "To the disciple... (*śiṣye...*) [and so forth].

The conjunction of the disciple’s self, his own mind, and the recollection [of the deity]; the conjunction of the disciple’s self, (l. 8) ... the mind, and the vital air (*samīraṇa*)—that is, the *prāṇa*—is a relationship characterized by mutual predominance. This first *viṣuva*, which is the *praṇava* and the junction related to the *prāṇa*, should occur. Thus it has been said: "Having joined the self, the mind, and the two *prāṇas*, [one attains] the *viṣuva*... (l. 9).

The *praṇava* is known as the *viṣuva* (equinox), pertaining to both the disciple and one’s own mind. One should offer the lotus existing at the root of the *kanda* and the *ādhāra*. From the subtle utterance (*tanūccāra*), that is, from the utterance of the mantra; through reflection upon that which is called *nāda*;

within the *nāda*, in the midst of the resonance (*dhvani*)—[through] meditation on the nature of the unity of the self. [This is] the second *manuviṣu* (equinox of the mind), the *mantraviṣu* (equinox of the mantra); and it has been said: "But the dissolution of the self in the midst of the *nāda*..."

Having reflected upon the weeping [of the breath], through the application of the conjunction of the phonemes *a*, *ā*, *u*, and so forth, [from] the heart (*hṛdaya*) up to the end of the *bala* [channel]— this is the "joined with the mantra" (*mantrasañjuktam*). Due to the cutting of the knots and the piercing of the ten knots beginning with the *meḍhra*, from the emergence of the *nāda* in their midst, and because the *suṣumnā* is preeminent in the center of all [channels],
the equinox of the channels (*nāḍīviṣuva*) occurs from the manifestation of the *nāda* situated in the middle of the *suṣumnā*.

And the third [place] has been described as being in the region of the genitals; then the bulb (*kanda*), the navel, the heart, the throat, the uvula, the tip of the palate, the middle of the eyebrows, the forehead, the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmabila*), the power (*śakti*), and the end of the twelve (*dvādaśānta*)—these ten knots in sequence. Having pierced them with the trident of the root-mantra, the Sound (*nāda*) [emerges]. Through the union with the channel of intoxication (*mādanāḍī*), that channel is considered the equinox (*viṣuva*). Here too, among all the channels, it is situated in the center.

That [channel] is to be known as Suṣumnā, which goes from the power (*śakti*) at the navel to Śiva. Therein one should cause [the breath] to flow... [it is called] the equinox (*viṣuva*). Having abandoned the six [elements] beginning with the primordial digit (*ādikalā*)—namely, those known as *a*, *u*, *m*, *bindu*, *nāda*, and the end of *nāda* (*nādānta*)—[one proceeds] through the six locations known as the heart, throat, palate, the space between the eyebrows, the aperture, and the "end of the twelve" (*dvādaśānta*), [where reside] Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra...

By abandoning [the sequence] through the six causal lords known as Śva, Rasadāśiva, and Anāhata, there is the dissolution of the self into the seventh, the Power (Śakti), in the station of Power. This is called the fourth state, the "Tranquil" (praśānta). It is said: "Having abandoned in succession the letters 'A' and 'U', the letter 'M' designated as the Bindu, and those designated as Nāda and Nādānta within Brahmā and the others, one should lead the disciple's self into dissolution into the seventh, the midst of Power; that is the Tranquil."

One should know that [the state] is "one whose range of the senses is stilled. Within the Śakti, in the midst of the Śakti, the Sound (nāda) together with its resonance (sadhvani) should flow upward alone. And when it moves, then that which is designated as Śakti is the fifth [state], Viṣuva. And it has been said: "The Sound situated in the middle of the Śakti flows forth as far as the end of Samanā;
that is declared by the experts in Śakti to be the Viṣuva. By means of three *truṭis*, the duration is merely that required for a blink of the eyes.

Since it has been stated that "the time required for a mere movement of the eyebrows is proclaimed to consist of three *truṭis*," one should calculate seven, eight, and sixteen *kalās* by means of those *truṭis*, making them seventeen, eighteen, and sixteen in number respectively. Then, starting from the power (*śakti*)—[text missing]—up to the end of sound (*nādānta*), which is the level of the power *samanā*, one should conceive of this as threefold; that [threefold division] is the single mantra within the vital breath (*prāṇa*).

[The breath] is not divided into three in the threefold measure of the elements, [but rather] by the lower, the intermediate, and the higher. "Lower" (*apara*) refers to the equinox (*viṣuva*), which is called "time" (*kāla*) and named "time" (*kālanāmadheya*);
the meaning of this "equinox-mantra" (*viṣumantṛ*) is sixteen *truṭis*. (l.

2) In the upward movement of the breath (*prāṇoccāra*), the "lower time" (*aparakāla*) consists of seventeen *truṭis* and extends to the end of the pervasive state (*vyāpinī*). In the movement of the breath within the pervasive state, the "intermediate time" (*parāparakāla*) consists of eighteen *truṭis*.
The movement of the vital breath (*prāṇacāra*) at the end of the *samanā* is called the "supreme" (*parākhya*), which is indeed the supreme time (*paraḥ kālaḥ*).

Thus, [there is] dissolution in the equinox (*viṣuvat*) of the void of the digits (*kalā*), which is devoid of time and pervades all digits; this is the equinox of time (*kālaviṣuva*). And it has been said: "But the first [time], situated at the end of the vital breath within the sixteenfold [process], is proclaimed as lasting only the duration of a brow-flicker at the conclusion of the mantra."

Divide me [the breath] again into three ways: the lower (*apara*), the intermediate (*parāpara*), and the higher (*para*). The lower extends up to sixteen [fingers], and the intermediate up to seventeen. That time which follows beyond that is recorded as the eighteenth. Having thus known the breath (*prāṇa*) as a threefold time, one should then abandon it: the first [part] reaches the power (*śakti*) at the top, and the second extends to the pervasive one (*vyāpinī*). The third...

The time of the *samanā* is called the *viṣuva*. Beyond that, existing at the end of *unmanī*, it is the fixed (*dhruva*) and circularly encompassed station of Paraśiva, the abode of Paraśiva, which effects the manifestation of consciousness and brings about the manifestation of the Self.
That which is named "Reality" (*tatva*), bearing the name of reality, is the seventh *viṣuva*. It is declared to be at the end of *unmanī*.

The reality (*tattva*) is [to be understood as] "possessing consciousness" (*sa-jñuka*), because it has been stated that the Unstruck Sound (*unmanā*) resides in the Supreme. Thus, the meaning is that the union of the disciple's self with the supreme Śiva, who is beyond parts (*niṣkala*), is the "equinox of reality" (*tattvaviṣuva*). ||77||
In that [state],

one should join that [nectar] with ambrosia by means of the channel (*nāḍī*)— which has a beautiful stalk, is connected to the cavity of the lotus of one's own heart, and extends upward through the opening of the palate, dripping the nectar of the Lord from the Bindu— by pouring it into the interior of the body.

(…) one should likewise employ the *pūrṇā* [offering] characterized by a moment (*kṣaṇa*) and a digit (*kalā*). Preceded by the meditation on one’s own blood, he speaks of the *pūrṇāhuti* for the purpose of joining the disciple’s self with reality during the equinox (*viṣuva*). Regarding the word “in that” (*tasmin*): the “staff of the channels” (*nāḍīdaṇḍa*) refers to the staff of the beautiful central channel;
the meaning is that the staff of the tongue (*sṛkdaṇḍa*) itself is the central channel. “Sṛk” [refers to] the cavity of the heart-lotus, the throat... (p. 118b, number).

110 is mentioned in the middle of the folio with a pen.
