(l1) [................................... from the nectar flowing as drops from the opening made manifest in the path of the throat and palate for a long time; from the place of the drops, [the nectar flows] into one's own heart-lotus (*svahṛtpadma*), that is, into one's own heart-lotus, the cavity (*śvabhra*) which is like the mouth of a cavern (*sṛkvedibilam*); by means of that very mouth of the cavern joined [to it], just as... (l2)

The sequence refers to the heart-lotus. From the aperture above the throat and palate—the path from the throat to the palate where the opening becomes manifest—the stream of nectar flows from its own source, the place of the *bindu*. Having begun its expansion from that station of the *bindu*, it is joined with the supreme nectar (*para-śuddhāra*). Thus, having reached the state of internal contemplation (*antarbhāvanā*), it assumes the form of the eyebrows; the meaning is that the internal is imitated externally by means of the form of the eyebrows. In this way, through meditation on the stream, the manifestation of consciousness occurs in that station of Paraśiva.

From the beautiful jar-base (*kalaśa*) of the root, which is rich in nectar and free from rebirth, situated at the base of the stalk of blood filled with ambrosia— [from] that jar-base existing at the root, [a stream] emerges from the root by the falling of clarified butter,
a stream of clarified butter endowed with the contemplation of the supreme ambrosia.

One should unite with this [mantra]. One should join the disciple’s self with the aforementioned [mantra]. Having performed inhalation (pūraka) and retention (kumbhaka), one should purify all the gates. Relying on the root-practice, one should contemplate the mantra which possesses the two sounds; abiding in the divine instrument and endowed with the supreme state, one should extract the sixfold path from the disciple’s self, the jar, the fire, and also from the maṇḍala, and then project it [into the disciple].

Then, on the life-channel (*prāṇanāḍī*), at the tip [of the central channel]—as taught by the Guru—one should utter the mantra in sequence. Having pierced the knots one after another with the trident of the root-mantra, having led the path of the temple (*prāsādādhvan*) as far as the celestial palace situated at the crest (*śikhāntastha-dvimāna*), and having abandoned the mental [conception], one indeed pervades... (l. 8)

While the disciple, endowed with the nature of consciousness and perfected in the six qualities, remains in the resonance of *cidānanda*, the master, meditating on the self as a canopy, should slowly pour the full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*). He should remain in the breath-retention (*kumbhaka*) for as long as the stability of the clarified butter persists; then, for the sake of steadiness and for the purpose of unification, he should again cast the full oblation. (78)

Having joined [the disciple] into the fire of emanation (*sṛṣṭhyagni*), there, by means of the supreme power (*paradhā*), Śiva should then unite the disciple with the manifestation of consciousness (*cidvyakti*)—characterized by omniscience, self-satisfaction, and so forth—as well as with those known as autonomy (*svātantrya*). Endowed with the six qualities, he should cause [the disciple] to attain that which is filled with power (*śaktipūrṇimā*), possesses infinite objects, and is similar to Śiva through the fire. Thus, the state of the six qualities such as omniscience is established for the consciousness of the disciple.

Regarding the word "sṛṣṭyā" (by emission): for the disciple who has been initiated up to the *pūrṇāhuti* as previously described, [the teacher]— by means of the supreme (*parā*) [power], through the path of emission and non-emission (*sṛṣṭāsṛṣṭimārgeṇa*), by drawing forth the disciple’s consciousness (*caitanya*) which is the very nature of the manifestation of consciousness (*cidvyaktika*) consisting of vision and action (*dṛkkriyātmaka*)— having led it from his own root-center (*mūlasthāna*) up to the end of the twelve (*dvādaśānta*), [he then] again...

Having brought [the consciousness] from the *dvādaśānta* to the location of the *ghaṇṭikā*, one should meditate on it as being within the handful of flowers at the opening of the nose; then, having joined it by uniting it with the Śiva-fire existing there in the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), one should perform the offering with the *srava* ladle using three oblations each for the sake of the complete satisfaction of omniscience and so forth.

Endowed with the insatiability for omniscience, and possessing the notion of sovereignty over primordial consciousness (*anādibodha*), [the Lord] brings [the soul] to completion through His sovereign power—[a power] that is undecaying, infinite in its objects, and possessed of infinite potency. Having thus drawn [the soul] forth and caused it to enter [into manifestation], the meaning is that He generates it by means of the qualities belonging to the manifold creation, because it was previously established within the noose of the impurity of beginningless *mala*. Now, as for the word "nanu": [it is used here as an interrogative particle].

After the division of the words (*padacchedana*), following the *pūrṇāhuti* offering into the fire, and immediately after the mention of the six qualities (*ṣaḍguṇa*), [the soul] is extracted from the fire— this is the ellipsis— having been summoned from the fire which is endowed with the six qualities. Therefore, at that time, it becomes similar to Śiva, who by his very nature is free from the beginningless bonds (*pāśa*).
(…) one should apply the six qualities to the disciple and cause them to be integrated.

Likewise, at the end of the *Dīkṣāpaṭala* in the *Mṛgendra*, it says: "Having brought forth the qualities right there, one should sever [the bonds] such as servitude by means of three offerings to the Siddhas according to the procedure of the *Svatantra* and other [tantras]."
"Vipaścitim" (to Vipaścit). ||79||

Now follows the procedure for the initiation of the teacher (*ācāryābhiṣeka*). Having been consecrated with the excellent Guru, who is the liberator from bonds, by means of jewels, medicinal herbs, seeds, and full jars containing the elements, arranged upon a firm seat according to the ritual arts and surrounded by the five enclosures;

and having performed the worship of Śiva along with the Brahma-mantras and limbs accompanied by recitation (*japa*) in rites such as initiation and consecration; he shall become fit [for these], being chosen and invested with authority by the Guru after receiving the command bestowed before Śiva. [He is fit] for the three categories...

Because it has been said, "He who understands this compendium (*saṃhitā*), which bestows the fruits of the fourfold enjoyment and liberation—that disciple alone is worthy," [the author] now describes the procedure for the master’s consecration (*ācāryābhiṣeka*) for a disciple endowed with such qualities and conduct.
Regarding the word "consecrated" (*sikta*): [it refers to one consecrated] with jewels, medicinal herbs, seeds, and the five [substances] beginning with jewels.

Regarding the jewels, it is said: ruby, lapis lazuli, pearl, coral, and sapphire—these five are proclaimed as the [primary] gems. By the word "gem" (ratna), metals such as gold and minerals such as yellow orpiment are included; likewise, medicinal herbs along with the goddesses and so forth are included.

Likewise, in the *Mṛgendra*, [the herbs are]: Devī, Brāhmī, Trāyantī, Lakṣmaṇā, Śaṅkhapuṣpī, Abalā, Bījā, Jyotiṣmatī, Aparājitā, Viṣā, Balā, Moṭā, Bilva, Dhātrī, Abhayā, Amṛtā, Śatāvarī, Śārvarī, Dūrvā, Kuśa, Vyāghrī, and Punarnavā. The seeds are rice (*śāli*), white mustard (*siddhārtha*), barley (*yava*), and so forth.

With these *bhūtaghaṭas*— the five jars filled to the brim and placed in the directions starting from the west, north, south, east, and northeast— and furthermore, with what kind [of seats]: on a stable seat consisting of the complete assembly of the *ādhāraśakti* and so forth,
and the seven types of grains beginning with rice.

He is consecrated by means of the *kala*s, which are sequentially assigned according to the five enclosures (*pañcāvṛta*), each accompanied by its respective fivefold enclosure; these are joined with the worship of the limbs (*aṅga*) and Śiva, and with the recitation (*japa*) of the five Brahmans—Sadyojāta and the others—along with their respective mantras in due order.

He is sprinkled from the jars that are joined with the worship of the limbs and Śiva for each individual limb, as well as with the recitation of the root mantra (*mūlamantra*) one hundred and eight times for each.

He was thus consecrated, as it has been said: "The western [face] with the *sadyojāta* mantra, the northern one situated on the left with the *vāmadeva*, and the southern one facing east with the *bahurūpa* man; having touched the eastern [face] with the *īśāna* mantra—all these by means of Śambhu together with Ambā. Thus, having received the command prescribed for the *śivāśrama*, he stood before Śiva... (l. 3)

Having performed [the initiation] in the presence of the Supreme Lord seated in the maṇḍala and other [sacred spaces], she acts thus hereafter as one who has accomplished her task. As it has been said: "O child, you must always perform the obligatory (*nitya*) and occasional (*naimittika*) rites received through the lineage of gurus while residing in the assembly of ten. From this day forward, having reflected upon it, you must act by the command of Śiva. Having received this command, the disciple promised "So be it," accepting the guru’s instruction.
"One who has undertaken the vow" (*uktavrataḥ*) means one who is engaged in the practice of the vows prescribed by the Guru.

As it is stated in the *Svāyambhuva*: "Now, the preceptor himself should indeed observe the supreme vow of the preceptor; he should practice the collection of mantras (*mantrasaṃhitā*) from Sadyojāta up to Śiva."

Sleeping on the ground for three fortnights, eating only at night, always subsisting on sacrificial oblations (*caru*), bathing three times a day, remaining unperturbed by dualities, self-restrained, wearing white garments, peaceful,
adorned with white garlands and unguents, and carrying a meditation belt, a rosary, and a girdle of muñja grass.

The bearer of the Victors' purifier should perform the recitation (*japa*) every day, one thousand times, without agitation. At the conclusion of the recitation, he should perform the fire-oblation (*homa*) daily according to his ability, in due order, with clarified butter, or with sesame seeds smeared with clarified butter, or with milk, or with rice grains.

(l8) Thus consecrated, the disciple shall be fit for initiation, consecration, and so forth; that is, he shall become worthy for initiation, the consecration of a *liṅga*, the performance of the *pavitra* rite, and other such acts.

The liberator from bonds (pāśavimocaka) is one who is skillful in [severing] the bonds of impurity and so forth. For this very reason, he should be the preeminent teacher (guruvara); by the term "preeminent teacher," [it refers to one who is] fit for performing initiation for all those to be subdued.

O Brahmins, [this rite] shall be effective in the installation and sprinkling [of the deity], in the ritual of atonement and consecration, in the exposition and other activities of the scripture— whether for one's own sake or for the sake of others— and in the worship of all the gods; likewise for the foremost Śaiva preceptor among Brahmins and others,
and for the caste-status of those two, [it applies] to initiation and installation.

Furthermore, for Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, and others—specifically for Kṣatriyas, Śūdras, and Vaiśyas, and for Vaiśyas and Śūdras—the initiation (*dīkṣā*) is desired even within their own respective castes. For one’s own sake, there are eight [types] in the case of a mobile linga (*calaliṅga*); however, in the installation (*pratiṣṭhā*), these three [are prescribed]. Even a Śūdra, in the case of a Śūdra-initiation, may perform the installation for his own sake when it concerns a mobile or fixed [linga], or even a stone linga (*bāṇaliṅga*), provided he is a lifelong student (*naiṣṭhika*) who has studied all the mantras, especially those concerning the knowledge of Śiva.

Even for a Śūdra householder, eligibility exists only for the obligatory daily rites (*nityeṣṭi*); even there, it is proclaimed that [the rites] must be performed with mantras devoid of [specific ritual] reverence. He is unfit for consecration (*abhiṣeka*), so how much less for installation (*sthāpana*) and other such acts? ||80||
From that Great Lord Bindu, who was marked by the Gāyatrī-śakti,

[the lineage] flowed here upon the earth to Durvāsas from the *suratna* [jewel] beginning with Vidyeśa; and through the arising of grace toward his disciples and others, it became endowed with the glorious primary Kadamba ornament in the year of Bhārata.

The *Cāmarmasajyāśrama*. In order to demonstrate the specific qualification for initiation (*dīkṣā*) as prescribed in the *Śivāgama*, he describes the lineage of the Śaiva family (*śaivakulakrama*), beginning from the *bindu*. By "from the *bindu*," he indicates that it is the material cause (*upādāna*) of the pure path (*śuddhādhvan*).

It is not from the *bindu* itself, but from Maheśvara abiding in the *bindu*; for the sake of the production of the world consisting of the moving and the non-moving, [the lineage proceeds] from Sadāśiva through the emission of the *bindu*. Therefore, starting from the *bindu*...

The term "partless" (*niṣkala*) is thus illuminated. For the sake of the world's emanation, [the Supreme Lord], through the agitation of the *bindu*... [is] indeed made manifest as the "partless. This is illuminated: the meaning is that at the time of the world's emanation, there occurs an outpouring of consciousness (*ciddoha*). By Sadāśiva, who possesses a body of consciousness, at the time of the agitation of the *bindu*, the agitation of the *bindu* is marked by the power of Gāyatrī; at that time, it is *parā*.

Sadāśiva was born from Vidyeśa, who is embodied in the *bindu*, having arisen from Niṣkala Śiva through the lineage of the primordial gods (*ādisurakrama*). From Vidyeśa, [the succession proceeds] through Ananteśa and the others; by Ananteśa, [he was born as] Śrīkaṇṭha, the lord of Kailāsa, in the midst of the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*).

Viṣṇu was born from Śrīkaṇṭha; from Viṣṇu, Brahmā; from Brahmā, Brahmā [himself]; and from Śrīkaṇṭha once again, all the gods beginning with Indra were produced. Durvāsas was likewise born; in this sequence, the lineage originating from Durvāsas and Dāśiva arose upon the earth in the world of mortals (bhūloka). Thus it has been stated by Jñānaśivācārya: "Indeed, the Lord was received from Paraśiva; from him, Śiva together with his consort, whose nature is sound (nādātmā), [was received]."

From that Lord [Śiva] came Sakalākala, then Ananteśa, Bhaṭṭa, and others; from him came Aṇḍaja, Viṣṇu, Vāsava, Vidhi, Śrīkaṇṭha, and Rudra; and from them came the eminent sage named Durvāsas, the Guru and the one who brought down the Tantras. Furthermore, on this earth, in the land of Bhārata within the region of Bharatakhaṇḍa, there was Durvāsas, who attained the grace of that [Lord] through the arising of sacrificial rites.

For a seer (*ṛṣi*) or similar being who has received the prescribed initiation, the name "Kāśika"—such as Kāśyapa, Agastya, Bhāradvāja, Gautama, and so forth—is used; by such a name, [he is known] in the land of Bharata (*bhāratavarṣa*), the region of Bharata (*bharatakhaṇḍa*), on the earthly world (*bhūloka*), in Jambudvīpa, situated in the southern part of the snowy mountain (*himagiri*) located to the south of the central Maru mountain. This is what is called the land of Bharata.

Adorned with the *kadamba* trees that were its primary ornaments, and possessing the decoration of the *kadamba* forest, it was the hermitage known as Āmardaka—[the place where] Āmardaka... Thus, by this assigned name, it became a penance grove (*tapovana*). By the word "and" (*ca*), another monastery not explicitly mentioned is indicated; first, the site of the Āmardaka monastery, a location established by Durvāsas, is named Āmardaka.
Because it is stated that [the lineage] was served by the venerable Durvāsas,

those such as Kauśika and Kāśyapa— who were residents of the Mardaka monastery under the leadership of Dūrvāsas— worshipped Śrīkaṇṭha in the form of Dakṣiṇāmūrti for the sake of the knowledge of the Āgamas;
having obtained the knowledge of the Āgamas from Śrīkaṇṭha, [they resided at] the Mardaka monastery.
The disciples who remained there became four, beginning with Sanatkumāra; from that Āmardaka Maṭha, three monasteries arose: Raṇabhadrī, Golakī, and Puṣpagiri.
For it is said that the place [originating] from there is Raṇa...la... as well as Puṣpagiri. The sages worship the form of Dakṣiṇāmūrti in the monasteries of Āmardaka and the others.
Agastya, Kauśika, Bhāradvāja, and Gautama—

[having learned] from the Supreme Lord the true meaning of the Āgamas, all those sages, with minds full of joy, as well as their disciples beginning with Sananta, attended upon them. Having obtained the meaning of the Āgamas, they [established themselves] through the office of *māṭhāpati*...

(…) they are established. The sage Sanatkumāra is the lord of the Āmardaka monastery; his lineage tree is the Kadamba tree, and those who belong to his lineage are some who [reside at] Puṣpagiri. The sage Sanaka is the lord of that monastery; his tree is the Arjuna tree, and those who belong to his lineage are some (l4).
The seer Sanātana is the leader of the Lakima monastery; his tree is the Jambuka tree, and his progeny are declared to be the lords of Raṇabhadra. Sanantana is [also] mentioned as the lord.
He is remembered as the Nyagrodha tree, and those who belong to his lineage dwell on the banks of the Godāvarī river.

That auspicious abode of the Śaivas is at Puramandhara on the Kālindī, where Śaṅkara resides. He was born specifically for the sake of the Śaiva teachers; there, surrounding the Lord Mandhara-Kālīśa, are the Cārumaṭhas.

Āmardakī, Puṣpagiri, Golaki, Karamabhadrakī, and Kauśika. [Objection: But how can Kauśika be a creation of Śiva, since he is well-known in the world as a creation of Brahmā? [Response: True. First, those such as Kauśika and Kāśyapa were born as creations of Śiva;
others, such as the Kāśikas and Kāśyapas, were born as creations of Brahmā; yet there are others who, by the same name, are identical to the Kauśikas and Kāśyapas.

They become twofold through the division of the creation of Śiva and Brahmā. Here, there is no fault [in the classification], as those such as Kāśyapa and others belong to the Śaiva tradition by virtue of being part of Śiva’s creation.
Likewise, in the *Kāmika* [Tantra], in the determination of lineages (*gotranirṇaya*), it is said: "Kauśika, Kāśyapa, Bhāradvāja, Gautama, Vasiṣṭha, Agastya, and Jamadagni."

The Bhārgavas, the Āṅgirasas, and the Mānavas—these others are proclaimed to be of two kinds: those sages who are endowed with the emanation of Śiva, and those who are devoid of it. These [sages] who are possessed of the emanation of Śiva have been initiated into the five faces; such are the sages beginning with Kauśika, who are present everywhere.

Thus it is stated in that very same *Arcanāṅga-paṭala*: "But those who are born from the mouth of Brahmā without the creative emission (*sṛṣṭi*) of Śiva are common; they do not have the qualification for the higher purpose. (81)

And there, the assembly of sages, having performed their recitations (*japa*) in the great [sacred] place, became intent upon the pair of spheres (*gocara-yuga*), beginning with the *prājāpatya* [observance]. Then, through purity, self-restraint, and discipline at the beginning and end [of the sessions], he arose from the true sphere; [he was] the illustrious teacher Śambhu, the foremost of gurus.

The lineage is thus established. Having described the fourfold nature of the single Amardaka monastery, he explains the sequence of his own lineage preceded by knowledge of the arts (*kalā*). Regarding the phrase "therein" (*tatra*):

born into the tradition of the aforementioned Amardaka monastery, the succession of sages (*munipaṅkti*)—the assembly of ṛṣis beginning with Kaśyapa—was known as the *Paitāmaha*. Within that, Manu, whose name is *Svāyambhuva*, was born under the designation "Manu"; the meaning is that he was known as Manu.
The fourteenth Manu is the first primary being, Svāyambhuva Manu.

[Those] who abide by the designation of "Sages" (*ṛṣi*)—meaning they exist through the tradition of the sages of the Āmardaka monastery until the end of the period of Svāyambhuva Manu—and who are all likewise [endowed with] the splendor of Svāyambhuva... (l6–l7).

And he is remembered as Vaisvata; Sūrya, Dakṣa, Brahmā, Dharma, Rudra, Sāvarṇi, [and others]—these are declared to be the fourteen Manus, beginning with Rucya and Bhavya. Then, immediately after the completion of the period of Svāyambhuva Manu, during the period of [the next] Manu, those whose faces are Prajāpati-like are named Prājāpatya; they are devoted to their own tradition regarding the *gocara-yuga* (the age of the spheres). [This is] the tradition of the *gocarās*.

In the [expired] yuga of Bhra...śāna, there were well-known traditions such as the Āmardaka-maṭha and others, numbering [four], as stated in the tradition; they came into existence in the period following the Rociṣmat-kalpa. The meaning is that they became the fourfold traditions beginning with the Āmardaka in the four maṭhas. In the four maṭhas... (l. 3)

The Śaiva Brāhmaṇas are of four kinds, as it has been said: "There is the place named Sthānamātrardaka, frequented by the venerable Dūrvāsas; from that [place] emerged the places Raṇarudra, Golaki, and likewise Puṣpagiri—thus the place is of four kinds. Those Śaivas born from these places are also of four kinds: the student (brahmacārin), the householder (gṛhastha), the forest-dweller (vānaprastha)..."
The ascetic (*yati*), however, states his own lineage succession with the words "from Āditya" (*ādityāditya*) and so forth.

Among the fourfold traditions of the monasteries (*maṭhasāṃpradāya*), [he is] endowed with purity and restraint (*śaucasaṃyama*). Purity and restraint consist of bathing to remove the impurities of *brāhma-bhūta* and so forth; "restraint" (*saṃyama*) refers to the control of the senses. This term "restraint" (*saṃyama*) is also indicative of the other limbs of yoga, such as observances (*niyama*) and the rest.

Accompanied by these [lineages], beginning with the *sadgocara* and including the lineages of Kāśyapa, Pārāśarya, and others, from the original Āmardaka Maṭha, at the time of the commencement of the Kali Yuga, there arose— that is, was born— the Great Guru named Śrīmadhyāpakaśambhu, who bestows both worldly enjoyment (*bhukti*) and liberation (*mukti*). Thus, the lineage is endowed with the succession of Gurus born in former times, together with the aforementioned earlier Gurus.

The lineage has remained in this manner, having been born down to the time of his own birth. And it is said: In this regard, there is a connection with a previous narrative: A king of the Colas named Rājendra Cola, while residing on the earth, came for the purpose of bathing in the Gaṅgā; having seen the excellent Śiva [liṅga] at that time, he bathed.
Having returned, he took those excellent Śaiva teachers and established them throughout the entire Colabhūmi region, including the center of Kāñcī, as follows: ||82||
[Thus ends the Kriyāpāda in the Siddhāntasārāvalī.]

May there be auspiciousness! Salutations to the illustrious Kālahastīśvara together with the illustrious Jñānāmbā. Salutations to Vedādrinātha. Salutations to Marundīśvara. (The remainder is blank. (From p123b, l1:
...arising from below the navel, it is the abode of the sprouts; and in the midst of that, within the body, they remain situated above the enclosure of a thousand *dhvā* sounds.

Emerging from the Piṅgalā and Kālī [nāḍīs], it extends to the right and left [nostrils]... the essence, supported by the yoke, is situated below the heart at the *dvādaśānta*. Now, desiring to speak of the Yoga-pāda, its purpose being the origin of all the channels (*nāḍī*) beginning with the Suṣumnā, because they are the source of [all things], it is said: [Note: The ellipses indicate missing or illegible portions of the manuscript.]

Regarding the phrase "below the navel" (*nābhyadhas*): here, "below the navel" does not intend to refer only to the region immediately adjacent to the navel; rather, it intends to include the lower region even far removed from the navel. This is because it is made known that the *kanda* originates from the navel. Thus, it is stated that the *kanda* has arisen below the navel; otherwise, since the *kanda* arises in the region below the genitals (*meḍhra*), the term "below the navel" would be redundant.
The location of the *kanda* is nine finger-breadths from the middle of the human body, as it has been stated.
Likewise, it is said in the *Siddhāntaśekhara*: "Two finger-breadths above the anus and two finger-breadths below the penis, the middle [point] is one finger-breadth; that is the middle of the body."

They explain [it as follows]: nine finger-breadths above that, resembling the top of a bulbous root (*kanda*), it is four finger-breadths in width and equal to that in height. The bulbous root is touched by the thumb; its center is called the navel.
From that, the wheel has arisen, endowed with twelve spokes and possessed of a uniform life-force.

In this wheel, by means of one's own karma mounted upon the vital breath (*prāṇa*), that which was spun twice in the wheel is indeed spun; by this wheel, as it revolves, this body proceeds from its growth, surrounded by the *kuṇḍalinī*.

Therefore, the *kanda* is formed by the *kuṇḍalī*, consisting of the eightfold nature (*aṣṭaprakṛti*), having the form of a sleeping serpent. Having firmly placed its hood within the lower opening of the navel of the *kanda*, [it remains there].

"Then, having completely blocked the pathways of the vital winds, one should coil Sumukha at the tail [of the body] and, remaining behind, stay together with it at the *brahmarandhra*. In this text, regarding the phrase 'nine finger-breadths above from that,' the meaning is that the *kanda* resides nine finger-breadths above—that is, in the upper portion—from the center of the body. Regarding the phrase 'the navel is said to be in its center'..."

The meaning is that the *nābhi* (navel-center) exists within the *kanda* in the form of a cavity; it is the abode, the dwelling place, of the sprouts of the channels (*nāḍyaṅkura*), which are the sources of the arising of all channel-sprouts. Within that—meaning within the middle of the *kanda*—there is a hollow passage (*kuhara*). Thus it has been said: "Having pierced through the six lotuses arisen from the hollow of the root-basin (*mūlālavāla-kuhara*), like flashes of lightning, there are two thousand seven hundred channels (*nāḍī*). (3)

In all embodied beings, there are seventy-two thousand channels (*nāḍī*) extending from the *kanda* [the root-center] downwards, across, and upwards throughout the pervasive body— from the lower region of the body’s center to its upper region.
Regarding the word "nā" (*nāmi*): among these channels (*nāḍī*), thirty-two channels are primary. Among those, three channels—Suṣumnā, Piṅgalā, and Iḍā—are the most primary.

Because they are the most primary, [the text] describes the pervasion of the channels beginning with Suṣumnā: the Piṅgalā channel, having emerged from the *kanda*, is produced from the *kanda*; it has emerged from the *kanda* as something distinct and separate.

The *iḍā* channel emerges from the center of the *kanda* on the right side of the *suṣumnā*; the *piṅgalā* is situated on the right side, while the *iḍā* is situated on the left side, extending from the aperture [of the *kanda*] up to the *brahmabila*. And it is said in the treatises on the channels (*nāḍiśāstra*) regarding *māyā*:

"...on the left is *iḍā*, and on the right is *piṅgalā*. He explains how *iḍā* and *piṅgalā* are situated as far as the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*): "Externally, in the body, in the external region, [they are] visible... (p124b, l1) They rest upon the pair of apertures; that is, they rest upon the pair of cavities, the pair of apertures of the nose. While *piṅgalā* has entered the *suṣumnā* channel, *iḍā* reaches the end of the aperture along with the *nāḍī*.

"Separately" (pṛthak) means that it rests upon the *suṣumnā* channel. [The phrase] "from the end of the twelve" (*dvādaśāntāt*) means from the tip of the crest of space; "situated in the lower part" means that having left the end of the twelve, it is situated together with the *suṣumnā* as far as the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*). ||118||
From the pair of thumbs and the lotus of the heart, [the channels] go upward in two ways and as one in the middle; supported by the row [of petals], they reach as far as the *dvādaśānta*.
The bulb (*kanda*) is joined with a lotus having four petals and veins; the navel has six petals;

the throat is endowed with a heart-lotus of eight petals and sixteen petals; the palate is a lotus of twenty-four petals; the earth is a lotus of four petals; and the head is a lotus of nine apertures.

Above the nine-petaled lotus is the thousand-petaled one, joined with the filaments of power (*śakti*) and provided with a pericarp by means of the Equal One (*samanā*). Above that are the orbs of the Sun, Moon, and Fire; pervading them at the end of the Transmental (*unmanā*) is Śiva. This occurs through the pervasion of the Suṣumṇā first.

He describes, in sequence, the nature of the lotus that serves as the seat of Paraśiva, starting from the *mūlādhāra* up to the *dvādaśānta*, according to the number of petals situated therein: "At the big toe" (*padāṅguṣṭhe*) means from the pair of big toes—that is, from the two big toes of the right and left feet; "the region of the bladder" (*vastisthānam*) refers to the location situated there, which is called the *vastisthāna*. From that point, [the sequence continues].
Extending as far as the stationary lotus, it is twice as bright and beautiful in the middle;

starting from the location of the *kanda* held in the center of the body, it extends upward to the end of the *brahmabila*. It is single-fold and uniform in form, a channel (*nāḍikā*) supported by a row, and from its support as a row, it has the form to be described later in the [sections on] the directions, etc. (p. 125a, l. 1).

The wheels (*cakras*) beginning from the support (*ādhāra*) situated in the *sukhyā* [channel] up to the end of the ten [channels]—namely, the *ādhāra*, *svādhiṣṭhāna*, *maṇipūra*, *anāhata*, *viśuddhi*, and ending with the one called *jñāna*—are exactly four above that. The channel named *suṣumṇā*, which exists pervading the ten *sadyas* [channels], extends as far as the end of the twelve channels; it has gone upward, reaching the limit of the "end of the twelve" (*dvādaśānta*).
Up to the *brahmarandhra* it has a form with parts (*sakalarūpā*); above that, up to the limit of the *dvādaśānta*, it has a partless form (*niṣkalarūpā*).

The meaning is that the *suṣumnā*, which is called the "Brahma-channel" (*brahmanāḍī*) by those learned in all the scriptures, resides as far as the *dvādaśānta*. "Bladder" (*vasti*) means the location below the *kanda*, that is, the foundation (*ādhāra*).
It is endowed with a lotus whose petals are the "Veda-vessels" (*vedasirā*). By the "Veda-vessel" (*vedasirā*)... [line 4]

The lotus with four petals is joined with the Vedas; the *vasti* (bladder) is accompanied by a lotus with four petals; the *kanda* (bulb) is joined with six petals; above that is the navel, from which ten petals emerge at the tip; the heart is endowed with eight petals;
the throat is joined with sixteen petals, possessing the digits (*kalā*); the palate is a lotus with twenty-four petals, for the Vedas are twenty-four.

The meaning is that there are twenty-four, being four times five. The palate-position is said to be accompanied by a lotus joined with petals of this number. Here, by the word *bhṛṅga* (bee), the middle of the eyebrows is meant. It is accompanied by four petals, [the number] of the Vedas.

The "aperture-lotus" (*randhrābja*) is the lotus situated at the *brahmarandhra*, possessing sixteen petals; it is the supreme *ka*, the head [of the alphabet]. Above that, existing further upward, is the "nine-petaled lotus," a lotus endowed with nine-fold leaves. Above that, at the "twelve-finger limit" (*dvādaśānta*), there exists a lotus accompanied by its filaments, numbering one thousand petals. He describes the nature of that lotus: "with the filaments of power" (*śaktisukesara*).

(.... joined with and accompanied by the filaments (*kiñjalka*) which are the nature of the letters beginning with *mā* and *dina*, together with *samanā*; (p125b, l1) (.... together with the pericarp (*karṇikā*) endowed with the fifty seed-syllables; on the resonance (*svarasi*) of the Sun (*rave*) and the Moon (*somaryo*), situated in the orb (*bimba*); accompanied by its own lord (*svādhipa*) and joined with the mandala; above that, the three mandalas (........................). (l2)

(................ It is supreme, upward-facing, all-pervading, and omnipresent. At the end of Unmanā, at the end of the power of Unmanīśa, or within Unmanī itself, there exists the Śaktimaṇḍala; there resides Śiva, the Supreme Śiva. ||3||
In a seat such as a silk cloth placed within a house surrounded by a circular pit,

the twice-born [practitioner], having first performed the *svastha-prāṇa-japa*, should cause [the breath] to flow through the throat and thighs; for the sake of purification, he should gradually fill the abdomen from the left with the lunar external air through the channels, while the solar [air] is measured by *tālas*.

Having performed *kumbhaka* in sequence, one should exhale this [air] by the power of *śakti* through the *piṅgalā* and *arka* channels; thus, being "without the embryo" (*nirgarbha*), one constantly performs the recitation (*japa*). Furthermore, through meditation joined with recitation while being "with the embryo" (*sagarbha*), he destroys all sin that must be purified. Again, at dawn and evening, standing in the day, he performs the direct realization of the principles (*tattva*) and so forth.

He describes the purification of the channels (*nāḍiśuddhi*), which is the cause for the practice of yoga, by means of fire: (l6) "In a *kuṇḍa*... [referring to] a house that has been wrapped in a single, double, or triple layer according to the requirements of the doubt, situated in the middle of the wrapped area, with two equal eyes wrapped in the middle. (l7)

Having prepared a place, covered with a cloth, a rug, a deerskin, or similar materials, one should sit comfortably and at ease upon a seat or pedestal arranged according to one's own preference. As it has been said: "One who eats wholesome and digested food, who is healthy, and who dwells in a house free from disturbances or in a forest and such places, should remain seated on his own seat facing north. Thus, he remains seated upon a prepared pedestal or seat, whether it be rectangular or circular in shape.

Here, by the word "posture" (*āsana*), the [ten] postures such as the lotus (*padma*), the swastika (*svastika*), and so forth, which have been practiced and mastered, are meant. And it is said in the *Siddhāntaśekhara*: "The lotus, the cow's mouth (*gomukha*), the swastika, the auspicious (*bhadra*), the peacock (*mayūra*), the cock (*kukkuṭa*), the hero's (*vīra*) throne, the lion's throne (*siṃhāsana*), the tortoise (*kūrma*), and the half-seat (*ardhapīṭha*); these are the ten in sequence. (Siddhāntaśekhara, l. 2)

It should be understood that this has been stated in the *Lakṣa* [Tantra] itself. "The twice-born (*dvija*) whose body is preceded by the syllable *pra*," meaning one who at dawn stands with his body erect in a straight posture;

here, by the word "twice-born" (*dvija*), one who is initiated (*dīkṣā-yukta*) and free from laziness and other such defects is meant. And it is said: "One who is liberated from laziness and the like, devoted to the Guru and the deities, and devoid of longing for all objects, [attains] the supreme..."

One who is endowed with qualities such as "relying on dispassion" (*vairāgyamāśritaḥ*) and so forth is praised for the purification of the channels (*nāḍīśuddhi*). Thus, the subject matter concerns the initial commencement at an auspicious moment (*lagne sumuhūrte*); or rather, one who is joined with the restraint of the mind (*amana*) and the body (*yama*) should exhale—that is, perform *recaka*.
And it has been said: "The rising of the breath... (*udayaḥ samīrasya*).

The *devakas* are the exhalations (*recakas*) from the outside; the restraint (*saṃyama*) of the filling of the air is through inhalation (*pūraka*). One should properly exhale the air from the belly slowly through the *piṅgalā*.

The retention (*kumbhaka*) of the air filled within the belly is known as such because of its holding. Thus, for the sake of the purification of the channels (*nāḍī*)—which is for the purpose of [attaining] mastery over the signs of the channels—one should, very gradually and slowly, [fill] the belly, the stomach, or the abdomen... on the left.

She should fill [the breath], that is, she should perform the filling; and it is said: "Then one should properly fill the external air through the *iḍā*. Thus, with the external wind of the side associated with the moon—the left side—[she fills] the external air situated outside by means of twelve *mihira*s. Since "Mihira," "Aruṇa," and "Pūṣan" are stated to be synonyms for the Sun (*sūrya*), [this is done] by means of twelve *tāla*s, that is, twelve measures (*mātrā*).

The definition of *mātrā* is twofold, according to the distinction of rotating the kneecap once or three times. Thus it is said in the *Siddhāntaśekhara*: "Having struck the ground three times with the kneecaps, one should perform the *kaniṣṭhā-mātrā* with a state of indifference."
Regarding the measurement of time, they say it is otherwise [than previously described]:

one should perform a single circumambulation of the knee and a single snap of the fingers; this is called a *mātrā*, and this is the measure of time. Here, because of the plural form "with *tālas*," the little finger (*kaniṣṭhā*) and the others are included, [referring to] twelve *tālas*.

The lowest [practice] consists of twenty [repetitions], the middling forty-eight, and the best is twice that. As it is stated in the Sarvajñānottara: "The *tāla* should be known as twelve; the lowest *prāṇāyāma* is [that many], the middling is twenty-four, and the best is double that."

Thinking "it shall be so," one who has filled the air [performs] *kumbhaka* in sequence; from that filling, O Omniscient One, having performed the nature of abandonment (*tyāga*) by the power of *śakti* according to one's capacity, through the grasping of time starting from the little finger (*kaniṣṭhā*), and by means of the flow through the *piṅgalā* channel—the path of the Sun—one emits that *kumbhaka*, performing the emission (*virecana*). The person should emit the air held in *kumbhaka*.
It has been stated by Budha that [the practice] with Piṅgalā is slow (*śanaiḥ*).
Thus, the meditation (*dhyāna*) on the *nirbhrama-mantra*—[wherein] breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) without a seed-syllable (*nirgarbha*) is so called—is as follows.

Likewise, in the *Siddhāntaśekhara*: "The *agarbha* and the *sagarbha*: indeed, that which is devoid of a mantra is *agarbhaka*; that which is joined with a mantra is *sagarbha*. And the mantras [beginning with] *praṇava*... [and so forth].

"The palace, the chanting swans, the Gāyatrī, and those headed by the Vyāhṛtis"—this was said regarding the command of the senses of the gods (*devānām indriyāṇām*). And it is further stated: "Even the embryo of the gods kills as they rush toward power. Here, "of the gods" (*devānām*) refers to [the senses] accompanied by the mind (*manas*).

The meaning is "of the three. From meditation (*dhyāna*), which consists of the recitation of mantras (*japa*) accompanied by the contemplation of Śiva, the well-known *sagarbha-prāṇāyāma* destroys—that is, annihilates—all sin committed during the night (*niśā*). This is because it has been stated that "sin committed at night [is destroyed] at the end of the day, whereas that committed during the day [is destroyed] at the end of the day. Furthermore, one should practice yoga repeatedly throughout the day until the attainment of perfection in yoga.

For a person practicing this yoga— performed during the morning, evening, and midday periods— this practice of yoga brings about the direct realization of reality and so forth; that is, it effects the direct perception of the true nature of each element, such as earth and the others.

The meaning is that for a person practicing yoga, [the practice] manifests the qualities such as fragrance and solidity residing in the earth and other elements within the body. Through the direct realization of earth, he becomes free from desire for external fragrance;
through the direct realization of fire, he perceives divine form and there is no longer the heat of fire; through the direct realization of air, he perceives the touch of a lamp.

The eightfold group of qualities beginning with *aṇimā* is accomplished; through the direct realization of the sky, one becomes possessed of divine knowledge and the power of moving through the celestial ether—such are the qualities that arise from the practice of yoga. ||5||
From the lotus-stamen of the water of Umā in the heart, [he perceives] the lunar orb, the fire, and the upward-pointing Śakti; joined with breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*), [there is] a stalk...

shining like a thread, a light that has entered therein; and beyond that, he sees his own [Self] situated at the *dvādaśānta*, and his own water, which has a similar radiance, as the Supreme Śiva through consciousness. Thus, day by day, he remains engaged in the practice of yoga... (Note: The ellipses indicate portions of the original text that were either illegible or omitted in the provided fragment.)
He says that the yogi perceives Paraśiva, who resides in his own *dvādaśānta*, through direct perception. "In the space of the heart" (*hṛdyoma*): Yoga is indeed union with Śiva;

it is connected to the first moment of oneness. A yogi endowed with such yoga, being joined with the union of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and the Self (*ātman*)—according as it occurs through the combined practices of inhalation (*pūraka*), retention (*kumbhaka*), and exhalation (*recaka*)—perceives within the lotus-heart the orb of the moon situated upon the sun-disk at its pericarp.

The flour [is] the upward-moving [light]; it is the sun, situated upon the pericarp of the lotus of the heart’s hollow—the lotus of the sky of the heart—and the moon. It is the light whose nature is luminosity existing above the two discs or orbs of those two, having the form of splendor, the supreme light situated within the heart-lotus, because it is described as "the supreme and the non-supreme" (*parāpara*). That...

With his mind gone [to Śiva], having attained direct perception of Śiva in the form of light residing within the heart-lotus, he does not go elsewhere; rather, by means of the consciousness of *cit*, he perceives through direct vision Paraśiva—who exists at his own *dvādaśānta* above the heart-lotus, who possesses a clear luster, whose radiance is similar [to that of the former], and whose beauty is like pure water. The meaning is that he becomes one who has seen [Śiva] directly. ||6||

In the heart-lotus at dawn, one should contemplate the form born of Supreme Śiva, resembling a mass of rising suns in the central channel; at midday, in the lotus of the clouds, the form of consciousness shining like the moon; in the evening, in the upper lotus, the resonance arising from itself which illuminates the ocean of nectar;
and at midnight, that which is to be known as the object of cognition, the meaning free from conceptual construction.

That great [reality] is at the *dvādaśānta*. He describes the sequence of remembering Śiva by means of the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) such as morning time and so forth. Regarding the word "in the heart" (*hṛdi*): in the lotus of the heart, at morning—that is, at the time of dawn prior to sunrise, up until the end of the first *nāḍikā*—[one should meditate on] that which resembles the rising of the sun, possessing a radiance equal to the mass of the rising sun, meaning it has many reddish colors, within the central channel (*madhyanāḍī*).
Having meditated upon [the deity] within the *suṣumnā*, one should contemplate...

at midday, in the lotus of the eyebrows (*bhrū-saroja*), the nature of the Supreme Śiva born from Paramaśiva. By this, the instrumental cause of the universe is described as being of the nature of consciousness (*cid-rūpa*), and its essence consists of knowledge and action (*jñāna-kriyā*). Its manifestation... [is revealed].

Having meditated upon [the deity] shining like the moon in the upper lotus situated at the *brahmarandhra* in the evening—shining like the ocean of nectar, radiant like the distant sea—the nature of the *nāda* arising from one's own *mūlādhāra* is expressed by this; thus, the nature of the *prāsāda-mantra* together with the boat (*aukāra*) is stated. At the half of the night, at midnight, it is immeasurable.
The mind is capable of knowing [the Self] through the intellect and other faculties;

it is complete, absolute, partless, and immovable—meaning devoid of movement. By this, it is stated that [the Self] is free from the exertion, authority, and activity of the powers of vision and action, for those [powers] have their functions withdrawn. Such is that [Self], which is attained at the "End of the Twelve."
One should contemplate the perfected Great One, whose form is radiant splendor. ||7||

The knowledge of one's own objects by means of the external and internal organs is the waking state (*jāgrat*); that knowledge whose object is the activity residing within the internal organ is the dream state (*svapna*); deep sleep (*suṣupti*) is [the state] beyond. However, when the body is devoid of the activity of the senses, it is the inexpressible fourth state (*turya*). When the agitation of the body ceases, one attains the consciousness of one's own Self, which transcends [all states]; this is the arising of Śiva-nature. Hereafter, [the states of] waking and so forth pertain to the impure self.

He states the sequence of the five stages: "External," etc. For the *aṇu* (the individual soul), which is a self possessed of impurity, there is here [the process] by means of the external and internal organs—the external organs being the eyes, ears, and so forth, and the internal organs being the mind (*manas*), intellect (*buddhi*), and ego (*ahaṅkāra*). Here, first, the self, together with the internal organs, [attains] knowledge of its own objects; subsequently, together with the external organs, it attains knowledge of the objects of its own [senses], such as the eyes and so forth.
The cognition of perceived objects such as form (*rūpa*) and so forth is well-known as the waking state (*jāgrat*), for one who abides in the waking condition. (p128b, l1) ...

The cognition of objects occurring within the mind (*manas*), intellect (*buddhi*), and ego (*ahaṅkāra*) is the dream state (*svapna*). Beyond the dream state, that which is distinct from the internal organs (*antaḥkaraṇa*) is deep sleep (*suṣupti*), the state of slumber within the body. (l2)

Devoid of the functions of the body and senses, distinct from the operation of the eyes and other organs, and beyond speech—that is, free from the state of verbal expression—the "intellect" (*mati*) intended here by the word *mati* is the consciousness capable of grasping what is to be grasped; it refers to the Self endowed with *prāṇa*. Moving in the fourth state (*turyaga*), when the agitation of the senses, mind, and so forth existing in the body has subsided—that is, when their movement and such have dissolved—this is one's own true consciousness.

The meaning is that self-knowledge alone, conjoined with the vital breath (*prāṇa*), constitutes the state of the Self (*ātman*). That which has passed refers to the state beyond the fourth state (*turyātītāvasthā*). Thus, there are five states for the impure Self; now, for the pure Self, there is the emergence of Śiva-nature, which is the attainment of the essential nature of Śiva.

Thus, in the *Cintyāgama*, the characteristic of impurity (*mala*) is stated: "The waking state is to be known as being in the mouth; the dream state is within the heart; beginning from the heart and extending to the navel, the state of deep sleep (*suṣuptika*) resides in the channels (*suṣi*); its [corresponding] meaning is the fourth state (*turya*), while that which transcends the fourth (*turyātīta*) resides in the *liṅga*. This refers to the waking state and so forth."

Thus, the locus is indeed said here to be the initiator. The fivefold [set] consists of the ear, skin, eye, tongue, and the nose; and sound, touch, form, taste, and smell as the fifth. The [five] organs of action are speech, hands, feet, the anus, and the generative organ as the fifth; their functions are speaking, grasping, moving, excretion, and sexual pleasure as the fifth. Furthermore, there are the vital breaths: prāṇa, apāna, vyāna, udāna, and samāna.

Nāga, Kūrma, Cakraka, Devadatta, and Dhanañjaya; (l8) mind, intellect, ego, consciousness, and the Knower of the Field—these five, along with the supreme [Self], are designated as the waking state. Sound and the other [objects], speech and the other [actions], the vital breaths and so forth, the mind and so forth—here, by the term "vital breaths" and so on, [are meant] Nāga and the others... (p129a, l1)

Because tools for cultivation such as hammers and the like are seen in dreams due to their existence [in that state], these indeed move within the remainder of the dream; one should conquer them. In the waking state there is the enjoyment of objects, and likewise supreme well-being. ... the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and the mind (*manas*), as well as the Knower of the Field (*kṣetrajña*), exist in deep sleep (*suṣupti*). The Self (*ātman*) is the vital breath in the fourth state (*turya*), while in the state beyond the fourth (*turyātīta*), it is emission (*visarga*). Here, by the term "the arising of Śiva-nature" (*śivatvodaya*):
The five states, beginning with waking, are said to belong to the stainless self (*nirmalātman*).

Likewise, it was stated by the divine teacher Īśāna: "The utterance of the seed-syllable (*bīja*) is the waking state; the grasping of the point (*bindu*) is dreaming; the conjunction with the resonance (*nāda*) is deep sleep; and the union with power (*śakti*) is the fourth state."
Thus, one should recite that which is past, dissolved, and tranquil within the Great Splendor (*mahasi*).
Thus it is recited. [Thus ends the Yoga-pāda in the Siddhāntasārāvalī.]
Having placed ten self-mantras facing westward as pure Śivas, and having likewise bent his knee beyond them,
that Lord Śiva himself directly taught the Śaiva scriptures from the end of the Śaiva [tradition].
Having awakened the eighteen Rudras, other Āgamas were spoken by them.

Now, desiring to explain the Caryāpāda, [the author] first states the rule for the nomenclature of the divisions of Śiva and the divisions of Rudra among the Kāmika and other Āgamas: "Ātman" refers to the knowledge of the Supreme Lord, which is of two kinds and consists of the nature of awakening.

Regarding the phrase "and the form of sound" (*śabdarūpaṃ ca*): therein, within Paramaśiva, exists the form of sound which is free from beginningless impurity, without beginning or end, the illuminator of all objects, the benefactor of all, auspicious (*śiva*), consisting of the knowledge of Śiva, and having the nature of pure consciousness (*avabodharūpa*). As for this form of sound, however, it is precisely the scripture (*śāstrarūpam eva*); the Supreme Lord, out of supreme compassion, at the time of creation, having made that very form of consciousness existing within His own self into the form of sound, [revealed it].
Having protected all [beings] with supreme devotion to the Guru,

he sets them in motion toward those who are worthy; and herein, the descent of the scripture (*śāstrāvatāra*)— characterized by the sequence of the great flood and characterized by the sequence of the Guru’s compendium— is of two kinds, possessing the supreme and subordinate prowess of the Guru.

In this context, having created from the upward emanation (*ūrdhvasṛṣṭi*) the ten-fold [principles] beginning with the *praṇava*— which are pure and devoid of anything else, endowed with manifested qualities such as omniscience for the sake of their function, and which are therefore auspicious (*śiva*), identical in nature to Śiva, and situated in the state of Sadāśiva— the Guru, through mere remembrance, [established] these [mantras] beginning with the *praṇava*.

Thus it is established that there is abiding in the state of Sadāśiva; so it is stated in the venerable *Svatantra*: "The Lord is complete through the sequence beginning with Oṃ. By "beginning with Oṃ" is meant beginning with the *praṇava*; [this refers] to those whose self-knowledge consists of the ten starting with the *praṇava*, who are intent upon awakening the Lord of Mantras.

The "awakening" (*prabodha*) of the lords of mantras (*mantrapatīnām*), namely the eight Vidyeśvaras beginning with Ananta, is the instruction of the knowledge derived from the *Āgama*. That very [instruction] is again "excellent" (*utkṛṣṭa*), meaning it is primordial (*paurvaka*). Therefore, after that awakening by the Vidyeśvara, the instruction of the *praṇava* and so forth was given; this is the meaning. Furthermore, the knowledge of Śiva, whose nature is knowledge and bliss (*jñānānanda-rūpa*), is liberated and whose form is unseen (*adṛṣṭa-vigraha*).
From the peaceful Śiva,

the supreme cause, the scripture— which is extremely difficult to obtain— emerged in the form of *nāda*. Having thus divided it into ten parts, that which was spoken in the *Svāyambhuva* [Tantra] concerns the bondage of karma known as *māyā*.

For the sake of liberation and for the manifestation of the state of Śiva-ness, the knowledge of Śiva proceeds. This single knowledge of Śiva is again divided in many ways—into ten, eighteen, and further into ten internal divisions.
Thus, the Lord Śiva, the Supreme Śiva who shines everywhere, taught this instruction directly through perception, having composed it in ten distinct parts beginning with the *Kāmika*.
Therefore, because the speakers and listeners possess the nature of Śiva, the ten Āgamas beginning with the *Kāmika* are established under the designation of "Śaiva.
Likewise, it is stated in the *Kiraṇatantra*: "Immediately after [the act of] emission, having remembered the tenfold [Āgamas], they arise as soon as they are known..."

Speak of the number: [the power] born of yoga belongs to the one named Praṇava and the one well-known as Suśiva; that which is called Dīpta is to be meditated upon, while the cause belongs to the one named Kāraṇa. Ajita belongs to the one named Suśiva, and [the power] belonging to the one named Samāraṃśa is... (l3) Dīptaka is subtle, but for the one known as Sūkṣma it is the thousandfold [power] of Time; Sughranta belongs to Gaṇeśa, and Aṃśumān belongs to the one named Aṃśu. Thus is the Prādhānika [system].

Furthermore, the sequence of the *yojagu* (or *nyojagu*) has been declared; it should be understood from the passage beginning with "the time of the *praṇava-ārtika* has arrived" and "Kāmika is obtained from the three times, O Hara," and so forth. [It concerns] the eighteen Rudras—those numbering eighteen—and the names of the Rudras beginning with Ananta.

Having awakened those endowed with knowledge and having favored only those established in the reality of the Lord, Śiva himself— having made that single non-awakened knowledge into the form of sound according to their respective capacities and having spoken it through the divisions of ritual action and so forth— taught other Āgamas by means of those Rudras, who were the venerable Śivabhaṭṭārikās, by way of establishing them as the essence of the sense of hearing.

The eighteen [tantras] beginning with Vijñāna, which are established under the designation of Rudra, are mentioned here because they are not included among the others; thus it is indicated that the states of being higher and lower are assigned respectively to the divisions of Śiva and the divisions of Rudra.
Likewise, in the Kiraṇa [Tantra]: (l8)

Furthermore, another supreme division of Rudras is considered to be by the number eighteen. O Bird, having first produced the Rudras by the number eighteen, the wise Śiva should then awaken them here by that same number. By him was spoken the *Vijaya*, the great tantra of the Supreme Lord; and the *Niśvāsa*, which is the glorious form of the Lord, was proclaimed.
That which was proclaimed by Daśārṇa beginning with "O Śūlin" (l. 2) is to be understood as follows:

there are three listeners for each of the Śiva-bodha scriptures such as the Kāmika; there are two listeners for each of the Rudra-bheda scriptures such as the Vijaya; and by combining both, they number sixty-six. (l. 3)
Since it has been stated that "the listeners [received it] in sequence from the sixty-six [sages] by the command of Śiva," their names are to be found in the root scriptures (mūlāgama). ||1||

But those who are connected [with the scriptures] know that there are six Śaiva Āgamas: (1) the *Raurava*, (2) the *Nātha* (Kāmika), (3) the *Śiva* (Yogaja), (4) the *Ānanta* (Vaimala), (5) the *Saumya* (Pārameśvara), and (6) the *Moma* (Lākula). Among these, the divine one is known as being situated within the interval between the gods; it has come down among the sages (*muni*). Although the divine one has gone to the gods, it is said to have come from the lord of sages (*munīndra*) to man (*nara*), and even though it has reached the disciples (*śiṣya*), it is not divine. Thus they know the six Śaiva Āgamas. Of the Śaiva Āgamas...

He states that there are six types [of connections] considered according to the distinction between speaker and listener. Regarding "the connection" (*saṃbandha*): it is the connection between *Aṇunātha* and *Śiva*. *Aṇunātha* is the Lord (*nātha*) numbering seventy million;
*ananteśvara-śiva* is Sadāśiva.

The Bhaṭṭāraka states that the first relationship, known as *subandha*, is the successive connection of the scriptures (*āgamas*) through the distinction between the listener and the speaker; here, Īśvara is called by the name Ananta, and Śrīkaṇṭha is called by the word Soma.
Ananteśvara is the speaker and Śrīkaṇṭha is the listener; the relationship between these two, known by the name *mahān*, is stated to be the second relationship. Thus it has been said:
In the venerable *Raurava*, it is stated that the Lord is the cause of the universe...

[to] the Guru... by him it was told... by the Lord of Uma (*Umāpati*) to the high-souled Śrīkaṇṭha. From Soma, from Śrīkaṇṭha, it went to the gods; it went to the gods beginning with Indra. It is known by the name "Intermediate" (*antarāla*). It is said... [line 2].
The fourth connection is that which has come from Indra and the other gods among the sages, and is accompanied by the name "Divya" (the Divine).

Because it has reached the sages who are the hearers from the gods who are the speakers, it is called "Divya. From the sages, it is "Adivya" (Non-divine); because it has reached the best of men who are the hearers from the sages who are the speakers, it is called "Divya. For this very reason...

From the Lord of Munis, the divine seer, [the lineage] was not [transmitted] to a human seer; thus the fifth [type of transmission] is proclaimed. From that seer, it reached his own disciple, who attained the connection as a non-divine [disciple]; thus the sixth [type] is declared. In this manner, [the transmission of] the Śaiva Āgamas...

The wise know that the various types [of scriptures], such as the Kāmika and others, have been spoken by the former teachers; the implied meaning is that they were uttered through the investigation of the meaning of the scriptures. Now, an objection may arise:

"In the Kāmika and other Tantras, it is heard that Praṇava and others are the listeners (śrotāraḥ). How then is the relationship between Śiva and Ananta established? The resolution to this doubt is found here in this work, because [Ananta] is contained within the womb of that [Śiva].
The connection characterized by the *āmalaka* has been explained;

in this very same way, the connection characterized by the sequence of the lineage of teachers (*gurukrama*) should be joined together. Following the awakening of Ananteśvara, because [the sequence] beginning with the *praṇava* is the means of attainment (*sādhanatvāt*), for that very reason the connection is twofold: the connection beginning with Ananteśvara and the connection beginning with the *praṇava*. This is the supreme connection between Śiva and the *praṇava*.

The relationship between the *praṇava* and the three times is "great" (*mahān*); between the three times and Hara it is "intermediate" (*antarāla*); between Hara and the god [Śiva] it is "divine" (*divya*); between the god and the sages it is "divine-and-non-divine" (*divyādivya*); and between the sages and humans it is "non-divine" (*adivya*). Thus, the relationship is sixfold; in this manner, they are to be inferred according to the distinctions of Śiva, Rudra, and so forth.

Through differentiation, the connection between the two supreme [beings] is indeed fivefold: the *para* [connection] between Śiva and Anādirudra; the *mahat* [connection] between Anādirudra and Parameśa; the *divya* [connection] between Parameśa and Deva; the *divyādivya* [connection] between Deva and Ṛṣi;
and the *adivya* [connection] between Ṛṣi and Manuṣya. Thus, because the tradition is seen to be uninterrupted down to Parameśvara, the authority of the scripture composed by Paraśiva is established.
Success!
Likewise, in the Mataṅga [Tantra] it is said:
"The single Praṇava... is the truth spoken by Īśvara. Now, some claim that because the scripture is eternal, it lacks authority; that is incorrect.
That very [nature] which is eternal is of the nature of awakening itself;

because it is established as being rooted in sound and so forth, the impermanence of the produced is proven, like the composition of a newly fashioned poetic work (*vākya*). However, the view held by some—that scripture (*āgama*) lacks the quality of being produced—is also incorrect.

The fact that the nature of consciousness is produced by being rooted in sound is perceived through direct perception; for those who deny direct perception, it would follow that they are [like] Īśvara, and because their cognition is false, it is therefore well known that the words of the scriptures composed by the Supreme [Being] possess authority alone. ||2||

The Śaivas [possess] the *Kāmika*, *Yogaja*, *Jīta*, and then the final one called *Dīpta*; the *Sūkṣma*, *Kāraṇa*, *Āśu*... and the *Sāhasraka*—these ten are the *Suprabhu* and *Audra*. Then there are the *Vijaya*, *Raurava*, *Niśvāsa*, *Āgneyaka*, *Saṃtāna*, the one named *Kiraṇa*, the *Siddha-vimala*, the venerable *Candrabhāsa*, *Para*... (p132a, l1) ...the *Calita-dvamākaṭa*, and then the venerable *Nārasaṃhama*.

Likewise, the auspicious lineages of the *Bimba* [tradition], beginning with the venerable *Svāyambhuva* and *Pārameśvara*, have been directly declared by him in that region from above, numbering ten. For he alone is truly the one who has attained all speech and possesses full knowledge. Through the contemplation of Śiva, there are ten divisions of Śiva in the center and in the east; as for the others...
Regarding the "ten divisions of the Rudras," [the author] states in pairs [which of] the twenty-eight tantras [belong to which group].

He says, "The Śaivas": although the author has stated that [the sequence is] *Kāmika*, *Yogaja*, *Ajitam*, and then *Cintyam*, nevertheless, in this work, the sequential order of the scriptures (*āgama*) according to their chronological succession is to be understood by way of their internal connection (*anvaya*). [This is] the meter... (l4)

Because they are stated in accordance with their respective divisions, the Śiva-bhedas are proclaimed as tenfold in number: the *Kāmika*, the *Yogaja*, the *Kāmika* [again], the *Yogaja*, the *Kāraṇa*, the *Ajita*, the *Dīpta*, the *Sūkṣma*, the *Sāhasra*, and the *Aṃśumān*; and the *Suprabheda*. Likewise, there are the *Vijaya*, the *Niśvāsa*, the *Svāyambhuva*, and the *Āgneyaka*.
The *Analatantra* is called by the name *Bhadrāhvaya*, while the *Vīratantra* is so designated.
Likewise, in the *Mṛgendra*, the *Svāyambhuva*, the *Āgneya*, the *Vīrabhadra*, the *Saurava*, the *Mākaṭa*, the *Vimala*, and the *Candrabhāsa* are said to be the *Candrajñāna*.

That which is joined with the face is called the *mukhabimba*; "udgīta" means "prodgīta"; "lalita" means "siddha"; "santāna" means "nārasiṃha," because it was spoken by Nṛsiṃha to Soma-deva; and it is called "śārvokta" because it was spoken by Śarva.
Likewise, in the *Kāmika*, it is stated that Somadeva attained the status of Narasiṃha through a number of two hundred thousand [verses] spoken by Śarva;
thus, there is a fivefold division from Soma. It is said that the *Parameśvara* is the *Kiraṇa*, and the *Parama* is the *Vātula*.
This is because the other [division], the *Aparahita*, is said to belong to the twelve divisions of the *Vātula*.

They are well known by the number eighteen through the mention of [the names] by their initial parts; they are called the divisions of Rudra (*raudraka*). (l2) Likewise, among the *kāraṇa* [tantras]: the *Kāmika*, the *Yogaja*, and finally the *Kāraṇaka*; likewise the *Ajita*, the *Dīpta*, the *Sūkṣma*, the *Sāhasra*, and the *Aṃśumān*. The *Suprabhedaka*, the *Vijaya*, the *Niśvāsa*, the *Svāyambhuva*, then the *Anila*, and the *Vīra*. (l3)

Raurava, Makuta, Vimala, Candrajñāna, Bimba, Prodgīta, Lalita, Siddha, Santāna, Śarvokta, Pārameśvara, Kiraṇa, and Vātula—these are the twenty-eight compendia (*sahitās*). Among them, the first ten are declared to be designated as the *Śivabheda*, while the other ten tantras are remembered as the *Rudrabheda*. Thus it was spoken by that perfected one, Sadeśa Sadāśiva.

From the upward-facing mouth, that of Īśāna, the *Kāmika* and other [Tantras] were directly (*sākṣāt*) proclaimed to you. Now, one might ask: how is it established in the Root Scriptures (*mūlāgama*) that the twenty-eight Tantras, beginning with the *Kāmika*, originated from the mouth of Īśāna, given that they are said to have emerged from all five faces?

Likewise, [the scriptures] beginning with Kāmika and ending with Ajita arise from the mouth of Sadyojāta; those beginning with Dīpta and ending with Suprabheda arise from the mouth of Vāmadeva; and these five, starting from Vijaya and ending with Vīra, are known as the Ghoras, [beginning with] Raurava... (l7)

"(... those ending in *tvam* originate from the mouth called Puruṣa; the eight Tantras beginning with Prodgīta originate from the mouth of Īśāna. Thus, here each of the five faces beginning with Sadyojāta possesses five faces of its own (... because it is stated [in that way]. Therefore, it is said "from the upward-facing mouth" because [the mantra] originated from the faces beginning with Sadyojāta, which are connected to the face of Īśāna.

Likewise, in the *Kāmika*, the forms of Sadyojāta, Vāmadeva, Mahāghora, Puruṣa, and Īśāna—[which are] the five faces endowed with [the respective powers]—are joined with the worldly and so forth. The divisions of the stream are proclaimed to be twenty-five-fold: the worldly (*laukika*), the Vedic (*vaidika*), the spiritual (*adhyātmika*), the trans-marginal (*atimārga*), and that which is called Mantra. Regarding these, [it is said]: *...* (text fragment) *...the worldly, the Vedic, and likewise the spiritual, as well as the trans-marginal and that which is called Mantra.* (p133a, l2)

In the *Maneka-vātas* themselves, that which is called the *mantra-tantra* emerged from the mouth of Sadāśiva; specifically, the knowledge [known as] the *Kāmika* and other [Tantras] issued from the upper face, the *Īśāna* face. It is said to have "Śiva-Rudra as its manifestation" through its divisions of ten and eighteen. Because it was composed by Śiva, who is endowed with omniscience, he states in the passage beginning with "He indeed...
that the knowledge of the Āgamas alone possesses authority (*prāmāṇya*), for he—the well-known Sadāśiva—is the supreme *āpta*, meaning one who is most excellently authoritative.

Regarding the meaning of things as they truly are (*yathābhūta*), [the word] *para* is employed here for the purpose of indicating that this person is indeed a trustworthy teacher (*āpta*) to the person [who seeks knowledge], because he teaches that "this object is an object as it truly is" solely by virtue of his own self-knowledge—
just as [one perceives] with eyes.

Having ascertained that "this is the true reality" (*bhūtārtha*), because He is the primordial source, all [others] bound by beginningless impurity are called *paśu* (bound souls). This one, moreover, is called the Supreme Lord (*paramapati*). By the word "thus" (*evam*), it is indicated that this one is the supreme attainer (*parāpta*), whereas others are merely attainers (*anvāpta*). For the sake of making this very meaning firm, He is described as "transcended" (*uttīrṇa*)—transcended from all the bonds (*pāśa*), such as beginningless impurity (*mala*) and *māyā*.
"Existing above," meaning free from connection with impurities and the like;
for this very reason, "possessing all knowledge," that is, endowed with all cognition, in the sense that he knows everything according to its true nature.
Likewise, in the *Mṛgendra* [Tantra]: "In the Vedānta, Sāṅkhya, and in the systems of the existent, non-existent, and the six categories of reality... and so forth.

In the Śiva-āgama, the distinction regarding the cause of liberation is clearly set forth by the All-Seeing One; such is the summary of the subject matter. That means [of attainment] should be practiced accordingly, for in the Śaiva tradition, all this is supreme. Thus it is established that knowledge alone, as imparted by the one who has attained Śiva, is the cause of the highest beatitude (*niḥśreyasa*). As it is said in the Raurava: "For the sake of the enjoyment and liberation from bonds, Śiva is the Lord of Beings (*paśupati*) who is authoritative (*āpta*); when the word of that authoritative one..."
"Then, the word of a trustworthy person is that scripture.
Likewise, in the *Vāyupurāṇa*, in the dialogue between Upamanyu and Kṛṣṇa, it is said: "The supreme knowledge declared in the Śivāgama was spoken by Śrīkaṇṭha for Śiva alone."

The Śivāgama is the sole means for those who stand at the forefront of auspiciousness to attain the highest good through compassion; therefore, one who is liberated from the bonds of impurity (*mala*) and the like by knowing its ancillaries, and one who is liberated by the knowledge of other scriptures, is in this context nothing but a bound soul (*paśu*).
Because the author of the treatise is a bound soul (*paśu*).

Likewise, it is stated in the *Kāmika* and other scriptures: "Those who are liberated in other systems are considered bound souls (*paśu*) in the Siddhānta. In the solar year, on the twelfth lunar day (*tithi*), Hari resides in his own [day]; when the bright fortnight has passed, he is extended through three [periods] from the Sūtra, yet he is attained in six months during the two new moons (*darśa*). When he rests upon any one of the joints located among the twice-born (*dvija*) and others...

Likewise, when [the sun] has entered that [sign] for ten yugas... (l7) ...if at that time there is the effort for the Pavitra in Leo, then he states the determination of the time for the Pavitra according to the solar view: "Arka" means when Arka, the Sun, has entered a pair, that is, when it has entered the sign of Gemini, Hari, who is Nārāyaṇa... (l8)

In that [month], during the bright fortnight, on his own lunar day—the twelfth—he sleeps; thereafter, following Hari’s sleep, the rite of *pavitraka* (the sacred thread) must be performed using materials such as silk, fine cloth, and cotton. By this [verse], the time for the commencement of the plowing is indicated, as well as the time for the preparation of the *pavitraka* which has arrived after the period of Nārāyaṇa’s sleep.

Likewise, in the *Mohaśūrottara*: "Even if one causes a purificatory rite (*pavitra*) to be performed while Janārdana is not asleep—whether out of delusion or ignorance—that sinner, deluded by sin, [must perform penance]. He should fast for five days and mutter [the mantra] 'Hara' ten thousand times. Indeed, in this world, the sleep of Viṣṇu is well known to occur on the twelfth day (*dvādaśī*) of the bright fortnight of the month of Āṣāḍha, when the sun has entered the sign of Gemini (*mithuna*) and the month of Jyeṣṭha has passed.

When the sun has entered the sign of Gemini during the bright fortnight of the month of Māgha, that lunar day belongs to Hari; for this very reason, in the northern course [of the sun], there are six months beginning with Māgha, which are of two kinds: solar and lunar. Likewise, in the southern course, there are six months beginning with Śrāvaṇa, [and] the month of Māgha...

When the month of Māgha is joined with the Sun in Aquarius (*makara*), it is primary as a solar month; when it is joined with the Sun in Aquarius, it is primary as a lunar month. Thus, for all months, the status of being solar or lunar is appropriate.
And so it is stated in the *Niśvāsakārikā*: "Starting from the month of Māgha and ending with Āṣāḍha, O auspicious one, the worldly [calendar] should be understood."

The supreme northern course (*uttarāyaṇa*) is to be known as beginning from the full moon of Śrāvaṇa and ending with Puṣya, O beautiful one. As for the supreme southern course (*dakṣiṇāyaṇa*), it is the worldly time [beginning] from the month of Māgha; these months are designated by the zodiac sign Capricorn (*makara-rāśi*), as stated in that very [text]. "He who, while Indra is stationed in the east, begins with the month of Māgha... [etc.]

Cancer and Leo are likewise declared to be Gemini; these six signs are proclaimed as the [six] months of the zodiac. Leo, Virgo, Libra, Scorpio, Sagittarius, and Capricorn are designated as the [six months] of the Sun in the south. Likewise, by the months known as Āṣāḍha and so forth, through the two groups of six months beginning with Māgha in due order, the six seasons are remembered. By the three [groups] beginning with Śiśira, the northern course of the sun is known.

Two [periods] beginning with two months each constitute a season (*ṛtu*); three of those seasons make a solstice (*ayana*). Two solstices—the northern and southern course of the sun—constitute a year (*vatsara*). Or likewise, in this very *Saṃhitā*, for whom there is also "the cool season" (*śiśira*)...

The end of summer occurs during the northern course (*uttarāyaṇa*), while the rains, autumn, and winter are situated within the southern course (*dakṣiṇāyana*); thus, the seasons are of two kinds, solar and lunar. And it has been said: "The seasons beginning with spring are twofold:

those following the moon start from the new moon (*darśa*), while those of the sun start from Aries (*meṣa*) up to Pisces (*mīna*). Here, [the solar reckoning] is from the movement of the sun's transits (*saṃkrānti*) starting from Aries.

The solar month and the lunar month [are defined as follows]: the lunar month is that which concludes at the new moon (*amāvāsyā*) occurring immediately after the full moon (*paurṇamāsī*)—the primary full moon associated with a particular constellation during its respective bright fortnight.
Likewise, it has been stated by Amarasiṃha: "The month of Pauṣa is that in which the full moon is conjoined with the Puṣya [constellation]... (and so forth).

By name, that is Pauṣa; and likewise, there are eleven others beginning with Māgha. Thus they desire the lunar month as the supreme [measure] for the new moon (darśa). Furthermore, in the Siddhāntaśekhara it is said: "The solar [month] is the period during which the Sun remains in a zodiacal sign. Likewise: "When the new moon occurs while the Sun is situated in Aries and so forth, that is known as the [lunar month] beginning with Caitra. For this very reason, here...

The lunar Āṣāḍha begins with Cancer, whereas the solar Āṣāḍha begins from [the sign] Aries... (l2) ...up to the new moon; both the lunar and the solar months are to be specifically understood. For the purpose of worldly transactions one should use the lunar month, while for auspicious rites one should use the solar month, according to the rule of those who know the light of the stars (*jyotiṣavid*). Thus, when matters are ordained by way of the solar reckoning... (l3)

It is stated in three places that the Pavitrārohaṇa should be performed during the months of Āṣāḍha, Śrāvaṇa, and Bhādrapada—when they are conjoined with the Leo zodiac sign—with the qualifications of being middling or inferior;

for it is said that these three months beginning with Āṣāḍha are middling and lowest (*madhyama-kanyasa*). Because of this restriction to "three [months]," it is indicated that performing the Pavitraka rite beyond that is forbidden; thus, it is not [permissible] after Bhādrapada.
One should perform [the rite] according to the Siddhānta, for there exists the scriptural injunction that "one would become a partaker of fault [otherwise].

(l5) For this very reason, when the moon is in the sign of Virgo (Kanyārāśi), one must first perform the expiation (*prāyaścitta*) and then perform the *pavitra* rite; one should never perform it during the sign of Libra (Tulā).
Likewise, in the *Ṣaṭsahasrikā*: "The three beginning with Āṣāḍha... (l6)

The months are auspicious for the fixing of the thread (*sūtra-ropaṇa*) when Janārdana is asleep, whether during the bright or the dark fortnight. However, it is joined with the increase of disease during the three [periods] beginning with *prapāsi* and when afflicted by the king.

He who does not perform the fixing of the thread while the Sun has entered the sign of Aries (*tanu*), should recite ten thousand times the mantra of Dakṣa and then perform it; [likewise] Citraka [is forbidden] in Libra (*tulā*) for Śambhu.

"In any way whatsoever" (*kathañcana*) means likewise elsewhere: "Having performed the *pavitraka* rite, one should recite the *aghora* mantra two hundred thousand times and then perform the *cāndrāyaṇa* penance. By the word "having performed," the time for the *pavitraka* [is indicated]. Regarding the specific [details]... [omitted]. (p135b, l1)
