Since the *pavitra* rite is prescribed immediately after the period of Viṣṇu’s sleep (*rāyaṇasvāpa*), that period of sleep occurs on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of Āṣāḍha when the sun has entered Gemini (*mithuna*)— calculated according to the solar system— in a year devoid of an intercalary month;

whereas [the period of awakening] occurs on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of Āṣāḍha when the sun has entered Cancer (*kaṭaka*)— calculated according to the lunar system— in a year containing an intercalary month,
provided it is the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of the second month joined with Cancer, excluding the case where the sun is in Pūrvāṣāḍhā.

He states the determination for the pure twelfth day of the month of Śravaṇa conjoined with Karkaṭaka... (l3) ...by means of the passage beginning with "vaṣaṭ svadhiketa" and so forth. Among the six months—the excellent months beginning with Caitra conjoined with Aries and the other signs—and among the five Vaiśākhas, in whichever [month]... (l4) ...sa...

When, in a particular year, there are two *darśa* [new moon] days at the time of the Aries ingress (*meṣasaṅkrānti*), and thus an intercalary month (*adhikamāsa*) occurs, then in that year he performs his reclining (*śayana*) in Cancer (*karkaṭa*). Following the reclining, among the months of the twice-born (*dvijātamāsa*)— namely Pūrvāṣāḍhā and Uttarāṣāḍhā— he remains in the junction (*sandhi*) for one month, and [then] in the following month...

The meaning is that [the month] was previously an intercalary month (*malamāsa*) because of the [solar] course. For it is stated: "When the sun transits having bypassed two new moons (*darśa*), that should be known as an intercalary month, excluded from all ritual acts. (l6–l7)

And in the *Pavitrakālanirṇaya*, it is stated that the twelfth day (*dvādaśī*) itself—whether bright or otherwise—is prescribed for [the rite] when [the Sun] has entered Gemini; it ordains sleep and indeed effects the sleeping of Hari. When the Sun is in the six signs beginning with Aries, [the following applies]:

(l8) ...if the Pavitraka rite is performed while Hari is asleep, then this expiation (*prāyaścitta*) is declared; otherwise, [it is as follows]. Thus, in the *Śrīmohaśūrottara*: "Now, here [in the month] of Āṣāḍha..."

Regarding the state of having two Āṣāḍhas: [if one asks] how Viṣṇu’s sleep occurs in the month of Āṣāḍha when it is conjoined with Cancer, excluding [the first] Āṣāḍha—whether within the six-month period beginning with Caitra, or whether his sleep occurs in a single [specific] Cancer—the resolution here is: "when [the Sun] is situated in Gemini... (l. 2).

When [the moon] touches two [new moons] in the month of Āṣāḍha, then the designation "Dvirāṣāḍha" (Double Āṣāḍha) is applied by the wise. Likewise, according to the science of astrology (*jyotiḥśāstra*), when the sun, having entered Gemini (*mithuna*), touches two new moons, it is called Dvirāṣāḍha; [this occurs] in all cases... (l3) Viṣṇu sleeps in Cancer (*karkaṭa*). Furthermore, elsewhere it is said that on the tenth day of the dark fortnight of Caitra, prior to the fourteenth day, when the sun has entered Aries (*meṣa*), there are two new moons in Gemini.

Just as there is a "double Āṣāḍha" (*dvirāṣāḍha*) for you in the month of Āṣāḍha, so too— according to the manner of attainment (*yathāprāptyena*)— by means of the designation "attainment of double Āṣāḍha," wherever an excess [of days] might occur within the six-month periods beginning with Mādhava, that [excess] should be... (l5)

Because it is prescribed by the designation "double Āṣāḍha" for the sake of that purpose, Viṣṇu’s sleeping is established in the month of Karkaṭaka during a year in which an intercalary [month] occurs within six months. And it has been said:

"In the five months other than Vaiśākha, one should sleep according to the single sequence; however, when there is a single *saṃkrānti* in two [months], it is in the secondary (*gauṇa*) double Āṣāḍha, and likewise elsewhere in the months beginning with Mādhava."

Six [months], one [month] of its own, and the month of Āṣāḍha—when this occurs twice, it should be known as a *dvirāṣāḍha* year; for according to the rule of those who know the stars (*jyotirvid*), this specific designation of a *dvirāṣāḍha* year is for the purpose of making known the Lord’s reclining in Cancer. (Line 8)

Thus, in the Śāstra, regarding the year that possesses an additional [month] among the six-month periods, this ritual (*kalpa*) for the Lord’s sleep in Vaikuṇṭha—concerning the image, the cloth-painting, and so forth—is declared as the primary [practice]. Likewise, because the designation "secondary *dvirāṣāḍha*" is applied to other months, the sleep in Cancer (*karkaṭasvāpa*) is established; otherwise, it would not be the secondary *dvirāṣāḍha*.

Because he is without a seat (*nirāsadatvāt*), Acyuta sleeps right here; for this very reason, he is referred to as being "in Karkaṭaka. Furthermore, if it be the month of Śrāvaṇa or Bhādrapada, then because it is the fifth month, the [observance] prescribed for the four-month period (*cāturmāsya*) is established.

Because it is established by scriptural authority (*jñāya*) that [the Lord] exists there, and because otherwise the injunctions and restrictive rules (*niyama*) prescribed for those months would result in meaninglessness; furthermore, since the sleep [of Viṣṇu] in the sign of Cancer is established even when an intercalary month (*adhimāsa*) occurs during Śrāvaṇa or Bhādrapada, there is no fault.

(From the *Mohaśūrottara*): "Where two new moon days (*darśa*) occur without the sun's transition into a zodiacal sign (*saṅkrānti*), that is to be known as an intercalary month, and Viṣṇu sleeps in Cancer. In the case of equal months...

But the *pavitraka* rite on the *savyaka* [day], when Harikeśa has been satisfied, otherwise one would become a partaker of fault; thus, among those who speak of illusion (*māyāvādins*), the designation of "double Āṣāḍha" (*dvirāṣāḍha*) is prescribed in a subsequent quarter-verse for the purpose of establishing the time for the installation of Viṣṇu. According to the opinion of some, the designation "double Āṣāḍha" applies to the end of the signs beginning with Aries and ending with Gemini.
If it is said that in the year [of the scripture],

for the sake of both [meanings], the designation "double Āṣāḍha" is prescribed, otherwise, during the six [months] beginning with the dark fortnight of Uttarā, the sleep [of the Buddha] occurs in the sign of Gemini in the current year increased by one; [and] in Cancer...

The meaning must be stated as follows: if, in the current year, an intercalary month occurs within the first three signs beginning with Aries, it is naturally associated with Āṣāḍhā and Cancer; [if] an intercalary month occurs in the signs beginning with Cancer, it is not associated with [the aforementioned]; likewise, its dormancy is established in Gemini. Thus, the statement regarding the dormancy prescribed for the current year must be demonstrated as consistent. This is so.
Because of the very absence of such a statement, Mādhava and others [hold that] in the sixth [month], one's own...

(l3) ...when there are two Āṣāḍhas, that is to be known as [the year of] double-Āṣāḍha; and the statement "Acyuta sleeps in Śrāvaṇa" is a declaration indicating the time for the prescribed sleep when Cancer is conjoined with the solar year. Regarding the subsequent [matter of] sleeping... (l4)
The statement that "when two new moons (*darśa*) occur within a year during the period from Aries to Gemini, Hari must necessarily sleep when the sun is in Gemini;

or when two new moons occur within a year during the triad beginning with Cancer, Hari must necessarily sleep when the sun is in Cancer" is a declaration concerning the time of sleep in the future. If the time of sleep does not occur in this manner—

It may be that, primarily on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Āṣāḍha, she has entered the sign of Gemini; it may be that at that very time her period of sleep necessarily occurs— by this unarisen [sign] during the time of sleep.

If [the month were established] by itself, numerous scriptural injunctions prescribed for the purpose of establishing the time of sleep would become redundant, and the designation "double Āṣāḍha" would likewise be meaningless. Therefore, it is established that—

apart from the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of a single Āṣāḍha— the sleep [of Viṣṇu] is to be observed on the pure twelfth day of Śrāvaṇa when it occurs as an intercalary month, provided there is a need for such a period.

Likewise, there is a statement in the Śivāgama: "It should also be performed in Āṣāḍha when [the world] has fallen asleep by Madhusūdana... it is known as being well-restrained; let the definitive conclusion be heard... one should perform [it] on the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of Āṣāḍha, and on the eighth and fourteenth days of both fortnights of Śrāvaṇa and Bhādrapada..."

By the phrase "on the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of Āṣāḍha," the time immediately following Viṣṇu’s sleep is obtained by itself. For this very reason, it will make known the meaning [of the expression] "while Madhusūdana has not yet slept" (as the text intends to convey). [This applies] in the months of Śrāvaṇa and Bhādrapada; provided there is an intercalary month (*adhimāsa*), [the rite is performed] on the twelfth day of Āṣāḍha while the sun is in Gemini (*mithuna*).

The sleep [of the deity] is established on the pure twelfth day of the month of Śrāvaṇa conjoined with the asterism Karkaṭa; thus it is stated in the *Tantrasāra*: “Āṣāḍha is indeed the best month, Śrāvaṇa is considered middling, and Bhādrapada is inferior;
one should perform [the rite] during the bright fortnight on the eighth or the fourteenth [day]. (l4–l5)
Or else, it should be performed on the new moon day or on the twelfth day; however, the dark fortnight is for the ancestors (*paitṛka*). One should perform the ritual of the *pavitrāropaṇa* there.

It should also be performed in the month of Āṣāḍha, when Janārdana has fallen asleep. Even while he is asleep, it should be performed on the eighth or the fourteenth day. Thus it is stated in this text. [It may be done] once in Āṣāḍha... [his] sleep.

It is not so; for it has been stated that when [the month] is Śrāvaṇa or Bhādrapada, then—excluding the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of Āṣāḍha joined with the constellation Mithuna—the commencement of the *pavitra* rite must be performed on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight joined with Karkaṭaka.
When [it is] Śrāvaṇa or Bhādra...

Or [the rite] should be performed on the day of the full moon in the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, or in Karkaṭaka-Āṣāḍha, or in Mithuna-Āṣāḍha... one should cause [the deity] to sleep. On the eighth [day] of the [month] of Svāpāvarta... for the sake of success, at that very time when the Pavitra begins... (l.

2) ...the application must be made, because of the force of the mention of the eighth [day]. This text does not concern the first Āṣāḍha; if it concerned the first Āṣāḍha, [it would apply] in the case of a double Āṣāḍha.
On the eighth day, [there is] the sleeping [of the deity].

(l3) [It is established that] the Pavitrāropaṇa should be performed in the second Śrāvaṇa, having omitted the first month [of Śrāvaṇa] which contains the mention of the eighth-day [observance]; for it is prescribed that the sleeping [of the deity] occurs on the eighth day of the bright fortnight of the first Śrāvaṇa. (l4)

Likewise, in the *Viṣṇurahasya*: "In the bright fortnight of Śrāvaṇa, when the sun is in Cancer, on the twelfth lunar day, the offering of the sacred thread (*pavitrārohaṇa*) for Vāsudeva is prescribed. Or [it may be performed] at the conjunction (*saṃhṛasta*) of the sun [with the asterism], or likewise when the sun has entered Virgo. This statement refers to the region [of the Magadhas]. If there is an intercalary month (*malamāsa*), it should be done except for the first enclosure (*prathamāvaraṇa*).

The offering of the sacred thread (*pavitrāropaṇa*) should be performed in the second month of Śrāvaṇa when Leo is in conjunction. Otherwise, the statement that it "should be done under Leo or the Sun" would be purposeless for the offering of the sacred thread;
[for this applies] to the lunar month... (l7)

The solar [month] alone is to be accepted; there, no suspicion of an intercalary month (*adhikamāsa*) exists, nor should it be so stated. Generally, regarding the *pavitrārohaṇa* [festival], the lunar [month] is intended as the middle one. Likewise, in the Vaiṣṇava [tradition], one should perform [the rite] on the day of the *cāga* [constellation] within the four months of the rainy season, starting from the fifteenth day of Āṣāḍha up until the twenty-ninth.

The day of the full moon; that [is] the number of Indras (14). But from the beginning of Cancer, the time for the Pavitrāropaṇa rite and the month and fortnight of those two [are calculated]; the solar [month] is known as the *madhyama* (intermediate).
Thus, in the *Vaighānasa*, in the *Triproktasahmitā*.

In the months of Āṣāḍha, Śrāvaṇa, and likewise Bhādrapada, during the bright fortnight of these months, one should perform the planting on the twelfth day. One may have it performed with the Heart-mantra, the Cāndramasa-mantra, or even the Saura-mantra. In the two months of Jyeṣṭha and Āṣāḍha, when the moon is in Karkaṭaka, one should perform it; and in the months of Kārttika and Mārgaśīrṣa, when the sun is in Tapa (Siṃha) and Aśleṣā, one should cause it to be done.

"Kecana" means that the *pavitrāropaṇa* (the ritual installation of the sacred thread) should be performed in the month of Jyeṣṭha, in Āṣāḍha, or in the two [months] together with Śrāvaṇa when the sun is in Cancer; the meaning is that if there are two [days] in Śrāvaṇa, one should perform it on the day of Śrāvaṇī.

Likewise, it is connected [to the previous rule] that one should perform [the rite] on the Śrāvaṇī day when there are two [days] in Bhādrapada and Āśvayuja. Regarding the phrase "when there are two," some say it should be understood as referring to an alternative option (*pakṣāntara*).

Likewise, in the *Kāmika*, it is said: "In the month of Āṣāḍha, on the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight, one should perform the Pavitraka rite; in other months, during both the bright and dark fortnights, on the eighth day of the dark fortnight, one should perform the Pavitraka according to the rule. For that ascetic, even when performing the Pavitraka in two months, [it should be done] during the bright fortnight in both cases."
The commencement is on the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of Āṣāḍha.

It is completed on the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of Bhādrapada, with the ritual bath (*avabhṛthasnāna*) performed on its full moon day. In the case of a one-month performance, the completion is on the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of Śrāvaṇa, with [the bath] on its full moon day.

One should perform the *avabhṛtha* (concluding bath) in the *pavitra* [rite]. Because it is stated that "the Guru [is the authority]," the commencement [of the rite] takes place on the eighth day of the bright fortnight of Śrāvaṇa, and its completion on the eighth day of the dark fortnight of Bhādrapada.

Alternatively, it may be performed starting from the first day of the bright fortnight until the fifteenth; however, due to the absence [of time], it may last for two months, one fortnight, or seven days, as it has been so stated.
The fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of Āṣāḍha, as well as the eighth day of the bright fortnight, bestows auspiciousness;

however, the dark [eighth] is the cause of liberation. Thus, according to the determination of lunar days for all months, on the eighth and the fourteenth, as well as the first, the full moon, and the fifteenth, an interval should be observed.

In the bright fortnight (*pūrvapakṣa*), it is produced on the second day; specifically, the fourth, sixth, and so forth, up to the eighth, should be performed, O best of the twice-born, for seven days in the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇapakṣa*). One should also cause it to be performed for three days [or] thirty-one days, ending on the eighth day of the dark fortnight, or on the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight.

The rite of the offering of the *pavitra* [sacred thread]. Thus, in the case of the seven-day period, it should be performed starting from the eighth day of the bright fortnight of Śrāvaṇa up until the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight. Likewise, when performing the daily *pavitra*, the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsa*) is on the thirteenth day, and the *pavitra* [offering] itself is on the fourteenth day.

The dedication should be performed there on the full fourteenth day; for it is said that when everything that is to be done on a single day is completed according to the full lunar date (*tithi*), then on that very day, O Śambhu, the *pavitraka* [should be offered]. Having performed the daily rites such as the *karṣa* and so forth, and having performed the occasional (*naimittikī*) twilight worship (*sandhyā*), one should properly offer the fragrant *pavitraka* once, and upon it, the flower *pavitraka*.
"Having given the *liṅga* to Caṇḍa, one should worship one's own [liṅga]... (l. 3).
When the fourteenth lunar day (*caturdaśī*) occurs twice, then the offering of the sacred thread (*pavitra*) should be performed on the fourteenth day joined with the following day.
Likewise, in the *Siddhāntaśekhara*, regarding the rite of the sacred thread (*pavitrakārya*)... (l. 4).

"The fourteenth day conjoined with the *parāgharpa* [moment] bestows auspiciousness, as does the eighth. Nevertheless, it is stated elsewhere: "When the lunar day (*tithi*) is fragmented (*khaṇḍatithi*), then one should offer the *gandhasūtra* and the *pavitra* during the two portions of that lunar day;

when the first fourteenth day is mixed with half of the full moon (*paurṇamāsī*), then it is beneficial at another time. Or rather, it should be performed right then and there if one is otherwise occupied."

Then, having performed the *godoha* [rite]... (l6) ...having made it *sādhivāsa-nivartaka*, one should perform it on the fourteenth day; on the remaining lunar day (*tithi*), one should practice [the rite]. The meaning of this is:
when at that time the *khaṇḍatithi*—a lunar day occurring across two days—is present, then at that time (l7)...

At the appropriate time, for the two parts of that lunar day—namely, the two parts associated with the *ghaṭikās* of the lunar day elapsed during the two watches of the day—one should, in due order, offer the *gandhasūtra*, the *pavitraka* presented on the day of consecration (*adhivāsana*), and again the *pavitraka* for presentation in the morning... [to] the Supreme Lord; this is the meaning: one should present it on the fourteenth day joined with the night.

The offering of the *pavitra* should be performed on the fourteenth day of the following month. When the fourteenth day of the following month coincides with the afternoon, it should be performed as previously described up until midday;
if [the fourteenth] belongs to the following day, then at that time—

He states that [the rite] should be performed at another time; or rather, since it has been said that when both times coincide, the fourteenth day itself must be taken on the following day, the fourteenth day—which is of a form common to the offering of both times—must be discarded. Thus, it is stated that it is prescribed for another time;
however, if one is distracted, it should be performed quickly right then and there.
If it is joined with that [time] while one is occupied, then on the fourteenth day, having created an interval in the middle until the time equivalent to the end of the milking (godoha),

one should perform the consecration (*adhivāsa*) of the *pavitra*. One must not perform the consecration during the night joined with the fourteenth day, because it would be of the same nature as the offering of the *pavitra* during the daytime of the preceding day.

The intention is that it is not suitable for the *adhivāsa* (preliminary consecration) to take place after that; as for the remaining rites, such as the circumambulation of the village and the festival, one should perform them on the final lunar day (*parāhṇe*) joined with the full moon. Thus it has been said: "Having performed [the rite] on the seventh or the thirteenth day..."

"The fragrant *pavitraka* should be performed on the following day; that is remembered as the *pavitra*. Some say this refers to the case of a lunar day (*tithi*) that is incomplete: the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsa*) takes place at night joined with the thirteenth day, the offering of the fragrant *pavitra* in the afternoon joined with the fourteenth day, and immediately thereafter, the offering of the *pavitra* in the morning joined with the fourteenth day.

Others have said that it should be performed sequentially over one day according to their respective order; or else, they say that by means of these two [substances], one [rite] should be performed on each day. Others [have declared] that the consecration (*adhivāsa*) should take place on the thirteenth lunar day and the following day, making it two days.
Other masters have stated that by means of these two—the perfumed thread (*gandhasūtra*) and the purifier (*pavitra*)—one [rite] should be performed for each day. Thus they spoke.

On the thirteenth day, the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsa*) must be performed; the removal of scents and threads and the offering of the sacred thread (*pavitra*) should be carried out. In the case where the consecration is to be performed immediately, on the fourteenth day, when [the moon] has waned, one should perform the offering of the sacred thread together with the consecration after having interposed the "burning of the cow" (*godāha*).

If the fourteenth day has only a few *ghaṭikās* remaining, then at the end of the fourteenth day, one should perform the consecration and the sacred thread offering. This is the excellent sacred thread.

This rule regarding the lunar days pierced by the full moon should also be understood to apply to the eighth day. This sequence is for the "ascension of the sacred thread" (*pavitrārohaṇa*). Having abandoned the month associated with the retrogression or heliacal setting of Jupiter and Venus, the *pavitrārohaṇa* must be performed in a pure month. When, due to the retrogression or setting of Jupiter and Venus at the end [of the month], the three months do not arise [as auspicious], then [the rite is still required] because the sacred thread is a constant auxiliary (*nityāṅga*) of the ritual.
It must certainly be performed.
Thus, in the Siddhāntaśekhara:
"When the planet [the Sun] has set in its pure state, and there is no rising for three months, even so one should perform the Pavitraka rite."

[Is it] because of its being occasional (*naimittikatva*), or because of its being a single [act]? Now, if during the three months beginning with Āśvina there should be no rising of Jupiter or Venus, then the performance of the *pavitraka* rite must take place in the month of Āśvina or Kārttika when they have risen;
for that month as well—
Because of its inclusion.

Likewise, in the *Kāmika*: "The three months beginning with Āṣāḍha are the summer [season], consisting of the middle and the lower; or else the two months of Aśvini and Kārttika are proclaimed [as such].
Even though it is stated thus regarding these three months, how [is it so]? (l5)

Regarding the objection concerning the "purification" (*pavitrakaraṇa*), the resolution is as follows: if the purification is not performed due to divine or other circumstances during the three-month period, the inclusion of these two months [of the year] is not intended in its primary sense; thus there is no fault, because the two months are primary in the context of the *pavitrakaraṇa*. Having kept all this in mind, the author stated in that verse, "in that [year], the pair of Darśas," and so forth. In that [verse]:

In the year when the Darśa [new moon] occurs within the Karkaṭaka [Cancer] zodiacal sign, then, because of its inherent nature, the effort for the Pavitra [rite]— the performance of the Pavitrārohaṇa and so forth— should be carried out in the month of Āṣāḍha, conjoined with Siṃha [Leo] and the Śravaṇa [constellation].

Once the first [rite], the hearing [of the mantra] and the sleeping [initiation], have been accomplished, the performance of the *pavitrarohaṇa* is established as occurring specifically in the month of Siṃha, because it is an intercalary month (*malamāsa*).
Thus it is stated in the *Mohaśūrottara*:

"One desiring one's own welfare should not perform initiation and the like, the installation and the like, or the *pavitra* rite and so forth during an intercalary month, even for Indra. Likewise, it is said in the *Smṛti*:

The *upākarma* and *utsarjana* rites, the offering of the *pavitra*, the presentation of *damanaka*, the *avaroha*, the offering during the winter season, the *bali* and the *iṣṭakā*; the *bali* for Īśāna, the sleeping and turning of Viṣṇu, and the installation and removal of Durga and Indra,
as well as the raising of the banner.

Regarding the statement, "The *Pūrva* [nakṣatra] belongs to the speaker (*vaktr*), while the *Para* and the *Antya* belong to the divine (*daivika*)," the phrase "here is the sleeping of Viṣṇu" refers to the prohibition of the month of *Pūrva* [Āṣāḍha]. Since Viṣṇu does not sleep during *Pūrvāṣāḍhā*, and since his sleep is established as occurring in the month of *Śrāvaṇa* (which corresponds to *Uttarāṣāḍhā*), it must be stated that this [phrase] does not refer to that [month of *Pūrva* Āṣāḍha].

Because the *pavitra* rite is performed immediately after Viṣṇu’s sleep, its commencement must be made on the fourteenth day (*caturdaśī*), excluding the pure eighth day (*śuddhāṣṭamī*) when the moon is in Gemini (*mithuna*). And it has been said: "Except for the pure eighth day, [the rite is performed] when the moon is in Gemini or Cancer during the months of Leo and Bhādrapada."

It should be performed on the white and black [fortnights], specifically on the fourteenth and eighth lunar days. A head-measure of one hundred threads made from new cotton is prepared; then, for the portion of worship, there are three [measures]. Furthermore, according to the number of threads, a knot is made with nine dots and five arrows. When the thread is measured at one cubit, it is divided by twenty-eight in rows, as heard in the Śruti.
In the Kilahṛta [system], there are eighteen knots. In the Bāṇādya [system]...

(l8) ...in those honored [systems], or if it is the sharp one, it is joined with one and eight [making nine]; or else, in the *ātmatattva*, there are thirty-one, known by the number of drops (*bindu*) and arrows (*śara*), beginning with *prakṛti*.

(p142a, l1) The lords of the names of the scents are the Śivas joined with the moon; the Śaiva kalās are a portion of the moon. The lords of the threads, beginning with the *praṇava*, extend up to the knees in the manifest [systems].
Now, for the purpose of ascending the *pavitra* [sacred thread],

he states the measurements for the knots (*granthi*) and so forth of the *pavitra*s known as the "Descent of Śiva’s Gaṅgā" (*śivagaṅgāvatāra*), beginning with the word *kārpāsa*. The meaning is that it should be made from cotton (*kārpāsa*)—
that is, produced from cotton and similar materials— by the daughters of the twice-born (*dvijakanyā*).
The *navātmasūtra* is called a "single thread" because it is formed by the nature of the number nine. It is fashioned with a count of one hundred and eight, arranged in the ten directions.
Likewise, in the *Somaśambhupaddhati*:

"In the Kali age, the purifying thread (*pavitraka*)—made of gold, silver, copper, or [iron] from the Kṛta age and so forth in due order, or even of cotton according to one's means—should be prepared by daughters of twice-born men."

The thread should be tripled and made into three strands; it may be white and auspicious, or other types of thread are also employed, such as those derived from silk, bark, lotus fibers, linen, *darbha* grass, hemp, or produced from *mūrvā* and so forth,
for the sake of the purificatory rite (*pavitra*).

"It is praised" means that for the blind, [the use of] silk (*paṭṭa*) and linen (*kṣauma*) is praised as being appropriate for those who possess wealth; likewise, for ascetics (*yati*), the use of *darbha* grass is praised as being appropriate for them; for the poor, [the use of] *mauñja* grass and so forth is appropriate. The word "twice-born" (*dvija*) refers to the sacraments (*saṃskāra*) of the twice-born; it is appropriate for those who have undergone such sacraments. In their absence, it is appropriate for those belonging to the [other] castes (*varṇa*). Here, the word "maiden" (*kanyā*) is intended solely to exclude widows. Regarding this, [there is the rule]: "eight hundred... (Sūtra 8).
Three [threads] constitute the best; half of that is the middle; half of that is the lowest.
Likewise, in the *Jñānaratnāvalī*: "A thread of one hundred and eight, equal in number to the Rudras, is always the best; in the absence of a thread, half of that [should be used]; half of that..."

Or one may fashion [the purifiers] numbering one hundred and eight and so forth; this refers to the purifiers being made for the sacrificial ground (*sthaṇḍila*) and other such objects. And it has been said: "The purifier should be made with one hundred and eight [threads];

on the sacrificial ground and so forth, one should apply half of that, or half of that again, or according to what is available. [This applies] to the sacrificial ground, to a mobile *liṅga*, to a *bāṇaliṅga*, and to a self-manifested (*svayambhū*) [liṅga]."

(13) There is no fixed rule regarding the recitation and so forth, as has been illustrated previously. One should never perform more than one hundred and eight [recitations]; O Śakra, this is the rule for all—such is the command of the Supreme Goddess. (14)
That *liṅga* is the "head-measure" (*śiromānaka*), the measure of the head being threefold; it consists of the three purifiers known as Ātman, Vidyā, and Śiva.

Likewise, in the *Ṣaṭsahasraka*, the circumference at the top of the *liṅga* is such that the circumference of the Ātman [portion] is as it is, and the circumference of the Vidyā-ātman portion is likewise, excluding two parts from that. Therefore, the two parts remaining are the new [portion] called Śiva, which is the purifier (*pavitraka*).
Here, by the word "atha" (now),

it is indicated that immediately following this, one should perform ten knots and so forth for each of the three principles (*tattva*); and on the sacrificial ground (*sthaṇḍila*), the linga, and other such objects, the purificatory thread (*pavitraka*) for the three principles should be made with eight finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) or more, as appropriate.

The ritual task is as follows: in the *Jñānaratnāvalī*, it is stated that the sacred thread (*pavitraka*) consists of twenty-one [threads] representing the Self (*ātman*), while the [sacred thread] of Vidyā and Śiva consists of fewer than that, according to what is auspicious;
this applies to both the immovable and the movable [lingas].

Having made the object of the rite (*kārya*) eight or more finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) in length, with ten knots (*granthi*) at intervals like those on a bracelet; likewise elsewhere, "provided with knots" means "with as many [knots] at equal intervals. Thus, three *pavitra* [strainers] provided with ten knots are for the subject matter of *liṅga*s and so forth according to the *Kalpaśīra* measurement; or, in the case of *liṅga*s with very large heads, the *pavitra* may be [determined] by the number of threads or in a manner appropriate [to the size].

(…) the rite is to be performed. Likewise, in the *Mṛgendra*, it is stated that for the sake of worship—specifically for the portion of the worship of the *liṅga*—the wise man should perform the auspicious "three-headed" (*mūrdhnitraya*) [rite], which consists of the three principles (*tattva*) and is measured by the number of knots desired for that purpose. For the fourth [portion], the *pavitraka* known as the "Descent of the Gaṅgā" (*gaṅgāvatāra*), as previously described, should be performed with one hundred and eight [knots] or more, according to the superior, middling, or inferior [grade].

Some maintain that the descent of the Gaṅgā should be fashioned with one hundred and eight threads. Likewise, in the *Siddhāntaśekhara*: "The excellent purifier (*pavitra*) should consist of one hundred and eight [threads], the middling half of that, and the other half of that; thus one should fashion the triad of purifiers, and the descent of the Gaṅgā with one hundred and eight [threads] by means of a fixed liṅga."
It is stated that the measurement for the *gaṅgāvatāra* (the descent of the Gaṅgā),

beginning from the top of the *liṅga* down to the end of the pedestal (*pīṭha*), should be made to hang down; this is called the fourth hundred-sūtra rule, known as the *gaṅgāvatāraka*, [applying] to a fixed *liṅga* from the head to the base.

And [the phrase] "not otherwise" refers to the Sūtra of One Hundred and Eight [Verses] and so forth; by virtue of the number—that is, according to the count—one should make a knot at the Gaṅgāvatāra, such is the remainder [of the sentence]. (l4)

Likewise, in the *Mṛgendra*, it is said: "The knots (*granthayaḥ*) are indeed enumerated as those hanging from the *āvedi*. This means that while hanging down as far as the pedestal (*pīṭha*), they hang from the points where the Gaṅgā descends. With the verse beginning with "binduśareṇa" and so forth, he states the enumeration of the types of threads and the enumeration of the nine types of knots for the nine liṅgas, ranging from the most excellent (*uttamottama*) to the lowest (*niṣṭha*). By the word "or" (*vā*), the sense of an alternative is indicated, as previously mentioned: the sacred thread (*pavitraka*) [is made] with one hundred and eight [threads] or with half of that, for the nine liṅgas.

The ritual action (*kārya*) should be performed in nine ways; that is, in the nine types of liṅgas ranging from nine cubits down to one cubit, starting from a row of one hundred and eight threads and dividing by the number ten.

When the hand-measure (*hastaliṅga*) is reduced, there are eighty-one threads for a six-cubit image; seventy-one threads for a five-cubit image; sixty-one threads for a four-cubit image; fifty-one threads for a three-cubit image; forty-one threads for a two-cubit image; and thirty-one threads for a one-cubit image. According to this method, [the proportions are determined]... (na... by a measurement of twenty-eight threads.

(13) And the number and measure of the *liṅga*-objects [in] the *Gaṅgāvatāra-sūtra* have been stated as eightfold, beginning from *bindu* and ending with *yānta*, within the nine *liṅgas* ranging from the eldest (*jyeṣṭha*) to the youngest (*kanyasa*). (14)
O Purandara, I have declared to you the number of threads for the three bracelets;

the measurement of the number of threads should be made in this manner. Regarding the measurement of the number of knots: for the Gaṅgāvatāra, twelve knots should be made, as stated for the Gandhiva, or [alternatively] nine knots on the Liṅga at the Gaṅgāvatāra.

By the word *bindu* (dot) and the word *śara* (arrow), the number five is expressed; if joined with *bindu*, the number fifty arises. One should form a knot at the fiftieth [mark], which serves as the removal of the Veda from the count. The meaning is that one should decrease the count by four, from nine cubits down to one cubit. In the case of a *liṅga* measuring nine cubits, [the Gaṅgā...]

Thereafter, the knots (*granthi*) should be made on the thread: forty-six for an eight-fingered [thread], forty-two for a seven-fingered, twenty-eight for a six-fingered, thirty-four for a five-fingered, thirty for a four-fingered, twenty-six for a three-fingered, twenty-two for a two-fingered, and eighteen knots for a one-fingered [thread]. Starting from the "dot" (*bindu*), the "arrows" (*bāṇa*), and the "shoulder" (*aṃsa*), this continues until there are the "serpents" (*nāga*) and "moons" (*candra*).

O best of gods, it is declared that due to the decrease of the *yugas*, the knots (*granthi*) [of the cord] are determined; when the sacred thread (*pavitra*) is removed, all the deities [reside] in the eldest daughter [of the knots]. Thus, regarding the ninefold *liṅga*, there is no fixed rule in the *Svāyambhuva* and other [ages]; rather, as previously stated, the performance should be carried out according to the superior, middling, or inferior [status], by means of one hundred and eight [recitations] and so forth, and it is also prescribed for the sacrificial ground (*sthaṇḍila*).

Regarding mobile liṅgas, such as Bāṇaliṅgas, self-manifested (*svayambhu*) liṅgas, and those grown from the earth (*viroha*), there is no fixed rule, as was previously illustrated; this is indicated here by the word "it is said" (*kila*) with respect to self-manifested liṅgas and the like, as well as images and the descent of the Gaṅgā.

It is indicated that eighteen knots (*granthi*) are to be made. And it has been said: "The *vedispṛk* [should extend] to the manifest and the unmanifest; among the manifest [parts], it reaches the knees and the *jambī* [region]. There, at the descent of the Gaṅgā (*gaṅgāvatāraka*), eighteen knots are traditionally prescribed. (l7) Furthermore, regarding the making of the eighteen knots, it is stated: "One should make two knots at the end at the descent of the Gaṅgā; there, having omitted the space between the *tāla*s, one should make them."
The four knots:

having made the four knots at intervals of two finger-breadths, they should likewise be made on both sides; thus, one should finally form sixteen such parts consisting of digits, composed of Śiva and Śakti, and again consisting of knots.

One should perform the investiture of the sacred thread (*pavitrārohaṇa*) for the *bāṇa* and other types of *liṅgas* according to the previously mentioned number of threads, such as one hundred and eight; he states that this is to be done with a single type of thread.

Regarding those *liṅgas* worshipped with any one [of these], such as the *bāṇa*—among the one hundred and eight threads starting from the *yāmyabhūva* and others—when the *liṅgas* have been worshipped with whichever one among those threads, or alternatively with barley and so forth...
The remainder [of the sentence] is that there are eighty-one threads (*sūtra*).

Alternatively, for the investiture of the sacred thread (*pavitrāropaṇa*), it should be performed with eight, thirty-two, or fifty threads, including those called *bindu*; this is the remainder [of the sentence].
Likewise, Somaśambhu [states] regarding the jeweled sacrificial ground (*ratnasthaṇḍila*): [l4]

When the arrow has moved and the knot is fixed by Svayambhū, one of the purifiers (pavitra) should be performed as previously instructed according to one's preference; thus, in the context of reality (tattva), the presiding deities of the ten knots of the *tattva-pavitra* are said to be Prakṛti and the others.

Likewise, Somaśambhu states: "In the *puruṣa*, there is *prakṛti*; [then] Virā, Parājitā ending with the fourth; Jayā as the other [fifth]; Vijayā as the sixth; likewise, Citi, Sadāśiva, and Manonmanī as the ninth; and Sarvatomukhī as the tenth. When the nine knots (*granthi*) have been made—or rather, when the powers beginning with Vāmā [are present]—these [powers] exist in the three principles (*tritattva*) concerning the many junctions (*sandhi*); so it is stated elsewhere."
In this way, the time periods are to be repeated;
having completed them in one part, they should be arranged elsewhere as appropriate. As it has been said by the Teachers: "These [time periods] are to be applied everywhere..."

Regarding the phrase "by the guides," he refers to the deities of the knots of the *Gaṅgāvatāra*, which consists of eighteen knots. By the words beginning with "Śiva," [he means] that in the second knot, above and below, it is "joined with Śiva," meaning accompanied by Śiva;

the sense is that the deity is Śakti. "The lunar rays" refers to the Śaiva *kalās* (the powers of Śiva). [The text continues: "accompanied by the lunar digits" refers to the Śaiva *kalās* together with the digits of the moon.

The sixteen digits (*kalā*) mentioned in the *Prāsāda* mantra are declared to be the deities of the lunar digits (*candrakalā*). (L2) The meaning is that they are to be installed (*nyāsanīya*). Here, some say that the sixteen digits contained within the *Prāsāda* mantra are to be installed together with Śiva and Śakti; others say that the lunar digits beginning with *Śaśinī* are to be installed together with Śiva and Śakti. Both [methods] are to be installed... (L3)

And it is said by others that those *kalās* are written according to the scriptures in their traditional order: A, U, M, the Bindu, Artha, Indu, Nirodhikā, Nāda, Nādānta, Śakti, Vyāpinī, Vyomarūpiṇī, Anantā, Anāśritā, Anāthā, Samanā, and Unmanī. These are the *kalās* of the Prāsāda-mantra; [the goddesses] Śākinī, Lakṣmī, and Kāminī reside in the Moon.

And Prabhā, as well as Puṣpiṇī, Suprabhā, [Amṛtā], Kumudā, Āśvāsī, Śāyinī, Vidyā, Mohinī, Pramohinī, Vitarkinī, Saumyā, and Amṛtā— the sixteen digits (kalās). Thus are the sixteen lunar digits at the descent of the Gaṅgā.

Regarding the knots (*granthi*), these very *kalās* are to be repeated and brought into close proximity; or else, even in the case of alternative options such as one hundred and eight, and even for the *pavitra* [threads], one hundred and eight Rudras are to be assigned according to the number of respective knots. The eighty-one squares (*pada*) are to be laid down; in the case of fifty [squares], there are fifteen syllables (*varṇa*), and in the case of thirty-eight, there are thirty-eight *kalās*.

Therefore, this rule regarding the number [of threads] has been stated in the *Jñānaratnāvalī*: "The one hundred and eight-threaded cord is always the most excellent, equal in number to the Rudras; in the absence of that, one should prepare half of it, or half of that again."

It is held that there are eighty-one *padas*, or fifty-five (*pañcā...*) [padas], or thirty-eight *kalās*; this is the consensus regarding all *liṅgas*. Having tripled the three qualities (*guṇas*) of the *sūtras*, the lords (*adhipatis*) of the nine *tantras* contained within the single *sūtra*—beginning with the *praṇava* and beginning with the letter *ka*—have been declared.

Likewise, in the *Somaśambhu*, [it is said]: "The *praṇava*, the Moon, Fire, Brahmā, Nāga, Guha, the Sun, the *sādākhya*, and all the gods are to be placed in sequence upon the nine threads. Alternatively, Brahmā and the others are to be installed.
Thus, (l3).

In the *Kālottara*: "One should install Aja, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśvara, and Sadāśiva, as well as the deities Moon, Sun, and Fire, upon the nine threads. The distinction here is that by this [statement], the nine deities are to be installed in a circular manner according to the number of the nine threads. In the case of manifest [icons] such as images, the descent of the Gaṅgā should be fashioned down to the knees—that is, reaching as far as the region of the knees.
The remainder— the triad of principles beginning with the Self (ātman)—

should be applied in sequence as far as the secret place, the navel, and the heart. Likewise, in the *Jñānaratnāvalī*, it is stated that there should be three bracelets for the forms [of the deities] from the head down to the knees.

"One should conceive of the fourth" means: while uttering the Śaiva mantra, which is joined with the *kalās* and joined with the locus of consciousness (*cetana-sthāna*), extending from the end of the *daṇḍa* up to the end of *manas*, one should offer the triad of principles beginning with the Self (*ātma-ādi-tattva-traya*) along with the fourth, called "the Soul of All" (*sarvātmā*), in succession, through the process of dissolution and utterance, ending at the end of all things for the sake of supreme unification (*paramīkṛti*). And for the sake of fulfillment, O Viye, [one offers] the flower.

In the year [blank], he states that the self is offered with three principles (*tattva*), all the deities with the fourth, and the three bracelets of Śiva with the descents of the Gaṅgā. Reciting the mantra related to Śiva (*śaiva*), he says "Śaivam" (p. 146b, l. 1).

(…) endowed with the purification of the five *kalās*, beginning with *nivṛtti* and ending with *kālā*. By this, the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*) is stated. "Endowed with the locus of consciousness" (*cetanāsthānayuk*):

by the word *cetanā*, the internal sacrifice, the oblation, and meditation are meant; by the word *sthāna*, the purification of the locus, the substance, the *liṅga*, and the mantra is meant. Accompanied by these, he says that the Self and so forth abide in the three *tattvas* and in the fourth, which is Śiva himself.
O Śivā, "up to the end of the *daṇḍa*, up to the end of the mind" means that the *daṇḍa* is *nāda*;

its end is *nādānta*; its end is *śakti*. By this, the pervasion of the three principles beginning with *ātman* is stated; [this occurs] by the Lord Brahmakāraṇa, whose pervasion extends from the principle of earth (*pṛthvī-tattva*) up to the principle of *prakṛti*.

When the *ātmatattva* is conjoined with Śiva as its presiding lord (*adhipati*), it is the utterance ending at that *tattva*. Likewise, when the *vidyātattva*—which extends from the *pṛthivītattva* up to the end of the *śuddhavidyātattva*—is conjoined with Viṣṇu as the Lord of Causes (*kāraṇeśvara*), Śiva alone is the presiding lord; this is the utterance ending at the *īśvaratattva*. Similarly, [when conjoined] with Rudra, [it refers to the *māyātattva*] which extends from the *pṛthivītattva* up to the end of the *śaktitattva*.

In the *śivatattva*, which is conjoined with the Lord of Causes (*kāraṇeśvara*), Śiva alone is the presiding deity; thus, having articulated [the mantra] up to the end of Śiva, and here too, starting from the *pṛthivītattva* up to the pervasion ending in the power of *samanā*,
[one reaches] Śiva, the supreme designator, who is the Supreme Śiva (*paraśiva*).

Regarding the phrase "the Lord" (*adhipati*) during the offering of the fourth purifier: the recitation extends up to *unmanā*. One should place the triad of principles (*tattva*) beginning with the Self (*ātman*)—namely, the triad of principles known as the Self-principle (*ātmatattva*), the Knowledge-principle (*vidyātattva*), and the Śiva-principle (*śivatattva*)—upon the top of the *liṅga*, as previously described.

Such is the sequence for the offering for one who desires liberation (*mumukṣu*); however, for one who desires worldly enjoyment (*bhukṣu*), there is the offering of the triad of principles known as Śiva, Knowledge, and the Self.

Likewise, Somaśambhu [states]: "In the *ātmatattva* (principle of self), ending with *prakṛti*, having recited up to the root *māyā* while [the principle] is protected by Padma..., one should worship Śiva with the *pavitra*. And in the *vidyātattva* (principle of knowledge), ending with *vidyā*, while [the principle] is protected by Viṣṇu as the cause, having recited up to *īśvara*, one should place the *pavitra*. Or, in the *śivatattva* (principle of Śiva), ending with Śiva..."

In the Rudrakāraṇapālita [tantra], having uttered the mantra ending with Śiva, [it describes] the form of the *pavitraka*. It is declared that for those seeking liberation (*umukṣu*), the *pavitraka* is taught by means of Ātman, Vidyā, and Śiva; whereas for those seeking enjoyment (*bubhukṣu*), it is prescribed in sequence by means of Śiva, Vidyā, and Ātman. Here, in the offering of the Śiva-tattva and so forth, [it is placed] upon all the *pavitrakas*.

Since it is improper for the Śiva-tattva that is already present to be placed below [the other tattvas], some say that the Śiva-tattva first offered should be removed after the offering of the Pavitra of the Vidyā-tattva and placed above the Vidyā-tattva;
likewise, after the offering of the Ātman-tattva, the Vidyā-tattva should be removed and placed above the Ātman-tattva. Others, however, say thus:

Because there is no statement regarding the dedication (*samarpaṇa*), it is not included within the three rings (*kaṅkaṇa*) which are broad according to the measurement; they say that dedication after having lifted [the elements] upward is not appropriate, because each of the three rings, starting from the principle of Śiva (*śivatattva*), has a height of two parts respectively.

Some maintain that three bracelets should be made because [the number] is slightly less [than four]. Having previously described the offering of the *pavitra* to Śiva as the presiding lord over the three principles (*tattva*) beginning with the Self (*ātman*), he now describes the offering of the *pavitra* to Śiva who presides by virtue of his power over all principles, [referring to Him] as the fourth, named "the Soul of All" (*sarvātmā*), whose nature is that of all deities, the descent of the Gaṅgā, and who is endowed with the sequence [of emanation].

In such a way that it is accompanied by the sequence of the renunciation of Brahmā and the others, one should offer [the oblation] through the upward resonance of dissolution (*layoccāra*), starting from the end of the twelve [finger-breadths] and proceeding from the resonance of the end of sound (*nādāntoccāra*).

In all the principles (*tattva*) that are to be protected by all causes, one who is firm in his vows (*suvrata*), having recited [the mantra] up to the root-abode (*mūlālaya*), should perform the descent of the Gaṅgā (*gaṅgāvatāraka*). The presiding deity over the principles is known as Sadyojāta and so forth; and Śiva, as described above, is the cause in the Yoga-pāda. That Supreme Lord exists either as one or through various distinctions of names, because of his nature as Brahman and because of his all-pervasiveness.

He is Brahmā by virtue of his union with Brahman; he is Viṣṇu because he protects; and he is Śiva because he is the source of the world. He is the Lord, the Master of the universe. Because he causes the destruction of suffering (*ruj*), he is Rudra; because of the destruction of suffering, he is the Destroyer of Pain. He is Sadāśiva, eternally peaceful; being ever-peaceful, he abides as Śiva.

"Thus, by means of various designations, the one Lord of the world alone abides. In this manner, during the rite of supreme unification (*paramīkṛti*), one should offer three handfuls of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*) while performing the unification of Śiva—who resides within the four principles beginning with the Self—at the very end of everything, concluding with the offering of the descent of the Gaṅgā. This is done by reciting the root mantra ending in *namaḥ* and then offering the three handfuls of flowers.
In the *Jñānaratnāvalī*,

because it is stated immediately after the dedication of the *Gaṅgāvatāra*, [the following is for] the completion of the ritual (*vidhi*)— that is, the performance of the rite— within one year (*vatsara*): namely, the avoidance of the omission of mantras (*mantra-lopa*), the omission of rites (*kriyā-lopa*), and the omission of ritual substances (*dravya-lopa*).

The remainder [of the sentence] is that one must perform the *pavitrārohaṇa* for the sake of the complete fulfillment of the ritual performed correctly; and it has been said: "...that which was joined with mantras, substances, and rites, through negligence, fate, delusion, or even distraction from duties—[if it is lost] due to fear of kings, thieves, laziness, or attachment to one's own [pleasures], [then this rite is prescribed]. (l8) (p148a, l1)

"A flaw inevitably arises; for the sake of filling that flaw and for the benefit of men, the eternal ancillary (*nityāṅga*) rite known as the *pavitra* is now described. Now, it has been stated here that the *pavitrārohaṇa* is an eternal ancillary. How can its status as an eternal ancillary be established? [A ritual act] is called "eternal" when it is performed regularly. If that very same eternal act is performed twice on specific lunar days such as the *saṅkrānti*, it is called an "eternal ancillary. And it has been said:

In the *Kālottara*, for both the *samayin* and the *putraka*, and especially for the *sādhaka*, it is taught according to the command of Śiva that this should be performed daily and sequentially throughout one's life: bathing, worship, recitation (*japa*), the twilight rites (*sandhyā*), and fifthly, the fire-oblation (*homa*). One should always perform these; they are called the "constant limbs" (*nityāṅga*).

On the eighth and fourteenth days of both fortnights, on the fifteenth day, at the end of the day, during a solar transit (*saṃkrānti*), during the southern course of the sun (*dakṣiṇāyana*), during an intercalary month, when there is an increase in the number of people, during the six *aśītimukha* periods, and likewise during lunar and solar eclipses—on these occasions, worship, recitation (*japa*), and so forth, should be performed twice as much. The same applies during the four-month period (*cāturmāsya*). One should observe the vow of eating only at night and consuming sacrificial food (*haviṣya*). And on the eighth day...
"One must never eat on the fourteenth day"—

this has been stated as a mandatory auxiliary element (*nityāṅga*). For this very reason, the *pavitrārohaṇa* (the offering of the sacred thread) is performed at a fixed time, such as the month of Āṣāḍha, by means of cotton threads as a specific ritual act (*karmaviśeṣa*).

How, then, can it be called a permanent (*nitya*) limb? For this very reason, whether it be occasional (*naimittika*), optional (*kāmya*), or expiatory (*prāyaścitta*), it is called "occasional" (*naimittika*) because it is performed by taking a specific occasion as its cause—such as the fixed time for the sleep of Viṣṇu. Even in this manner, its status as occasional is not tenable; for the definition of the occasional would suffer from the fault of being too narrow (*avyāpti*), since [the definition] exists [only in some cases].

For instance, there is no over-extension (*avyāpti*) [of the definition] to the occasional (*naimittika*) initiation (*dīkṣā*) and so forth performed at a time already brought about; yet it is included in the *Asahasrikā*, because it is stated: "Initiation and consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*)—these two types are occasional. Likewise, this applies to those rites such as the twilight worship (*sandhyāvandana*) which are to be performed at fixed times such as morning and so on.

Because even a name is occasioned by a cause, there would be the fallacy of over-extension (*ativyāpti*). Thus it has been said regarding the *pavitrāropaṇa*: "The twilight rite (*saṃdhyā*) that must be performed because of that [occasion] is therefore declared to be occasional (*naimittikī*), not because of an occasional ritual act (*naimittika-karma*). For this very reason, it is not merely occasional; likewise, it is not optional (*kāmya*), for the optional consists of [powers] such as *aṇimā*.

Subjugation (*vaśyādi*) and so forth come about. Furthermore, because it has been stated that the "optional" (*kāmya*) [rite] is for the sake of attaining powers such as *aṇimā* and the like, and because it is extensive, the claim that the optional rite is not established here—on the grounds that it is not prescribed—is incorrect. Because it has been stated that the "purification" (*pavitra*) is for the purpose of filling any gaps in the procedure of all worship, even when the ritual is performed over the course of a year, [the rite remains effective] despite omissions in the mantra, the substance, or the action.

It cannot be said that because the purificatory rite (*pavitrakarma*) was performed to fulfill that [requirement], there is an expiation (*prāyaścitta*); for at that time there is a lapse of the ritual, and it is at that time that the expiation is prescribed. (l6) Since the purificatory rite is not performed at all during the months of Āṣāḍha and so forth, there is no expiation; for in the world, [the rule holds] regarding the performance of what is enjoined by the injunctions. (l7)

It is heard in the scriptures that having prescribed an expiation, an expiation must be performed. However, in this case, regarding the Pavitraka rite, it is observed that when there has been an omission, the Pavitraka-ārohaṇa should be performed even without an expiation. And it is said: "He who does not perform the Sūtra-ārohaṇa during the three months [of the rainy season], when the sun has entered the sign of Virgo, he should perform the Pavitraka after reciting the mantra joined with the Dakṣa-syllable."
"But in no way [should there be] the consumption of *lāyā* for Śambhu," [it says] elsewhere. (l2) ...

"In this case, those who are twice-born, having performed the *pavitra* rite and recited the *aghora* mantra one hundred thousand times, should perform the *cāndrāyaṇa* penance" [is stated]. Having given [the gift] to the deity in whatever manner [possible] for the sake of fulfilling the omission of ritual acts...

And this expiation (*prāyaścitta*) would then have to be for the very act of performing the *pavitrāropaṇa*, because there is no expiation for an expiation; therefore, no expiation occurs. Consequently, having determined that this is a compulsory (*nitya*) rite, it was stated [as follows]. And it has been said: "Bathing, the twilight prayers (*saṃdhyā*), worship, recitation (*japa*), and fifthly, the fire-oblation (*homa*)—these are declared to be the compulsory limbs (*nityāṅga*); the *pavitrāropaṇa* is likewise."

"So be it. Here too, because it is to be performed [regularly] and because it is to be performed every year, there is a twofold nature: namely, the daily (*daivasika*) and the annual (*vārṣika*). That which is performed day by day is the daily; that which is performed year by year is the annual.

When it is asked how there can be a single site for the two annual [festivals] given their twofold nature, [the answer is that] because the *pavitraka* rite is performed daily due to its abundance, one becomes incapable [of completing it all at once].
(l7) Even though the *pavitraka* is performed every day with flowers, *kuśa* grass, and so forth as substitutes for the thread, it remains incomplete; therefore, by this very [means]...

"It is brought to completion" (149b, l1). Thus, by the exhaustion of the daily [obligations], the annual [obligation] is established. Furthermore, because an expiation is prescribed for the omission of the daily *bhūta-pavitra*—just as there is for the omission of the daily vows (*nityavrata*) and the twilight prayers (*sandhyāvandana*)—if this is so, let the daily rite remain; the annual [rite] is of such a nature... (l2).

When it is said "that [pavitra]," in the absence of the daily [pavitra], the annual one should be used because of its primacy; for in the *Nityotsava*, it is stated that the worship performed on that occasion is the "annual festival" (*sāṃvatsarotsava*). For this very reason, it is said that compared to the daily [pavitra], the annual *pavitra* is indeed a permanent auxiliary (*nityāṅga*).

Likewise, in the *Mohaśūrottara*: "One should fashion a purifier (*pavitra*) for Śambhu every day with strips of cloth, flowers, or *kuśa* grass, out of a desire to accumulate great merit. Thus has the daily rite been explained; now hear again the occasional (*naimittika*) rite. One should take [the thread] from the bright fortnight of Āṣāḍha, and from both the bright and dark fortnights of Śrāvaṇa...
[text fragment].

If it is established that the *pavitrārohaṇa* is occasional (*naimittika*), how can it be called a regular constituent part (*nityāṅga*)? To this, the reply is: while the daily *pavitra* is being performed as a regular rite, [it serves] for the purpose of removing defects in all ritual acts, binding [the practitioner], and providing the primary knowledge of the connection [to the deity]. Thus, the designation "occasional" is applied to the annual [rite] for that specific purpose, but not [because it is inherently occasional].

Because it is joined with the characteristic of being occasional (*naimittika*). For this very reason, the word *naimittika* has the suffix *-ika* in its own sense (*svārtha-eka-pratyaya*), since it is stated that "the occasional [rite] is precisely the daily occasion (*daivasika-nimitta*) or the annual [occasion] (*vārṣaka*). Thus, it is established that it is a constant limb (*nityāṅga*).
Likewise, in the *Kālottara*: "Initiation... (l. 8).

That which is eternally remembered as consisting of ritual action (*kriyātmaka*), which depends upon substances, mantras, and rites, and which would otherwise be incomplete and fruitless for women—therefore, this *pavitrārohaṇa* is considered an eternal limb (*nityāṅga*) [of that rite]. Due to the aforementioned deficiencies, there is a terrible... [omitted] ...the *pavitraka*. Therefore, it should be performed at the proper time before the previously mentioned *parameṣṭhin*. By that, the annual worship (*sāṃvatsarī-pūjā*) clearly becomes complete; [one should perform] the worship...
"Having gone [there], the *pavitraka* must always be performed;
for it is said that without the *pavitraka*, one is proclaimed to be *tāmasī*.
Regarding this, some [hold] that in the *Mohaśūrottara*, a Śiva-āgama, it is called *naimittika* because it is performed on specific occasions, since its cause is a fixed time."
They say it is effective [in all respects] (l3);

they say it is eternally so; they say that because it is a limb of the eternal, it should be performed by one of skillful vision. Even when the Sun and Jupiter have set, or even during the three months [of their absence], there should be no [restriction]; nevertheless, one should perform the Pavitraka rite. (l4)
"Whether because it is occasional (*naimittika*) or because it is obligatory (*naimityaka*)," so it is stated in the *Siddhāntaśekhara*. (7)
One should place the [syllable] Kha, enriched with Kalā, upon the right and left ears; likewise, upon the nose, one should place the [syllables] Sakala and Akala;

and within the eyes, one should place Kṣapaṇaka. Having visualized Viriñci, Keśava, Hara, Īśāna, Śakti, and Śiva in the previously mentioned locations, one should then perform the visualization and grasping of the face in the void.
Nor with the lip. ||8||
Having performed the swallowing, gathering, binding, throwing, tasting, releasing, downward movement, and reaching the lips of the morsel;

and having [performed these] from the "all-made" (sakala) vessel which is empty, as well as from the "partless" (niṣkala) through meditation, one who is free from decay and pride should consume the food to be licked and so forth.

The egg of Brahmā is the food, while the Blessed One Maheśa himself is the enjoyer; Maheśvara is also the giver. Or rather, if the object of enjoyment consists of his own [nature], then Maheśvara is indeed its creator, and Śiva is the supreme enjoyer.
One who possesses strength and wisdom should eat even at lowly times, observing the coming and going of the prāṇa and apāna breaths.

In this way, even if a preeminent teacher eats in the house of great sinners—whether it be the remnants of their food or the impure food of a *śrāddha* ceremony—if he eats this only once, ten million learned and unlearned people who have eaten with him shall go to Śiva, delivering twenty-one generations of their kin; so it is stated in the *Niśvāsa*. 11. (l4)

In this world, there are indeed lineages that remain unbroken, as well as those whose lineages have been broken. Regarding those in whose homes the lineage has been broken, there is a lack of knowledge;

thinking that by performing [acts such as] eating and so forth, a fault would accrue to those who possess the lineage, and in order to avoid that, [one should perform the rite] preceded by the eightfold installation of the temple-mantra (*prāsādamantranyāsa*).

"Eating, one does not incur fault"—this [is stated] by the following passage beginning with "of the two ears" (*śrutyor*). One should place the mantra named *khamala* into the two ears, that is, the right and left ears; one should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) in the right ear, and likewise, one should place the mantra named *kalāḍhya* in the left ear.
In the nose, [and] in the nostril,
one should place the two mantras known as *sakala* and *akala*, and that called *sakalaniṣkala*, respectively upon the right and left [nostrils] of the nose. [One should also place] the mendicant,
the mantra known as *kṣapaṇaka*.

One should place the *antastha* mantra, known as the *antastha*, upon the two eyes—the right and left visions. Within the previously mentioned mantras beginning with *kha* and *mala*, one should place Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and Īśvara, starting from Viriñca [the East] up to Hara [the North-East].

Likewise, one should place Śakti and Śiva. Immediately after this placement, below [the forehead], one should perform the "display of food" (*annadarśana*) by means of the vision—the eye—using the mantra called *śūnya*.

One should gaze at the cooked rice placed in a vessel of bell-metal or similar material. With the mantra known as Oṣṭhya-karṇoṣṭhya, one should perform the gathering and consolidation of the house and its components. Furthermore, there is the extraction of the eightfold temple.

It should be understood from the *Śrīkālottarāgama*: "The Sakala, Niṣkala, Śūnya, Kalāḍhya, Khamala, Kṛta, Kṣapaṇa, Kṣamaya, and Tastha—these are remembered as the eight, ending with Kaṇṭhoṣṭha. From the *Kṣapaṇa* mantra, the collection—that is, the grouping together—of the *khaṇḍa* and so forth, which exist in the form of *khaṇḍa* and so forth, must be performed; for indeed, after the grouping has been completed below, the binding follows.
The mixing of [the food] with soup and so forth; likewise, lifting up— that is, raising the morsel of food from the hand— and tasting, which is the eating,
and releasing [it].

The release of that which has reached the lips and that which has reached the hands: "reached the lips" refers to the movement of the hand—that is, the contact known as the lip—from one complete mantra to another complete mantra, from a mantra consisting of space to a mantra consisting of space, from a void mantra to a void mantra, and from a partless mantra to its cessation; having performed this through meditation on the mantra situated within the state of cessation, thus...

Having performed the five activities, such as binding and so forth, by means of the five mantras, that person who performs such placement (*nyāsa*), meditation, and so on— by means of the mantras *unnatoṣṭha* and *anuta*, and [the mantras] ending with *unnatā* and *kaṇṭhoṣṭha*— should consume food, such as that which is to be licked (*lehya*), drunk (*peya*), and chewed (*khādya*).

One should perform [the following]: at the commencement of the meal, one should meditate that the food of Brahman (*brahmānna*) is of the very nature of Brahman. The "Taste" (*rasa*)—the six flavors such as sweet and so forth present in food and other things—is the Lord Hari, whose form is Nārāyaṇa; he is the Blessed One endowed with the six divine qualities (*ṣāḍguṇya*), the Great Lord (*maheśvara*). He himself is the eater, the performer of the act of eating; thus, it is the Great Lord himself.

One should perform meditation [as follows]: that all things, beginning with food, are beyond [the self]; or else, one should meditate that every object fit for consumption is of the nature of one's own *māyā*, and furthermore, that it is the very form of the path of *māyā* and the exertion of *māyā*.

The creator of that which consists of illusion is this very Maheśvara, who is supreme and superior to all. Śiva, the possessor of power, is endowed with power; he is the enjoyer (*bhoktā*), meaning that by his own capacity he performs the act of enjoyment. "The one who knows the coming and going of prāṇa and apāna" means, according to the previously mentioned method, that he possesses knowledge of the upward and downward movement of the prāṇa and apāna winds.
"Matimān" means possessed of intelligence;

that is to say, one whose intellect is dedicated to Maheśvara. He should eat—that is, he should take his meal—even from those who are lowly or from those whose traditional lineage has been interrupted.
Thus, in the manner previously described.

The best of teachers, the supreme guide who is truly engaged in meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*), even while eating in the house of great sinners—performing the act of eating—does not incur fault because he is endowed with such cultivation. Likewise, [the text implies] that even when engaged in the consumption of food at a *śrāddha* or other such [inauspicious] occasions, he does not become tainted. In that case, as previously stated, for the best of guides who is joined with meditation, [it occurs] only once.

When one has eaten a meal once in the house of someone while they are performing a feast, it is as if ten million [brāhmaṇas] who are knowers of the Vedas—endowed with knowledge of the Vedic scriptures—have been fed by that person; the meaning is that he possesses the fruit of having fed ten million brāhmaṇas.
This stated meaning was spoken in the *Niśvāsa* (*Niśvāsāgama*), for the purpose of illuminating the significance of the brāhmaṇa.

For the donor, that excellent teacher who provides food and other necessities, twenty-one generations of his lineage—seven born of his father, seven born of his mother, and seven born of himself—thus comprising twenty-one types; or alternatively, ten ancestors, ten descendants, and himself as the twenty-first—shall go, shall proceed, to Śiva, the state of Śiva. 11.

In order to avoid the fault of accepting wealth from sinners, he describes the placement of the eightfold grace (*prasāda*) in two ways using two verses: One should place the mantras beginning with *sakala* and ending with *aṣṭa* upon the heart, the interior, the exterior, the head, the eyes, the right [side], the left, as well as the crest, the mouth, and the body. Likewise, one should place the *sakalāṅgaka* mantra, which has the luster of nectar, upon the eight [locations].
The Guide should place the entire fifth radiance in the region of the heart as empty through meditative cultivation.
The *kṣipaṇaka* [is] of a splendor equal to vermilion-red at the site of the crest and at the eyes;

the conch-like [mark], the lotus, and the beautiful reddish [mark] are situated within; the lotus and water-lily [are] in the face, shining like jasmine and the moon; externally as well as internally in the body, it is partless (*niṣkala*).
This placement (*nyāsa*) removes the acquisition of sinful substances and more than a hundred-fold impurities.

In the heart, in the *hṛdaya*, in the station of Brahman; within the heart and in the external station, at the head (*mūrdhan*), the crown of the head (*mastaka*), and the eyes—the right eye and the left eye (*savya*); at the crest (*cūḍā*) or tuft (*śikhā*), the face (*vadana*), and the body (*tanu*). (L2) In the entire body, from the beginning of the *sakala* mantras up to the end of the *oṣṭha*: he has made [the deities] the *sakala*, the *niṣkala*, the *śūnya*, the *kalāḍhya*, the pure void (*khamala*), the destroyer (*kṣapaṇa*), and that which abides in the throat and lips (*kaṇṭhoṣṭha*).

"And the eighth is remembered"—by this manner it is said that one who would perform the placement (*nyāsa*) of the mantras according to their sequence; or else (*yadi*), the meaning is that the placement should be performed by another method. *Oṃ ṣaṃ* is the mantra for the throat and lips, likewise as previously stated, [to be placed] upon the entire body (*sakalāṅgake*), which is the whole physical form, [as] the radiance of nectar (*amṛtarucam*).

Having meditated [on him] as being endowed with nectar-like beauty, the instructor— the *ācārya*— should place the *sakala* mantra, known as the "complete" mantra, in the region of the heart— that is, the area of the heart— by means of contemplation (*bhāva*), that is, through the meditation on emptiness (*śūnyadhyāna*). (L5) One should place the *kṣapaṇaka* mantra, which possesses a radiance red like vermilion and a luster equal to minerals and gems such as red ochre (*gairika*), at the site of the crest— that is, the location of the topknot— and in the two eyes.

In the two eyes, one should place the mantra that is conch-like (*śaṅkhābha*), meaning white like a conch; the mantra that is pure-colored, stainless, and ruddy (*aruṇa*), meaning red-colored, which is rich in its digits (*kalāḍhya*). Because it is mentioned twice—*abja-ambuja*—it is like a white lotus and a red lotus, [meaning] white and red in color; one should place the mantra that resides within, namely *kṣamayantastha*.

One should place [the mantra] in the mouth—that is, on the face. One should place the partless (*niṣkala*) mantra, which has a color equal to that of the *kunda* flower and the moon—shining like the *kunda* flower and the moon—upon the body, both externally and internally. This placement (*nyāsa*), which removes sins such as the appropriation of forbidden substances, is said to be fifty and a half [times] effective in warding off the great sins arising from the possession of wealth and grain by persons joined with evil.
"Equal to the deposition of one hundred and fifty [of those]" means that it is equal to whatever fruit is obtained when one hundred and fifty other mantras have been performed. ||14||

He describes the procedure for the funeral rites (*antyeṣṭi*) of those who have been initiated (*dīkṣita*) in three verses: A sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) measuring one cubit [is prepared]; with the earth from that [pit], a platform (*vedikā*) is made. Toward the northwest, it is two cubits [wide] and its inner space is one cubit; toward the southeast, it is four cubits long and half of that [in width]. The funeral pyre (*citā*) is eight cubits [long] and five cubits [wide], divided by the *vasu* (eight), *nata* (nine), and *āpa* (four) measures; it is placed upon the ground at the center of the five parts.
The lords of birth [are the following]. ||15||

In the southwest, in the group of four, [the lords are] Jala, Hari, Śveta, Sṛg, Agni, Śikhin, Rudra; in the northwest, Īśvara; and in the green square, [the lord is] Aiśa. That region [is thus defined]. In the directions, [starting from the east, are] Indra, [Agni], Yama, Nairṛta, Varuṇa, Vāyu, Kubera, and Īśāna. [The colors are: white, black, yellow, and white; red, yellow, and the lord of the fire-corner (Rudra); and between Indra and Agni [is the center]. 16.
Upon the departure of one who has performed the *saddīkṣā* and is adorned with [virtuous] conduct, there occurs the sacrifice for the auspicious name (*sunāmadheṣṭi*).
For those who harbor doubts regarding their conduct due to the prior intentional transgression of knowledge, and for the purification of the impurities of the residual karma that initiates the body,
there is the *dīkṣā* consisting of the propitiation of the ancestors of the thirty-three gods and the performance of the Śiva-śrāddha.
Enough! ||17||

Regarding the passage beginning with "the pit" (*kuṇḍa*) and so forth: prior to the construction of the pit near this reservoir, it is stated that a pavilion (*maṇḍapa*) of nine cubits or seven cubits should be made. As it is said:

"Having constructed a pavilion measuring nine cubits, covered with cloth, or measuring seven cubits, with its door facing south and provided with an archway (*toraṇa*). Therein, in the center of that pavilion, the pit is four cubits square.
It should be made one cubit in measure;
its enclosure wall is six finger-breadths [high]. For that *kuṇḍa*, a single girdle (*mekhalā*) should be made, six finger-breadths in width and height.
Having constructed it with that [wall], or with the earth excavated from that *kuṇḍa*, [one should place it] in the northwest of the pavilion.

In the northwest corner from the pit (*kuṇḍa*), according to the measurement of that [pit] and the measurement of its girdle (*mekhalā*), the meaning is that it should be six finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) in height. Inside, an altar (*vedikā*) should be made, measuring one cubit (*hasta*) in width. In the northeast corner of the pit within the fire-pavilion (*maṇḍapa*), there is a ground known as the "funeral pyre" (*citā*), four cubits in length and four cubits in width, provided with a half-circle of two cubits in breadth.

It should be made with a depression of eight finger-breadths at the base of the *vasu* [section]; this is the remainder [of the requirement]. It is stated in some places that a pit (*khāta*) should be made on the southern side of the sacrificial fire-pit (*kuṇḍa*), like a funeral pyre (*citā*). And it is said: "There, the fire-pit, measuring one cubit, having four corners and a single girdle (*mekhalā*), should be raised by one finger-breadth."

Having prepared that earthen altar for Vāyu to the southeast of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), one should construct a funeral pyre (*citā*) with a trench (*khāta*) measuring four cubits; this [trench] should be two cubits wide and auspiciously one finger-breadth deep. Some authorities maintain that the funeral pyre and the trench may be constructed somewhere to the south of the pit. Having thus completed these three, one should smear them all with cow dung. Regarding the phrase "to the south of the pit," the word "south" (*dakṣiṇa*) refers to the southern direction.
The meaning is "on the right side" (vāmetara-pārśve), not in the direction of the south-western corner (kuṇḍayāmya-digbhāge).

Likewise, in the Kāmika [Tantra]: "Having constructed either a peak (kūṭa) or a water-shed (prapā) in that very interval, [one should fashion] a single girdle (mekhalā) possessing a height of six finger-breadths."

Having constructed a quadrangular pit (*kuṇḍa*) of one cubit according to the ritual procedure, one should designate that mound (*sthaṇḍila*) in the northwest wind-quarter. To the south of the pit, one should fashion a funeral pyre (*citā*) measuring four cubits in length, two cubits in width, and eight finger-breadths in depth. Having thus completed these three, the Guru [proceeds]. The ground for the pyre is divided by twenty-five parts; the pyre itself consists of twenty-five parts.

Having performed the ritual action, [one should place] those [syllables] within twenty-five squares in the center of the five [rows]. One square is in the middle; one square each is in the directions immediately to its east, south, west, and north. Within the five squares located in the center, the father [is marked] with yellow pigment (*haridrā-cūrṇa*), [and they are] of that color.

In this [mandala], the Earth, presided over by the Lotus-born (Brahmā), should be prepared; she is to be worshipped in the southwest with white rice-flour and white-colored substances within four squares. On the fourth square, Nārāyaṇa, together with water, is to be worshipped along with jars filled with water.
