In the southeast, in the red-colored fourth square, Rudra, the Fire-crested (Śikhin), together with fire, is to be worshipped. In the northwest, in the black-colored [square], [the deity] is to be worshipped.

In the four-petalled [lotus] situated in the wind-corner (vāyukoṇa), Īśvara is to be worshipped; in the green sign, he has the color of a fruit-eater, and his splendor is green. In the northeast (aiśa), in the four corners extending toward Īśāna, that region is Sadāśiva, who is to be worshipped together with Ākāśa.

In the remaining directions—namely the east, south, west, and north—the lords Indra, Antaka (Yama), Pāśī (Varuṇa), and Yakṣapati (Kubera) are to be worshipped. They are respectively golden, white, red, and yellow; that is, they possess the colors yellow, black, white, and red. Indra and the others are to be honored with these aforementioned colors, and their respective positions are to be established accordingly.
The lord of the corner situated in the southeast (pītākṛśānukoṇagapatiḥ):

within the pit (kuṇḍamadhye), one should draw a square with yellow powder; by the word "fire" (kṛśānu), red is meant. With red powder, one should draw a triangle in its center. The lord of the corner refers to this corner.
Having attained sovereignty, one should worship Śakra and Anala—namely Indra and Agni—in the middle of the mandala; the remainder implies that in some cases Brahmā and Rudra are to be worshipped.

Likewise, in the Jñānaratnāvalī: "When the sacrificial pit has been consecrated there, having drawn a square with yellow powder, one should worship Brahmā; then, having drawn a triangle in the middle of that with red powder, one should worship Kālāgni there."
Thus, for one who is adorned by the practice of true initiation— that is,

for one who has been properly initiated (*saddīkṣā*)— and for the teacher and the spiritual son (*putraka*), who are likewise adorned by the practice following initiation through the performance of conduct prescribed by the scriptures and who have correctly carried out that practice.
"And when there is the departure— that is, the relinquishing— of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*), then after the abandonment of life, the *iṣṭi*, the final rite (*antyeṣṭi*), shall take place. Here too,

for those of virtuous conduct— the teachers, the practitioners (*sādhaka*), and the sons— the final rite is joined with the purification of the paths (*adhvaśuddhi*), even though the purification of the paths had already occurred at the time of initiation."

Because there is an absence of purification of the paths (*adhvaśuddhi*) due to the transgression of the rules of conduct (*samayācāra*), the final rite (*antyeṣṭi*) for those who possess the pledges (*samayin*) is one that is devoid of the purification of the paths; this is because there is no purification of the paths in the initiation of the pledges (*samayadīkṣā*). And it is said in the *Jñānaratnāvalī*: "For those who abide in reality until the end of life and who possess virtuous conduct..."

For those men who have lost their sense of self through diversion in the meaning of the Siddhānta, one should burn the body with the fire of Śiva; however, for those practitioners (*kriyāvat*) who are joined with improper conduct (*anācāra*), the purification of the path (*adhvaśuddhi*) is prescribed. One should perform the purification of the path for the sons of the *sādhaka* and the *ācārya*, but not for one who desires liberation (*mokṣakāṅkṣin*) if he has transgressed the rule (*samaya*) by previously committing improper conduct (*anācāra*) through the violation of the command (*ājñālaṅghana*).
For embodied beings, according to the Śiva-śāstra, this [command] is indeed to be carried out as "this must be done" and "this must not be done.

Even so, for those who possess the abandonment of dense [ignorance], there is the transgression of a command by a king through lack of prior awareness—such as out of fear of thieves—and thus it constitutes intentional (buddhi-pūrvaka) transgression of a command performed by one's own intellect. [The portion regarding] non-intentional (abuddhi... [transgression follows].

Regarding the priority of the conduct established by embodied beings: when the performance of virtuous deeds (*satkarmānuṣṭhāna*) is being carried out, there arises a doubt among those who wonder whether the fruit produced by the impressions (*saṃskāra*) of the actions currently being performed exists or does not exist—“By whom has this been seen? [Such people are] those whose bodies are defiled by residual karma from previous lives, who are possessed of a desire for worldly enjoyments, and who, while beginning the undertaking of karma that initiates a new body, are stained by the remaining karma that was not yet exhausted.

For the sake of purifying the three [categories] beginning with the *sādhaka*, the final rite (*antyeṣṭi*) accompanied by the purification of the paths (*adhvaśuddhi*) must be performed here; because it is stated that this is done "with conscious intent" (*buddhipūrvaka*), for those who have violated their commitments (*samaya*) and so forth through such conscious intent, [the rite is for] their own ignorance... (l5)

For practitioners and others who have not performed atonement for transgressions against the deities, the funeral rite (*antyeṣṭi*) accompanied by the purification of the paths (*adhvaśuddhi*) is prescribed; however, for those who have committed lapses regarding the rules (*samaya*) and so forth through negligence and have not performed atonement, the funeral rite must be performed devoid of the purification of the paths.

Likewise, in the *Kāmika*: "Whether they be the Ācāryas, the Sādhakas, or the Putrakas established in the Samaya, when their [time] has come, the final rite (*antyeṣṭi*) should be performed for them by those well-initiated. If these three, beginning with the Ācārya, are devoid of proper conduct and do not perform penance, yet have properly performed the rites of purification (*mṛtikarma*) while avoiding what is forbidden—for such ones who are free from negligence, the mere final rite is prescribed, setting aside the purification of the principles (*tattvaśuddhi*)."

For those who have violated an agreement made intentionally and have not performed the prescribed penance, even if a funeral rite (*antyeṣṭi*) is performed accompanied by the purification of the elements (*tatvaśuddhi*), it does not become purified. If it were to become purified, it would follow that all the scriptures on penance (*prāyaścitta-śāstra*) consist of meaningless statements.

Because there is also a contradiction with the words of the *Āgama*, it is stated: "Due to the transgression of the rule (*samaya*), the state of being a flesh-eater (*kravyāda*) is proclaimed for a hundred years... If this were so, one might conclude that for those who have intentionally committed [sins] and performed the required expiation (*prāyaścitta*), the final purificatory sacrifice (*adhvaśuddhi-iṣṭi*) need not be performed; however, that is not the case—it must indeed be performed. Once it has been performed, [the period of punishment lasts] for up to a hundred years... ...until the end.

Following the *piśāca*-stage with devotion, the attainment of the stage of Śiva (*śivapada*) shall occur as a matter of course. Therefore, for those [transgressions] committed intentionally that have been subject to prescribed expiations, purification of the path (*adhvaśuddhi*) must be performed; the intention is that this is because they were committed intentionally. And so it has been stated in the *Dviśatikā*:

In the *Kālottara*: "If one who has been initiated at a later time should transgress the rules (*samaya*), he becomes a partaker of great sins regarding the deity and the gurus. For those who have not abandoned doubt and those who belong to the final [class] consisting of the rules, the funeral rite (*antyeṣṭi*) has not been taught by me for the sake of removing their dense mass of sin. Likewise, in the *Tattva*: "Regarding one who is ignorant of the rules at a time subsequent to initiation, or due to a lack of instruction..."

The funeral rite (*antyeṣṭi*) has been described for the purpose of purifying one who has performed the penance (*prāyaścitta*) but has violated the rules of conduct (*samayācāra*). [Objection: But surely, if this [rite] were a purification for [sins such as] intentional malice toward a guru, then all the scriptures on penance would become useless, and it would contradict the Veda; for it is heard in the Śruti: "The rules of conduct (*samaya*)," etc. (l. 2).

It is said that through leaping (*laṅghana*), one attains the state of a flesh-eater (*kravyāda*) for a hundred years. It is taught that immortality (*viśvāmara*) is attained by the propitiation of the ancestors (*pitṛ*) presiding over two or three [levels] and by the Śiva-śrāddha; for initiation (*dīkṣā*) is indeed sufficient.
"The two Viśvas" refers to the Viśvedevas—meaning two gods and three [levels]. Corresponding to that number are the existing Īśas and Pitṛs: Īśa, Sadāśiva, and Śānta.

By these names, in their respective order, the ancestors—the father, grandfather, and great-grandfather—along with the two Viśvedevas named Rudra and Ananta, are referred to. The Śiva-śrāddha is said to be that which is performed by means of the satiation of these ancestors through the offering of food and other gifts.
Accompanied by that śrāddha, [the recipient becomes] free from the distress of the beginningless cycle of existence.

It is "fully capable," meaning it correctly bestows its fruit. By this, it is indicated that the *śrāddha* must necessarily be performed, because it serves to remove the afflictions associated with the ancestors; this is the intended meaning. That which is performed by sons, disciples, and others, directed toward their fathers and gurus, through the giving of food and other offerings to worthy recipients (*satpātra*), is called *śrāddha*. And it has been said: "I shall describe the procedure for the *Śiva-śrāddha*."

The meaning is that by means of rites such as worship and fire-offerings (*homa*), one removes the debt to the teachers and so forth; and by means of this constant recitation of the *Ṛṇaskhalitavāra*, one should pay the debt to the teachers and so forth through the performance of the *dīkṣita-śrāddha* rite. It is given with faith by the disciples.
"That wealth which is intended for the gurus, when bestowed upon worthy recipients by the learned, is indeed declared to be *śrāddha*.
A *śrāddha* performed for the Viśvedevas known as Rudra and Ananta, and for the ancestors known as Īśa, Sadāśiva, and Śānta, is called a *Śiva-śrāddha*.

Likewise, in the Kāmika [Tantra]: "Īśa, Sadāśiva, and Śānta are proclaimed for the Śiva-śrāddha; Rudra and Ananta are mentioned for the Viśva[-śrāddha]," so say the twice-born. (l. 2) Īśa, Sadāśiva, and Śānta—this is declared the Śiva-śrāddha. Therein, the invocation of Īśa should be performed with the heart-mantra using the name "Father" (pitṛ), and that of Sadāśiva with his own mantra.

One should visualize the Grandfather (Pitāmaha) as Śiva using his own seed-mantra (*svasaṃjñāmūla*). [The visualization of] the Great-Grandfather (*prapitāmaha*) is likewise. For those initiated according to the *Śivadharma*, this is how it should be performed; for those initiated according to the *Lokadharma* who have attained the state of Rudra, [the deities are] the Viśvedevas and Nandi and Mahākāla.

The Pitṛs are the lords of the hosts of *skandas*; they are Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Īśa for those initiated for the sake of attaining the station of a Bhuvaneśa according to the worldly path (*lokadharmin*).
Yama and Aruṇa are the Viśvedevas.
Likewise, in the Somaśambhu [tradition]... (l5)

In the Śiva-śrāddha for ascetics, Īśa, Sadāśiva, and Śāntā are the [deities]; the Rudras and the one named Ananta are the two Viśvedevas present there. For those who are initiated, the deities are the portions of Rudra; otherwise it is different. In that [rite], Nandin and Mahākāla are the two Gaṇa-Viśvedevas. Caṇḍa, Skanda, and Gaṇādhīśa are the Gaṇas in the three [rites] respectively. In the worldly [rite]... Viṣṇu and Īśa.
The two Viśvedevas, Yama and Aruṇa, [are worshipped] in five parts...

(l7) However, in all cases, two persons are worshipped. One should arrange three [figures] together by dividing them into head and shoulders. In the division at the base of the arms... the two Viśvedevas are in the second [position]. Together in one arm... (l8)

Or one may perform five [types] together. That *śrāddha* is of five kinds according to the distinctions of the obligatory (*nitya*) and so forth. Thus, in the *Kāmika*: "The obligatory, the occasional (*naimittika*), the optional (*kāmya*), the prosperity-rite (*vṛddhi*), and the ancestral rite on specific lunar days (*pārvaṇa*)—having known these five types of *śrāddha*, one should perform the ritual. The *pārvaṇa* [śrāddha] is prescribed; the *vṛddhi-śrāddha* occurs at marriages and other such occasions (.................................. (l2), so it should be understood. ||18||

The *pīṭha* is Umā, the *liṅga* is Śiva; the union of these two is declared to be *pratiṣṭhā*. When conjoined with *vidyā*, it is of the nature of action (*kriyā*) for the sake of the supreme vision (*paradṛk*), and is said to consist of five deities.
In the case of a *liṅga* such as the *brahmaśilā* and so forth, [the installation] is the *sthāpana* of Śiva.

In the case of a *pīṭha*, it is the *sthitasthāpana*. In the case of a *bāṇa-liṅga*, there is only *sthāpana*; therefore, according to the *beraja* tradition, there are both *sthāpana* and *utthāpana*. Thus, *pratiṣṭhā* is indeed *sthāpana*.

He says that *pratiṣṭhā* (consecration) is fivefold: *sthitasthāpana*, *utthāpana*, *āsthāpana*, [................], and *pratiṣṭhā*. The pedestal (*pīṭha*), the base (*piṇḍikā*), and the *liṅga* constitute the locus for the worship of the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*). The *liṅga* and *pīṭha* fashioned from stone and other materials are so designated. [In] due order, the pedestal [is established... (l5).

Umā is the Śakti and Liṅga is Śiva; for that reason, the *pratiṣṭhā*—the connection between these two, Umā and Śiva, established by rule—is declared to be the yoga taught in the Śiva scriptures. It is the foundation (*pratiṣṭhā*) because the gods are firmly established (*pra-sthā*) within this image. It is the body consisting of supreme vision and action, whose nature is the power of supreme knowledge and the power of action.

Therefore, by means of the body whose nature is the power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*), [Śiva] is called the "signified" (*lakṣya*) and the "linga"; by means of the body whose nature is the power of action (*kriyāśakti*), the "seat" (*pīṭha*) is called the "signifier" (*lakṣaṇa*). By this, the state of Śiva having power as his body (*śaktidehatva*) is established as the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*).

The *liṅga* consists of the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*), and the pedestal (*pīṭha*) consists of the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*). When their union is being performed by a Śaiva teacher who speaks according to [the truth] and follows the ninefold path taught in the scriptures, that conjunction is called "installation" (*pratiṣṭhā*). For in this way, [the deity] is directly present there as Śiva himself.

It is understood that [the Lord] exists as the agent and instrument of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) by means of a knowledge characterized by an internal consciousness that is distinct from other consciousnesses, which is of the nature of a mass of *cit*. For this very reason, it is stated in the venerable *Mataṅga*: "Now, the presiding power of the Lord consists of the rays of His own *śakti*. That *Pratiṣṭhā* is fivefold; [it exists] in five ways... (l3)

That has been stated. Likewise, it was said by Varuṇaśiva: "The installation (*pratiṣṭhā*) is the union of the pedestal with the power of action (*kriyāśakti*) according to the prescribed rite, within the *liṅga* which consists of the power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*); that [installation] is fivefold. Thus, he describes the characteristics of the divisions of the fivefold installation in sequence, beginning with the word "liṅga": "in the *liṅga* and so forth," where "brahmaśilā" refers to the foundation stone (*ādhāraśilā*), and "and so forth" refers to the *liṅga*.

The ritual act of installation (*pratiṣṭhākarma*), when performed according to the procedure prescribed in the scriptures upon a linga characterized by [the presence of] the *ātman* and so forth, receives the designation "installation" (*pratiṣṭhā*). This is the intended meaning: in that installation, following the placement of the foundation stone (*ādhāraśilā*), [the rite is performed] within the pit for that foundation stone for the circumference of the linga.
Having performed the entry (*praveśana*), the union with the pedestal (*piṇḍikā*) is effected; that is called *pratiṣṭhā*. And it is said:

"Pratiṣṭhā, sthāpana, likewise sthitasthāpana, āsthāpana as the fourth, and similarly uddhāpana—thus the determination of that [ritual] is declared to be fivefold *pratiṣṭhā*. Wherein, in the midst of the Brahma-stone (*brahmaśilā*)..."

Having fashioned the *liṅga* (l8), or having fashioned a faceless (*avaktra*) mouth-*liṅga* or the pedestal-binding (*pīṭhabandha*), and having reached the pure conjunction (*śuddhalagna*), that which is performed with the *piṇḍikā* (the pedestal) [is] the installation (*pratiṣṭhā*); thus says Śiva... (p158a, l1).

In this case, no separate *liṅga* is mentioned; rather, it refers to the rite of consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*) performed upon a pedestal (*pīṭha*) that is inseparable from the *liṅga*, such as in the case of crystal and other materials. As it has been said: "When the *piṇḍikā* (pedestal) is not distinct from the *liṅga*, [the consecration] is performed on the crystal and so forth; where the purification (*saṃskāra*) is applied, that is called 'establishing what is already situated' (*sthitasthāpana*). Regarding the *bāṇa* or *bāṇaliṅga*, the consecration and installation (*sthāpana*) being performed is called *sthitasthāpana*. [This applies to those made of] metal or gems.
The *liṅga* may be made of stone or of metal such as iron.

Having divided that *liṅga* into five parts or having divided it into three, and having understood the relative strength or weakness of the *liṅga*—whether two parts or one part—is placed in the center of the pedestal (*piṇḍikā*); that is declared to be the "image-born" (*beraja*) installation.

The sequence of installation (*pratiṣṭhākrama*) for the emergence of the image of Śiva’s form and so forth is now described. It is said: "Having fashioned a manifest linga (*vyaktaliṅga*) measuring four cubits or more, or likewise a pedestal (*pīṭha*) joined with a *piṇḍikā*, and having performed the purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) within the temple, that wherein it is thus established is called 'installation' (*sthāpana*). Furthermore, regarding that which is worn out, such as a linga or other object, where it is restored to its original state...

The rite of installation (*pratiṣṭhā*) performed upon a *liṅga* or similar object receives the name "raising" (*utthāpana*). And it has been said: "When a *liṅga* that is defiled by defects such as those of the *liṅga* itself is carefully removed and another is installed in its place, that is called 'raising. Thus, five types [of rites] for the Śiva-liṅga have been declared by the learned."

[The measurements for] the liṅga for the worship of the Supreme Lord, which removes the difficulty of forgetting [the proportions], are as follows: one and a half parts; eight, seven, four, four, and a quarter; nine, seven, four, eight, and eight; ten, six, seven, three, and thirty; eleven, twenty-three, and twenty-eight; two, two, six, eight, and four oceans; and thirty-two parts added to those [preceding] fractions. [These are] for the sake of making all [parts] equal. The liṅga... [is established].

Since [the measurement] is greater than that by [an amount], he says "sārdhāṃśa" (with half a part), stating that the *liṅga* must be made with its proper characteristics (*salakṣaṇa*). Regarding the characteristics of the *liṅga*, although they are of many kinds in the scriptures, for fear of excessive prolixity, [he describes them as follows]:
"of the wealthy, the poor, the lord of the gods, and the one equal in all parts. (l. 3)
He explains the sequence of the expansion of the fourfold marks (*liṅga*) in their proper order: first, the *liṅga* is of two kinds, mobile and immobile; each of these, in turn, is threefold:
manifest (*vyakta*), manifest-unmanifest (*vyaktāvyakta*), and unmanifest (*avyakta*).

That which is manifest is said to be all the images and so forth. The manifest-unmanifest is the "face-liṅga" (*mukhaliṅga*), which is both with parts (*sakala*) and without parts (*niṣkala*). The unmanifest is the partless liṅga (*niṣkalaliṅga*) [to be installed] in houses.

The immovable *liṅga* that has been worshipped, the *liṅga* installed in temples, and the *liṅga* installed as a mobile one—this is called the stable (*sthira*) *liṅga*. That stable *liṅga* is fivefold: the self-manifested (*svayambhu*), the divine (*daivika*), the astrological (*gāṇaka*), the rishi-made (*ārṣa*), and the human (*mānuṣa*).

The *liṅga* is said to be their defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*). And it has been stated: "Thus, the characteristics of the types and marks of crystal gems have not been mentioned here because they are already stated in the *Jñānaratnāvalī*, the *Siddhāntaśekhara*, and other such works. (l7) This should be consulted. It is taught that a *liṅga* made of stone and other materials should be fashioned with a size ranging from one cubit to nine cubits. And it is said: "One cubit, two cubits, and three cubits—these are the three smallest sizes."
By those [measures] of five and six, there shall be the middle [type];

by nine cubits, the superior—thus it is remembered as being threefold. This means that for one who has thus taken up the *liṅga*, having tripled the eight [parts], it is divided into twenty-four parts within the octad (*aṣṭaka*).
[This is] the measurement of the portions of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra...

(.... with a half-part of the nose (.... and a good half-Sindhu; then the Brahmā-part is raised as a square, and within twenty-four parts, it consists of eight parts together with a half-part and a half-part.

Viṣṇu [is] Śo-vasa (................ (l3) joined with a part; the Rudra-part consists of seven parts together with a half-Sindhu and a half-part. A liṅga made according to these measurements is called "prosperous" (āḍhya). Likewise...

It is said: "Having performed the cleansing of the *liṅga*, the lotus-seat (*kajāsana*) is formed with eight and a half parts; the seat of Īśa is formed with seven and a half [parts]; and in the case of the *āḍhya* [liṅga], Hari is formed with eight parts. This means that, having performed the cleansing of the *liṅga*, one should divide it into twenty-four parts.
The *kajāsana* means the portion belonging to Brahmā; here, the portions of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra should be fashioned respectively as a square, an octagon, and a circle.
Likewise, in the *Siddhāntaśekhara*:
"One should determine the length of the *liṅga* and divide it into three parts; at the base, the middle, and the top are the portions of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva. The portion of Brahmā is square."

One should make the portion of Viṣṇu octagonal, circular, or even sixteen-sided; it may also be joined with thirty-two sides or sixty-four sides. The portion of Brahmā is neuter, the portion of Viṣṇu is feminine, and the portion of Rudra is masculine.

The irrelevant portion: That which is made of iron is the best; that made of wood is middling. The fire from the domestic hearth of the twice-born and so forth is proclaimed as the lowest. That produced by a sun-crystal (*sūryakānta*) is the best; that born of wood is middling; the fire produced from the mouth of a *śrotriya* is proclaimed as the inferior.
